Orestes, after looking vainly round the room for a place to escape, had quietly subsided into his chair again; and by the time that the slaves knocked at the door he had so far recovered his philosophy as to ask, not for the torturers, but for a page and wine.

“Oh, you Jews!” quoth he, trying to laugh off matters. “The same incarnate fiends that Titus found you!”

===Chinese===
「我们走着瞧！」俄瑞斯忒斯叫道，「来人，奴才！」他大声鼓掌。

「阁下请息怒，」拉斐尔起身道，「门已锁了；窗上有纱帘；这柄匕首是淬了毒的。我若有个三长两短，你便得罪了所有的犹太放贷人，不出三日便要在极大的痛苦中死去，错过了与老米利暗的约会，失去了你最称意的伴侣，还使你本人的财务和总督府的财务，都陷入相当可观的窘境。何不坐下来，像一个真正的希帕蒂娅门生那样，以哲人的心境，听我把话讲完，又何必强人所难，要一个把实情真不知道的人说出来呢。」

俄瑞斯忒斯徒然四下张望，想找个脱身之处，已悄然又缩回到他的椅子里；待奴才们敲门时，他已恢复了相当的哲学风度，所要的不是拷问手，而是一名侍童和酒。

「哦，你们这些犹太人！」他道，想把事情一笑带过，「还是提图斯（Titus）当日所见的那同一群肉身魔鬼！」

===Original===
“The very same, my dear prefect. Now for this matter, which is really important﻿—at least to Gentiles. Heraclian will certainly rebel. Synesius let out as much to me. He has fitted out an armament for Ostia, stopped his own wheat-ships, and is going to write to you to stop yours, and to starve out the Eternal City, Goths, senate, emperor, and all. Whether you will comply with his reasonable little request depends of course on yourself.”

“And that again very much on his plans.”

“Of course. You cannot be expected to﻿—we will euphemise﻿—unless it be made worth your while.”

Orestes sat buried in deep thought.

===Chinese===
「正是同一群，我亲爱的总督。如今说这桩事，它确是紧要——至少对非犹太人而言。赫拉克利安一定要造反。叙内西乌斯对我漏了口风。他已为远征奥斯提亚（Ostia）备好一支军备，停了自己的麦船，还要写信给你，叫你也停你的，要以此饿死那座永恒之城——哥特人、元老院、皇帝，一锅端。你依不依他这小小的一点合理要求，自然全在你自己。」

「而这又很取决于他的打算。」

「当然。不能指望你——我们委婉一点说——除非这事值得你去做。」

俄瑞斯忒斯深深陷入沉思。

===Original===
“Of course not,” said he at last, half unconsciously. And then, in sudden dread of having committed himself, he looked up fiercely at the Jew.

“And how do I know that this is not some infernal trap of yours? Tell me how you found out all this, or by Hercules” (he had quite forgotten his Christianity by this time) “﻿—by Hercules and the Twelve Gods, I’ll﻿—”

“Don’t use expressions unworthy of a philosopher. My source of information was very simple and very good. He has been negotiating a loan from the Rabbis at Carthage. They were either frightened, or loyal, or both, and hung back. He knew﻿—as all wise governors know when they allow themselves time﻿—that it is no use to bully a Jew; and applied to me. I never lend money﻿—it is unphilosophical: but I introduced him to old Miriam, who dare do business with the devil himself; and by that move, whether he has the money or not, I cannot tell: but this I can tell, that we have his secret﻿—and so have you now; and if you want more information, the old woman, who enjoys an intrigue as much as she does Falernian, will get it you.”

“Well, you are a true friend, after all.”

===Chinese===
「当然不能，」他末了半不自觉地说。随即忽然怕自己漏了口风，猛抬头凶狠地瞪着那犹太人。

「我怎么知道这不是你设的什么恶毒圈套？告诉我你是怎么探出这一切的，否则凭赫拉克勒斯——」（这时他已全然忘了自己的基督徒身份）「——凭赫拉克勒斯和十二天神起誓，我要——」

「别说有失哲学家身份的话。我的消息来源十分简单，又十分可靠。他一直在与迦太基（Carthage）的拉比们洽借一笔款子。他们或出于害怕，或出于忠心，或两者兼有，踌躇不前。他懂得——一切聪明的总督，只要肯给自己留出时间，都懂得——威逼一个犹太人是无用的；于是来找我。我从不放贷——那是不合哲学的：可我把他引见给老米利暗，她连和魔鬼本人也敢做买卖；这一手下去，他拿到了钱没有，我不知道：可这一点我知道——我们捏住了他的秘密——如今你也捏住了；你若要更多的消息，那老太婆，她之乐于一桩密谋不亚于一杯法勒那（Falernian）好酒，自会替你弄来。」

「到底，你终究是个真正的朋友。」

===Original===
“Of course I am. Now, is not this method of getting at the truth much easier and pleasanter than setting a couple of dirty negroes to pinch and pull me, and so making it a point of honour with me to tell you nothing but lies? Here comes Ganymede with the wine, just in time to calm your nerves, and fill you with the spirit of divination.﻿ ﻿… To the goddess of good counsels, my lord. What wine this is!”

“True Syrian﻿—fire and honey; fourteen years old next vintage, my Raphael. Out, Hypocorisma! See that he is not listening. The impudent rascal! I was humbugged into giving two thousand gold pieces for him two years ago, he was so pretty﻿—they said he was only just rising thirteen﻿—and he has been the plague of my life ever since, and is beginning to want the barber already. Now, what is the count dreaming of?”

“His wages for killing Stilicho.”

“What, is it not enough to be Count of Africa?”

===Chinese===
「我当然是。如今，这样探得真相的法子，难道不比派两个脏兮兮的黑人去又捏又拽我、逼得我以不说一句真话为荣，要容易得多、惬意得多么？伽倪墨得斯（Ganymede）拿酒来了，正好给你压压神经，又灌你一肚子预言的神气。……祝那位善谋的女神康健，大人。这是何等的美酒！」

「地道的叙利亚酒——火与蜜；到下个酿酒节就满十四年了，我的拉斐尔。出去，希波克里丝玛（Hypocorisma）！看看他没在偷听。这无赖的小子！两年前我被人诓了，花了两千金币买下他，只因他生得俊俏——他们说他才刚过十三岁——从此他便是我这一生的祸害，如今已开始要找剃头匠了。说罢，那位伯爵在做什么梦？」

「梦见他杀死斯提里科（Stilicho）的赏钱。」

「怎么，做非洲伯爵还不够吗？」

===Original===
“I suppose he sets off against that his services during the last three years.”

“Well, he saved Africa.”

“And thereby Egypt also. And you too, as well as the emperor, may be considered as owing him somewhat.”

“My good friend, my debts are far too numerous for me to think of paying any of them. But what wages does he want?”

“The purple.”

Orestes started, and then fell into thought. Raphael sat watching him a while.

===Chinese===
「我想，他是要拿过去三年的功劳来抵一抵。」

「也罢，他保全了非洲。」

「因而也保全了埃及。而你，与皇帝一样，也可算欠着他一份人情。」

「我的好朋友，我所欠的债太多了，哪有心思去还其中任何一笔。可他要的是怎样的赏钱？」

「紫袍。」

俄瑞斯忒斯一惊，随即陷入沉思。拉斐尔坐着端详了他一会儿。

===Original===
“Now, most noble lord, may I depart? I have said all I have to say; and unless I get home to luncheon at once, I shall hardly have time to find old Miriam for you, and get through our little affair with her before sunset.”

“Stay. What force has he?”

“Forty thousand already, they say. And those Donatist ruffians are with him to a man, if he can but scrape together wherewith to change their bludgeons into good steel.”

“Well, go.﻿ ﻿… So. A hundred thousand might do it,” said he, meditating, as Raphael bowed himself out. “He won’t get them. I don’t know, though; the man has the head of a Julius. Well﻿—that fool Attalus talked of joining Egypt to the Western Empire.﻿ ﻿… Not such a bad thought either. Anything is better than being governed by an idiot child and three canting nuns. I expect to be excommunicated every day for some offence against Pulcheria’s prudery.﻿ ﻿… Heraclian emperor at Rome﻿ ﻿… and I lord and master on this side the sea. The Donatists pitted again fairly against the orthodox, to cut each other’s throats in peace﻿ ﻿… no more of Cyril’s spying and talebearing to Constantinople.﻿ ﻿… Not such a bad dish of fare.﻿ ﻿… But then﻿—it would take so much trouble!”

With which words, Orestes went into his third warm bath for that day.

===Chinese===
「如今，最高贵的爵爷，我可以告退了么？该说的我都说了；我若不即刻回去用午饭，怕就来不及替你去找老米利暗，也来不及在日落之前把咱与她那桩小事办妥了。」

「慢着。他有多少兵？」

「据说已有四万。而那些多纳图斯派（Donatist）的暴徒，只要他能凑得出钱，把他们手中的木棍换成好钢，便个个都与他同党。」

「好，去罢。……这样。十万之数或可成事，」他沉思着，那时拉斐尔已鞠躬而出。「他弄不到的。可谁知道呢；此人有一颗尤里乌斯（Julius）般的头脑。也罢——那傻子阿塔卢斯（Attalus）曾说起把埃及并入西部帝国。……这主意倒也不坏。无论如何，总好过被一个白痴孩童和三个伪善的修女治理。我每日都等着因触犯了普尔凯丽娅的假道学而被革出教门。……赫拉克利安在罗马称帝……而我，在这一边海作主作王。多纳图斯派与正统派重新旗鼓相当地对峙，好相安无事地互相割喉……再没有区利罗那一套刺探和搬弄是非告到君士坦丁堡去。……这盘菜倒不坏。……可那——要费那么大的力气！」

说完这话，俄瑞斯忒斯便去洗他当日第三次温水澡了。

## III / III

### The Goths / 哥特人

===Original===
For two days the young monk held on, paddling and floating rapidly down the Nile-stream, leaving city after city to right and left with longing eyes, and looking back to one villa after another, till the reaches of the banks hid them from his sight, with many a yearning to know what sort of places those gay buildings and gardens would look like on a nearer view, and what sort of life the thousands led who crowded the busy quays, and walked and drove, in an endless stream, along the great highroads which ran along either bank. He carefully avoided every boat that passed him, from the gilded barge of the wealthy landlord or merchant, to the tiny raft buoyed up with empty jars, which was floating down to be sold at some market in the Delta. Here and there he met and hailed a crew of monks, drawing their nets in a quiet bay, or passing along the great watery highway from monastery to monastery: but all the news he received from them was, that the canal of Alexandria was still several days’ journey below him. It seemed endless, that monotonous vista of the two high clay banks, with their sluices and waterwheels, their knots of palms and date-trees; endless seemed that wearisome succession of bars of sand and banks of mud, every one like the one before it, every one dotted with the same line of logs and stones strewn along the water’s edge, which turned out as he approached them to be basking crocodiles and sleeping pelicans. His eye, wearied with the continual confinement and want of distance, longed for the boundless expanse of the desert, for the jagged outlines of those far-off hills, which he had watched from boyhood rising mysteriously at morn out of the eastern sky, and melting mysteriously into it again at even, beyond which dwelt a whole world of wonders, elephants and dragons, satyrs and anthropophagi﻿—ay, and the phoenix itself. Tired and melancholy, his mind returned inward to prey on itself, and the last words of Arsenius rose again and again to his thoughts. “Was his call of the spirit or of the flesh?” How should he test that problem? He wished to see the world that might be carnal. True; but, he wished to convert the world﻿ ﻿… was not that spiritual? Was he not going on a noble errand?﻿ ﻿… thirsting for toil, for saintship, for martyrdom itself, if it would but come and cut the Gordian knot of all temptations, and save him﻿—for he dimly felt that it would save him﻿—a whole sea of trouble in getting safe and triumphant out of that world into which he had not yet entered﻿ ﻿… and his heart shrank back from the untried homeless wilderness before him. But no! the die was cast, and he must down and onward, whether in obedience to the spirit or the flesh. Oh, for one hour of the quiet of that dear Laura and the old familiar faces!

===Chinese===
整整两日，那年轻的修士一路撑舟，顺着尼罗河（Nile）的水流飞快地向下游漂去，把一座又一座的城池留在左右两岸，目光里满是眷恋；他频频回望一幢又一幢的别墅，直到河湾一道道地遮断了视线。他心里怀着无尽的渴望，想知道那些鲜艳的楼阁与花园走近了看会是什么模样；想知道那成千上万、摩肩接踵于繁忙码头的人群过的是怎样的日子；他们川流不息地步行着、乘车着，沿着两岸的大道来来去去。凡是有船从身旁经过，他都小心避开——无论是富有的地主或商人那金碧辉煌的游舫，还是用空坛子浮起来、正顺流漂下去要到三角洲（Delta）某处集市去发卖的小小筏子。他时或遇见一队修士，在幽静的河湾里收网，或沿着这条宽阔的水上通衢从一座修院去往另一座修院，便向他们招呼问候；可他从他们口中得来的消息，无非是：去亚历山大城的那条运河，还在他下游好几日的路程之外。那两道高高的黏土河岸，连同岸上的水闸、水车、一簇簇的棕榈与枣椰，单调的景象仿佛永无尽头；那一段接一段的沙洲与泥岸，更是乏味得似无止境，每一段都与前一段一模一样，每一段水边都同样散落着一排木头与石块，待他凑近了才看清——原来是晒太阳的鳄鱼和酣睡的鹈鹕。他的眼睛被这长久的逼仄、这无处可看远的景况折磨得疲倦不堪，渴望着沙漠那一望无际的辽阔，渴望着远方群山那参差的轮廓——自幼年起他便望着它们在清晨从东方天际神秘地升起，到了傍晚又神秘地消融回那天际之中；山的那一边，住着一整个奇境的世界：大象与巨龙、萨提尔（satyr，半羊之妖）与食人族（anthropophagi）——啊，还有那不死鸟（phoenix）本身。他身心俱疲，满怀愁绪，心思便转回内里，反噬起自身来；阿尔塞尼乌斯（Arsenius）最后的那几句话，在他心头一遍又一遍地浮起。「他的呼召，是出于圣灵，还是出于肉体呢？」他该怎样去勘破这道难题？他渴望去看那世界——这或许是出于肉体。不错；可他更渴望去归化那世界……这难道不属圣灵？他所行的，难道不是一桩崇高的大业？……他渴慕劳苦，渴慕成圣，甚至渴慕殉道本身——只要它肯降临，一刀斩断一切试探的戈尔迪之结（the Gordian knot），救拔他——因为他隐约觉得，那样便能救拔他——免去他将要陷入的那一整个大海般的麻烦，使他安然、凯旋般地脱出那个他尚未踏入的世界……然而一面对眼前这片未曾尝试过的、无家可归的荒野，他的心又退缩了。可是不！骰子既已掷下，他便只能顺流而下、向前再向前，无论是顺从圣灵，还是顺从肉体。唉，只要能得那亲爱的劳拉一小时的清静，再见一见那些熟悉的老脸也好啊！

===Original===
At last, a sudden turn of the bank brought him in sight of a gaudily-painted barge, on board of which armed men, in uncouth and foreign dresses, were chasing with barbaric shouts some large object in the water. In the bows stood a man of gigantic stature, brandishing a harpoon in his right hand, and in his left holding the line of a second, the head of which was fixed in the huge purple sides of a hippopotamus, who foamed and wallowed a few yards down the stream. An old grizzled warrior at the stern, with a rudder in either hand, kept the boat’s head continually towards the monster, in spite of its sudden and frantic wheelings; and when it dashed madly across the stream, some twenty oars flashed through the water in pursuit. All was activity and excitement; and it was no wonder if Philammon’s curiosity had tempted him to drift down almost abreast of the barge ere he descried, peeping from under a decorated awning in the afterpart, some dozen pairs of languishing black eyes, turned alternately to the game and to himself. The serpents!﻿—chattering and smiling, with pretty little shrieks and shaking of glossy curls and gold necklaces, and fluttering of muslin dresses, within a dozen yards of him! Blushing scarlet, he knew not why, he seized his paddle, and tried to back out of the snare﻿ ﻿… but somehow, his very efforts to escape those sparkling eyes diverted his attention from everything else: the hippopotamus had caught sight of him, and furious with pain, rushed straight at the unoffending canoe; the harpoon line became entangled round his body, and in a moment he and his frail bark were overturned, and the monster, with his huge white tusks gaping wide, close on him as he struggled in the stream.

Luckily Philammon, contrary to the wont of monks, was a bather, and swam like a waterfowl: fear he had never known: death from childhood had been to him, as to the other inmates of the Laura, a contemplation too perpetual to have any paralysing terror in it, even then, when life seemed just about to open on him anew. But the monk was a man, and a young one, and had no intention of dying tamely or unavenged. In an instant he had freed himself from the line; drawn the short knife which was his only weapon; and diving suddenly, avoided the monster’s rush, and attacked him from behind with stabs, which, though not deep, still dyed the waters with gore at every stroke. The barbarians shouted with delight. The hippopotamus turned furiously against his new assailant, crushing, alas! the empty canoe to fragments with a single snap of his enormous jaws; but the turn was fatal to him; the barge was close upon him, and as he presented his broad side to the blow, the sinewy arm of the giant drove a harpoon through his heart, and with one convulsive shudder the huge blue mass turned over on its side and floated dead.

===Chinese===
终于，河岸一个猛然的转弯，把他带进了一艘彩绘斑斓的大游舫的视野之内。舫上，一群披挂兵刃、穿着粗野异邦衣裳的汉子，正以野蛮的呐喊追逐水里一头硕大的活物。船头立着一个身量魁梧的巨人，右手挥舞着一柄鱼叉，左手攥着第二根叉的绳索——那叉头已深深扎进一头河马紫红的庞大侧腹；那河马口吐白沫、翻滚挣扎，在下游几码之处。船尾一位须发斑白的老将，双手各执一柄舵，不顾那巨物突然而狂乱的回旋，始终把船头对准它；待它发疯似地横冲过河面，便有二十来支桨如闪电般划破水面，紧紧追来。满船上下都是忙碌与亢奋；也难怪菲拉蒙（Philammon）被好奇心勾了去，几乎漂到了与那游舫并排的位置，才猛然发现：船尾一顶华美的帷幔之下，探出十来双水汪汪的黑眼睛，时而被引向那场猎戏，时而被投向了他自己。这些蛇精！——叽叽喳喳地笑着、说着，发出娇滴滴的小声尖叫，摇晃着一头油亮亮的卷发和金项链，薄薄的细布裙衫翩翩翻飞，竟离他只有十几码远！他涨红了脸，红得像胭脂，自己也不知是为什么，赶忙抓起桨，想从这张罗网里退出来……可不知怎的，他越想躲开那双双闪亮的眼睛，便越把心思从别处统统引开：那河马已瞧见了他，负痛发狂，直冲着这只无辜的独木舟扑来；鱼叉的绳索缠住了他的身子，一眨眼间，他与他那脆弱的小舟便一齐被掀翻了，那巨物张开它巨大的白牙，在他于水中挣扎之际，已近在咫尺。

所幸菲拉蒙与一般修士不同，是个惯于沐浴的，游起来像只水鸟：他从未尝过恐惧的滋味；自幼便如劳拉里其他同伴一样，死亡于他是一种太过恒久的沉思，反倒没有了令人瘫痪的恐怖——即便在此时，当生命仿佛又要在他眼前重新展开之际，亦复如是。然而这位修士到底是个人，而且是个年轻人，断无束手待毙、白白送死的打算。说时迟那时快，他已挣脱了那绳索；抽出他唯一的兵器——那把短刀；猛地一个潜水，避开了那巨物的猛扑，从它背后反攻，一刀一刀地戳将过去——那一刀虽戳得不深，每一刀下去却都把河水染红了一片。那些蛮子欢呼雀跃起来。那河马狂怒地转身扑向这新的袭击者，哎呀！只一合它那巨颌便把那只空空的独木舟咬成了碎片；可这一转身，却要了它的命：大舫已紧逼上来，当它把宽阔的侧腹暴露在打击之下，那巨人青筋暴突的手臂便将一柄鱼叉直透它的心窝；那庞大的蓝色身躯痉挛似地一抖，翻身侧倒，浮在水上，死了。

===Original===
Poor Philammon! He alone was silent, amid the yells of triumph; sorrowfully he swam round and round his little paper wreck﻿ ﻿… it would not have floated a mouse. Wistfully be eyed the distant banks, half minded to strike out for them and escape,﻿ ﻿… and thought of the crocodiles,﻿ ﻿… and paddled round again,﻿ ﻿… and thought of the basilisk eyes;﻿ ﻿… he might escape the crocodiles, but who could escape women?﻿ ﻿… and he struck out valiantly for shore﻿ ﻿… when he was brought to a sudden stop by finding the stern of the barge close on him, a noose thrown over him by some friendly barbarian, and himself hauled on board, amid the laughter, praise, astonishment, and grumbling of the good-natured crew, who had expected him, as a matter of course, to avail himself at once of their help, and could not conceive the cause of his reluctance.

Philammon gazed with wonder on his strange hosts, their pale complexions, globular heads and faces, high cheekbones, tall and sturdy figures; their red beards, and yellow hair knotted fantastically above the head; their awkward dresses, half Roman or Egyptian, and half of foreign fur, soiled and stained in many a storm and fight, but tastelessly bedizened with classic jewels, brooches, and Roman coins, strung like necklaces. Only the steersman, who had come forward to wonder at the hippopotamus, and to help in dragging the unwieldy brute on board, seemed to keep genuine and unornamented the costume of his race, the white linen leggings, strapped with thongs of deerskin, the quilted leather cuirass, the bears’-fur cloak, the only ornaments of which were the fangs and claws of the beast itself, and a fringe of grizzled tufts, which looked but too like human hair. The language which they spoke was utterly unintelligible to Philammon, though it need not be so to us.

===Chinese===
可怜的菲拉蒙！在满舫得意的欢呼声中，唯独他默然无声；他凄然地围着他那只薄纸般的小破船游了一圈又一圈……那船，连一只老鼠都浮不起了。他眼巴巴地望着远处的岸，几乎想拼力游过去逃命……可一想到鳄鱼，便又划着水转了一圈……又想到那双双妖蛇似的眼睛；……鳄鱼或许还躲得过，可女人，谁躲得过呢？……于是他鼓起勇气朝岸上划去……谁知冷不丁地被挡住了去路——游舫的船尾已逼到了他跟前，一位好心的蛮子把一个活结套甩到了他身上，他就这样被拽上了船；那群好心肠的汉子又是笑、又是夸、又是惊、又是嘟囔，他们原以为他理所当然会立刻接受他们的援手，想不通他这番推三阻四究竟为着什么。

菲拉蒙惊异地打量着他这群古怪的主人：他们肤色苍白，头脸浑圆，颧骨高耸，身量高大而结实；他们生着红胡子，黄头发在头顶上绾成奇形怪状的发髻；他们的衣衫笨拙不雅，半是罗马或埃及式样，半是异邦的毛皮，被一场场风雨与厮杀弄得污渍斑斑，却又俗气地缀满了古典的宝石、胸针，还有像项链一样串起来的罗马钱币。只有那舵手——他这时已走上前来，对那河马啧啧称奇，并帮着把那笨重的畜生拖上船——似乎还忠实无饰地保留着他本族的装束：白色亚麻的绑腿，用鹿皮条束紧；绗缝的皮革胸甲；熊皮斗篷；它唯一的装饰，便是那畜生本身的獠牙与利爪，外加一圈灰白的穗子，那穗子看起来未免太像人的头发。他们所说的话，菲拉蒙一句也听不懂——不过，在我们却未必不能懂。

===Original===
“A well-grown lad and a brave one, Wulf the son of Ovida,” said the giant to the old hero of the bearskin cloak; “and understands wearing skins, in this furnace-mouth of a climate, rather better than you do.”

“I keep to the dress of my forefathers, Amalric the Amal. What did to sack Rome in, may do to find Asgard in.”

The giant, who was decked out with helmet, cuirass, and senatorial boots, in a sort of mongrel mixture of the Roman military and civil dress, his neck wreathed with a dozen gold chains, and every finger sparkling with jewels, turned away with an impatient sneer.

“Asgard﻿—Asgard! If you are in such a hurry to get to Asgard up this ditch in the sand, you had better ask the fellow how far it is thither.”

Wulf took him quietly at his word, and addressed a question to the young monk, which he could only answer by a shake of the head.

“Ask him in Greek, man.”

“Greek is a slave’s tongue. Make a slave talk to him in it, not me.”

“Here﻿—some of you girls! Pelagia! you understand this fellow’s talk. Ask him how far it is to Asgard.”

“You must ask me more civilly, my rough hero,” replied a soft voice from underneath the awning. “Beauty must be sued, and not commanded.”

“Come, then, my olive-tree, my gazelle, my lotus-flower, my﻿—what was the last nonsense you taught me?﻿—and ask this wild man of the sands how far it is from these accursed endless rabbit-burrows to Asgard.”

===Chinese===
「好一个壮实的小伙子，还挺有胆气，沃尔夫·奥维达之子（Wulf the son of Ovida），」那巨人对手披熊皮斗篷的老英雄说道，「论起在这火炉口一般的天气里穿毛皮，他可比你懂得多哩。」

「我守着我祖上传下来的装束，阿玛尔里克，阿玛尔王族（Amalric the Amal）。」老人答道，「当年能穿着它去攻陷罗马，如今便能穿着它去找阿斯加德（Asgard）。」

那巨人头戴钢盔，身披胸甲，足蹬元老式的高筒靴，一身上不伦不类地糅合了罗马军装与文官服饰；脖子上缠着十几条金链，每根指头上都闪着宝石。他一脸不耐的冷笑，转过脸去。

「阿斯加德——阿斯加德！你既急着要沿这条沙地里的沟渠逆流而上、去寻阿斯加德，不如问问这家伙：到那儿还有多远？」

沃尔夫竟不声不响地依了他的话，向那少年修士发了一问；那修士听不懂，只能摇了摇头。

「用希腊话问他呀，老兄。」

「希腊话是奴隶的话。叫个奴隶去跟他说，别叫我。」

「喂——你们这群丫头！佩拉吉娅（Pelagia）！你懂这家伙的鸟语。问问他到阿斯加德还有多远。」

「你可得对我客气些，我的莽英雄，」帷幔底下传来一个柔媚的声音，「美人是求来的，不是唤来的。」

「那么来吧，我的橄榄树，我的小羚羊，我的莲花，我的——你上回教我的那句傻话是怎么说的来着？——去问问这个沙地里的野人：从这些可恶的、没完没了的兔窟窿到阿斯加德，还有多远？」

===Original===
The awning was raised, and lying luxuriously on a soft mattress, fanned with peacock’s feathers, and glittering with rubies and topazes, appeared such a vision as Philammon had never seen before.

A woman of some two-and-twenty summers, formed in the most voluptuous mould of Grecian beauty, whose complexion showed every violet vein through its veil of luscious brown. Her little bare feet, as they dimpled the cushions, were more perfect than Aphrodite’s, softer than a swan’s bosom. Every swell of her bust and arms showed through the thin gauze robe, while her lower limbs were wrapped in a shawl of orange silk, embroidered with wreaths of shells and roses. Her dark hair lay carefully spread out upon the pillow, in a thousand ringlets entwined with gold and jewels; her languishing eyes blazed like diamonds from a cavern, under eyelids darkened and deepened with black antimony; her lips pouted of themselves, by habit or by nature, into a perpetual kiss; slowly she raised one little lazy hand; slowly the ripe lips opened; and in most pure and melodious Attic, she lisped her huge lover’s question to the monk, and repeated it before the boy could shake off the spell, and answer.﻿ ﻿…

“Asgard? What is Asgard?”

The beauty looked at the giant for further instructions.

“The City of the immortal Gods,” interposed the old warrior, hastily and sternly, to the lady.

“The city of God is in heaven,” said Philammon to the interpreter, turning his head away from those gleaming, luscious, searching glances.

His answer was received with a general laugh by all except the leader, who shrugged his shoulders.

“It may as well be up in the skies as up the Nile. We shall be just as likely, I believe, to reach it by flying, as by rowing up this big ditch. Ask him where the river comes from, Pelagia.”

===Chinese===
帷幔掀了起来：只见一位美人慵懒地倚在一张柔软的垫褥上，有人拿孔雀羽扇给她扇着风，她周身红宝石、黄玉闪闪放光——这般景象，菲拉蒙生平从未见过。

那是一个看上去约莫二十二三岁的女子，按希腊美神最肉感的模子塑成；她的肤色是一层甘美的褐色，每一根青紫的脉络都隐约透见。那双赤裸的小脚踩在软垫上，一捏一个窝儿，比阿佛洛狄忒（Aphrodite）的脚还要完美，比天鹅的胸脯还要柔嫩。她酥胸与玉臂的每一道起伏，都透过那层薄如蝉翼的纱裙显露出来；她的下半身裹着一条橘黄色的丝巾，上头绣着一圈圈的贝壳与玫瑰。她那乌黑的秀发仔细地摊在枕上，化作上千个卷发，缠着金丝与宝石；她那一双水汪汪的眼睛，像洞穴里的钻石一般灼灼放光，眼皮则被黑色的锑粉描得又浓又深；她的双唇习惯性地、抑或天生地噘着，仿佛永远在索取一个吻。她缓缓地抬起一只懒洋洋的小手；那熟透的双唇缓缓张开；她用最纯正动听的阿提卡（Attic）希腊话，把她那巨人情人要问的话，娇滴滴地向那修士转述了一遍，又重复了一遍——那少年这才如梦初醒，能够作答……

「阿斯加德？阿斯加德是什么？」

那美人向那巨人投去一瞥，想讨个进一步的吩咐。

「是不朽众神之城。」那老战士匆促而严厉地向那女子插了一句。

「上帝的城在天上。」菲拉蒙对那位通译说，一面把头从那双双灼灼的、甜腻腻的、洞穿人心的目光里转开。

他的回答引来众人一阵大笑，唯独那首领不笑，只是耸了耸肩。

「它要是在天上，倒也跟在尼罗河上游差不多。依我看，我们要飞上去抵达它，跟划着船沿这条大沟上去抵达它，怕是同样有指望。佩拉吉娅，问问他这条河是从哪儿来的。」

===Original===
Pelagia obeyed﻿ ﻿… and thereon followed a confusion worse confounded, composed of all the impossible wonders of that mythic fairyland with which Philammon had gorged himself from boyhood in his walks with the old monks, and of the equally trustworthy traditions which the Goths had picked up at Alexandria. There was nothing which that river did not do. It rose in the Caucasus. Where was the Caucasus? He did not know. In Paradise﻿—in Indian Aethiopia﻿—in Aethiopian India. Where were they? He did not know. Nobody knew. It ran for a hundred and fifty days’ journey through deserts where nothing but flying serpents and satyrs lived, and the very lions’ manes were burnt off by the heat.﻿ ﻿…

“Good sporting there, at all events, among these dragons,” quoth Smid the son of Troll, armourer to the party.

“As good as Thor’s when he caught Snake Midgard with the bullock’s head,” said Wulf.

It turned to the east for a hundred days’ journey more, all round Arabia and India, among forests full of elephants and dog-headed women.

“Better and better, Smid!” growled Wulf, approvingly.

“Fresh beef cheap there, Prince Wulf, eh?” quoth Smid; “I must look over the arrowheads.”

—To the mountains of the Hyperboreans, where there was eternal night, and the air was full of feathers.﻿ ﻿… That is, one-third of it came from thence, and another third came from the Southern ocean, over the Moon mountains, where no one had ever been, and the remaining third from the country where the phoenix lived, and nobody knew where that was. And then there were the cataracts, and the inundations﻿—and﻿—and﻿—and above the cataracts, nothing but sand-hills and ruins, as full of devils as they could hold﻿ ﻿… and as for Asgard, no one had ever heard of it﻿ ﻿… till every face grew longer and longer, as Pelagia went on interpreting and misinterpreting; and at last the giant smote his hand upon his knee, and swore a great oath that Asgard might rot till the twilight of the gods before he went a step farther up the Nile.

===Chinese===
佩拉吉娅遵命而去……于是一场乱上加乱便接踵而来：这一头，是菲拉蒙自幼与那些老修士散步时、把那一脑门子的神话仙境的种种荒诞奇闻胡乱塞进肚里；那一头，是哥特人（Goth）在亚历山大城东拼西凑来的、同样靠不住的种种传闻。那条河无所不能。它发源于高加索（Caucasus）。高加索在哪儿？他不知道。在乐园里——在印度人的埃塞俄比亚（Aethiopia）——在埃塞俄比亚人的印度。那又在哪儿？他不知道。谁也不知道。它在沙漠里一流就是一百五十日的路程；那沙漠里只住着会飞的蛇和萨提尔，连狮子的鬃毛都被热气烤焦了。……

「无论怎样，那里的那些龙，倒是可以好好猎上一猎。」队伍里的兵器匠斯密德·特罗尔之子（Smid the son of Troll）说道。

「跟托尔（Thor）用公牛头钓起尘世巨蛇（Snake Midgard）那一手，不相上下。」沃尔夫说。

那河又转而向东，再流一百日的路程，绕过阿拉伯与印度全境，两岸尽是密林，林中满是象群与狗头的女人。

「越说越来劲了，斯密德！」沃尔夫赞许地嘟囔。

「那里的鲜肉便宜，沃尔夫亲王，是不是？」斯密德道，「我得把箭镞拾掇拾掇了。」

——再往上去，便是极北族人（Hyperboreans）的群山了，那里长夜漫漫，空中飘满了羽毛。……也就是说，这条河，三分之一的水从那里来；又有三分之一，从南海而来，越过那从来无人到过的月亮山脉；剩下的三分之一，从不死鸟所居的国度而来——可谁也不知道那国度在哪儿。再者便是那些大瀑布，那些泛滥……还有……还有……还有那大瀑布之上，除了沙丘与废墟，便一无所有，里面塞满了群魔，塞得满满当当……至于阿斯加德，从来没有人听说过这么个地方……听着听着，每张脸都越拉越长——佩拉吉娅一路译着，又一路口译着；末了，那巨人一掌拍在膝上，发下一个毒誓：阿斯加德大可烂在那里，等到众神的黄昏再說，他绝不再沿尼罗河往上走一步。

===Original===
“Curse the monk!” growled Wulf. “How should such a poor beast know anything about the matter?”

“Why should not he know as well as that ape of a Roman governor?” asked Smid.

“Oh, the monks know everything,” said Pelagia. “They go hundreds and thousands of miles up the river, and cross the deserts among fiends and monsters, where anyone else would be eaten up, or go mad at once.”

“Ah, the dear holy men! It’s all by the sign of the blessed cross!” exclaimed all the girls together, devoutly crossing themselves, while two or three of the most enthusiastic were half-minded to go forward and kneel to Philammon for his blessing; but hesitated, their Gothic lovers being heathenishly stupid and prudish on such points.

“Why should he not know as well as the prefect? Well said, Smid! I believe that prefect’s quill-driver was humbugging us when he said Asgard was only ten days’ sail up.”

“Why?” asked Wulf.

“I never give any reasons. What’s the use of being an Amal, and a son of Odin, if one has always to be giving reasons like a rascally Roman lawyer? I say the governor looked like a liar; and I say this monk looks like an honest fellow; and I choose to believe him, and there is an end of it.”

“Don’t look so cross at me, Prince Wulf; I’m sure it’s not my fault; I could only say what the monk told me,” whispered poor Pelagia.

===Chinese===
「该死的修士！」沃尔夫嘟囔道，「这么个可怜虫似的畜生，哪能知道这档子事？」

「他凭什么就不能知道？跟那只罗马总督派来的猴子，难道不一样？」斯密德反问。

「哎哟，修士们可是无所不知的，」佩拉吉娅道，「他们沿河逆流而上几百几千里的，又穿过沙漠，一路都是妖魔怪兽——换了别人，早被吃了，要不就发疯啦。」

「啊，亲爱的圣人们！这全靠那有福的十字架的圣号！」姑娘们一齐喊起来，虔诚地画着十字；其中两三个最热心激动的，几乎想走上前去，跪求菲拉吉娅的祝福；可终究犹豫了——她们的哥特情人在这等事上头，异教徒似的又蠢又矫情。

「他凭什么不能跟总督一样知情？说得在理，斯密德！我看那总督手下那摇笔杆子的，说阿斯加德只在向上行十日水路之处，准是在蒙咱们。」

「怎见得？」沃尔夫问。

「我从不讲什么道理。一个人要是身为阿玛尔王族，身为奥丁（Odin）之子，还得像那无赖罗马律师似的，事事都得讲道理，那活着还有什么意思？我说那总督看着就像个骗子；我说这修士看着像个老实人；我偏要信他，事情就这么定了。」

「别那样气鼓鼓地瞪着我呀，沃尔夫亲王；这可怨不得我；修士说什么，我原样转述罢了。」可怜的佩拉吉娅悄声道。

===Original===
“Who looks cross at you, my queen?” roared the Amal. “Let me have him out here, and by Thor’s hammer, I’ll﻿—”

“Who spoke to you, you stupid darling?” answered Pelagia, who lived in hourly fear of thunderstorms. “Who is going to be cross with anyone, except I with you, for mishearing and misunderstanding, and meddling, as you are always doing? I shall do as I threatened, and run away with Prince Wulf, if you are not good. Don’t you see that the whole crew are expecting you to make them an oration?”

Whereupon the Amal rose.

“See you here, Wulf the son of Ovida, and warriors all! If we want wealth, we shan’t find it among the sand-hills. If we want women, we shall find nothing prettier than these among dragons and devils. Don’t look angry, Wulf. You have no mind to marry one of those dog-headed girls the monk talked of, have you? Well, then, we have money and women; and if we want sport, it’s better sport killing men than killing beasts; so we had better go where we shall find most of that game, which we certainly shall not up this road. As for fame and all that, though I’ve had enough, there’s plenty to be got anywhere along the shores of that Mediterranean. Let’s burn and plunder Alexandria: forty of us Goths might kill down all these donkey-riders in two days, and hang up that lying prefect who sent us hereon this fool’s errand. Don’t answer, Wulf. I knew he was humbugging us all along, but you were so open-mouthed to all he said, that I was bound to let my elders choose for me. Let’s go back; send over for any of the tribes; send to Spain for those Vandals﻿—they have had enough of Adolf by now, curse him!﻿—I’ll warrant them; get together an army, and take Constantinople. I’ll be Augustus, and Pelagia, Augusta; you and Smid here, the two Caesars; and we’ll make the monk the chief of the eunuchs, eh?﻿—anything you like for a quiet life; but up this accursed kennel of hot water I go no farther. Ask your girls, my heroes, and I’ll ask mine. Women are all prophetesses, every one of them.”

===Chinese===
「谁敢气鼓鼓地瞪你，我的王后？」阿玛尔大吼，「你叫他出来，凭托尔的雷锤起誓，我非——」

「谁跟你说话了，你这个蠢宝贝？」佩拉吉娅答道——她平素时时刻刻都怕着打雷。「谁要跟谁过不去？除了我要跟你过不去——谁叫你耳背、谁叫你误会、谁叫你多管闲事，这一桩桩你哪样不干？我说过的那话可要算数：你再不老实，我就跟沃尔夫亲王私奔啦。你没瞧见么，全船上下都等着你给他们来上一篇演说呢？」

于是那阿玛尔站起身来。

「你们都听着，沃尔夫·奥维达之子，还有众位将士！我们要的是金银，沙丘里头可挖不出金银来。我们要的是女人，那些龙呀魔呀的地方，找不出比眼前这些更俏的来了。别瞪眼，沃尔夫。你总不至于想娶那修士所说的狗头女子当中的一个吧，啊？那么好，我们既有了钱，又有了女人；若还要消遣，杀人可比杀畜生有意思得多；所以我们还是上那类猎物最多的地方去——沿这条路上去，断乎是找不着的。至于名声那一类玩意儿，我虽说捞够了，可那地中海（Mediterranean）沿岸一带，到处都还多得是。咱们回去罢，去烧去抢亚历山大城：咱们哥特人，四十条好汉，不出两日便可把这些骑驴的杀个精光，再把那个打发咱们来跑这趟蠢差事、满嘴谎言的总督吊起来。你别开口，沃尔夫。我早知道他一直在蒙咱们；只是你对他那套话张着大嘴听得那么入神，我也只好让长辈替我拿主意。咱们回去罢；派人去把哪个部族都叫来；派人去西班牙（Spain）把那些汪达尔人（Vandal）叫来——他们在阿道夫（Adolf）手底下也受够了，该死的他！——保他们乐意；凑起一支大军，去拿下君士坦丁堡（Constantinople）。我做奥古斯都（Augustus），佩拉吉娅做奥古斯塔（Augusta）；你和这里的斯密德，就做两员凯撒（Caesar）；咱们再叫那修士去做掌理太监的头儿，好不好？——只要图个清静，随你们怎么安排都成；只是这一条该死的热水沟，我是绝不再往上走了。诸位英雄，问问你们的姑娘罢，我也问问我这位。女人个个都是女先知，没一个不是。」

===Original===
“When they are not harlots,” growled Wulf to himself.

“I will go to the world’s end with you, my king!” sighed Pelagia; “but Alexandria is certainly pleasanter than this.”

Old Wulf sprang up fiercely enough.

“Hear me, Amalric the Amal, son of Odin, and heroes all! When my fathers swore to be Odin’s men, and gave up the kingdom to the holy Annals, the sons of the Aesir, what was the bond between your fathers and mine? Was it not that we should move and move, southward and southward ever, till we came back to Asgard, the city where Odin dwells forever, and gave into his hands the kingdom of all the earth? And did we not keep our oath? Have we not held to the Amals? Did we not leave Adolf, because we would not follow a Balth, while there was an Amal to lead us? Have we not been true men to you, son of the Aesir?”

“No man ever saw Wulf, the son of Ovida, fail friend or foe.”

“Then why does his friend fail him? Why does his friend fail himself? If the bison-bull lie down and wallow, what will the herd do for a leader? If the king-wolf lose the scent, how will the pack hold it? If the Yngling forgets the song of Asgard, who will sing it to the heroes?”

“Sing it yourself, if you choose. Pelagia sings quite well enough for me.”

===Chinese===
「当她们不是娼妓的时候。」沃尔夫自言自语地嘟囔。

「我愿随你到天涯海角，我的王！」佩拉吉娅叹道，「不过亚历山大城可比这儿惬意得多，这是真的。」

老沃尔夫腾地一下跳了起来，怒气冲冲。

「你听我说，阿玛尔王族的阿玛尔里克，奥丁之子，还有众位将士！当年我的祖上立誓做奥丁的人，把王国献与那神圣的阿萨神族（the holy Annals，即 Aesir 众神）——阿萨神族之子——那时候，你祖上与我祖上立的约是什么？岂不是：我们要前行、前行，永远向南、向南，直到回到阿斯加德——奥丁永居之城——把全天下的王国都交到他手里？这誓约，我们岂不是守了？我们岂不是始终追随阿玛尔王族？我们岂不是因为不肯追随一个巴尔王族（Balth）的阿道夫——只要还有一个阿玛尔王族的人领着我们——便离开了他？我们待你，阿萨神族之子，岂不是忠义之人？」

「从来没有人见过沃尔夫·奥维达之子失信于友、或失信于敌。」

「那么他的朋友为何要失信于他？他的朋友为何要失信于自己？野牛之王若躺倒打滚，牛群还能跟谁去？狼王若失了嗅迹，狼群还能撑得住么？英格林（Yngling）王裔若忘了那阿斯加德之歌，又有谁来向众英雄歌唱它？」

「你自己唱罢，你愿意唱就唱。佩拉吉娅唱得，对我来说已经够好的了。」

===Original===
In an instant the cunning beauty caught at the hint, and poured forth a soft, low, sleepy song:﻿—

“Loose the sail, rest the oar, float away down,
						
						Fleeting and gliding by tower and town;
						
						Life is so short at best! snatch, while thou canst, thy rest,
						
						Sleeping by me!”

“Can you answer that, Wulf?” shouted a dozen voices.

“Hear the song of Asgard, warriors of the Goths! Did not Alaric the king love it well? Did I not sing it before him in the palace of the Caesars, till he swore, for all the Christian that he was, to go southward in search of the holy city? And when he went to Valhalla, and the ships were wrecked off Sicily, and Adolf the Balth turned back like a lazy hound, and married the daughter of the Romans, whom Odin hates, and went northward again to Gaul, did not I sing you all the song of Asgard in Messina there, till you swore to follow the Amal through fire and water until we found the hall of Odin, and received the mead-cup from his own hand? Hear it again, warriors of the Goths!”

“Not that song!” roared the Amal, stopping his ears with both his hands. “Will you drive us blood-mad again, just as we are settling down into our sober senses, and finding out what our lives were given us for?”

“Hear the song of Asgard! On to Asgard, wolves of the Goths!” shouted another; and a babel of voices arose.

===Chinese===
那一瞬，那机灵的美人立刻抓住了这暗示，倾泻出一支柔媚、低回、慵懒的歌来：——

「松了帆，歇了桨，任舟儿顺流荡，
　　掠过一塔又一塔，一城又一乡；
　　人生至苦短呵！能偷闲处且偷闲，
　　伴我入梦乡！」

「这一手你怎么答，沃尔夫？」十几条嗓子一齐喊起来。

「听这阿斯加德之歌罢，哥特的将士们！阿拉里克王（Alaric the king）当年岂不是爱煞了它？我岂不是曾在凯撒们的皇宫里，当着他的面唱过它，唱得他发誓——尽管他是个基督徒——也要南下、去寻那圣城？后来他归了瓦尔哈拉（Valhalla，英灵殿），船队在西西里（Sicily）海外失事，那巴尔王族的阿道夫像条懒狗一样折了回去，娶了那个奥丁所痛恨的罗马人的女儿，再度北上回到高卢（Gaul）——我岂不是在墨西拿（Messina），给你们众人唱起那阿斯加德之歌，唱得你们发誓要追随阿玛尔王族，赴汤蹈火，直到我们找到奥丁的大殿、亲口从他手里接过那蜜酒杯？再听一遍罢，哥特的将士们！」

「不要唱那歌！」阿玛尔大吼，双手捂住耳朵，「我们正要静下心来、正要弄明白这辈子活着为的是什么，你又要惹得我们杀红了眼么？」

「听那阿斯加德之歌！向阿斯加德去，哥特的群狼！」另一个喊道；顿时众声喧哗，乱作一团。

===Original===
“Haven’t we been fighting and marching these seven years?”

“Haven’t we drunk blood enough to satisfy Odin ten times over? If he wants us lot him come himself and lead us!”

“Let us get our winds again before we start afresh!”

“Wulf the Prince is like his name, and never tires; he has a winter-wolf’s legs under him; that is no reason why we should have.”

“Haven’t you heard what the monk says?﻿—we can never get ever those cataracts.”

“We’ll stop his old wives’ tales for him, and then settle for ourselves,” said Smid; and springing from the thwart where he had been sitting, he caught up a bill with one hand, and seized Philammon’s throat with the other﻿ ﻿… in a moment more, it would have been all over with him.﻿ ﻿…

For the first time in his life Philammon felt a hostile grip upon him, and a new sensation rushed through every nerve, as he grappled with the warrior, clutched with his left hand the uplifted wrist, and with his right the girdle, and commenced, without any definite aim, a fierce struggle, which, strange to say, as it went on, grew absolutely pleasant.

The women shrieked to their lovers to part the combatants, but in vain.

“Not for worlds! A very fair match and a very fair fight! Take your long legs back, Itho, or they will be over you! That’s right, my Smid, don’t use the knife! They will be overboard in a moment! By all the Valkyrs, they are down, and Smid undermost!”

===Chinese===
「这七年里，我们打的仗、走的路还少么？」

「我们喝的血，就是把奥丁灌足十回也够了吧？他要我们，就让他自己来领我们！」

「让我们喘口气再重新上路罢！」

「沃尔夫亲王人如其名，永不知疲倦；他胯下生着一条冬狼的腿；那可不是我们也得生一条的理由。」

「你们没听见那修士怎么说么？——我们永远过不了那些大瀑布。」

「咱们先堵了他那张讲老婆子故事的嘴，再自己拿主意。」斯密德说罢，从他坐的横座上一跃而起，一手抄起一柄战戟，另一手便掐住了菲拉蒙的喉咙……再过一刻，菲拉蒙这条命便要交代了……

菲拉蒙有生以来头一遭感到一只敌意的手攥住了自己；一种全新的感觉掠过他每一根神经——他迎着那战士扑上去，左手死死攥住那高高举起的腕子，右手揪住对方的腰带，毫无明确章法地，便开始了一场凶猛的扭打；说来也怪，这扭打进行得越久，竟越发地痛快起来。

女人们尖叫着，求她们的情人把这两个厮打的人拉开，却是徒然。

「拿金山银海来换也不成！旗鼓相当，一场好打！把你的长腿收回去，伊托（Itho），不然就要压到你身上了！这才对，我的斯密德，别动刀子！他们马上就要翻到水里去啦！凭诸位瓦尔基里（Valkyrs）起誓，他们倒下了，斯密德在底下！」

===Original===
There was no doubt of it; and in another moment Philammon would have wrenched the bill out of his opponent’s hand, when, to the utter astonishment of the onlookers, he suddenly loosed his hold, shook himself free by one powerful wrench, and quietly retreated to his seat, conscience-stricken at the fearful thirst for blood which had suddenly boiled up within him as he felt his enemy under him.

The onlookers were struck dumb with astonishment; they had taken for granted that he would, as a matter of course, have used his right of splitting his vanquished opponent’s skull﻿—an event which they would of course have deeply deplored, but with which, as men of honour, they could not on any account interfere, but merely console themselves for the loss of their comrade by flaying his conqueror alive, “carving him into the blood-eagle,” or any other delicate ceremony which might serve as a vent for their sorrow and a comfort to the soul of the deceased.

Smid rose, with a bill in his hand, and looked round him﻿—perhaps to see what was expected of him. He half lifted his weapon to strike.﻿ ﻿… Philammon, seated, looked him calmly in the face.﻿ ﻿… The old warrior’s eye caught the bank, which was now receding rapidly past them; and when he saw that they were really floating downwards again, without an effort to stem the stream, he put away his bill, and sat himself down deliberately in his place, astonishing the onlookers quite as much as Philammon had done.

“Five minutes’ good fighting, and no one killed! This is a shame!” quoth another. “Blood we must see, and it had better be yours, master monk, than your betters’,”﻿—and therewith he rushed on poor Philammon.

===Chinese===
这一点毫无疑问；再过一刻，菲拉蒙便要从对手手里夺下那柄战戟了——谁知，令旁观者大惊失色的是：他竟忽然松了手，一个猛劲挣脱了身，悄然退回自己的座位上去——原来当他把敌人压在身下之时，一种可怕的嗜血之渴猛地在他心里沸腾起来，他为之心惊肉跳。

旁观者都看得目瞪口呆；他们原以为，他理所应当会行使他那把败将的头颅劈开的权利——这一结局他们当然会深表遗憾，但作为讲体面的人，他们绝不能插手干预，只能以活剥那胜者的皮、「把他雕成血鹰（blood-eagle）」、或任何别种雅致的仪式，来发泄他们的哀痛、慰藉死者的亡灵，借此聊以自慰，弥补失去同伴的损失。

斯密德立起身来，手提一柄战戟，四下里张望——也许是想看看众人期望他怎样。他把兵器提起一半，似要砍下……坐着的菲拉蒙，平静地直视他的脸……那老战士的目光瞥到了河岸——那岸正从他们身旁飞速向后退去；他一看，他们确乎又在顺流而下了，毫无再逆流而上的意思，便收了战戟，从容地坐回原位——这一手令旁观者之惊愕，不下于方才菲拉蒙那一下。

「痛痛快快打了五分钟，竟没死一个人！这算什么话！」又一个说道，「血，我们是非见不可的；与其见贵人们的血，倒不如见你的血，修士先生。」说着便朝可怜的菲拉蒙扑了过来。

===Original===
He spoke the heart of the crew; the sleeping wolf in them had been awakened by the struggle, and blood they would have; and not frantically, like Celts or Egyptians, but with the cool humorous cruelty of the Teuton, they rose altogether, and turning Philammon over on his back, deliberated by what death he should die.

Philammon quietly submitted﻿—if submission have anything to do with that state of mind in which sheer astonishment and novelty have broken up all the custom of man’s nature, till the strangest deeds and sufferings are taken as matters of course. His sudden escape from the Laura, the new world of thought and action into which he had been plunged, the new companions with whom he had fallen in, had driven him utterly from his moorings, and now anything and everything might happen to him. He who had promised never to look upon woman found himself, by circumstances over which he had no control, amid a boatful of the most objectionable species of that most objectionable genus﻿—and the utterly worst having happened, everything else which happened must be better than the worst. For the rest, he had gone forth to see the world﻿—and this was one of the ways of it. So he made up his mind to see it, and be filled with the fruit of his own devices.

And he would have been certainly filled with the same in five minutes more, in some shape too ugly to be mentioned: but, as even sinful women have hearts in them, Pelagia shrieked out﻿—

“Amalric! Amalric! do not let them! I cannot bear it!”

“The warriors are free men, my darling, and know what is proper. And what can the life of such a brute be to you?”

Before he could stop her, Pelagia had sprung from her cushions, and thrown herself into the midst of the laughing ring of wild beasts.

“Spare him! spare him for my sake!” shrieked she.

“Oh, my pretty lady! you mustn’t interrupt warriors’ sport!”

===Chinese===
他说出了全船人的心声：他们心中那头沉睡的狼，已被方才那场厮杀唤醒，他们非要见血不可；他们不像克尔特人（Celt）或埃及人那样狂乱行事，而是带着条顿人（Teuton）那种冷静而带几分戏谑的残忍，一齐起立，把菲拉蒙掀翻在地，商议着该叫他怎样一个死法。

菲拉蒙静静地任他们摆布——如果「任人摆布」一词还能用来形容这样一种心境的话：纯粹的惊愕与新奇，已把人性中一切积习打得粉碎，以至最离奇的所作所为、所受所苦，都被他当作理所当然。他突然逃离劳拉、他被投入其中的那一个思想与行动的新天地、他新结识的这群伙伴，已把他原来停泊的锚索彻底崩断；如今，任何事情、一切事情都可能落在他头上。他这个曾立誓永不看女人一眼的人，竟因着自己无从掌握的境遇，落到了满满一船那最可厌的种群之中、最最可厌的物种之间——而最最坏的事既已发生，往后无论再发生什么，总不会比最坏更坏了。再者，他本就是出来看世界的——而这便是这世界的样子之一。于是他打定主意看个究竟，饱尝自己计谋结出的果子。

再过五分钟，他确实就要被那果子填个满满当当了，填以一种丑陋得不忍言说的样子：然而，即便是罪孽的女人，心里也长着一颗心呢——佩拉吉娅尖叫起来——

「阿玛尔里克！阿玛尔里克！别让他们这样！我受不了！」

「将士们都是自由人，我的宝贝，他们自有分寸。这么个畜生的命，又与你有什么相干？」

他还没来得及拦住她，佩拉吉娅已从垫褥上一跃而起，扑进了那一圈嬉笑的野兽中间。

「饶了他！看在我的分上饶了他！」她尖叫道。

「哎哟，我漂亮的姑娘！你可不能搅了将士们的乐子！」

===Original===
In an instant she had torn off her shawl, and thrown it over Philammon; and as she stood, with all the outlines of her beautiful limbs revealed through the thin robe of spangled gauze﻿—

“Let the man who dares, touch him beneath that shawl!﻿—though it be a saffron one!”

The Goths drew back. For Pelagia herself they had as little respect as the rest of the world had. But for a moment she was not the Messalina of Alexandria, but a woman; and true to the old woman-worshipping instinct, they looked one and all at her flashing eyes, full of noble pity and indignation, as well as of mere woman’s terror﻿—and drew back, and whispered together.

Whether the good spirit or the evil one would conquer, seemed for a moment doubtful, when Pelagia felt a heavy hand on her shoulder, and turning, saw Wulf the son of Ovida.

“Go back, pretty woman! Men, I claim the boy. Smid, give him to me. He is your man. You could have killed him if you had chosen, and did not; and no one else shall.”

“Give him us, Prince Wulf! We have not seen blood for many a day!”

“You might have seen rivers of it, if you had had the hearts to go onward. The boy is mine, and a brave boy. He has upset a warrior fairly this day, and spared him; and we will make a warrior of him in return.”

And he lifted up the prostrate monk.

“You are my man now. Do you like fighting?”

Philammon, not understanding the language in which he was addressed, could only shake his head﻿—though if he had known what its import was, he could hardly in honesty have said, No.

“He shakes his head! He does not like it! He is craven! Let us have him!”

“I had killed kings when you were shooting frogs,” cried Smid. “Listen to me, my sons! A coward grips sharply at first, and loosens his hand after a while, because his blood is soon hot and soon cold. A brave man’s grip grows the firmer the longer he holds, because the spirit of Odin comes upon him. I watched the boy’s hands on my threat; and he will make a man; and I will make him one. However, we may as well make him useful at once; so give him an oar.”

“Well,” answered his new protector, “he can as well row us as he rowed by us; and if we are to go back to a cow’s death and the pool of Hela, the quicker we go the better.”

===Chinese===
说时迟那时快，她已扯下身上的丝巾，把它罩在了菲拉蒙身上；她这一站，那条缀着亮片的薄纱裙下，秀美肢体的每一道轮廓都显露无遗——

「谁敢动他一动手，就是在这条丝巾底下！——哪怕它是一条番红色的！」

哥特人都退了回去。说起佩拉吉娅其人，他们原也跟世上别的人一样，对她没什么敬意。可这一刻，她不是亚历山大城的那个梅莎琳娜（Messalina，淫后），而是一个女人；他们恪守着古老的崇拜女人的本能，一齐望着她那双灼灼的眼睛——眼里满是高贵的怜悯与义愤，也满是一个寻常女子的惊恐——于是他们退了回去，交头接耳起来。

是善神得胜，还是恶神得胜，一时似未可知；正在此时，佩拉吉娅感到一只沉甸甸的手按在了她肩头，回头一看，是沃尔夫·奥维达之子。

「回去罢，漂亮的女人！众将士，这小子我认下了。斯密德，把他给我。他是你手下败将。你本可以杀他，却没有下手；那么除你之外，谁也不许动他。」

「把他给我们罢，沃尔夫亲王！我们好多天没见血啦！」

「你们若是真有心再往前走，本可以见到血流成河的。这小子是我的，是个有胆气的小子。今日他公公平平地摔倒了一位战士，又饶了他一命；咱们便投桃报李，把他造就成一个战士罢。」

说着，他把那倒在地上的修士扶了起来。

「你如今是我的人了。你可喜欢厮杀打仗？」

菲拉蒙听不懂向他说的这话，只能摇了摇头——其实他若懂得这话的意思，凭着良心也未必能答一个「不」字。

「他摇头！他不喜欢！他是个孬种！把他交给我们罢！」

「你们还在拿弹弓打青蛙的时候，我已杀过国王了。」斯密德喊道，「听我说，孩子们！懦夫起手时抓得紧，过一会儿手就松了，因为他的血来得快，凉得也快。好汉却是越攥得久，攥得越紧，因为奥丁的神气降临到了他身上。方才我威胁那小子时，盯着他的手瞧；他抓得越来越紧——他会成为一个汉子；我也要叫他成为一个汉子。不过，我们不妨立刻就叫他派上点用场；给他一支桨罢。」

「好罢，」他这位新保护人答道，「他自己划船经过我们，原也好好的；让他替我们划，也划得。我们既是要回去受一种母牛般的死法、回到海拉（Hela，死神之女）的水池里去，那么越快回去越好。」

===Original===
And as the men settled themselves again to their oars, one was put into Philammon’s hand, which he managed with such strength and skill that his late tormentors, who, in spite of an occasional inclination to robbery and murder, were thoroughly good-natured, honest fellows, clapped him on the back, and praised him as heartily as they had just now heartily intended to torture him to death, and then went forward, as many of them as were not rowing, to examine the strange beast which they had just slaughtered, pawing him over from tusks to tail, putting their heads into his mouth, trying their knives on his hide, comparing him to all beasts, like and unlike, which they had ever seen, and laughing and shoving each other about with the fun and childish wonder of a party of schoolboys; till Smid, who was the wit of the party, settled the comparative anatomy of the subject for them﻿—“Valhalla! I’ve found out what he’s most like!﻿—One of those big blue plums, which gave us all the stomachache when we were encamped in the orchards above Ravenna!”

===Chinese===
众人各自回到桨位坐下，一支桨也塞进了菲拉蒙的手里。他使起桨来气力既大、手法又巧，引得方才那班折磨他的人——这班人虽说偶尔也起意抢劫杀人，骨子里却是彻底的好脾气、老实汉子——一齐拍着他的背夸他，夸得跟方才真心实意要折磨死他时一般热烈。随后，那些不用划桨的，便一窝蜂拥到船头，去细看他们刚刚宰杀的那只怪兽：他们从獠牙摸到尾巴，把脑袋塞进它嘴里，拿刀在它皮上试锋，把它跟平生见过的种种走兽比来比去，说它像这个、又不像那个，又推又搡地嬉笑哄闹，活像一群学童，满脸是稚气的惊奇；末了还是斯密德——他是众人中的活宝——替他们把这怪兽的比较解剖学一锤定音——「瓦尔哈拉！我琢磨出来它最像什么啦！——就像拉文纳（Ravenna）城外那片果园里驻营时、那些叫我们个个闹肚子的紫蓝色大李子！」

## IV / IV

### Miriam / 米利暗

===Original===
One morning in the same week, Hypatia’s favourite maid entered her chamber with a somewhat terrified face.

“The old Jewess, madam—the hag who has been watching so often lately under the wall opposite. She frightened us all out of our senses last evening by peeping in. We all said she had the evil eye, if anyone ever had—”

“Well, what of her?”

“She is below, madam, and will speak with you. Not that I care for her; I have my amulet on. I hope you have?”

“Silly girl! Those who have been initiated as I have in the mysteries of the gods, can defy spirits and command them. Do you suppose that the favourite of Pallas Athene will condescend to charms and magic? Send her up.”

The girl retreated, with a look half of awe, half of doubt, at the lofty pretensions of her mistress, and returned with old Miriam, keeping, however, prudently behind her, in order to test as little as possible the power of her own amulet by avoiding the basilisk eye which had terrified her.

Miriam came in, and advancing to the proud beauty, who remained seated, made an obeisance down to the very floor, without, however, taking her eyes for an instant off Hypatia’s face.

Her countenance was haggard and bony, with broad sharp-cut lips, stamped with a strangely mingled expression of strength and sensuality. Put the feature about her which instantly fixed Hypatia’s attention, and from which she could not in spite of herself withdraw it, was the dry, glittering, coal-black eye which glared out from underneath the gray fringe of her swarthy brows, between black locks covered with gold coins. Hypatia could look at nothing but those eyes; and she reddened, and grew all but unphilosophically angry, as she saw that the old woman intended her to look at them, and feel the strange power which she evidently wished them to exercise.

===Chinese===
同一周里的一天早晨，希帕蒂娅（Hypatia）最得意的侍女走进她的卧房，脸上带着几分惊惶。

「那个犹太老婆子，夫人——就是近来老在对面的墙根底下窥伺的那个。昨儿傍晚她探头探脑地往里张望，把我们个个吓得魂飞魄散。我们都说，若世上真有什么人不长着恶眼，便是她了——」

「嗯，她怎么了？」

「她在楼下，夫人，要见您说话呢。我倒不怕她；我戴着护身符呢。但愿您也戴着？」

「傻丫头！像我这样在众神的奥秘里受过启蒙的人，能够蔑视群魔、号令群魔。你以为帕拉斯·雅典娜（Pallas Athene）的宠儿，会降格去信什么符咒与巫术么？叫她上来。」

那侍女退了下去，对女主人这般自负的口气，半是敬畏、半是怀疑；她把老米利暗（Miriam）领了进来，自己却谨慎地躲在老人身后——为的是尽量少拿自己那枚护身符去冒险，能躲开那双吓得她的蛇怪眼便躲开。

米利暗走了进来，径直走到那位端坐不动的傲慢美人跟前，深深行了一个大礼，直弯到地板上；然而她的眼却一刻也不曾离开过希帕蒂娅的脸。

她的面容枯瘦嶙峋，阔而薄削的嘴唇上，印着一种力量与肉欲奇妙交织的神情。可那一点——那一点登时攫住希帕蒂娅注意、叫她身不由己无法移开的——却是那双干燥、灼灼发亮、乌黑如炭的眼睛，从她那黝黑眉弓下灰白的眉穗之间、从覆着金币的黑发之间瞪将出来。希帕蒂娅除了那双眼，什么也看不见了；她涨红了脸，几乎要一反其哲人的镇定而动起怒来——因为她看得出来，这老婆子是故意要她看着这双眼，要她感受这双眼中显然有意施展的那股古怪力量。

===Original===
After a moment’s silence, Miriam drew a letter from her bosom, and with a second low obeisance presented it.

“From whom is this?”

“Perhaps the letter itself will tell the beautiful lady, the fortunate lady, the discerning lady,” answered she, in a fawning, wheedling tone. “How should a poor old Jewess know great folks’ secrets?”

“Great folks?—”

Hypatia looked at the seal which fixed a silk cord round the letter. It was Orestes’; and so was the handwriting.… Strange that he should have chosen such a messenger! What message could it be which required such secrecy?

She clapped her hands for the maid. “Let this woman wait in the anteroom.” Miriam glided out backwards, bowing as she went. As Hypatia looked up over the letter to see whether she was alone, she caught a last glance of that eye still fixed upon her, and an expression in Miriam’s face which made her, she knew not why, shudder and turn chill.

“Foolish that I am! What can that witch be to me? But now for the letter.”

“To the most noble and most beautiful, the mistress of philosophy, beloved of Athene, her pupil and slave sends greeting.…”

“My slave! and no name mentioned!”

===Chinese===
默然片刻之后，米利暗从怀中抽出一封信，又深施一礼，呈了上来。

「这是谁送来的？」

「这封信本身，大约会对那位美丽的夫人、有福的夫人、明察的夫人说明白罢，」她用一种谄媚讨好的腔调答道。「一个可怜的犹太老婆子，哪里晓得大人物们的秘密呢？」

「大人物？——」

希帕蒂娅看了看那枚把一根丝绳固定在信上的火漆印。那是俄瑞斯忒斯（Orestes）的印章；字迹也是他的。……真奇怪，他竟挑了这么一个信使！这会是怎样一封需要如此隐秘的信呢？

她拍了拍手唤侍女来。「让这女人在前厅等候。」米利暗倒退着滑了出去，一路行礼。希帕蒂娅从信上抬起眼，想看看左右是否无人，恰好又瞥见那双眼仍死死盯着自己，米利暗脸上那副神情使她——她说不清为什么——打了个寒噤，浑身发凉。

「我这傻瓜！那巫婆与我有什么相干？还是看信罢。」

「致最尊贵、最美丽的、哲学之女主、雅典娜之所爱——她的学生与奴仆敬上问候。……」

「我的奴仆！竟然不署名！」

===Original===
“There are those who consider that the favourite hen of Honorius, which bears the name of the Imperial City, would thrive better under a new feeder; and the Count of Africa has been despatched by himself and by the immortal gods to superintend for the present the poultry-yard of the Caesars—at least during the absence of Adolf and Placidia. There are those also who consider that in his absence the Numidian lion might be prevailed on to become the yokefellow of the Egyptian crocodile; and a farm which, ploughed by such a pair, should extend from the upper cataract to the Pillars of Hercules, might have charms even for a philosopher. But while the ploughman is without a nymph, Arcadia is imperfect. What were Dionusos without his Ariadne, Ares without Aphrodite, Zeus without Hera? Even Artemis has her Endymion; Athene alone remains unwedded; but only because Hephaestus was too rough a wooer. Such is not he who now offers to the representative of Athene the opportunity of sharing that which may be with the help of her wisdom, which without her is impossible. *Φωνᾶντα συνέτοισιν.* Shall Eros, invincible for ages, be balked at last of the noblest game against which he ever drew his bow?”.…

If Hypatia’s colour had faded a moment before under the withering glance of the old Jewess, it rose again swiftly enough, as she read line after line of this strange epistle; till at last, crushing it together in her hand, she rose and hurried into the adjoining library, where Theon sat over his books.

“Father, do you know anything of this? Look what Orestes has dared to send me by the hands of some base Jewish witch!”—And she spread the letter before him, and stood impatient, her whole figure dilated with pride and anger, as the old man read it slowly and carefully, and then looked up, apparently not ill pleased with the contents.

“What, father?” asked she, half reproachfully. “Do not you, too, feel the insult which has been put upon your daughter?”

“My dear child,” with a puzzled look, “do you not see that he offers you—”

===Chinese===
「有人说，霍诺留（Honorius）皇帝所养、那以帝国都城为名的心爱母鸡，换一个喂养人会更肥壮些；而那位非洲伯爵（the Count of Africa）既蒙他本人、又蒙不朽众神之差遣，已前去暂且照管凯撒们的家禽棚——至少在阿道夫（Adolf）与普拉西迪娅（Placidia）不在的时候。也有人以为，趁他不在，那只努米底亚的狮子或许可以说动，与那埃及的鳄鱼共挽一犁；由这样一对耕出来的田庄，从上游的大瀑布一直延展到赫拉克勒斯之柱（the Pillars of Hercules），便是对于一个哲学家，也不无诱人之处。然而耕地的人若无山林仙女相随，那田园便不算圆满。狄俄倪索斯（Dionusos）若无他的阿里阿德涅（Ariadne）、阿瑞斯（Ares）若无阿佛洛狄忒（Aphrodite）、宙斯（Zeus）若无赫拉（Hera），成何体统？便是阿尔忒弥斯（Artemis）也有她的恩底弥翁（Endymion）；唯独雅典娜终身不嫁——可那也只是因为赫淮斯托斯（Hephaestus）求起婚来太过粗鲁。如今向雅典娜的代表之人献上机会的，却并非这样一位求婚者；他邀她共享之事，有她的智慧便可成就，没有她便绝无可能。*Φωνᾶντα συνέτοισιν.*（有智之士自能领悟。）那战无不胜了千百年的厄洛斯（Eros），难道到头来竟要在他所曾张弓相向的最尊贵的猎物前，一无所获么？」……

方才在犹太老婆子那蚀人的一瞥之下，希帕蒂娅脸上的血色若是褪去了一阵，此刻读着这封古怪信札一行又一行，那血色便又飞快地涌了上来；末了，她把信攥在手里揉成一团，起身冲进相连的图书室，提昂（Theon）正坐在那儿对着他的书。

「父亲，您可知这事？您看俄瑞斯忒斯竟敢托一个下贱的犹太巫婆给我送来什么！」——她把信摊在他面前，不耐烦地站着，整个身形因骄傲与愤怒而挺得高高的；老人慢慢地、仔细地读着，读罢抬头，看神情对此内容竟颇为满意。

「怎么，父亲？」她半带责备地问。「难道连您也体会不到加在您女儿身上的这份侮辱么？」

「我亲爱的孩子，」他一脸困惑，「你没看出来他这是要给你——」

===Original===
“I know what he offers me, father. The Empire of Africa.… I am to descend from the mountain heights of science, from the contemplation of the unchangeable and ineffable glories, into the foul fields and farmyards of earthly practical life, and become a drudge among political chicanery, and the petty ambitions, and sins, and falsehoods of the earthly herd.… And the price which he offers me—me, the stainless—me, the virgin—me, the untamed—is—his hand! Pallas Athene! dost thou not blush with thy child?”

“But, my child—my child—an empire—”

“Would the empire of the world restore my lost self-respect—my just pride? Would it save my cheek from blushes every time I recollected that I bore the hateful and degrading name of ‘wife’?—The property, the puppet of a man—submitting to his pleasure—bearing his children—wearing myself out with all the nauseous cares of wifehood—no longer able to glory in myself, pure and self-sustained, but forced by day and night to recollect that my very beauty is no longer the sacrament of Athene’s love for me, but the plaything of a man;—and such a man as that! Luxurious, frivolous, heartless—courting my society, as he has done for years, only to pick up and turn to his own base earthly uses the scraps which fall from the festal table of the gods! I have encouraged him too much—vain fool that I have been! No, I wrong myself! It was only—I thought—I thought that by his being seen at our doors, the cause of the immortal gods would gain honour and strength in the eyes of the multitude.… I have tried to feed the altars of heaven with earthly fuel.… And this is my just reward! I will write to him this moment—return by the fitting messenger which he has sent, insult for insult!”

“In the name of Heaven, my daughter!—for your father’s sake!—for my sake! Hypatia!—my pride, my joy, my only hope!—have pity on my gray hairs!”

And the poor old man flung himself at her feet, and clasped her knees imploringly.

===Chinese===
「我知道他给我什么，父亲。给我非洲的帝位。……要我从一个科学的高峰之巅、从对那不变、不可言说的荣耀的凝思冥想之中，降落到尘世实务那污秽的田地与家禽棚里去，去做政治倾轧的苦工，去钻营于尘世芸芸众生那点渺小的野心、罪恶与谎言之间。……而他给我的代价——给我这纤尘不染的、给我这童贞的、给我这桀骜不驯的——竟是——他的一只手！帕拉斯·雅典娜！你不为你的孩子脸红么？」

「可是，我的孩子——我的孩子——一个帝国——」

「便是全世界的帝国，能找回我失去的自尊——我那理所应当的骄傲么？能使我每逢想起自己担着『妻子』这个可憎可鄙的名头时，脸颊不再发烫么？——做一个人的财产、一个人的玩偶——任他取乐——为他生儿育女——为妻的种种令人作呕的操劳把我的心血耗干——再也不能以一己之纯洁、自足而自傲，倒要日夜被迫想起：我这容颜再不是雅典娜爱我的圣礼，不过是男人手里的玩物；——何况是这样一个男人！奢靡、浮薄、无心肝——他多年来逢迎我的交往，不过是捡拾众神宴席上落下的残羹冷炙，拿去为他尘世的下贱用途罢了！我太纵容他了——我这个虚荣的傻瓜！不，我冤枉了自己！我不过是——我以为——我以为他常在我们门前露面，不朽众神的事业在众人眼中便多了几分体面与力量罢了。……我这是想拿尘世的柴薪去供奉天上的祭坛。……而这便是我应得的报答！我此刻便要回他一封信——就用他派来的那位合宜的信使，把侮辱原样奉还！」

「看在老天份上，我的女儿！——看在你父亲的份上！——看在我的份上！希帕蒂娅！——我的骄傲、我的欢乐、我唯一的盼头！——可怜可怜我这一头白发罢！」

可怜的老人竟扑到她脚下，抱住她的双膝苦苦哀求。

===Original===
Tenderly she lifted him up, and wound her long arms round him, and laid his head on her white shoulder, and her tears fell fast upon his gray hair; but her lip was firm and determined.

“Think of my pride—my glory in your glory; think of me.… Not for myself! You know I never cared for myself!” sobbed out the old man. “But to die seeing you empress!”

“Unless I died first in child bed, father, as many a woman dies who is weak enough to become a slave, and submit to tortures only fit for slaves.”

“But—but—” said the old man, racking his bewildered brains for some argument far enough removed from nature and common sense to have an effect on the beautiful fanatic—“but the cause of the gods! What you might do for it!… Remember Julian!”

Hypatia’s arms dropped suddenly. Yes; it was true! The thought flashed across her mind with mingled delight and terror.… Visions of her childhood rose swift and thick—temples—sacrifices—priesthoods—colleges—museums! What might she not do? What might she not make Africa? Give her ten years of power, and the hated name of Christian might be forgotten, and Athene Polias, colossal in ivory and gold, watching in calm triumph over the harbours of a heathen Alexandria.… But the price!

And she hid her face in her hands, and bursting into bitter tears, walked slowly away into her own chamber, her whole body convulsed with the internal struggle.

===Chinese===
她温柔地扶起他，把长长的双臂缠住他，把他的头按在自己洁白的肩上，眼泪扑簌簌地落在他灰白的头发上；可她的嘴唇却抿得紧、抿得坚决。

「想想我的骄傲——我以你的荣耀为荣耀；想想我吧。……不是为我自己！你知道我从不为自己打算的！」老人抽抽搭搭地说。「可我死前要看见你做皇后啊！」

「除非我先死在产床上，父亲——多少软弱到甘心去做奴隶、去受那只有奴隶才配受的苦刑的女人，都是那样死的。」

「可是——可是——」老人说着，绞尽脑汁要寻一个论据，那论据须离天理人情、离常识都足够远，方能打动这位美丽的狂徒——「可是众神的事业呢！你能为它做多少事啊！……想想尤利安（Julian）罢！」

希帕蒂娅的双臂蓦地垂了下来。是的；这是真的！这念头闪过她心头，伴着交杂的狂喜与恐惧。……童年时的一幕幕景象又密又急地涌上心头——神庙——祭祀——祭司——学院——博物馆！她有什么做不到的？她有什么不能把非洲改成的样？给她十年的权柄，那可憎的『基督徒』之名或许便被人遗忘了，而雅典娜·波利亚斯（Athene Polias），以象牙与黄金铸成巨像，将在平静的凯旋之中，俯瞰着异教的亚历山大城的诸港口。……可那代价呢！

她把脸埋进双手里，迸出苦涩的泪，缓缓走回自己的卧房，全身因内心的交战而阵阵抽搐。

===Original===
The old man looked after her, anxiously and perplexed, and then followed, hesitating. She was sitting at the table, her face buried in her hands. He did not dare to disturb her. In addition to all the affection, the wisdom, the glorious beauty, on which his whole heart fed day by day, he believed her to be the possessor of those supernatural powers and favours to which she so boldly laid claim. And he stood watching her in the doorway, praying in his heart to all gods and demons, principalities and powers, from Athene down to his daughter’s guardian spirit, to move a determination which he was too weak to gainsay, and yet too rational to approve.

At last the struggle was over, and she looked up, clear, calm, and glorious again.

“It shall be. For the sake of the immortal gods—for the sake of art, and science, and learning, and philosophy.… It shall be. If the gods demand a victim, here am I. If a second time in the history of the ages the Grecian fleet cannot sail forth, conquering and civilising, without the sacrifice of a virgin, I give my throat to the knife. Father, call me no more Hypatia: call me Iphigenia!”

“And me Agamemnon?” asked the old man, attempting a faint jest through his tears of joy. “I daresay you think me a very cruel father; but—”

“Spare me, father—I have spared you.”

And she began to write her answer.

===Chinese===
老人忧心忡忡、满头雾水地望着她的背影，迟疑着跟了上去。她正坐在桌前，脸埋在手里。他不敢惊动她。除了那份亲情、那份智慧、那份他整颗心日日所寄的灿烂的美之外，他还深信她确确实实拥有她那样大胆地声称自己拥有的超自然的能力与恩宠。他便站在门口守着她，心里向着一切神魔、一切有位与掌权的——从雅典娜直到他女儿的守护灵——祷告，求他们去打动那一项他太软弱而不敢反驳、却又太清醒而不便附和的决心。

终于，这场交战结束了，她抬起头来，又是那般澄明、镇定、光彩照人了。

「就这么定了。为了不朽众神的缘故——为了艺术、科学、学问与哲学的缘故。……就这么定了。众神若要一个祭品，我便是。倘若在千古的史上这是第二回：希腊的舰队若不献上一个少女为祭，便无法扬帆出征、去征服、去开化——那么我把我的咽喉送上去挨刀罢。父亲，不要再叫我希帕蒂娅：叫我伊菲革涅亚（Iphigenia）罢！」

「那便叫我阿伽门农（Agamemnon）么？」老人问道，想从欢喜的眼泪里挤出一个勉强的笑话来。「你一定觉得我是个十分狠心的父亲罢；可是——」

「饶了我罢，父亲——我已经饶过您了。」

她便动手写回信。

===Original===
“I have accepted his offer—conditionally, that is. And on whether he have courage or not to fulfil that condition depends—Do not ask me what it is. While Cyril is leader of the Christian mob, it may be safer for you, my father, that you should be able to deny all knowledge of my answer. Be content. I have said this much—that if he will do as I would have him do, I will do as you would have me do.”

“Have you not been too rash? Have you not demanded of him something which, for the sake of public opinion, he dare not grant openly, and yet which he may allow you to do for yourself when once—”

“I have. If I am to be a victim, the sacrificing priest shall at least be a man, and not a coward and a timeserver. If he believes this Christian faith, let him defend it against me; for either it or I shall perish. If he does not—as he does not—let him give up living in a lie, and taking on his lips blasphemies against the immortals, from which his heart and reason revolt!”

And she clapped her hands again for the maidservant, gave her the letter silently, shut the doors of her chamber, and tried to resume her Commentary on Plotinus. Alas! what were all the wire-drawn dreams of metaphysics to her in that real and human struggle of the heart? What availed it to define the process by which individual souls emanated from the universal one, while her own soul had, singly and on its own responsibility, to decide so terrible an act of will? or to write fine words with pen and ink about the immutability of the supreme Reason, while her own reason was left there to struggle for its life amid a roaring shoreless waste of doubts and darkness? Oh, how grand, and clear, and logical it had all looked half an hour ago! And how irrefragably she had been deducing from it all, syllogism after syllogism, the nonexistence of evil!—how it was but a lower form of good, one of the countless products of the one great all-pervading mind which could not err or change, only so strange and recondite in its form as to excite antipathy in all minds but that of the philosopher, who learnt to see the stem which connected the apparently bitter fruit with the perfect root from whence it sprang. Could she see the stem there?—the connection between the pure and supreme Reason, and the hideous caresses of the debauched and cowardly Orestes? was not that evil pure, unadulterate with any vein of good, past, present, or future?…

===Chinese===
「我答应了他——是有条件地答应。至于他有没有胆子去履行那条件——就不要问我是什么条件了。区利罗（Cyril）如今既是那班基督徒暴民的领袖，那么您——我的父亲——若能全然否认对我的回信知情，于您或许更安全。您便知足罢。我所能说的只是——他若肯照我所愿的去做，我便照您所愿的去做。」

「你不是太莽撞了么？你向他开的，岂不是那样一个条件——碍于舆论，他不敢公然应允，可一旦——一旦如何，他或可容你自己去做？」

「我便是。我若要做祭品，那行祭的祭司至少得是个男人，不可是个懦夫与骑墙之徒。他若信这基督的道，便叫他来向我辩一辩罢；因为不是这道亡、便是我亡。他若不信——他确实不信——便叫他别再活在一个谎言里，别再口里说着那亵渎众神的话，而他的心与理智却对那些话厌恶至极！」

她又拍了拍手唤来侍女，默默地把信交给她，关上卧房的门，试着接着写她那部《波菲利（Plotinus）注疏》。可叹！在这般真实而属乎人心的交战之中，那些形而上学的玄想梦呓，于她又算得了什么？去界定个别灵魂如何从那太一之中流溢而出，于她又有什么用处——当她自己的灵魂，正独自一人、独自担起全责，要去定夺这样一桩可怕的意志之举？或是用笔墨去写那些关于『至高理性之不变』的漂亮字眼，于她又有什么用——当她自己的理性正被抛在那儿、在一片咆哮的无涯的疑虑与黑暗之海里为求活命而苦挣？唉，半个时辰之前，这一切显得何等恢宏、何等澄明、何等合乎逻辑！而她又何等坚不可摧地从这一切之中，一个三段论接一个三段论地，推出『恶之不存在』的结论！——推出恶不过是善的较低形式，是那一个伟大、无所不在、不能出错也不能改变的心智所生出的无数产物之一，只不过其形式太过古怪、太过深奥，故而除哲学家之外、一切心智见之皆生反感；而那哲学家却学着去看那根茎——它把那看来苦涩的果子，连到它所由生的那完美的根上。这一回她能看见那根茎么？——能看见那纯粹至高的理性，与那荒淫懦弱的俄瑞斯忒斯那可憎的爱抚之间，有什么相连之处？那岂不是纯粹的恶——不掺一丝善的脉络，过去、现在、将来都不掺？……

===Original===
True;—she might keep her spirit pure amid it all; she might sacrifice the base body, and ennoble the soul by the self-sacrifice.… And yet, would not that increase the horror, the agony, the evil of it—to her, at least, most real evil, not to be explained away—and yet the gods required it? Were they just, merciful in that? Was it like them, to torture her, their last unshaken votary? Did they require it? Was it not required of them by some higher power, of whom they were only the emanations, the tools, the puppets?—and required of that higher power by some still higher one—some nameless, absolute destiny of which Orestes and she, and all heaven and earth, were but the victims, dragged along in an inevitable vortex, helpless, hopeless, toward that for which each was meant?—And she was meant for this! The thought was unbearable; it turned her giddy. No! she would not! She would rebel! Like Prometheus, she would dare destiny, and brave its worst! And she sprang up to recall the letter.… Miriam was gone; and she threw herself on the floor, and wept bitterly.

And her peace of mind would certainly not have been improved, could she have seen old Miriam hurry home with her letter to a dingy house in the Jews’ quarter, where it was unsealed, read, and sealed up again with such marvellous skill, that no eye could have detected the change; and finally, still less would she have been comforted could she have heard the conversation which was going on in a summer-room of Orestes’ palace, between that illustrious statesman and Raphael Aben-Ezra, who were lying on two divans opposite each other, whiling away, by a throw or two of dice, the anxious moments which delayed her answer.

===Chinese===
诚然；——她尽可以在这其中守住一颗洁净的心；她尽可以献上那卑贱的肉身，以这舍己之举使灵魂升华。……然而，那岂不更要加重其中的可怖、痛楚、其中的恶——于她至少是再真实不过、再无法用巧辩化解的恶——可众神却偏偏要它？他们在此事上算得公义、算得慈悲么？他们忍心这样折磨她——他们最后一个未曾动摇的信徒？当真是他们要它么？岂不是某个更高的权能向他们要的——而他们不过是那权能的流溢、工具、傀儡？——又是某个还要高的权能向那个更高的权能要的——某个无名的、绝对的命运，俄瑞斯忒斯与她、以及天地间一切，都不过是它的牺牲，被裹在一个无可挽回的漩涡里，无助无望地，被拖向各自注定要去的地方？——而她注定要去的，竟是这个！这念头教人受不了；她直发晕。不！她不愿！她要反叛！她要像普罗米修斯（Prometheus）一样，去挑衅命运，去顶住它最恶的一击！她纵身而起，要去追回那封信。……米利暗早已去了；她扑倒在地上，痛哭失声。

而倘若她能看见老米利暗如何带着她的信匆匆赶回犹太区一间昏暗的屋子，那信在那里被拆开、被读过、又被以神乎其技的手法重新封好，神到任何一双眼睛都看不出破绽——那她的心境定然不会更好；而倘若她能听见俄瑞斯忒斯府上一间夏堂里正在进行的对话，她就更加不得安慰了：那位显赫的政治家与拉斐尔·阿本-以斯拉（Raphael Aben-Ezra）正对躺在两张长榻上，用掷一回两回骰子的法子，消磨着等候她回音时那焦灼的片刻。

===Original===
“Trays again! The devil is in you, Raphael!”

“I always thought he was,” answered Raphael, sweeping up the gold pieces.…

“When will that old witch be back?”

“When she has read through your letter and Hypatia’s answer.”

“Read them?”

“Of course. You don’t fancy she is going to be fool enough to carry a message without knowing what it is? Don’t be angry; she won’t tell. She would give one of those two grave-lights there, which she calls her eyes, to see the thing prosper.”

“Why?”

“Your excellency will know when the letter comes. Here she is; I hear steps in the cloister. Now, one bet before they enter. I give you two to one she asks you to turn pagan.”

“What in? Negro-boys?”

“Anything you like.”

“Taken. Come in, slaves!”

And Hypocorisma entered, pouting.

“That Jewish fury is outside with a letter, and has the impudence to say she won’t let me bring it in!”

“Bring her in then. Quick!”

“I wonder what I am here for, if people have secrets that I am not to know,” grumbled the spoilt youth.

“Do you want a blue ribbon round those white sides of yours, you monkey?” answered Orestes. “Because, if you do, the hippopotamus hide hangs ready outside.”

“Let us make him kneel down here for a couple of hours, and use him as a dice-board,” said Raphael, “as you used to do to the girls in Armenia.”

“Ah, you recollect that?—and how the barbarian papas used to grumble, till I had to crucify one or two, eh? That was something like life! I love those out-of-the-way stations, where nobody asks questions: but here one might as well live among the monks in Nitria. Here comes Canidia! Ah, the answer? Hand it here, my queen of go-betweens!”

===Chinese===
「又掷出三个三！你身上有鬼，拉斐尔！」

「我也一向这么觉得，」拉斐尔答道，把那些金币一把扫了过来。……

「那老巫婆什么时候回来？」

「等她把你的信、还有希帕蒂娅的回信从头到尾读完的时候。」

「读它们？」

「当然。你总不至于以为，她会蠢到替人送信却不知信里写的是什么？别动怒；她不会说出去的。她情愿拿她那两盏坟前的灯——也就是她叫做眼睛的那两盏——里的任何一盏，来看这事成事。」

「为什么？」

「大人等信到了便知。她来了；我听见回廊里有脚步声。来，他们进来之前咱们再赌一回。我以二对一跟你打赌：她要你改宗异教。」

「赌什么？黑奴男孩？」

「随你赌什么。」

「一言为定。进来，奴才们！」

许珀科里斯玛（Hypocorisma）噘着嘴走了进来。

「那犹太母老虎在外面拿着一封信，竟有脸说，不让我把它拿进来！」

「那就叫她进来。快！」

「我倒不懂，人家的事都有我不该知道的秘密，那还要我在这屋里做什么？」这被宠坏的少年嘟囔着。

「你想叫你那白白的两肋上绑一条蓝缎带么，你这只猴子？」俄瑞斯忒斯答道。「因为你要是想，河马皮的鞭子正挂在外面候着呢。」

「咱们不如叫他在这儿跪上两个钟头，拿他的背当骰子盘使，」拉斐尔说，「就像你从前在亚美尼亚（Armenia）对那些女孩子干的那样。」

「啊，你还记得那个？——还有那些蛮族的『爸爸』们怎样嘟嘟囔囔，直到我不得不把一两个钉上十字架，呃？那才叫日子！我就爱那些天高皇帝远的任所，那儿没人多问一句：可在这儿住着，简直跟在尼特拉（Nitria）那群修士里头差不多。卡尼迪娅（Canidia）来啦！啊，回信？拿来罢，我的牵线王后！」

===Original===
Orestes read it—and his countenance fell.

“I have won?”

“Out of the room, slaves! and no listening!”

“I have won then?”

Orestes tossed the letter across to him, and Raphael read—

“The immortal gods accept no divided worship; and he who would command the counsels of their prophetess must remember that they will vouchsafe to her no illumination till their lost honours be restored. If he who aspires to be the lord of Africa dare trample on the hateful cross, and restore the Caesareum to those for whose worship it was built—if he dare proclaim aloud with his lips, and in his deeds, that contempt for novel and barbarous superstitions, which his taste and reason have already taught him, then he would prove himself one with whom it were a glory to labour, to dare, to die in a great cause. But till then—”

And so the letter ended.

“What am I to do?”

“Take her at her word.”

“Good heavens! I shall be excommunicated! And—and—what is to become of my soul?”

“What will become of it in any case, my most excellent lord?” answered Raphael blandly.

“You mean—I know what you cursed Jews think will happen to everyone but yourselves. But what would the world say? I an apostate! And in the face of Cyril and the populace! I daren’t, I tell you!”

“No one asked your excellency to apostatise.”

“Why, what? What did you say just now?”

“I asked you to promise. It will not be the first time that promises before marriage have not exactly coincided with performance afterwards.”

===Chinese===
俄瑞斯忒斯读着——脸色便沉了下来。

「我赢了？」

「出去，奴才们！不准偷听！」

「那我赢了？」

俄瑞斯忒斯把信甩给他，拉斐尔念道——

「不朽众神不受二主分立之敬；凡欲得他们女先知之指授者，须记得：众神失去的尊荣未得恢复之前，绝不会赐她任何启迪。那志在为非洲之主的人，若是敢践踏那可憎的十字架，把凯撒里乌姆（the Caesareum）归还给那本为他们的敬拜而建此庙的人——若是敢口里说出来、行动上做出来，他那品味与理智早已教他学会的、对这新奇而野蛮的迷信之鄙夷——他便证明了自己是这样一个人：与他共事，与他一同冒险，与他一同为一桩大业而死，都是荣耀。但在此之前——」

信便到此为止。

「我该怎么办？」

「就依她的话办。」

「老天！我要被逐出教会的！而且——而且——我的灵魂怎么办？」

「无论如何您的灵魂又当如何呢，我至为卓越的大人？」拉斐尔温文地答道。

「你是说——你们这些该死的犹太人怎样想，我全知道，你们以为除你们之外人人如此。可世人会怎样说？我成了叛教者！而且是在区利罗和那群暴民面前！我不敢，我跟你说！」

「没有人请大人叛教啊。」

「咦，什么？你刚才说什么来着？」

「我请的是您许个诺。婚前的承诺与婚后并不尽然相符，这又不是头一遭了。」

===Original===
“I daren’t—that is, I won’t promise. I believe, now, this is some trap of your Jewish intrigue, just to make me commit myself against those Christians, whom you hate.”

“I assure you, I despise all mankind far too profoundly to hate them. How disinterested my advice was when I proposed this match to you, you never will know; indeed, it would be boastful in me to tell you. But really you must make a little sacrifice to win this foolish girl. With all the depth and daring of her intellect to help you, you might be a match for Romans, Byzantines, and Goths at once. And as for beauty—why, there is one dimple inside that wrist, just at the setting on of the sweet little hand, worth all the other flesh and blood in Alexandria.”

“By Jove! you admire her so much, I suspect you must be in love with her yourself. Why don’t you marry her? I’ll make you my prime minister, and then we shall have the use of her wits without the trouble of her fancies. By the twelve Gods! If you marry her and help me, I’ll make you what you like!”

Raphael rose and bowed to the earth.

“Your serene high-mightiness overwhelms me. But I assure you, that never having as yet cared for anyone’s interest but my own, I could not be expected, at my time of life, to devote myself to that of another, even though it were to yours.”

“Candid!”

“Exactly so; and moreover, whosoever I may marry, will be practically, as well as theoretically, my private and peculiar property.… You comprehend.”

“Candid again.”

“Exactly so; and waiving the third argument, that she probably might not choose to marry me, I beg to remark that it would not be proper to allow the world to say, that I, the subject, had a wiser and fairer wife than you, the ruler; especially a wife who had already refused that ruler’s complimentary offer.”

===Chinese===
「我不敢——我是说，我不愿许这个诺。我如今想想，这必是你们犹太人钩心斗角的什么圈套，无非是要哄着我表明立场、去与那些基督徒作对——你们恨透了那些基督徒。」

「我敢担保，我对全人类鄙视之深，远到不屑于去恨他们。当初我向您提这门亲事时，我的主意是何等无私，您永远也不会知道；说真的，由我来讲给您听，倒像是在自夸了。可您总得稍微做点牺牲，才能赢得这个傻丫头啊。有她那份心思的深沉与胆识来帮您，您便足以同时对付罗马人、拜占庭人（Byzantines）与哥特人（Goths）。至于美嘛——嘿，她那只手腕内侧、恰在那只纤纤小手接下去的地方，有一个酒窝，抵得上亚历山大城里旁人所有的血肉。」

「凭朱庇特（Jove）起誓！你这样爱慕她，我疑心你自己必是爱上她了。你何不娶她？我封你做我的首相，这样咱们既能用她的脑子，又不必招惹她的脾气。凭十二大神起誓！你若娶了她、又肯帮我，你要什么我便封你做什么！」

拉斐尔起身，深深一揖到地。

「您这般威严尊贵的殿下，真叫小人消受不起。可我敢说，我至今除自己的利益外，从未关心过任何人的利益；要我到了这把年纪再去为另一个人尽心——哪怕是为您——原也不该指望了。」

「坦白！」

「正是；况且，我无论娶了谁，她在实际上、也如同在理论上一样，将是我私有的、独一无二的财产。……您明白的。」

「又一句坦白。」

「正是；此外且撇开第三个理由不论——她大抵不肯嫁我——我倒要提一句：若任世人说，我这个臣子之妻，竟比您这位为君者的妻更聪明、更美，那可不大合适；何况这位夫人已经回绝过那位为君者的殷勤相聘了。」

===Original===
“By Jove! and she has refused me in good earnest! I’ll make her repent it! I was a fool to ask her at all! What’s the use of having guards, if one can’t compel what one wants? If fair means can’t do it, foul shall! I’ll send for her this moment!”

“Most illustrious majesty—it will not succeed. You do not know that woman’s determination. Scourges and red-hot pincers will not shake her, alive; and dead, she will be of no use whatsoever to you, while she will be of great use to Cyril.”

“How?”

“He will be most happy to make the whole story a handle against you, give out that she died a virgin-martyr, in defence of the most holy catholic and apostolic faith, get miracles worked at her tomb, and pull your palace about your ears on the strength thereof.”

“Cyril will hear of it anyhow: that’s another dilemma into which you have brought me, you intriguing rascal! Why, this girl will be boasting all over Alexandria that I have offered her marriage, and that she has done herself the honour to refuse me!”

“She will be much too wise to do anything of the kind; she has sense enough to know that if she did so, you would inform a Christian populace what conditions she offered you, and, with all her contempt for the burden of the flesh, she has no mind to be lightened of that pretty load by being torn in pieces by Christian monks; a very probable ending for her in any case, as she herself, in her melancholy moods, confesses!”

===Chinese===
「凭朱庇特起誓！她竟当真拒绝了我！我要叫她后悔莫及！我当初开口去求她，真是蠢透了！养这些卫队有什么用，若不能强迫所要的东西到手？软的不成，便来硬的！我这就叫人去把她传来！」

「至为显赫的陛下——这可不成。您不知道那女人的决心。鞭子、烧红的铁钳，都休想叫活着的她动一动；而她若死了，对您便一无所用，反倒大有利于区利罗。」

「怎么说？」

「他会十分乐意把整件事当成一把对付您的把柄，四处宣扬她是为护卫至圣至公、使徒所传之信仰而死的童贞殉道者，在她的坟上行出种种神迹，再据此把您的府邸拆到您头上来。」

「无论如何区利罗都会听说的：这又是你把我推进的一个两难，你这诡计多端的坏胚！嗳呀，这丫头要在亚历山大城四处夸口，说我曾向她求婚，而她竟赏脸拒绝了我！」

「她绝顶聪明，断不至做这种事；她有那个脑子，知道她若这样做，您便会把当初她开出的条件告诉那群基督徒暴民——她虽则口口声声轻贱『肉身之累』，可也没意思让基督徒的修士们把她这副漂亮的累赘撕成碎片；无论如何，这结局于她原是大有可能的，她自己心情低落时也这般承认！」

===Original===
“What will you have me do then?”

“Simply nothing. Let the prophetic spirit go out of her, as it will, in a day or two, and then—I know nothing of human nature, if she does not bate a little of her own price. Depend upon it, for all her ineffabilities, and impassibilities, and all the rest of the seventh-heaven moonshine at which we play here in Alexandria, a throne is far too pretty a bait for even Hypatia the pythoness to refuse. Leave well alone is a good rule, but leave ill alone is a better. So now another bet before we part, and this time three to one. Do nothing either way, and she sends to you of her own accord before a month is out. In Caucasian mules? Done? Be it so.”

“Well, you are the most charming counsellor for a poor perplexed devil of a prefect! If I had but a private fortune like you, I could just take the money, and let the work do itself.”

“Which is the true method of successful government. Your slave bids you farewell. Do not forget our bet. You dine with me tomorrow?”

And Raphael bowed himself out.

===Chinese===
「那你要我怎么办呢？」

「什么都不办。让她那点先知的神气，照它自己那样，过一两日便散去；到那时——若她不自降身价，那我便算不懂人情了。您放心好啦，任她怎样不可言说、怎样无动于中，任她在亚历山大城里玩的那套第七重天的玄虚把戏再怎么花哨——一顶宝座，毕竟是太美的诱饵，便是希帕蒂娅这位皮同女祭司也拒之不得。『顺境莫搅』是一条好规矩，『逆境莫搅』则更好。那么临别前咱们再赌最后一回，这回三对一。两边都别动手，不出一个月，她自会差人来找您。赌高加索（Caucasian）骡子？一言为定？便这么着罢。」

「嘿，对一个倒霉、左右为难的总督来说，你可真是个最讨人喜欢的谋士！我要是有你那样一份私产，便可只管收钱，让事情自己去成了。」

「这方是治国致治之正道。小人与您告辞。可别忘了咱们的赌注。明日您来我处赴宴？」

拉斐尔一揖而退。

===Original===
As he left the prefect’s door, he saw Miriam on the opposite side of the street, evidently watching for him. As soon as she saw him, she held on her own side, without appearing to notice him, till he turned a corner, and then crossing, caught him eagerly by the arm.

“Does the fool dare?”

“Who dare what?”

“You know what I mean. Do you suppose old Miriam carries letters without taking care to know what is inside them? Will he apostatise? Tell me. I am secret as the grave!”

“The fool has found an old worm-eaten rag of conscience somewhere in the corner of his heart, and dare not.”

“Curse the coward! And such a plot as I had laid! I would have swept every Christian dog out of Africa within the year. What is the man afraid of?”

“Hellfire.”

“Why, he will go there in any case, the accursed Gentile!”

“So I hinted to him, as delicately as I could; but, like the rest of the world, he had a sort of partiality for getting thither by his own road.”

“Coward! And whom shall I get now? Oh, if that Pelagia had as much cunning in her whole body as Hypatia has in her little finger, I’d seat her and her Goth upon the throne of the Caesars. But—”

“But she has five senses, and just enough wit to use them, eh?”

“Don’t laugh at her for that, the darling! I do delight in her, after all. It warms even my old blood to see how thoroughly she knows her business, and how she enjoys it, like a true daughter of Eve.”

“She has been your most successful pupil, certainly, mother. You may well be proud of her.”

===Chinese===
他刚走出总督府门，便看见街对面米利暗分明是在等他。她一见他，便装作不曾留意他，只在自己那一侧走着，等他拐了个弯，她才穿过街来，急切地一把抓住他的胳膊。

「那蠢货敢不敢？」

「谁敢什么？」

「你懂我说的是什么。你以为老米利暗替人送信，会不弄清楚信里写的什么？他肯不肯叛教？告诉我。我守口如瓶，如坟墓一般！」

「那蠢货在他心窝某个角落里翻出了一条蛀坏了的、名叫良心的破布，便不敢了。」

「该死的懦夫！我布下了那样一盘好棋！本可以在一年之内，把非洲的每一条基督徒狗都扫地出门的。他怕什么？」

「地狱的火。」

「嘿，他横竖都是要下地狱的，这可咒的外邦人（Gentile）！」

「我也尽可能婉转地向他指出过这一点；可是，正如世上旁人一样，他对于走自己的那条路下地狱，颇有一点偏爱。」

「懦夫！那我如今还能找谁？唉，那佩拉吉娅（Pelagia）若有一身子机心，赶得上希帕蒂娅一根小指头里的，我早把她和她的哥特人一起送上凯撒的宝座了。可惜——」

「可惜她有五官，也恰好够一点机灵来使唤这五官，是么？」

「别为此笑她，这小宝贝！我到底还是疼她的。看她把那一套本事使得多么到家、又是多么乐在其中——像夏娃（Eve）一个地道的女儿——连我这一把老骨头都跟着暖了起来呢。」

「她确是你最得意的学生啊，母亲。你尽可以为她自豪。」

===Original===
The old hag chuckled to herself a while; and then suddenly turning to Raphael—“See here! I have a present for you;” and she pulled out a magnificent ring.

“Why, mother, you are always giving me presents. It was but a month ago you sent me this poisoned dagger.”

“Why not, eh?—why not? Why should not Jew give to Jew? Take the old woman’s ring!”

“What a glorious opal!”

“Ah, that is an opal, indeed! And the unspeakable name upon it; just like Solomon’s own. Take it, I say! Whosoever wears that never need fear fire, steel, poison, or woman’s eye.”

“Your own included, eh?”

“Take it, I say!” and Miriam caught his hand, and forced the ring on his finger. “There! Now you’re safe. And now call me mother again. I like it. I don’t know why, but I like it. And—Raphael Aben-Ezra—don’t laugh at me, and call me witch and hag, as you often do. I don’t care about it from anyone else; I’m accustomed to it. But when you do it, I always long to stab you. That’s why I gave you the dagger. I used to wear it; and I was afraid I might be tempted to use it some day, when the thought came across me how handsome you’d look, and how quiet, when you were dead, and your soul up there so happy in Abraham’s bosom, watching all the Gentiles frying and roasting forever down below. Don’t laugh at me, I say; and don’t thwart me! I may make you the emperor’s prime minister some day. I can if I choose.”

“Heaven forbid!” said Raphael, laughing.

“Don’t laugh. I cast your nativity last night, and I know you have no cause to laugh. A great danger hangs over you, and a deep temptation. And if you weather this storm, you may be chamberlain, prime minister, emperor, if you will. And you shall be—by the four archangels, you shall!”

And the old woman vanished down a by-lane, leaving Raphael utterly bewildered.

===Chinese===
老婆子独自咯咯笑了好一会儿；然后忽然转向拉斐尔——「看这儿！我有一件礼物送你；」她掏出一枚极华丽的戒指。

「怎么啦，母亲，您总在送我东西。不过一个月前您才送了我那把毒匕首。」

「有什么不该，呃？——有什么不该？犹太人赠犹太人，有何不可？收下这老婆子的戒指罢！」

「好一颗夺目的蛋白石（opal）！」

「嘿，这才叫蛋白石呢！上面还刻着那不可言说之名；简直跟所罗门（Solomon）王自己那枚一模一样。我说，收下罢！谁戴上它，便再不必怕火、怕钢、怕毒药，也不必怕女人的眼。」

「连您自己的眼也包括在内，呃？」

「我说，收下！」米利暗一把抓住他的手，把戒指硬套上他的指头。「这不！如今你安全啦。这便再叫我一声母亲。我爱听。不知为什么，我就是爱听。还有——拉斐尔·阿本-以斯拉——别再笑话我，别再像你常做的那样叫我巫婆、叫我丑老婆子。别人这样叫我，我不在乎；我听惯了。可你这样叫我，我便总是恨不得捅你一刀。这便是我把那匕首送给你的缘故。我从前一直佩着它；我怕自己哪一天忍不住真会用上它——每当我想到：你死了该多俊、多安静，你的灵魂高高在上、坐在亚伯拉罕（Abraham）的怀里多么幸福，眼看着下面那些外邦人永永远远地被煎、被烤。我说，别笑话我；也别与我作对！我说不定哪一日便封你做皇帝的首相。只要我愿意，我办得到。」

「上天不容！」拉斐尔笑道。

「别笑。昨夜我替你算了星命，我知道你没有可笑的缘由。一桩大险正悬在你头上，还有一桩深重的诱惑。你若能熬过这一场风暴，你便可做内侍长、首相、皇帝，随你所欲。而你也必将成为——凭四大天使起誓，你必将成为！」

老婆子说着便消失在一条小巷里，撇下拉斐尔一头雾水。

===Original===
“Moses and the prophets! Does the old lady intend to marry me? What can there be in this very lazy and selfish personage who bears my name, to excite so romantic an affection? Well, Raphael Aben-Ezra, thou hast one more friend in the world beside Bran the mastiff; and therefore one more trouble—seeing that friends always expect a due return of affection and good offices and whatnot.
