Facts, objects, are but phantoms matter-woven—ghosts of this earthly night, at which the soul, sleeping here in the mire and clay of matter, shudders and names its own vague tremors sense and perception. Yet, even as our nightly dreams stir in us the suspicion of mysterious and immaterial presences, unfettered by the bonds of time and space, so do these waking dreams which we call sight and sound. They are divine messengers, whom Zeus, pitying his children, even when he pent them in this prison-house of flesh, appointed to arouse in them dim recollections of that real world of souls whence they came. Awakened once to them; seeing, through the veil of sense and fact, the spiritual truth of which they are but the accidental garment, concealing the very thing which they make palpable, the philosopher may neglect the fact for the doctrine, the shell for the kernel, the body for the soul, of which it is but the symbol and the vehicle. What matter, then, to the philosopher whether these names of men, Hector or Priam, Helen or Achilles, were ever visible as phantoms of flesh and blood before the eyes of men? What matter whether they spoke or thought as he of Scios says they did? What matter, even, whether he himself ever had earthly life? The book is here—the word which men call his. Let the thoughts thereof have been at first whose they may, now they are mine. I have taken them to myself, and thought them to myself, and made them parts of my own soul. Nay, they were and ever will be parts of me; for they, even as the poet was, even as I am, are but a part of the universal soul. What matter, then, what myths grew up around those mighty thoughts of ancient seers? Let others try to reconcile the Cyclic fragments, or vindicate the Catalogue of ships. What has the philosopher lost, though the former were proved to be contradictory, and the latter interpolated? The thoughts are there, and ours. Let us open our hearts lovingly to receive them, from whencesoever they may have come. As in men, so in books, the soul is all with which our souls must deal; and the soul of the book is whatsoever beautiful, and true, and noble we can find in it. It matters not to us whether the poet was altogether conscious of the meanings which we can find in him. Consciously or unconsciously to him, the meanings must be there; for were they not there to be seen, how could we see them? There are those among the uninitiate vulgar—and those, too, who carry under the philosophic cloak hearts still uninitiate—who revile such interpretations as merely the sophistic and arbitrary sports of fancy. It lies with them to show what Homer meant, if our spiritual meanings be absurd; to tell the world why Homer is admirable, if that for which we hold him up to admiration does not exist in him. Will they say that the honour which he has enjoyed for ages was inspired by that which seems to be his first and literal meaning? And more, will they venture to impute that literal meaning to him? can they suppose that the divine soul of Homer could degrade itself to write of actual and physical feastings, and nuptials, and dances, actual nightly thefts of horses, actual fidelity of dogs and swineherds, actual intermarriages between deities and men, or that it is this seeming vulgarity which has won for him from the wisest of every age the title of the father of poetry? Degrading thought! fit only for the coarse and sense-bound tribe who can appreciate nothing but what is palpable to sense and sight! As soon believe the Christian scriptures, when they tell us of a deity who has hands and feet, eyes and ears, who condescends to command the patterns of furniture and culinary utensils, and is made perfect by being born—disgusting thought!—as the son of a village maiden, and defiling himself with the wants and sorrows of the lowest slaves!"

"It is false! blasphemous! The Scriptures cannot lie!" cried a voice from the farther end of the room.

===Chinese===
「真理？除了灵魂自身之中，真理又何在？事实、外物，不过是物质织就的幻影——这尘世之夜的鬼魅；灵魂睡在此间物质的泥淖与黏土之中，因它们而战栗，并把自己那模糊的颤动，命名为感觉与知觉。然而，恰如我们夜间的梦境，会在我们心中唤起一种疑心，疑心那不受时空羁绊的、神秘的、非物质的存在之存在；我们这些所谓的视觉与听觉的清醒之梦，亦复如是。它们是神圣的使者——宙斯（Zeus）怜悯他的儿女，即便当他将他们囚入这血肉的牢狱之时，也派遣它们来唤醒他们对那个灵魂之真世界的隐约记忆，那是他们所从来的本乡。一旦向它们觉醒，透过感官与事实的面纱，看见它们不过是其偶然外衣所遮蔽、却又使其彰明的那一层属灵真理，哲人便可以重教义而轻事实，重内核而轻外壳，重灵魂而轻肉体——后者不过是前者的象征与载体。那么，对于哲人，赫克托耳（Hector）或普里阿摩斯（Priam），海伦（Helen）或阿喀琉斯（Achilles）这些名字，是否曾以血肉之躯的幻影显现在世人眼前，又有什么要紧？他们是否如希俄斯（Scios）的那位所言的那般言与思，又有什么要紧？甚至他本人是否曾有过尘世的生命，又有什么要紧？书在这里——即世人称作他的那部书。书中的思想最初是谁的，由它去吧；如今它们是我的。我把它们据为己有，独自将它们思量，使它们成为我自己灵魂的一部分。不仅如此，它们过去是、将来也永远是属于我的一部分；因为它们，正如那位诗人一样，正如我一样，不过是那普世灵魂的一部分而已。那么，围绕着古代先知那些伟大的思想，长出了什么样的神话，又有什么要紧？让别人去设法调和史诗组诗（Cyclic）的残篇吧，让别人去替「船名录」（Catalogue of ships）辩护吧。纵使前者被证明自相矛盾，后者被证明羼入伪作，哲人又损失了什么？思想在那里，是我们的。让我们敞开心怀、满怀爱意地去领受它们，不论它们来自何方。正如看人看其灵魂，读书亦读其灵魂，我们的灵魂所当与之交往的，唯有那灵魂而已；而书之灵魂，便是我们能在其中寻得的一切美、真与高贵之处。那位诗人是否完全意识到我们能在其中读出的种种含义，与我们无关。不论他是否意识到，那些含义必然在那里；因为倘若它们不在那里、不为人所见，我们又怎能看见它们？未入秘传的凡夫俗子当中——也有披着哲学外衣、而其心仍属未入秘传之人——有人斥责这种诠释不过是诡辩、是幻想的任性游戏。那么，倘若我们的属灵诠释荒谬可笑，就请他们来指教荷马（Homer）究竟何意；倘若我们推崇荷马所凭借的那一切、在他身上根本不存在，就请他们来告诉世人荷马究竟可取在何处。难道他们要说，他千百年来所享的尊荣，竟源自于那看起来最表层的字面含义？更进一步，他们竟敢把那种字面含义归之于他么？他们能设想荷马那神圣的灵魂，竟会自贬身价去写什么实在的、肉体的筵席、婚礼与舞蹈，写什么夜里实打实地盗马，写什么狗与猪倌的实打实的忠诚，写什么神与人的实打实的联姻么？他们能设想，正是这一层表面的鄙俗，才为他赢得了历代最智者授予的「诗歌之父」之衔么？堕落的念头！只配那粗鄙的、为感官所缚的一族去想——他们除了感官与目力所及的粗浅之物，便不能欣赏任何东西！这样看来，倒不如去信那基督教的《圣经》算了——它告诉我们有一位有手有脚、有眼有耳的神祇，居然纡尊降贵地去吩咐家具与厨具的样式，又借着降生——恶心的念头！——做一个乡村少女之子、而得以完全，还以最低贱的奴隶的匮乏与忧患来玷污自己！」

「这是胡言！是亵渎！《圣经》不会说谎！」一个声音从讲堂的远端传来。

===Original===
It was Philammon's. He had been listening to the whole lecture; and yet not so much listening as watching, in bewilderment, the beauty of the speaker, the grace of her action, the melody of her voice, and last, but not least, the maze of her rhetoric, as it glittered before his mind's eye like a cobweb diamonded with dew. A sea of new thoughts and questions, if not of doubts, came rushing in at every sentence on his acute Greek intellect, all the more plentifully and irresistibly because his speculative faculty was as yet altogether waste and empty, undefended by any scientific culture from the inrushing flood. For the first time in his life he found himself face to face with the root-questions of all thought—"What am I, and where?" "What can I know?" And in the half-terrified struggle with them, he had all but forgotten the purpose for which he entered the lecture-hall. He felt that he must break the spell. Was she not a heathen and a false prophetess? Here was something tangible to attack; and half in indignation at the blasphemy, half in order to force himself into action, he had sprung up and spoken.

A yell arose. "Turn the monk out!" "Throw the rustic through the window!" cried a dozen young gentlemen. Several of the most valiant began to scramble over the benches up to him; and Philammon was congratulating himself on the near approach of a glorious martyrdom, when Hypatia's voice, calm and silvery, stifled the tumult in a moment.

"Let the youth listen, gentlemen. He is but a monk and a plebeian, and knows no better; he has been taught thus. Let him sit here quietly, and perhaps we may be able to teach him otherwise."

And without interrupting, even by a change of tone, the thread of her discourse, she continued—

"Listen, then, to a passage from the sixth book of the *Iliad*, in which last night I seemed to see glimpses of some mighty mystery. You know it well: yet I will read it to you; the very sound and pomp of that great verse may tune our souls to a fit key for the reception of lofty wisdom. For well said Abamnon the Teacher, that 'the soul consisted first of harmony and rhythm, and ere it gave itself to the body, had listened to the divine harmony. Therefore it is that when, after having come into a body, it hears such melodies as most preserve the divine footstep of harmony, it embraces such, and recollects from them that divine harmony, and is impelled to it, and finds its home in it, and shares of it as much as it can share.'"

===Chinese===
那是菲拉蒙（Philammon）的声音。他一直听着整场讲演；可他与其说是在听，不如说是困惑地注视着讲演者的美貌、她举手投足的优雅、她嗓音的旋律，以及——最后却并非最不重要的——她那座修辞的迷宫，它在他心灵的眼前闪烁，如同挂满露珠的蛛网。海一般的新想法与新疑问——若非怀疑的话——从每一句话中涌来，冲击着他那敏锐的希腊人的头脑；这股潮流格外地浩大、格外地不可抵挡，因为他的思辨力至今仍是一片全然的荒芜与空旷，没有任何科学的修养来抵御这股涌入的洪水。他有生以来第一次，发现自己与一切思想的根本问题面对面——「我是谁？我在何处？」「我能知道什么？」他在与这些问题的搏斗中既惧且惊，几乎已忘记了自己进这讲堂来的本意。他觉得非打破这符咒不可。她岂不是个异教徒、一个假女先知么？这里总算有件可以着手攻击的实在之物；他一半是出于对那亵渎的义愤，一半是为了强迫自己行动起来，便一跃而起，喊了出来。

一阵叫骂响起。「把那修士赶出去！」「把那乡巴佬从窗户扔出去！」十几个公子哥儿嚷道。几个最英勇的开始翻过长凳朝他爬过来；菲拉蒙正暗自庆幸一场光荣的殉道在即，希帕蒂娅那沉静如银的嗓音响起，顷刻间便压下了骚动。

「让那少年听着吧，先生们。他不过是个修士、一个平民，不懂得什么；人家就是这样教他的。让他在这里安静地坐着，说不定我们还能教他明白些别的。」

她连语调都不曾变一变，便毫无间断地接着自己原来的话头说下去——

「那么，请听《伊利亚特》（*Iliad*）第六卷中的一段——昨夜我仿佛从中瞥见了几丝某个伟大奥秘的微光。你们都很熟悉它；我仍要读给你们听；那伟大诗行的音响与壮丽，或可将我们的灵魂调到适合领受崇高智慧的弦上。因为教师阿巴姆农（Abamnon）说得真好：『灵魂首先由和谐与韵律所成，在它将自己交付肉体之前，曾聆听过那神圣的和谐。因此之故，当它进入肉体之后，一旦听到那些最能保存和谐之神圣足音的旋律，便会拥抱它们，并从其中重新忆起那神圣的和谐，被它所驱迫，在它之中寻得归宿，并尽可能多地分享它。』」

===Original===
And therewith fell on Philammon's ear, for the first time, the mighty thunder-roll of Homer's verse—

So spoke the stewardess: but Hector rushed
From the house, the same way back, down stately streets,
Through the broad city, to the Scaian gates,
Whereby he must go forth toward the plain,
There running toward him came Andromache,
His ample-dowered wife, Eetion's child—
Eetion the greathearted, he who dwelt
In Thebe under Placos, and the woods
Of Placos, ruling over Kilic men.
His daughter wedded Hector brazen-helmed,
And met him then; and with her came a maid,
Who bore in arms a playful-hearted babe,
An infant still, akin to some fair star,
Only and well-loved child of Hector's house,
Whom he had named Scamandrios, but the rest
Astyanax, because his sire alone
Upheld the weal of Ilion the holy.
He smiled in silence, looking on his child
But she stood close to him, with many tears;
And hung upon his hand, and spoke, and called him.
"My hero, thy great heart will wear thee out;
Thou pitiest not thine infant child, nor me
The hapless, soon to be thy widow;
The Greeks will slay thee, falling one and all
Upon thee: but to me were sweeter far,
Having lost thee, to die; no cheer to me
Will come thenceforth, if thou shouldst meet thy fate;
Woes only: mother have I none, nor sire.
For that my sire divine Achilles slew,
And wasted utterly the pleasant homes
Of Kilic folk in Thebe lofty-walled,
And slew Eetion with the sword! yet spared
To strip the dead: awe kept his soul from that.
Therefore he burnt him in his graven arms,
And heaped a mound above him; and around
The damsels of the Aegis-holding Zeus,
The nymphs who haunt the upland, planted elms.
And seven brothers bred with me in the halls,
All in one day went down to Hades there;
For all of them swift-foot Achilles slew
Beside the lazy kine and snow-white sheep.
And her, my mother, who of late was queen
Beneath the woods of Placos, he brought here
Among his other spoils; yet set her free
Again, receiving ransom rich and great.
But Artemis, whose bow is all her joy,
Smote her to death within her father's halls.
Hector! so thou art father to me now,
Mother, and brother, and husband fair and strong!
Oh, come now, pity me, and stay thou here
Upon the tower, nor make thy child an orphan
And me thy wife a widow; range the men
Here by the fig-tree, where the city lies
Lowest, and where the wall can well be scaled;
For here three times the best have tried the assault
Round either Ajax, and Idomeneus,
And round the Atridai both, and Tydeus' son,
Whether some cunning seer taught them craft,
Or their own spirit stirred and drove them on."
Then spake tall Hector, with the glancing helm:
"All this I too have watched, my wife; yet much
I hold in dread the scorn of Trojan men
And Trojan women with their trailing shawls,
If, like a coward, I should skulk from war.
Beside, I have no lust to stay; I have learnt
Aye to be bold, and lead the van of fight,
To win my father, and myself, a name.
For well I know, at heart and in my thought,
The day will come when Ilios the holy
Shall lie in heaps, and Priam, and the folk
Of ashen-speared Priam, perish all.
But yet no woe to come to Trojan men,
Nor even to Hecabe, nor Priam king,
Nor to my brothers, who shall roll in dust,
Many and fair, beneath the strokes of foes,
So moves me, as doth thine, when thou shalt go
Weeping, led off by some brass-harnessed Greek,
Robbed of the daylight of thy liberty,
To weave in Argos at another's loom,
Or bear the water of Messeis home,
Or Hypereia, with unseemly toils,
While heavy doom constrains thee, and perchance
The folk may say, who see thy tears run down, 'This was the wife of Hector, best in fight
At Ilium, of horse-taming Trojan men.'
So will they say perchance; while unto thee
Now grief will come, for such a husband's loss,
Who might have warded off the day of thrall.
But may the soil be heaped above my corpse
Before I hear thy shriek and see thy shame!"
He spoke, and stretched his arms to take the child,
But back the child upon his nurse's breast
Shrank crying, frightened at his father's looks.
Fearing the brass and crest of horse's hair
Which waved above the helmet terribly.
Then out that father dear and mother laughed,
And glorious Hector took the helmet off,
And laid it gleaming on the ground, and kissed
His darling child, and danced him in his arm;
And spoke in prayer to Zeus, and all the gods:
"Zeu, and ye other gods, oh grant that this
My child, like me, may grow the champion here
As good in strength, and rule with might in Troy.
That men may say, 'The boy is better far
Than was his sire,' when he returns from war,
Bearing a gory harness, having slain
A foeman, and his mothers heart rejoice.
Thus saying, on the hands of his dear wife
He laid the child; and she received him back
In fragrant bosom, smiling through her tears.

===Chinese===
于是，荷马那雄浑如雷的诗句，第一次落进了菲拉蒙的耳中——

女管家如此说罢；赫克托耳却已
冲出屋子，沿原路折返，穿过巍峨的街衢，
横贯宽阔的城池，直奔斯开埃门，
他须从那里出城，奔赴平原。
在那里，迎着他跑来的，是安德洛玛刻，
他那妆奁丰厚的妻子，厄厄提翁之女——
厄厄提翁，那位心胸伟大的，他住在
普拉科斯山下的忒拜，住在那片
普拉科斯山林之中，统治着基利基亚人。
他的女儿嫁给了铜盔的赫克托耳，
此时迎上前来；随她同来的，还有一名侍女，
怀中抱一个顽皮的婴孩，
尚是襁褓中的婴儿，好比一颗明星，
是赫克托耳家中独一的、钟爱的孩子，
父亲给他取名斯卡曼德里奥斯，
旁人却唤他阿斯提阿那克斯，
因为他的父亲一人，
独自撑持着神圣的伊利昂的福祉。
他默然微笑，看着自己的孩子；
她却贴近他身旁，泪流不止；
拉住他的手，唤他，对他诉说。
「我的英雄啊，你那颗伟大的心要累垮了你；
你既不怜惜你的婴孩，也不怜惜我——
这苦命人，眼看就要做你的寡妇；
希腊人必将杀你，他们一个接一个
扑向你：然而对我而言，远为甜蜜的是，
既已失去你，便死去；从此再无欢慰
临到我，若是你命归黄泉；
唯有哀愁：我既无母亲，也无父亲。
因为我那神圣的父亲，阿喀琉斯所杀，
又将基利基亚人在高墙的忒拜
那些宜人的家宅，尽数夷为平地，
更用剑杀了厄厄提翁！却又不肯
剥下死者的铠甲：敬畏之心阻住了他。
于是他将死者连同镂花的甲胄一并火化，
在上面堆起一座坟丘；四围则有
执掌神盾的宙斯的众侍女——
那些出没于山岭的宁芙，种下了榆树。
与我同在厅堂里长大的七个兄弟，
同在一日之内下了冥府；
因为捷足的阿喀琉斯把他们
一个个都杀了，在慵懒的牛群与雪白的羊群之旁。
而她——我的母亲，近来还是
普拉科斯林荫之下的王后——他把她
连同别的战利品一并掳到此处；却又放她
归去，收下了丰厚贵重的赎金。
但阿尔忒弥斯（Artemis），她的全部欢乐都在弓上，
却在她的父亲家中将她射杀。
赫克托耳啊！如今你可作我的父亲，
母亲、兄弟，以及英武的夫君！
哦，来吧，可怜可怜我，你就留在这里
塔楼之上，莫叫你的孩子成了孤儿，
莫叫你的妻子做了寡妇；把兵士
列在这棵无花果树旁，这里城墙
最低，最容易被人攀越；
因为最善战的将领们已三度在此猛攻，
围着大埃阿斯与小埃阿斯，围着伊多墨纽斯，
围着两位阿特里代，以及堤丢斯之子，
不知是某个精明的先知教了他们计谋，
还是他们自己的心志鼓动驱策了他们。」
高大的赫克托耳，顶着闪亮的头盔，说道：
「这些我也都看在眼里，我的妻子；然而
我极怕特洛亚的男子
和拖着长裙的特洛亚女子耻笑我，
倘若我像个懦夫一样，逃避战争。
况且，我无意留下；我已学会
永远奋勇争先，做战阵的先锋，
为我的父亲、也为我自己，赢得声名。
因为我心中深知，骨子里明白，
那日子终将到来，神圣的伊利昂
将化为废墟，普里阿摩斯，以及
持灰木枪的普里阿摩斯的臣民，将悉数覆亡。
然而，特洛亚的男子们将临的灾祸，
乃至赫卡柏、乃至普里阿摩斯王，
乃至我的兄弟们——他们将在敌军的
击打之下，众多而英武地滚倒在尘埃里——
这些都还不曾如此牵动我的心，如你将去的
那日那般：你将
哭泣着被人领走，被某个披铜甲的希腊人掳走，
被夺去你那白昼般的自由，
去阿尔戈斯在别人的织机前织布，
或者去打墨塞伊斯的水，
或许珀瑞亚的水回家，受那难堪的劳役，
沉重的命运辖制着你，也许
看见你泪落如雨的人会说：『这是赫克托耳的妻子，
在伊利昂，在驯马的特洛亚男子中，他最善战。』
他们也许会这样说；而对你而言，
此刻哀愁将至，因为失去了这样一位丈夫，
他本可挡住那沦为奴隶的日子。
但愿泥土已堆在我的尸骸之上，
在我听见你的哀号、看见你的羞辱之前！」
他说罢，伸出双臂要去抱孩子，
可孩子却缩回奶娘的怀里
哭了起来，被他父亲的脸吓着了。
他怕那黄铜与马鬃的盔缨，
那在头盔之上恐怖地晃动。
那时，慈父与慈母都笑了，
光荣的赫克托耳摘下头盔，
把它闪着光放在地上，亲吻
他的心肝宝贝，把他抱在臂间颠晃；
并向宙斯与众神祈祷：
「宙斯啊，以及你们众神，求你们恩准
这孩子像我一样，在此长大成
勇武堪与我媲美的勇士，以威权统治特洛亚。
使人能说：『这孩子远胜过
他的父亲』——当他从战场上归来，
带着血污的铠甲，因他已
斩杀一个敌人，使他母亲的心欢喜。
说罢，他把孩子放到爱妻的
手上；她接过他，
贴在芬芳的胸怀里，含泪微笑。

===Original===
"Such is the myth. Do you fancy that in it Homer meant to hand down to the admiration of ages such earthly commonplaces as a mother's brute affection, and the terrors of an infant? Surely the deeper insight of the philosopher may be allowed without the reproach of fancifulness, to see in it the adumbration of some deeper mystery!

"The elect soul, for instance—is not its name Astyanax, king of the city; by the fact of its ethereal parentage, the leader and lord of all around it, though it knows it not? A child as yet, it lies upon the fragrant bosom of its mother Nature, the nurse and yet the enemy of man—Andromache, as the poet well names her, because she fights with that being, when grown to man's estate, whom as a child she nourished. Fair is she, yet unwise; pampering us, after the fashion of mothers, with weak indulgences; fearing to send us forth into the great realities of speculation, there to forget her in the pursuit of glory, she would have us while away our prime within the harem, and play forever round her knees. And has not the elect soul a father, too, whom it knows not? Hector, he who is without—unconfined, unconditioned by Nature, yet its husband?—the all-pervading, plastic Soul, informing, organising, whom men call Zeus the lawgiver, Aether the fire, Osiris the lifegiver; whom here the poet has set forth as the defender of the mystic city, the defender of harmony, and order, and beauty throughout the universe? Apart sits his great father—Priam, the first of existences, father of many sons, the Absolute Reason; unseen, tremendous, immovable, in distant glory; yet himself amenable to that abysmal unity which Homer calls Fate, the source of all which is, yet in Itself Nothing, without predicate, unnameable.

"From It and for It the universal Soul thrills through the whole Creation, doing the behests of that Reason from which it overflowed, unwillingly, into the storm and crowd of material appearances; warring with the brute forces of gross matter, crushing all which is foul and dissonant to itself, and clasping to its bosom the beautiful, and all wherein it discovers its own reflex; impressing on it its signature, reproducing from it its own likeness, whether star, or daemon, or soul of the elect:—and yet, as the poet hints in anthropomorphic language, haunted all the while by a sadness—weighed down amid all its labours by the sense of a fate—by the thought of that First One from whom the Soul is originally descended; from whom it, and its Father the Reason before it, parted themselves when they dared to think and act, and assert their own free will.

===Chinese===
「神话便是如此。难道你们以为，荷马在其中想要传诸后世、令万代景仰的，竟是一个母亲的兽性般的慈爱、以及一个婴孩的惊吓之类的人间俗事么？哲人那更为深刻的洞见，总可以不受『想入非非』之讥，而在其中看出某个更深奥秘的影子吧！

「譬如说，那蒙选的灵魂——它岂不是名为阿斯提阿那克斯、即『城邦之王』么？这是凭它那属天的出身，纵使它自己尚不自知，它已是周围一切的主宰与首领？它尚是一个婴孩，躺在它母亲——自然——那芬芳的胸怀之上；自然是人的乳母，却又是人的仇敌——诗人称她为安德洛玛刻（Andromache），这名号起得真好，因为她与之交战的，正是她幼时所哺育、长大成人之后的那同一个存在。她是美丽的，却并不明智；她像一切母亲那样，以软弱的溺爱娇纵我们；她惧怕把我们送进那广阔的思辨之真境、使我们因追逐荣耀而忘记她，便要我们尽把盛年的光阴消磨在内闱之中，永远在她的膝前嬉戏。而那蒙选的灵魂，岂不也有一位父亲，却并不认识他？赫克托耳，那在外者——不受自然所拘束、所限定，却是她的夫君？——那是无所不在的、赋形的灵魂，赋予万物以形相与组织，人们称他为立法者宙斯（Zeus）、称他为火以太（Aether）、称他为赐生命的奥西里斯（Osiris）；诗人正是在此将他表现为那座神秘之城的捍卫者、宇宙间和谐、秩序与美的捍卫者。他的大父则坐在远处——普里阿摩斯，那最初的存在，众子之父，即绝对的理性（Absolute Reason）；不可见、可畏、不可移易，居于遥远的荣耀之中；然而他自己亦臣服于那渊深的太一——荷马称之为命运——万物皆从此出，而它自身却是『无』，无任何谓词，不可名状。

「普世灵魂从此而出、为此而行，震颤着穿透整个造化，奉行那理性——它本从理性中满溢而出，不情愿地倾注于物质表象的风暴与喧嚣之中——的吩咐；与粗浊物质的蛮力争战，粉碎一切对自身而言污秽而刺耳之物，将一切美的、一切它能在其中照见自己倒影的，拥入怀中；将自己的印记盖在上面，从其中复现自己的形象——或是星辰，或是精灵（daemon），或是蒙选者的灵魂：——然而，正如诗人以拟人化的语言所暗示的，它始终被一种悲哀所萦绕——在它的一切劳作中，被一种命运的意识所重压——被那太初之一的思想所重压；灵魂本是从此而降，它与它的父亲理性，当初正是因为胆敢自去思想、自去行动、自立自由意志，才与那太初之一分道扬镳。

"And in the meanwhile, alas! Hector, the father, fights around, while his children sleep and feed; and he is away in the wars, and they know him not—know not that they the individuals are but parts of him the universal. And yet at moments—oh! thrice blessed they whose celestial parentage has made such moments part of their appointed destiny—at moments flashes on the human child the intuition of the unutterable secret. In the spangled glory of the summer night—in the roar of the Nile-flood, sweeping down fertility in every wave—in the awful depths of the temple-shrine—in the wild melodies of old Orphic singers, or before the images of those gods of whose perfect beauty the divine theosophists of Greece caught a fleeting shadow, and with the sudden might of artistic ecstasy smote it, as by an enchanter's wand, into an eternal sleep of snowy stone—in these there flashes on the inner eye a vision beautiful and terrible, of a force, an energy, a soul, an idea, one and yet million-fold, rushing through all created things, like the wind across a lyre, thrilling the strings into celestial harmony—one lifeblood through the million veins of the universe, from one great unseen heart, whose thunderous pulses the mind hears far away, beating forever in the abysmal solitude, beyond the heavens and the galaxies, beyond the spaces and the times, themselves but veins and runnels from its all-teeming sea.

"Happy, thrice happy! they who once have dared, even though breathless, blinded with tears of awful joy, struck down upon their knees in utter helplessness, as they feel themselves but dead leaves in the wind which sweeps the universe—happy they who have dared to gaze, if but for an instant, on the terror of that glorious pageant; who have not, like the young Astyanax, clung shrieking to the breast of mother Nature, scared by the heaven-wide flash of Hector's arms, and the glitter of his rainbow crest! Happy, thrice happy! even though their eyeballs, blasted by excess of light, wither to ashes in their sockets!—Were it not a noble end to have seen Zeus, and die like Semele, burnt up by his glory? Happy, thrice happy! though their mind reel from the divine intoxication, and the hogs of Circe call them henceforth madmen and enthusiasts. Enthusiasts they are; for Deity is in them, and they in It. For the time, this burden of individuality vanishes, and recognising themselves as portions of the universal Soul, they rise upward, through and beyond that Reason from whence the soul proceeds, to the fount of all—the ineffable and Supreme One—and seeing It, become by that act portions of Its essence. They speak no more, but It speaks in them, and their whole being, transmuted by that glorious sunlight into whose rays they have dared, like the eagle, to gaze without shrinking, becomes an harmonious vehicle for the words of Deity, and passive itself, utters the secrets of the immortal gods! What wonder if to the brute mass they seem as dreamers? Be it so.… Smile if you will. But ask me not to teach you things unspeakable, above all sciences, which the word-battle of dialectic, the discursive struggles of reason, can never reach, but which must be seen only, and when seen confessed to be unspeakable. Hence, thou disputer of the Academy!—hence, thou sneering Cynic!—hence, thou sense-worshipping Stoic, who fanciest that the soul is to derive her knowledge from those material appearances which she herself creates!… hence—; and yet no: stay and sneer if you will. It is but a little time—a few days longer in this prison-house of our degradation, and each thing shall return to its own fountain; the blood-drop to the abysmal heart, and the water to the river, and the river to the shining sea; and the dewdrop which fell from heaven shall rise to heaven again, shaking off the dust-grains which weighed it down, thawed from the earth-frost which chained it here to herb and sward, upward and upward ever through stars and suns, through gods, and through the parents of the gods, purer and purer through successive lives, till it enters The Nothing, which is The All, and finds its home at last.…"

「然而在此期间，呜呼！赫克托耳，那位父亲，在外四围征战，他的孩子们却睡的睡、吃的吃；他在沙场之上，他们却不认识他——不知道他们这些个人，不过是他那普世灵魂的组成部分。然而总有这样的时候——啊！三倍有福的人哪，他们的属天出身使这种时刻成了他们命中注定的一部分——总有这样的时候，那不可言说的奥秘，会如电光一般闪现于人之子的心头。在夏夜那缀满繁星的辉煌之中——在尼罗河洪流的轰鸣之中，每一波浪涛都挟着丰饶席卷而下——在神庙至圣所那可怖的深处——在古昔俄耳甫斯教（Orphic）歌者那狂野的旋律之中，或在那众神造像之前——希腊那些神圣的神智学者曾瞥见诸神完美之美的一抹转瞬即逝的影子，便以艺术狂喜的突然伟力，如受术士魔杖的一击，将它击入一场雪白大理石的永恒沉睡——在这一切之中，内心之眼会瞥见一个既美且怖的异象：一种力量、一种能量、一个灵魂、一个理念，是一又是百万，贯穿一切受造之物，如风掠过里拉琴，使琴弦震颤出天界的和声——那是整个宇宙百万条静脉中共同流淌的一种生命之血，出自一颗广大的、不可见的心，它的雷鸣般的脉搏，心灵远远听见，永远在那渊深的孤寂中跳动，在诸天与星河之外，在一切空间与时间之外——而那一切空间与时间，本身不过是从它那孕育一切的海洋中分流而出的血脉与溪涧。

「幸福啊，三倍的幸福！凡曾敢于——纵然气喘吁吁、被可畏之喜的泪水迷了双眼、因感到自己不过是横扫宇宙之风中的枯叶、而在全然无助中跪倒在地——凡敢于凝视、哪怕只是一瞬，那光辉行列的可怖景象之人！他们没有像幼小的阿斯提阿那克斯那样，被赫克托耳甲胄那横亘天宇的闪光、被他那彩虹般盔缨的照耀所惊吓，尖叫着紧紧抱住母亲自然的胸乳！幸福啊，三倍的幸福！纵然他们的眼珠被过量的光焰灼伤，在眼眶中化为灰烬！——曾亲眼看见宙斯、如塞墨勒（Semele）一般被他的荣耀所焚毁而死，岂非一个高贵的终局？幸福啊，三倍的幸福！纵然他们的心智在那神圣的沉醉中天旋地转，纵然喀耳刻（Circe）的猪群从此称他们为狂人、为入迷者。他们是入迷者；因为神明在他们之内，他们在神明之内。在那一刻，这『个体性』的重担消失了，他们认出自己是普世灵魂的一部分，便向上升腾，穿过并超越那灵魂所从出的理性，升到万有之源——那不可言说的、至高的太一——看见它，便因这一举动而成为它本质的一部分。他们不再说话，而是它在他们里面说话；他们的整个存在，被那荣耀的日光所点金——他们曾如雄鹰一般，毫不退缩地直视那光芒——化作神明之言的和谐载体，自身无所作为，却道出不朽众神的秘密！倘若在那一团愚钝的大众眼中，他们看起来如同梦中人，又有什么奇怪？由它去吧。……你们要笑便笑吧。但不要请我教你们那些不可言说之事——它凌驾于一切学问之上，那是辩证法的唇枪舌剑、理性的迂回挣扎所永不能及的，它只能被看见，而一旦被看见，便只能被承认为不可言说。去吧，学园里好辩的你！——去吧，冷嘲的犬儒派！——去吧，崇拜感官的斯多葛派，你妄想灵魂能从她自己创造的那些物质表象中获取知识！……去吧——；然而不：留下吧，要冷嘲就冷嘲吧。时间已所剩无几——在这座我们受辱的牢狱中再待上几日，万物便将各归其源；血滴归那深渊的心，水归河流，河流归那波光粼粼的大海；而那从天上落下的露珠，将再升至天上，抖落压着它的尘粒，融化那使它束缚在此、附着于草木与草皮之上的地霜，永远向上升腾、向上升腾，穿过群星与太阳，穿过众神，穿过众神之父众神之母，经历一次又一次的生命而愈加纯洁，直到它进入那『无』——那无即是『万有』——而最终寻得归宿。……」

And the speaker stopped suddenly, her eyes glistening with tears, her whole figure trembling and dilating with rapture. She remained for a moment motionless, gazing earnestly at her audience, as if in hopes of exciting in them some kindred glow; and then recovering herself, added in a more tender tone, not quite unmixed with sadness—

"Go now, my pupils. Hypatia has no more for you today. Go now, and spare her at least—woman as she is after all—the shame of finding that she has given you too much, and lifted the veil of Isis before eyes which are not enough purified to behold the glory of the goddess.—Farewell!"

She ended: and Philammon, the moment that the spell of her voice was taken off him, sprang up, and hurried out through the corridor into the street.…

So beautiful! So calm and merciful to him! So enthusiastic towards all which was noble! Had not she too spoken of the unseen world, of the hope of immortality, of the conquest of the spirit over the flesh, just as a Christian might have done? Was the gulf between them so infinite? If so, why had her aspirations awakened echoes in his own heart—echoes too, just such as the prayers and lessons of the Laura used to awaken? If the fruit was so like, must not the root be like also?… Could that be a counterfeit? That a minister of Satan in the robes of an angel of light? Light, at least, it was purity, simplicity, courage, earnestness, tenderness, flashed out from eye, lip, gesture.… A heathen, who disbelieved?… What was the meaning of it all?

===Chinese===
讲者戛然而止，她眼中泪光闪烁，整个身躯因狂喜而颤抖、而膨胀。她一动不动地静立了片刻，恳切地凝视着听众，仿佛盼望在他们心中点燃一抹相同的光焰；随后她收摄心神，以更为温柔的、不无悲凉的语调补充道——

「去吧，我的门生们。希帕蒂娅今日再无话给你们了。去吧，至少饶了她——她到底不过是个女子——不必叫她蒙受那等羞辱：发现自己给的太多，竟在尚未洁净到可以瞻仰女神荣光的眼睛之前，过早地揭起了伊西斯（Isis）的面纱。——再会！」

她说完了：菲拉蒙一从她那嗓音的符咒下脱身，便一跃而起，匆匆穿过走廊，奔到街上。……

她竟这般美！对他这般沉静而宽厚！对一切崇高之物这般热诚！她不也谈到那不可见的世界、谈到灵魂不死的盼望、谈到灵魂对肉体的征服么——不正像一个基督徒所会说的那样么？那么，他们之间的鸿沟竟如此深不可测么？若是如此，为何她的向往在他自己心中激起了回响——而这些回响，又恰与劳拉（the Laura）里的祈祷与教导所曾激起的回响如出一辙？倘若果子如此相像，根岂不也该相像？……那会是赝品么？会是撒但（Satan）的差役，披着光明天使的外袍么？光明，至少那是纯洁、是纯朴、是勇气、是诚恳、是温存——从她的眼、唇、举手投足间闪现出来。……一个异教徒，一个不信的人？……这一切究竟是怎么回事？

===Original===
But the finishing stroke yet remained which was to complete the utter confusion of his mind. For before he had gone fifty yards up the street, his little friend of the fruit-basket, whom he had not seen since he vanished under the feet of the mob in the gateway of the theatre, clutched him by the arm, and burst forth, breathless with running—

"The—gods—heap their favours—on those who—who least deserve them! Rash and insolent rustic! And this is the reward of thy madness!"

"Off with you!" said Philammon, who had no mind at the moment to renew his acquaintance with the little porter. But the guardian of parasols kept a firm hold on his sheepskin.

"Fool! Hypatia herself commands! Yes, you will see her, have speech with her! while I—I the illuminated—I the appreciating—I the obedient—I the adoring—who for these three years past have grovelled in the kennel, that the hem of her garment might touch the tip of my little finger—I—I—I—"

"What do you want, madman?"

"She calls for thee, insensate wretch! Theon sent me—breathless at once with running and with envy—Go! favourite of the unjust gods!"

"Who is Theon?"

"Her father, ignorant! He commands thee to be at her house—here—opposite—tomorrow at the third hour. Hear and obey! There they are coming out of the Museum, and all the parasols will get wrong! Oh, miserable me!" And the poor little fellow rushed back again, while Philammon, at his wits' end between dread and longing, started off, and ran the whole way home to the Serapeium, regardless of carriages, elephants, and foot-passengers; and having been knocked down by a surly porter, and left a piece of his sheepskin between the teeth of a spiteful camel—neither of which insults he had time to resent-arrived at the archbishop's house, found Peter the Reader, and tremblingly begged an audience from Cyril.

===Chinese===
然而，那使他心智彻底混乱的最后一击，尚在后面。因为他在街上还没走满五十步，他那位提果篮的小朋友——自从上次在剧院门口的人潮脚下消失之后，他便再没见过这孩子——便一把抓住他的胳膊，气喘吁吁地、跑得上气不接下气地嚷道——

「众——神——将恩宠——堆在那些——最不配的人身上！你这莽撞放肆的乡巴佬！这便是你那番癫狂的报酬了！」

「去你的！」菲拉蒙说，他此刻无心与这小门房再续旧交。然而那位「阳伞守护者」却紧紧揪住他的羊皮不放。

「蠢货！希帕蒂娅亲自传唤！是的，你要见她了，要和她说话了！而我——我这蒙光照的人——我这有鉴赏力的人——我这顺从的人——我这崇拜的人——三年来一直匍匐在阴沟里，只为她衣裳的边能触到我小指的指尖——我——我——我——」

「你这疯子，你到底要干什么？」

「她传唤你呢，你这没心肝的家伙！提昂差我来的——我一来跑得上气不接下气，二来嫉妒得上气不接下气——去吧！不公正的众神的宠儿！」

「提昂是谁？」

「她的父亲，你这无知的人！他命你明日第三时辰到她府上——就在这里——对面——。听命遵行吧！他们正从博物院里出来呢，所有的阳伞都要乱了套了！唉，我真命苦！」那可怜的小家伙奔回去了；而菲拉蒙，在恐惧与渴望之间走投无路，便撒腿飞奔，一口气跑回塞拉匹斯神庙（the Serapeium），什么马车、大象、行人一概不顾；中途被一个凶神恶煞的脚夫撞翻在地，又被一头恶脾气的骆驼扯下了一块羊皮——这两桩侮辱他都无暇计较——终于跑到大主教的府邸，找到了读经员彼得（Peter the Reader），战战兢兢地求见区利罗。

## IX / IX

### The Snapping of the Bow / 弓弦的崩断

===Original===
Cyril heard Philammon's story and Hypatia's message with a quiet smile, and then dismissed the youth to an afternoon of labour in the city, commanding him to mention no word of what had happened, and to come to him that evening and receive his order when he should have had time to think over the matter. So forth Philammon went with his companions, through lanes and alleys hideous with filth and poverty, compulsory idleness and native sin. Fearfully real and practical it all was; but he saw it all dimly as in a dream. Before his eyes one face was shining; in his ears one silvery voice was ringing. … "He is a monk, and knows no better. …" True! And how should he know better? How could he tell how much more there was to know, in that great new universe, in such a cranny whereof his life had till now been past? He had heard but one side already. What if there were two sides? Had he not a right—that is, was it not proper, fair, prudent, that he should hear both, and then judge?

Cyril had hardly, perhaps, done wisely for the youth in sending him out about the practical drudgery of benevolence, before deciding for him what was his duty with regard to Hypatia's invitation. He had not calculated on the new thoughts which were tormenting the young monk; perhaps they would have been unintelligible to him had he known of them. Cyril had been bred up under the most stern dogmatic training, in those vast monastic establishments, which had arisen amid the neighbouring saltpetre quarries of Nitria, where thousands toiled in voluntary poverty and starvation at vast bakeries, dyeries, brick-fields, tailors' shops, carpenters' yards, and expended the profits of their labour, not on themselves, for they had need of nothing, but on churches, hospitals, and alms. Educated in that world of practical industrial production as well as of religious exercise, which by its proximity to the great city accustomed monks to that world which they despised; entangled from boyhood in the intrigues of his fierce and ambitious uncle Theophilus, Cyril had succeeded him in the patriarchate of Alexandria without having felt a doubt, and stood free to throw his fiery energy and clear practical intellect into the cause of the Church without scruple, even, where necessary, without pity. How could such a man sympathise with the poor boy of twenty, suddenly dragged forth from the quiet cavern-shadow of the Laura into the full blaze and roar of the world's noonday? He, too, was cloister-bred. But the busy and fanatic atmosphere of Nitria, where every nerve of soul and body was kept on a lifelong artificial strain, without rest, without simplicity, without human affection, was utterly antipodal to the government of the remote and needy, though no less industrious commonwealths of Coenobites, who dotted the lonely mountain-glens, far up into the heart of the Nubian desert. In such a one Philammon had received, from a venerable man, a mother's sympathy as well as a father's care; and now he yearned for the encouragement of a gentle voice, for the greeting of a kindly eye, and was lonely and sick at heart. … And still Hypatia's voice haunted his ears, like a strain of music, and would not die away. That lofty enthusiasm, so sweet and modest in its grandeur—that tone of pity—in one so lovely it could not be called contempt—for the many; that delicious phantom of being an elect spirit, unlike the crowd. … "And am I altogether like the crowd?" said Philammon to himself, as he staggered along under the weight of a groaning fever-patient. "Can there be found no fitter work for me than this, which any porter from the quay might do as well? Am I not somewhat wasted on such toil as this? Have I not an intellect, a taste, a reason? I could appreciate what she said.—Why should not my faculties be educated? Why am I only to be shut out from knowledge? There is a Christian Gnosis as well as a heathen one. What was permissible to Clement"—he had nearly said to Origen, but checked himself on the edge of heresy—"is surely lawful for me! Is not my very craving for knowledge a sign that I am capable of it? Surely my sphere is the study rather than the street!"

===Chinese===
区利罗（Cyril）静静地微笑着，听菲拉蒙（Philammon）讲了事情的经过，也收下了希帕蒂娅（Hypatia）的口信，随后便打发这少年去城里做一下午的劳作，嘱咐他对所发生的事只字不提，傍晚再到他那里去领命——他要等有了斟酌的时间再作决断。于是菲拉蒙便跟着同伴们出去了，穿过一条条污秽贫穷的小巷与弄堂，那里满是被迫的游手好闲和与生俱来的罪孽。这一切可怕地真实、可怕地切近；可他却像在梦中一样，看什么都模模糊糊。他眼前只有一张脸在发光；他耳中只有一个银铃般的声音在回响。……「他是个修士，不懂得更好的。」是啊！他又怎能懂得更好的呢？他怎知道，在那个崭新的浩瀚宇宙里——他此前的半生便是在它某个偏僻的角落度过的——还有多少是他所不知道的呢？他至今只听过一面之词。倘若还有另一面呢？他难道没有权利——也就是说，让他兼听两面、然后再作判断，岂不是妥当的、公允的、审慎的么？

区利罗在替这少年决断他对希帕蒂娅邀约该尽何等本分之前，先打发他出去干些慈善的粗活，这做法恐怕未必明智。他没有料到那些正折磨着这年轻修士的新念头；就算知道，恐怕也难以理解。区利罗是在最严苛的教条训练下调教出来的，那是在尼特拉（Nitria）附近的硝石采石场间兴起的庞大修院群落里，那里有数以千计的人自愿守贫挨饿，在巨大的面包房、染坊、砖窑、裁缝铺、木匠作坊里劳作，而把劳作所得的利润，不花在自己身上——因为他们一无所需——而是花在教会、医院和施舍上。他既在那兼有实际工业生产与宗教操行的世界里受过教育——那地方紧邻大城，使修士们习于他们所鄙视的那个世俗世界；又自幼卷入他那位凶狠而野心勃勃的叔父提奥菲鲁斯（Theophilus）的种种阴谋——区利罗便这样毫无疑虑地继其叔之后登上了亚历山大城的宗主教之位，得以毫无顾忌、必要时甚至毫无怜悯地，将他炽烈的精力与清明务实的才智投入教会的事业。这样的人，又怎能体恤一个二十岁的可怜少年，突然被从劳拉那幽静的洞穴阴影里拖出来，抛入这世界正午的烈焰与喧嚣之中呢？他自己也是在修院里长大的。可尼特拉那忙碌而狂热的空气——在那里，灵魂与肉体的每一根神经都被终身置于一种人为的紧张之中，没有安息，没有纯朴，没有人的情爱——与那些遥远而贫苦、却同样勤勉的独居修士团体（Coenobites）的治理之道，截然相反；那些团体星罗棋布地散落在孤独的山间幽谷里，远至努比亚（Nubian）沙漠腹地。菲拉蒙所来的，正是那样一个团体，他从一位可敬的长者那里，既受了慈母般的体恤，也得着严父般的照拂；而此刻，他渴望一个温柔声音的鼓励，渴望一道和善目光的致意，他孤独，他心里发闷。……而希帕蒂娅的声音仍如一缕乐音，萦绕在他耳畔，挥之不去。那崇高的热忱，在其壮美之中如此甘美而谦逊；那怜悯的声调——出自如此美丽的人口中，便算不得轻蔑——对芸芸众生的怜悯；那甘美的幻影：他是个蒙选的灵，与芸芸众生不同。……「我当真与他们全然相同么？」菲拉蒙背负着一个呻吟的热病病人、踉跄前行时，自言自语道。「难道就找不出比这更适合我的活计么？这活儿码头上的任何一个苦力都能干得一样好。我干这种苦工，岂不是有些浪费？我难道没有理智、没有趣味、没有理性么？她说的那些话，我是能够领会的。——为什么我的心智就不该受到栽培？为什么唯独我要被拒于知识之外？既有异教的灵知（Gnosis），也有基督教的灵知啊。对克莱门特（Clement）所许可的——」他险些说出对奥利金（Origen）所许可的，却在异端的边缘硬生生收住了口——「对我自然也是合法的！我对知识的这份渴慕本身，岂不正是我能承受它的凭据么？我的天地分明是书房，而不是街头！」

===Original===
And then his fellow-labourers—he could not deny it to himself—began to grow less venerable in his eyes. Let him try as he might to forget the old priest's grumblings and detractions, the fact was before him. The men were coarse, fierce, noisy … so different from her! Their talk seemed mere gossip—scandalous too, and hard-judging, most of it; about that man's private ambition, and that woman's proud looks; and who had stayed for the Eucharist the Sunday before, and who had gone out after the sermon; and how the majority who did not stay could possibly dare to go, and how the minority who did not go could possibly dare to stay. … Endless suspicions, sneers, complaints … what did they care for the eternal glories and the beatific vision? Their one test for all men and things, from the patriarch to the prefect, seemed to be—did he or it advance the cause of the Church?—which Philammon soon discovered to mean their own cause, their influence, their self-glorification. And the poor boy, as his faculty for faultfinding quickened under the influence of theirs, seemed to see under the humble stock-phrases in which they talked of their labours of love, and the future reward of their present humiliations, a deep and hardly-bidden pride, a faith in their own infallibility, a contemptuous impatience of every man, however venerable, who differed from their party on any, the slightest, matter. They spoke with sneers of Augustine's Latinising tendencies, and with open execrations of Chrysostom, as the vilest and most impious of schismatics; and, for aught Philammon knew, they were right enough. But when they talked of wars and desolation past and impending, without a word of pity for the slain and ruined, as a just judgment of Heaven upon heretics and heathens; when they argued over the awful struggle for power which, as he gathered from their words, was even then pending between the Emperor and the Count of Africa, as if it contained but one question of interest to them—would Cyril, and they as his bodyguard, gain or lose power in Alexandria? and lastly, when at some mention of Orestes, and of Hypatia as his counsellor, they broke out into open imprecations of God's curse, and comforted themselves with the prospect of everlasting torment for both; he shuddered and asked himself involuntarily—were these the ministers of a Gospel?—were these the fruits of Christ's Spirit? … And a whisper thrilled through the inmost depth of his soul—"Is there a Gospel? Is there a Spirit of Christ? Would not their fruits be different from these?"

Faint, and low, and distant, was that whisper, like the mutter of an earthquake miles below the soil. And yet, like the earthquake-roll, it had in that one moment jarred every belief, and hope, and memory of his being each a hair's-breadth from its place. … Only one hair's-breadth. But that was enough; his whole inward and outward world changed shape, and cracked at every joint. What if it were to fall in pieces? His brain reeled with the thought. He doubted his own identity. The very light of heaven had altered its hue. Was the firm ground on which he stood after all no solid reality, but a fragile shell which covered—what?

The nightmare vanished, and he breathed once more. What a strange dream! The sun and the exertion must have made him giddy. He would forget all about it.

===Chinese===
于是他的同伴们——他无法对自己否认——在他眼中开始显得不那么可敬了。任他怎样努力忘却那老神父的牢骚与毁谤，事实毕竟摆在那里。这些人粗鄙、凶悍、聒噪……与她是何等不同！他们的谈话似乎不过是些闲言碎语——而且大多是在搬弄是非、苛责论断：论到某人的私心野心，某妇人的傲慢神色；论到上个主日谁留下来领了圣餐（Eucharist）、谁听了讲道便走了出去；又论到那些未曾留下的大多数怎敢擅自离去，而那些未曾离去的少数又怎敢擅自留下。……无尽的猜疑、讥诮、怨言……他们哪里在乎那永恒的荣耀与那荣福的异象（beatific vision）呢？他们衡量一切人事的唯一尺子——从宗主教到总督（prefect）——似乎是：他或它是否促进了教会的事业？——而菲拉蒙很快便发现，那无非是他们自己的事业、他们的影响力、他们自我荣耀的工具。这可怜的少年，在他人的影响下，自己找岔的本事也跟着灵敏起来，他似乎看透了：在他们用以谈论自己爱心劳作、谈论自己今日屈辱将来必得赏赐的那一套谦卑套话底下，藏着一种根深蒂固、难以抑制的骄傲，一种对自己绝无谬误的信心，一种对凡与本党有丝毫分歧之人——无论他多么可敬——所抱的轻蔑的不耐。他们带着讥诮谈论奥古斯丁（Augustine）的拉丁化倾向，又公然咒诅屈梭多模（Chrysostom），视其为最卑劣、最不敬的分裂派；就菲拉蒙所知，他们也许并不算错。可当他们谈论已成过往的与将要临到的战乱与荒芜，对那些被杀被灭之人竟无半句怜悯，只当作上天对异端与异教徒的公义审判；当他们议论着——据他听话中之意——当时正在皇帝与非洲伯爵（the Count of Africa）之间酝酿的那场争夺权力的可怕斗争，仿佛其中对他们唯有唯一值得关心的问题：区利罗、以及身为他扈从的他们，在亚历山大城里是得势还是失势？最后，当他们一提到俄瑞斯忒斯（Orestes）、提到希帕蒂娅是他的谋臣，便公然祈求上帝的咒诅降在他们身上，又以二人将受永刑的前景来自慰——这时他战栗起来，不由自主地问自己：这些人，难道就是那福音的执事么？——这些，难道就是基督之灵（Christ's Spirit）所结的果子么？……有一个低语，颤栗着掠过他灵魂的最深处——「果真有福音么？果真有基督之灵么？它的果子，岂不该与这些全然不同么？」

那低语，又微弱，又低沉，又遥远，仿佛在地下数英里深处隆隆作响的地震。然而，正如地震的滚动，它就在那一瞬间，把他每一样信念、每一样盼望、每一样记忆，都从原处震开了一发之差。……只是一发之差。可这便够了；他整个内在与外在的世界都变了形，处处接缝都裂开了口。倘若它整个坍塌下来，又将如何？一念及此，他脑中一阵眩晕。他怀疑起自己的本相来。连天上的光，也变了颜色。他所站立的那块实地，难道终究不是什么坚固的现实，而不过是一层薄薄的脆壳，其下覆盖着——什么？

那场噩梦消散了，他重新喘过气来。好一场怪梦！必是日头和劳顿叫他的头发了晕。他要把这一切统统忘掉。

===Original===
Weary with labour, and still wearier with thought, he returned that evening, longing and yet dreading to be permitted to speak with Hypatia. He half hoped at moments that Cyril might think him too weak for it; and the next, all his pride and daring, not to say his faith and hope, spurred him on. Might he but face the terrible enchantress, and rebuke her to her face! And yet so lovely, so noble as she looked! Could he speak to her, except in tones of gentle warning, pity, counsel, entreaty? Might he not convert her—save her? Glorious thought! to win such a soul to the true cause! To be able to show, as the firstfruits of his mission, the very champion of heathendom! It was worth while to have lived only to do that; and having done it, to die.

The archbishop's lodgings, when he entered them, were in a state of ferment even greater than usual. Groups of monks, priests, parabolani, and citizens rich and poor, were banging about the courtyard, talking earnestly and angrily. A large party of monks fresh from Nitria, with ragged hair and beards, and the peculiar expression of countenance which fanatics of all creeds acquire, fierce and yet abject, self-conscious and yet ungoverned, silly and yet sly, with features coarsened and degraded by continual fasting and self-torture, prudishly shrouded from head to heel in their long ragged gowns, were gesticulating wildly and loudly, and calling on their more peaceable companions, in no measured terms, to revenge some insult offered to the Church.

===Chinese===
他那天傍晚回来时，身因劳作而倦，心因思虑而更倦，既盼望、又害怕获准与希帕蒂娅一谈。他时而甚至巴望区利罗会嫌他太过软弱、不堪此任；可下一刻，他全部的骄傲与胆气——更不用说他的信心与盼望——又策马般催他向前。但愿他能直面那可怕的妖姬，当面斥责她！可她又显得那样美、那样高贵！他对她说话，岂能不用温柔的告诫、怜悯、劝导与恳求的口吻？他难道不能归化她——拯救她？光荣的念头啊！竟能赢得这样一颗灵魂归入真理的事业！竟能拿出异教世界的头号护法，作为他使命的初熟果子！单为这一桩，便值得活这一场；既做成了，便死也甘心。

他踏进大主教的寓所时，那里正处于比平日更加鼎沸的骚动之中。一群群的修士、神父、抚慰弟兄会（parabolani）的成员，以及贫富各色的市民，在院子里挤来挤去，谈得又恳切又激愤。一大群刚从尼特拉下来的修士，须发蓬乱，带着一切教派的狂热者所共有的那种独特的面相——既凶狠又卑微，既自知又失控，既愚昧又狡黠——因长年禁食与自虐而粗糙、堕落了的五官，拘谨地从头顶到脚跟裹在他们长长的破袍子里，正狂乱地、大声地比划着、叫嚷着，用极不客气的言辞，呼喊他们较为平和的同伴去为教会所受的某桩侮辱复仇。

===Original===
"What is the matter?" asked Philammon of a quiet portly citizen, who stood looking up, with a most perplexed visage, at the windows of the patriarch's apartments.

"Don't ask me; I have nothing to do with it. Why does not his holiness come out and speak to them? Blessed virgin, mother of God! that we were well through it all!—"

"Coward!" bawled a monk in his ear. "These shopkeepers care for nothing but seeing their stalls safe. Rather than lose a day's custom, they would give the very churches to be plundered by the heathen!"

"We do not want them!" cried another. "We managed Dioscuros and his brother, and we can manage Orestes. What matter what answer he sends? The devil shall have his own!"

"They ought to have been back two hours ago: they are murdered by this time."

"He would not dare to touch the archdeacon!"

"He will dare anything. Cyril should never have sent them forth as lambs among wolves. What necessity was there for letting the prefect know that the Jews were gone? He would have found it out for himself fast enough, the next time he wanted to borrow money."

===Chinese===
「出了什么事？」菲拉蒙问一位安静敦厚的市民，那人正一脸茫然地仰望着宗主教住所的窗户。

「别问我；这事与我无干。圣座怎么不出来对他们说几句话呢？童贞圣母、上帝之母啊！但愿我们能平平安安地熬过这一切！——」

「懦夫！」一个修士在他耳边咆哮。「这些开店的人只惦着他们摊子的安稳。宁可让教会本身被异教徒洗劫，也不肯少做一天生意！」

「我们才不需要他们！」另一个嚷道。「我们收拾了狄奥斯科鲁斯（Dioscuros）兄弟，也能收拾俄瑞斯忒斯。他回什么话有何打紧？魔鬼自该收下他的同类！」

「他们两个时辰前便该回来了：这会儿怕是已经遭了毒手。」

「他不敢动会吏长（archdeacon）一根毫毛！」

「他什么都敢干。区利罗根本不该把他们像羔羊一般送进狼群。何必非让总督知道犹太人已经走了呢？等他下一回想借钱时，自然便会发觉。」

===Original===
"What is all this about, reverend sir?" asked Philammon of Peter the Reader, who made his appearance at that moment in the quadrangle, walking with great strides, like the soul of Agamemnon across the meads of Asphodel, and apparently beside himself with rage.

"Ah! you here? You may go tomorrow, young fool! The patriarch can't talk to you. Why should he? Some people have a great deal too much notice taken of them, in my opinion. Yes; you may go. If your head is not turned already, you may go and get it turned tomorrow. We shall see whether he who exalts himself is not abased, before all is over!" And he was striding away, when Philammon, at the risk of an explosion, stopped him.

"His holiness commanded me to see him, sir, before—"

Peter turned on him in a fury. "Fool! will you dare to intrude your fantastical dreams on him at such a moment as this?"

"He commanded me to see him," said Philammon, with the true soldierlike discipline of a monk; "and see him I will in spite of any man. I believe in my heart you wish to keep me from his counsels and his blessing."

Peter looked at him for a moment with a right wicked expression, and then, to the youth's astonishment, struck him full in the face, and yelled for help.

If the blow had been given by Pambo in the Laura a week before, Philammon would have borne it. But from that man, and coming unexpectedly as the finishing stroke to all his disappointment and disgust, it was intolerable; and in an instant Peter's long legs were sprawling on the pavement, while he bellowed like a bull for all the monks in Nitria.

===Chinese===
「这到底是怎么回事，可敬的先生？」菲拉蒙问读经员彼得（Peter the Reader），那人此刻正好走进院中，迈着大步，活像阿伽门农（Agamemnon）的灵魂走过常春花草地，一副怒不可遏的模样。

「啊！你在这儿？你明天可以走了，小傻子！宗主教顾不上跟你说话。他何必跟你说话？依我看，有些人被人瞧得太起，已远远过了头。是了；你可以走了。你那脑袋要是还没被冲昏，明天尽管去让它冲昏好了。咱们走着瞧，凡自高的，临到末了必降为卑！」他正要大步走开，菲拉蒙冒着惹他发作的危险，拦住了他。

「圣座吩咐过我，此前要见他——」

彼得勃然大怒，转过身来：「蠢货！这种时候你还敢拿你那些痴人说梦来缠他？」

「他吩咐过我，要见他，」菲拉蒙说，带着修士那种真正的兵卒般的纪律；「无论是谁拦阻，我也要见他。我心里确信，你是要阻挡我领受他的指教和祝福。」

彼得带着一种着实恶毒的神情看了他片刻，随即——令这少年大吃一惊——一拳直打在他脸上，一面高声呼救。

若是这一拳在一周前由劳拉里的庞波（Pambo）打来，菲拉蒙也就忍了。可出拳的是这个人，又来得这样猝不及防，作为他一路失望与厌恶的总收尾，他再也按捺不住；转眼之间，彼得的长腿已经四仰八叉地摊倒在石板上，而他则像公牛一般怒吼，直呼唤尼特拉所有的修士前来救他。

===Original===
A dozen lean brown hands were at Philammon's throat as Peter rose. "Seize him! hold him!" half blubbered he. "The traitor! the heretic! He holds communion with heathens!"

"Down with him!" "Cast him out! Carry him to the archbishop!" while Philammon shook himself free, and Peter returned to the charge.

"I call all good Catholics to witness! He has beaten an ecclesiastic in the courts of the Lord's house, even in the midst of thee, O Jerusalem! And he was in Hypatia's lecture-room this morning!"

A groan of pious horror rose. Philammon set his back against the wall.

"His holiness the patriarch sent me."

"He confesses, he confesses! He deluded the piety of the patriarch into letting him go, under colour of converting her; and even now he wants to intrude on the sacred presence of Cyril, burning only with the carnal desire that he may meet the sorceress in her house tomorrow!"

"Scandal!" "Abomination in the holy place!" and a rush at the poor youth took place.

His blood was thoroughly up. The respectable part of the crowd, as usual in such cases, prudently retreated, and left him to the mercy of the monks, with an eye to their own reputation for orthodoxy, not to mention their personal safety; and he had to help himself as he could. He looked round for a weapon. There was none. The ring of monks were baying at him like hounds round a bear: and though he might have been a match for any one of them singly, yet their sinewy limbs and determined faces warned him that against such odds the struggle would be desperate.

===Chinese===
彼得爬起来时，已有十来只精瘦棕黑的手扼住了菲拉蒙的喉咙。「抓住他！按住他！」他半哭半嚷。「叛徒！异端！他跟异教徒有来往！」

「揍他！」「把他扔出去！押到大主教那里去！」菲拉蒙奋力挣脱，彼得又再扑上前来。

「我请一切善良的公教信徒作证！他竟在主殿的院子里殴打了一位教职人员——耶路撒冷啊，就在你当中！而且他今早还在希帕蒂娅的讲学堂里！」

一阵虔诚的惊骇之呻吟四起。菲拉蒙把背抵住墙。

「圣座宗主教差我来的。」

「他招了，他招了！他用归化那女人为名，哄骗了宗主教的敬虔，骗得放他去；如今他还要闯到区利罗的圣驾跟前，满心所烧着的，不过是那明天到那妖妇家中与她相会的肉欲！」

「大逆不道！」「圣地之中的可憎之事！」众人便向这可怜的少年一拥而上。

他的血已全然沸腾起来。人群中那一群体面的，在这种场合照例都谨慎地退了开去，听任修士们处置他——一则顾着自己正统的名声，二则也顾着自家性命安危；他只得尽力自救。他四下张望想寻件兵器。却没有。那圈修士像一群猎犬围着一头熊，向他狂吠；他纵能单打独斗胜过其中任何一人，可那一身身青筋盘结的肢体、一张张决绝的面孔，都在警告他：以一敌众，这一场必是拼死之斗。

===Original===
"Let me leave this court in safety! God knows whether I am a heretic; and to Him I commit my cause! The holy patriarch shall know of your iniquity. I will not trouble you; I give you leave to call me heretic, or heathen, if you will, if I cross this threshold till Cyril himself sends for me back to shame you."

And he turned, and forced his way to the gate, amid a yell of derision which brought every drop of blood in his body into his cheeks. Twice, as he went down the vaulted passage, a rush was made on him from behind, but the soberer of his persecutors checked it. Yet he could not leave them, young and hotheaded as he was, without one last word, and on the threshold he turned.

"You! who call yourselves the disciples of the Lord, and are more like the demoniacs who abode day and night in the tombs, crying and cutting themselves with stones—"

In an instant they rushed upon him; and, luckily for him, rushed also into the arms of a party of ecclesiastics, who were hurrying inwards from the street, with faces of blank terror.

"He has refused!" shouted the foremost. "He declares war against the Church of God!"

"Oh, my friends," panted the archdeacon, "we are escaped like the bird out of the snare of fowler. The tyrant kept us waiting two hours at his palace-gates, and then sent lictors out upon us, with rods and axes, telling us that they were the only message which he had for robbers and rioters."

"Back to the patriarch!" and the whole mob streamed in again, leaving Philammon alone in the street—and in the world.

Whither now?

===Chinese===
「让我平平安安地离开这院子！我是不是异端，上帝知道；我的案子，我交托给祂！你们的恶行，圣座宗主教自会知晓。我不必与你们纠缠；我许你们称我为异端、为异教徒，悉听尊便——只要我跨过这道门槛，直至区利罗亲自召我回来羞辱你们之时。」

他转身，硬挤到门口，一片嘲骂的嚎叫顿时把他全身上下每一滴血都涌到了脸上。在那拱顶的过道里，他身后两度有人扑来，却被那些较为清醒的施虐者阻住了。可他到底年轻气盛，临走不能不撂下最后一句，于是在门槛上又转过身来。

「你们！自称是主的门徒，却更像那些昼夜住在坟茔里、又喊叫、又用石头砍自己的鬼附之人——」

转眼间他们已一拥而上；而于他幸运的是，也正一拥而上地撞进了另一群教职人员的怀抱——那些人正满脸煞白地惊惶，从街上匆匆赶进来。

「他拒绝了！」当先一个喊道。「他向上帝的教会宣战了！」

「噢，我的朋友们，」会吏长喘着气说，「我们已像鸟儿逃脱了捕鸟人的罗网。那暴君在宫门口叫我们干等了两个时辰，然后放出执笞棒斧钺的扈从来对付我们，告诉我们：对于那些强盗和暴民，这便是他唯一的口信。」

「回宗主教那里去！」整个人群又潮水般涌了回去，把菲拉蒙一个人撇在了街上——也撇在了这世上。

如今向何处去呢？

===Original===
He strode on in his wrath some hundred yards or more before he asked himself that question. And when he asked it, he found himself in no humour to answer it. He was adrift, and blown out of harbour upon a shoreless sea, in utter darkness; all heaven and earth were nothing to him. He was alone in the blindness of anger.

Gradually one fixed idea, as a light-tower, began to glimmer through the storm. … To see Hypatia, and convert her. He had the patriarch's leave for that. That must be right. That would justify him—bring him back, perhaps, in a triumph more glorious than any Caesar's, leading captive, in the fetters of the Gospel, the Queen of Heathendom. Yes, there was that left, for which to live.

His passion cooled down gradually as he wandered on in the fading evening light, up one street and down another, till he had utterly lost his way. What matter? He should find that lecture-room tomorrow at least. At last he found himself in a broad avenue, which he seemed to know. Was that the Sun-gate in the distance? He sauntered carelessly down it, and found himself at last on the great Esplanade, whither the little porter had taken him three days before. He was close then to the Museum, and to her house. Destiny had led him, unconsciously, towards the scene of his enterprise. It was a good omen; he would go thither at once. He might sleep upon her doorstep as well as upon any other. Perhaps he might catch a glimpse of her going out or coming in, even at that late hour. It might be well to accustom himself to the sight of her. There would be the less chance of his being abashed tomorrow before those sorceress eyes. And moreover, to tell the truth, his self-dependence, and his self-will too, crushed, or rather laid to sleep, by the discipline of the Laura, had started into wild life, and gave him a mysterious pleasure, which he had not felt since he was a disobedient little boy, of doing what he chose, right or wrong, simply because he chose it. Such moments come to every free-willed creature. Happy are those who have not, like poor Philammon, been kept by a hotbed cultivation from knowing how to face them? But he had yet to learn, or rather his tutors had to learn, that the sure path toward willing obedience and manful self-restraint, lies not through slavery, but through liberty.

===Chinese===
他在盛怒之中大步前行了百来码开外，才向自己提出这个问题。而待他问出时，却全无心情去作答。他已是随波逐流，被吹出了港湾，漂泊在无边无际、漆黑一片的大海上；天地万物于他皆已无谓。他独自一人，困在愤怒的盲目之中。

渐渐地，一个固定的念头，像一座灯塔，开始在风暴里若隐若现。……去见希帕蒂娅，去归化她。这件事他有宗主教的许可。那必定是对的。那便能为他正名——也许还能领着他凯旋而归，那荣耀胜过任何一个凯撒（Caesar）的凯旋，让他用福音的锁链，牵着那异教世界的女王为俘虏。是的，还留下这一件事，值得他为之而活。

他在渐渐暗淡的暮色里，从一条街踅到另一条街，怒气渐渐平息下来，直走到彻底迷了路。那有何妨？至少明天他总能找到那座讲学堂。末了，他来到一条宽阔的大道上，似觉眼熟。远处那莫不是日城门（the Sun-gate）么？他漫不经心地踱了下去，终于走到了那片大游廊（Esplanade）上——三日之前，那个小门房便是领着他到这里来的。这么说来，他已离博物院（Museum），离她的家，近在咫尺了。命运在不知不觉间，已把他引到了他那番事业的现场。这是吉兆；他要立刻就去那里。他睡在她家门槛上，与睡在别处并无二致。说不定，纵然夜已深，他还能瞥见她进出。先让自己看惯她的模样，也许是好的。这样，明天在那双妖眼之前，他心慌意乱的可能便小些。再者，老实说，他那自立之心——以及他那自行其是之心——本已被劳拉的纪律压垮，或者毋宁说催眠了，此刻却野性复萌，给他带来了一种神秘的快意：做着自己所选择的事，不论对错，只因为是他自己所选的——这种快意，自从他还是个不听话的小男孩以来，便从未尝过。这样的时刻，凡有自由意志的生灵都难免经历。那些人，不像可怜的菲拉蒙这般被温室的栽培所误、竟不知如何面对此等时刻，岂不是有福的么？不过，他尚有待学得一课——或者说，他的老师们尚有待学得一课——那通往甘心顺服与丈夫般自制之可靠道路，并不在奴役之中，而在自由之中。

===Original===
He was not certain which was Hypatia's house; but the door of the Museum he could not forget. So there he sat himself down under the garden wall, soothed by the cool night, and the holy silence, and the rich perfume of the thousand foreign flowers which filled the air with enervating balm. There he sat and watched, and watched, and watched in vain for some glimpse of his one object. Which of the houses was hers? Which was the window of her chamber? Did it look into the street? What business had his fancy with woman's chambers? … But that one open window, with the lamp burning bright inside—he could not help looking up to it—he could not help fancying—hoping. He even moved a few yards to see better the bright interior of the room. High up as it was, he could still discern shelves of books—pictures on the walls. Was that a voice? Yes! a woman's voice—reading aloud in metre—was plainly distinguishable in the dead stillness of the night, which did not even awaken a whisper in the trees above his head. He stood, spellbound by curiosity.

Suddenly the voice ceased, and a woman's figure came forward to the window, and stood motionless, gazing upward at the spangled star-world overhead, and seeming to drink in the glory, and the silence, and the rich perfume. … Could it be she? Every pulse in his body throbbed madly. … Could it be? What was she doing? He could not distinguish the features; but the full blaze of the eastern moon showed him an upturned brow, between a golden stream of glittering tresses which hid her whole figure, except the white hands clasped upon her bosom. … Was she praying? were these her midnight sorceries? …

And still his heart throbbed and throbbed, till he almost fancied she must hear its noisy beat—and still she stood motionless, gazing upon the sky, like some exquisite chryselephantine statue, all ivory and gold. And behind her, round the bright room within, painting, books, a whole world of unknown science and beauty … and she the priestess of it all … inviting him to learn of her and be wise! It was a temptation! He would flee from it!—Fool that he was!—and it might not be she after all!

He made some sudden movement. She looked down, saw him, and shutting the blind, vanished for the night. In vain, now that the temptation had departed, he sat and waited for its reappearance, half cursing himself for having broken the spell. But the chamber was dark and silent henceforth; and Philammon, wearied out, found himself soon wandering back to the Laura in quiet dreams, beneath the balmy, semi-tropic night.

===Chinese===
他拿不准哪一处是希帕蒂娅的宅子；可博物院的大门他是忘不了的。于是他就在花园墙根下坐定，被清凉的夜色、被圣洁的寂静、被那千万株异国花卉沁人欲醉的浓香所抚慰。他就那样坐着守望，望了又望，却望不见那唯一身影的半点踪影。那几所宅子，哪一处是她的？哪一扇是她闺房的窗？那窗子是不是朝着街？他的心思怎竟与女子的闺房牵扯起来？……可是那一扇敞开的窗，里面灯亮得通明——他禁不住抬头望它——他禁不住去想——去盼望。他甚至挪动了几步，好把那灯光明亮的室内看得更清。那窗虽高，他仍依稀辨得出一架一架的书——墙上的画。那是声音么？是了！一个女子的声音——在按着韵律诵读——在这死寂的夜里清晰可辨，连他头顶树梢上的一声细语都未被它惊起。他站着，被好奇心所惑住，如中咒语。

忽然那声音停了，一个女子的身影走上窗前，一动不动地站着，仰望头顶那繁星点缀的星空，仿佛在饮尽那光辉、那寂静、那浓香。……莫非是她？他身上每一下脉搏都狂乱地跳动起来。……莫非是她？她在做什么？他辨不清她的面貌；可东方满月的光华，照给他看一张仰起的脸，夹在两股闪闪发光的金色发流之间，那发流遮住了她整个身形，唯有交握在胸前的一双白手露在外面。……她在祷告么？这就是她半夜的巫术么？……

他的心仍是一下接一下地跳，跳得他几乎以为她必能听见那咚咚的声响——她仍一动不动地站着，凝视着天空，像一尊精妙绝伦的黄金象牙神像（chryselephantine statue），通身是象牙与黄金。在她身后、那明亮的房间四壁之间，是画作、是书籍、是一整个他所不知的科学之世界、美之世界……而她便是这一切的女祭司……邀请他前去向她求学，得以有智！这是试探！他要逃离它！——他真是个傻瓜！——况且那也许根本不是她呢！

他忽然动了一下。她低下头，看见了他，随即放下帘子，那夜便隐去了。那试探既已离去，他坐在那里干等它再现，却是徒然，半是懊恼自己打断了那道魔咒。但那间内室从此便漆黑寂静了；菲拉蒙疲倦已极，在这馥郁的亚热带之夜下，不知不觉便神游起来，在恬静的梦里回到了那遥远的劳拉。

## X / X

### The Interview / 接见

===Original===
Philammon was aroused from his slumbers at sunrise the next morning by the attendants who came in to sweep out the lecture-rooms, and wandered, disconsolately enough, up and down the street; longing for, and yet dreading, the three weary hours to be over which must pass before he would be admitted to Hypatia. But he had tasted no food since noon the day before: he had but three hours’ sleep the previous night, and had been working, running, and fighting for two whole days without a moment’s peace of body or mind. Sick with hunger and fatigue, and aching from head to foot with his hard night’s rest on the granite-flags, he felt as unable as man could well do to collect his thoughts or brace his nerves for the coming interview. How to get food he could not guess; but having two hands, he might at least earn a coin by carrying a load; so he went down to the Esplanade in search of work. Of that, alas! there was none. So he sat down upon the parapet of the quay, and watched the shoals of sardines which played in and out over the marble steps below, and wondered at the strange crabs and sea-locusts which crawled up and down the face of the masonry, a few feet below the surface, scrambling for bits of offal, and making occasional fruitless dashes at the nimble little silver arrows which played round them. And at last his whole soul, too tired to think of anything else, became absorbed in a mighty struggle between two great crabs, who held on stoutly, each by a claw, to his respective bunch of seaweed, while with the others they tugged, one at the head and the other at the tail of a dead fish. Which would conquer?﻿﻿ … Ay, which? And for five minutes Philammon was alone in the world with the two struggling heroes.﻿﻿ … Might not they be emblematic? Might not the upper one typify Cyril?—the lower one Hypatia?—and the dead fish between, himself?﻿﻿ … But at last the deadlock was suddenly ended—the fish parted in the middle; and the typical Hypatia and Cyril, losing hold of their respective seaweeds by the jerk, tumbled down, each with its half-fish, and vanished head over heels into the blue depths in so undignified a manner, that Philammon burst into a shout of laughter.

===Chinese===
次日日出时分，菲拉蒙被进来打扫讲学堂的仆役们从睡梦中唤醒，便郁郁寡欢地在街上来回踱步；他既盼着、又怕熬过那令人疲倦的三个时辰——非等这三个时辰过去，他才能获准见希帕蒂娅（Hypatia）。可是从前一日中午起他便粒米未进；前一夜只睡了三个钟头，而整整两天里他都在劳碌、奔跑、厮打，身心不得片刻安宁。饥疲交加，又因夜里睡在花岗岩石板上而浑身酸痛，他觉得简直从来没有像此刻这般无力收拢心神、鼓起勇气去应付即将到来的会面。怎样弄到吃的，他无从猜想；但他有两只手，至少可以替人扛一扛货，挣一枚小钱；于是他朝大游廊（the Esplanade）走去，去找活干。唉，哪里有什么活儿！他便在码头的石栏上坐下，望着成群的沙丁鱼在下方大理石阶上进进出出地嬉游，惊奇地打量着那些奇异的蟹和海蝗，它们在石壁表面、水面以下几尺的地方爬上爬下，争抢着零星的残渣烂肉，时而徒劳地向那些围着自己穿梭的敏捷小银箭扑去。末了，他那颗累得无力再想别事的心，整个被两只大蟹之间的一场鏖战吸引住了——它们各用一只钳死死攥住各自的那丛海草，又各用另一只钳去争夺一条死鱼，一个拽头，一个拉尾。谁会赢呢？……是啊，谁呢？有整整五分钟，菲拉蒙与这两位挣扎中的好汉独处于天地之间。……它们莫非是个隐喻？上面那只莫非象征着区利罗（Cyril）？——下面那只是希帕蒂娅？——中间那条死鱼，便是他自己？……然而僵局终于戛然了结——那条鱼从中间断成两截；象征式的希帕蒂娅与区利罗被这一震，各自松了爪下的海草，带着各自的半条鱼一个倒栽葱跌了下去，消失在碧蓝的深处，姿态极不雅观，菲拉蒙不禁哈哈大笑，放声大叫起来。

===Original===
“What’s the joke?” asked a well-known voice behind him; and a hand patted him familiarly on the back. He looked round, and saw the little porter, his head crowned with a full basket of figs, grapes, and watermelons, on which the poor youth cast a longing eye. “Well, my young friend, and why are you not at church? Look at all the saints pouring into the Caesareum there, behind you.”

Philammon answered sulkily enough something inarticulate.

“Ho, ho! Quarrelled with the successor of the Apostles already? Has my prophecy come true, and the strong meat of pious riot and plunder proved too highly spiced for your young palate? Eh?”

Poor Philammon! Angry with himself for feeling that the porter was right; shrinking from the notion of exposing the failings of his fellow-Christians; shrinking still more from making such a jackanapes his confidant: and yet yearning in his loneliness to open his heart to someone, he dropped out, hint by hint, word by word, the events of the past evening, and finished by a request to be put in the way of earning his breakfast.

===Chinese===
「有什么好笑的？」身后一个熟悉的声音问道；一只手熟稔地在他背上拍了一下。他回过头，看见那小门房，头上顶了满满一篮无花果、葡萄和西瓜，可怜的少年眼巴巴地盯着那些果子。「喏，我的小朋友，你怎么不去教堂？瞧瞧你身后，圣徒们正鱼贯涌进凯撒里乌姆（the Caesareum）里去呢。」

菲拉蒙闷闷地咕哝了几句含混不清的话。

「嗬，嗬！这么快就跟使徒的继任者闹翻了？莫非我的预言应了验，那虔诚的暴动与劫掠的荤腥对你的嫩胃口来说太过辛辣？嗯？」

可怜的菲拉蒙！他心里明知小门房说得对，却又为此生自己的气；既不愿张扬同道基督徒的过失，更不愿把心事托付给这样一个轻佻的小丑；然而在孤独之中他又那么渴望向什么人敞开心扉，便一字一句、一点一滴地把昨夜的事抖落出来，末了请小门房替他指一条挣得早饭的路。

===Original===
“Earning your breakfast! Shall the favourite of the gods—shall the guest of Hypatia—earn his breakfast, while I have an obol to share with him? Base thought! Youth! I have wronged you. Unphilosophically I allowed, yesterday morning, envy to ruffle the ocean of my intellect. We are now friends and brothers, in hatred to the monastic tribe.”

“I do not hate them, I tell you,” said Philammon. “But these Nitrian savages—”

“Are the perfect examples of monkery, and you hate them; and therefore, all greaters containing the less, you hate all less monastic monks—I have not heard logic lectures in vain. Now, up! The sea woos our dusty limbs: Nereids and Tritons, charging no cruel coin, call us to Nature’s baths. At home a mighty sheatfish smokes upon the festive board; beer crowns the horn, and onions deck the dish; come then, my guest and brother!”

Philammon swallowed certain scruples about becoming the guest of a heathen, seeing that otherwise there seemed no chance of having anything else to swallow; and after a refreshing plunge in the sea, followed the hospitable little fellow to Hypatia’s door, where he dropped his daily load of fruit, and then into a narrow by-street, to the ground-floor of a huge block of lodgings with a common staircase, swarming with children, cats, and chickens; and was ushered by his host into a little room, where the savoury smell of broiling fish revived Philammon’s heart.

===Chinese===
「挣你的早饭！众神所宠的人——希帕蒂娅的座上客——岂能在我还有一个俄玻罗斯（obol）可与他分的时候，去挣他的早饭？卑鄙的念头！少年！我冤枉你了。昨日清晨，我真不该任凭嫉妒搅乱我心智的汪洋，这太不哲学了。如今你我已是朋友、是兄弟，一同仇恨那修士一族。」

「我跟你说了，我并不恨他们，」菲拉蒙说。「可是尼特拉（Nitria）那些野人——」

「正是修道的完美典范，所以你恨他们；既然大者包含小者，你也就恨一切较逊的修士——我听逻辑课可没白听。起来吧！大海正向我们蒙尘的肢体招手：涅瑞伊得斯（Nereids）与特里同（Tritons）不收分文，召唤我们去大自然的浴池。我家那条肥大的六须鲇已在节庆的案上冒着热气；啤酒斟满了牛角，洋葱点缀着菜肴；那么来吧，我的客人、我的兄弟！」

菲拉蒙把做异教徒座上客的几点顾虑咽了下去——因为若不如此，看来他没别的东西可咽了；在海水里爽爽快快地一浸之后，他跟着这位好客的小个子来到希帕蒂娅门前，小门房放下每日那担水果，又带他拐进一条窄巷，进了一大片带公共楼梯的出租公寓的底层；那里猫、鸡、孩子乱哄哄挤成一团；主人把他领进一间小屋，烤鱼扑鼻的香味使菲拉蒙为之一振。

===Original===
“Judith! Judith! where lingerest thou? Marble of Pentelicus! foam-flake of the wine dark main! lily of the Mareotic lake! You accursed black Andromeda, if you don’t bring the breakfast this moment, I’ll cut you in two!”

The inner door opened, and in bustled, trembling, her hands full of dishes, a tall lithe negress, dressed in true negro fashion, in a snow-white cotton shift, a scarlet cotton petticoat, and a bright yellow turban of the same, making a light in that dark place which would have served as a landmark a mile off. She put the dishes down, and the porter majestically waved Philammon to a stool; while she retreated, and stood humbly waiting on her lord and master, who did not deign to introduce to his guest the black beauty which composed his whole seraglio.﻿﻿ … But, indeed, such an act of courtesy would have been needless; for the first morsel of fish was hardly safe in poor Philammon’s mouth, when the regress rushed upon him, caught him by the head, and covered him with rapturous kisses.

Up jumped the little man with a yell, brandishing a knife in one hand and a leek in the other; while Philammon, scarcely less scandalised, jumped up too, and shook himself free of the lady, who, finding it impossible to vent her feelings further on his head, instantly changed her tactics, and, wallowing on the floor, began frantically kissing his feet.

“What is this? before my face! Up, shameless baggage, or thou diest the death!” and the porter pulled her up upon her knees.

“It is the monk! the young man I told you of, who saved me from the Jews the other night! What good angel sent him here that I might thank him?” cried the poor creature, while the tears ran down her black shining face.

===Chinese===
「犹滴！犹滴！你磨蹭到哪儿去了？彭忒利科斯（Pentelicus）的大理石！暗酒色大海的浪花！马里奥蒂斯湖（Mareotic lake）的百合！你这该死的黑皮肤的安德洛墨达（Andromeda），要你这会儿不把早饭端来，我把你劈成两半！」

里头的门开了，一个高挑柔软的黑女人哆哆嗦嗦地闯了进来，两手满满捧着菜碟；她打扮得是地道的黑人模样：雪白的棉布罩衫，猩红的棉布裙子，头上一条亮黄色的同色头巾，在这暗屋里亮得几乎一里开外都能当路标。她放下碟子，小门房庄重地挥手请菲拉蒙坐到一张小凳上；她则退到一旁，谦恭地站着侍候她的主子老爷——老爷并不屑于把他这整座后宫里唯一的黑美人介绍给客人。……其实这般客气也大可不必；因为可怜的菲拉蒙嘴里那第一口鱼还没来得及咽稳，这位黑女人便猛扑过来，一把捧住他的头，狂喜地在他脸上亲了又亲。

小个子一声大叫蹦了起来，一手挥着刀、一手挥着一根韭葱；菲拉蒙几乎同样惊骇，也跳了起来，使劲挣脱了这位女士；她见再也无法在他的头上发泄感情，当即变了招，趴在地上，疯了似的去亲他的脚。

「这是什么？当着我的面！起来，你这无耻的贱货，不然就叫你死！」小门房把她拽得跪了起来。

「这就是那个修士！就是那一夜我把你从犹太人手里救出来的那个年轻人！是什么好天使送他到这里来，好叫我向他道谢？」可怜的女人哭喊着，眼泪从她乌黑发亮的脸上直淌下来。

===Original===
“I am that good angel,” said the porter, with a look of intense self-satisfaction. “Rise, daughter of Erebus; thou art pardoned, being but a female. What says the poet?—

“‘Woman is passion’s slave, while rightful lord
						

						O’er her and passion, rules the nobler male.’﻿”

Youth! to my arms! Truly say the philosophers, that the universe is magical in itself, and by mysterious sympathies links like to like. The prophetic instinct of thy future benefits towards me drew me to thee as by an invisible warp, hawser, or chain-cable, from the moment I beheld thee. Thou went a kindred spirit, my brother, though thou knewest it not. Therefore I do not praise thee—no, nor thank thee in the least, though thou hast preserved for me the one palm which shadows my weary steps—the single lotus-flower (in this case black, not white) which blooms for me above the mud-stained ocean wastes of the Hylic Borboros. That which thou hast done, thou hast done by instinct—by divine compulsion—thou couldst no more help it than thou canst help eating that fish, and art no more to be praised for it.”

===Chinese===
「我便是那个好天使，」小门房说，满面得意之色。「起来，厄瑞玻斯（Erebus）的女儿；你被赦免了，因为你不过是个女人。诗人怎么说来着？——

「『女人是激情的奴隶，而合法的主宰——
						

　　　　统治着她与激情的，是更高贵的男性。』」

少年！投入我的怀抱吧！哲人们说得对，宇宙本身便自有其魔力，凭着神秘的同情把同类与同类相牵。你日后对我施恩的那点预言之本能，从我一见你的那一刻起，便像一根看不见的经线、缆绳、或是锚链，把我引到你身边。你原是我同气连枝的灵魂，我的兄弟，虽然你自己并不知道。所以我并不夸你——不，也一点也不谢你，尽管你替我保住了那唯一为我疲倦的脚步遮荫的棕榈——保住了那唯一一朵为我而开、绽出于泥斑斑的欲质泥沼（Hylic Borboros）之上的莲花（这一朵是黑的，不是白的）。你所做的，乃是出于本能——出于一种神圣的驱使——你禁不住不做此事，正如你禁不住不去吃那条鱼，因此并不值得称赞。」

===Original===
“Thank you,” said Philammon.

“Comprehend me. Our theory in the schools for such cases is this—has been so at least for the last six months; similar particles, from one original source, exist in you and me. Similar causes produce similar effects; our attractions, antipathies, impulses, are therefore, in similar circumstances, absolutely the same; and therefore you did the other night exactly what I should have done in your case.”

Philammon thought the latter part of the theory open to question, but he had by no means stopped eating when he rose, and his mouth was much too full of fish to argue.

===Chinese===
「多谢，」菲拉蒙说。

「你且听我说。我们学园里对这类情形的理论是这样的——至少这半年以来是如此：你与我身上都存在着同出于一本的相似微粒。相似的因生相似的果；故而我们的好恶与冲动，在相似的境况之下，便绝对地相同；所以那夜你所做的，正与你换作我时我会做的一模一样。」

菲拉蒙心里觉得这后半截理论颇可商榷，无奈他起身时并未停止进食，嘴里塞满了鱼，无从辩驳。

===Original===
“And therefore,” continued the little man, “we are to consider ourselves henceforth as one soul in two bodies. You may have the best of the corporeal part of the division﻿﻿ … yet it is the soul which makes the person. You may trust me, I shall not disdain my brotherhood. If anyone insults you henceforth, you have but to call me; and if I be within hearing, why, by this right arm—”

And he attempted a pat on Philammon’s head, which, as there was a head and shoulder’s difference between them, might on the whole have been considered, from a theatric point of view, as a failure. Whereon the little man seized the calabash of beer, and filling therewith a cow’s horn, his thumb on the small end, raised it high in the air.

“To the Tenth Muse, and to your interview with her!”

And removing his thumb, he sent a steady jet into his open mouth, and having drained the horn without drawing breath, licked his lips, handed it to Philammon, and flew ravenously upon the fish and onions.

===Chinese===
「因此，」小个子继续说道，「从此以后，你我便当看作一体而两身。你大可拿去这分配中肉身那较好的一半……然而造人的乃是灵魂。你尽可放心，我不会嫌弃这兄弟之份。从今往后若有人侮辱你，你只管唤我；我若在听得见的地方，嘿，凭这只右臂——」

他本想拍一下菲拉蒙的头，无奈两人身高差着一个头加一肩，从戏剧效果上看，这一拍大体上只能算是失败。于是小个子抓起那只盛啤酒的葫芦，用拇指堵住小口，往一只牛角里斟满了酒，高高举向空中。

「为第十位缪斯（the Tenth Muse），也为你与她的会面！」

他把拇指一松，让一道稳稳的酒柱直射进他张开的嘴里，一口气饮尽那角中酒，舔了舔嘴唇，把牛角递给菲拉蒙，自己如饿鹰扑食般地扑向鱼和洋葱。

===Original===
Philammon, to whom the whole was supremely absurd, had no invocation to make, but one which he felt too sacred for his present temper of mind: so he attempted to imitate the little man’s feat, and, of course, poured the beer into his eyes, and up his nose, and in his bosom, and finally choked himself black in the face, while his host observed smilingly—

“Aha, rustic! unacquainted with the ancient and classical customs preserved in this centre of civilisation by the descendants of Alexander’s heroes? Judith! clear the table. Now to the sanctuary of the Muses!”

Philammon rose, and finished his meal by a monkish grace. A gentle and reverent “Amen” rose from the other end of the room. It was the negress. She saw him look up at her, dropped her eyes modestly, and bustled away with the remnants, while Philammon and his host started for Hypatia’s lecture-room.

===Chinese===
菲拉蒙对这一切觉得荒唐透顶，没有什么祝祷要发，唯有一句他奉为太圣洁、不合他此刻心境的话：于是他试着学那小个子的本事，结果自然是把啤酒灌进了眼睛、灌进了鼻子、灌进了怀里，末了憋得脸发黑，几乎岔了气，而他的主人却笑吟吟地看着，说道——

「啊哈，乡下人！不晓得这文明中心由亚历山大诸英雄的后裔所保存的古代典雅风俗么？犹滴！收拾桌子。现在，向缪斯的神殿进发！」

菲拉蒙站起来，用一段修士的谢饭祷告结束了这一餐。一声温柔而虔诚的「阿们」从屋子另一头响起。是那黑女人。她见他抬头看她，便羞答答地垂下眼，收拾残局匆匆离去，菲拉蒙便与他的主人一同动身往希帕蒂娅的讲学堂去。

===Original===
“Your wife is a Christian?” asked he when they were outside the door.

“Ahem—! The barbaric mind is prone to superstition. Yet she is, being but a woman and a negress, a good soul, and thrifty, though requiring, like all lower animals, occasional chastisement. I married her on philosophic grounds. A wife was necessary to me for several reasons: but mindful that the philosopher should subjugate the material appetite, and rise above the swinish desires of the flesh, even when his nature requires him to satisfy them, I purposed to make pleasure as unpleasant as possible. I had the choice of several cripples—their parents, of ancient Macedonian family like myself, were by no means adverse; but I required a housekeeper, with whose duties the want of an arm or a leg might have interfered.”

“Why did you not marry a scold?” asked Philammon.

“Pertinently observed: and indeed the example of Socrates rose luminous more than once before my imagination. But philosophic calm, my dear youth, and the peaceful contemplation of the ineffable? I could not relinquish those luxuries. So having, by the bounty of Hypatia and her pupils, saved a small suns, I went out bought me a negress, and hired six rooms in the block we have just left, where I let lodgings to young students of the Divine Philosophy.”

“Have you any lodgers now?”

“Ahem! Certain rooms are occupied by a lady of rank. The philosopher will, above all things, abstain from babbling. To bridle the tongue, is to—But there is a closet at your service; and for the hall of reception, which you have just left—are you not a kindred and fraternal spark? We can combine our meals, as our souls are already united.”

===Chinese===
「你妻子是基督徒？」出了门，他问。

「咳——！蛮族的心性本易陷于迷信。不过她既然不过是个女人、又是个黑女人，倒是个好人，节俭会过日子，只是跟一切低等动物一样，间或需要责罚一番。我是出于哲学上的理由娶她的。我有几桩缘故非有妻子不可：但我记挂着哲学家应当制服肉体的贪欲，即使天性非满足它不可，也当凌驾于那属乎肉体的猪一般的欲望之上，于是打算使这桩乐事尽可能变得乏味。我有好几个残废可挑选——他们的父母与我一样，都是古马其顿（Macedonian）旧家，并不见得反对；可我需要一个管家的，缺一只手或一条腿，怕要误事。」

「你为何不娶一个泼妇？」菲拉蒙问。

「说得在理：的确，苏格拉底（Socrates）的榜样在我心目中也不止一次光辉地浮现。可是哲学的宁静，我亲爱的少年，对那不可言说之物的安详观照呢？这几样奢侈我却舍不得放弃。于是我凭着希帕蒂娅及其门徒的慷慨资助，攒下一小笔钱，出去买了一个黑女人，又在咱们刚才离开的那片公寓里租了六间房，分租给神圣哲学的年轻学子。」

「你眼下可有房客？」

「咳！有几间房住着一位贵妇人。哲学家最要紧的便是戒掉饶舌。勒住舌头，便是——不过这里有一个小间供你使用；至于你刚才待过的那间待客厅——你岂不是与我同气连枝的兄弟么？我们大可合起来吃饭，正如我们的灵魂已经合在一起了。」

===Original===
Philammon thanked him heartily for the offer, though he shrank from accepting it; and in ten minutes more found himself at the door of the very house which he had been watching the night before. It was she, then, whom he had seen!﻿﻿ … He was handed over by a black porter to a smart slave-girl, who guided him up, through cloisters and corridors, to the large library, where five or six young men were sitting, busily engaged, under Theon’s superintendence, in copying manuscripts and drawing geometric diagrams.

Philammon gazed curiously at these symbols of a science unknown to him, and wondered whether the day would ever come when he too would understand their mysteries; but his eyes fell again as he saw the youths staring at his ragged sheepskin and matted locks with undisguised contempt. He could hardly collect himself enough to obey the summons of the venerable old man, as he beckoned him silently out of the room, and led him, with the titters of the young students ringing in his ears, through the door by which he had entered, and along a gallery, till he stopped and knocked humbly at a door.﻿﻿ … She must be within! knocked together under him. His heart sank and sank into abysses! Poor wretch!﻿﻿ … He was half minded once to escape and dash into the street﻿﻿ … but was it not his one hope, his one object?﻿﻿ … But why did not that old man speak? If he would have but said something!﻿﻿ … If he would only have looked cross, contemptuous!﻿﻿ … But with the same impressive gravity, as of a man upon a business in which he had no voice, and wished it to be understood that he had none, the old man silently opened the door, and Philammon followed.﻿﻿ … There she was! looking more glorious than ever; more than when glowing with the enthusiasm of her own eloquence; more than when transfigured last night in golden tresses and glittering moonbeams. There she sat, without moving a finger, as the two entered. She greeted her father with a smile, which made up for all her seeming want of courtesy to him, and then fixed her large gray eyes full on Philammon.

===Chinese===
菲拉蒙真心实意地谢了他的好意，却不好意思接受；十分钟后，他已站在昨夜一直守望的那所宅子的门前。那么，昨夜他所见的，竟是她！……一个黑人门房把他交给一个俏丽的奴婢，那奴婢领着他穿过回廊与曲廊，上到那间大图书室，那里有五六个少年正坐在提昂（Theon）的监督下，忙着抄写手稿、绘制几何图形。

菲拉蒙好奇地望着这些他所不懂的科学符号，暗想是否终有一日他也能领会其中的奥秘；可一见那些少年毫不掩饰地、鄙夷地盯着他破旧的羊皮和纠结的乱发，他的眼睛又垂了下去。他几乎定不下神去听从那位令人肃然起敬的老人无声的召唤——老人默默地招手把他领出房间，在少年们窃窃的嗤笑声中，领他穿过进来时的那扇门，沿一条画廊走去，末了停下来，恭恭敬敬地叩了一扇门。……她必在里面！他膝盖在身下直打架。他的心一沉再沉，沉入无底的深渊！可怜的人啊！……他一度几乎想逃，冲到街上去……可是这岂不是他唯一的希望、唯一的目标么？……可是那老人为何不开口？他要是说句什么就好了！……他哪怕板着脸、露出不屑的神情就好了！……可那老人只是带着一种凝重的庄严——像一个受命办事、且要人明白他对这事并无发言权的人那样——默默地开了门，菲拉蒙跟了进去。……她就在那儿！比往日更为光辉照人；比她为自己口若悬河的雄辩所燃烧时更光辉；比昨夜在金发与闪烁的月光中变形时更光辉。两人进去时，她坐在那里，连一根手指都不动。她对父亲嫣然一笑——这一笑足以补偿她对他似乎失礼的一切——然后把那双灰色的大眼睛定定地投向菲拉蒙。

===Original===
“Here is the youth, my daughter. It was your wish, you know; and I always believe that you know best—”

Another smile put an end to this speech, and the old man retreated humbly toward another door, with a somewhat anxious visage, and then lingering and looking back, his hand upon the latch—

“If you require anyone, you know, you have only to call—we shall be all in the library.”

Another smile; and the old man disappeared, leaving the two alone.

===Chinese===
「这就是那个年轻人，女儿。这是你的意思，你知道；我一向相信你知道得最清楚——」

又是一笑，止住了这番话，老人面带几分忧虑，恭顺地朝另一扇门退去，又依依不舍地回头看着，手搭在门闩上——

「你要是需要人，你知道，只要唤一声——我们都在图书室里。」

又是一笑；老人便不见了，留下他们两人独处。

===Original===
Philammon stood trembling, choking, his eyes fixed on the floor. Where were all the fine things he had conned over for the occasion? He dared not look up at that face, lest it should drive them out of his head. And yet the more he kept his eyes turned from the face, the more he was conscious of it, conscious that it was watching him; and the more all the fine words were, by that very knowledge, driven out of his head.﻿﻿ … When would she speak? Perhaps she wished him to speak first. It was her duty to begin, for she had sent for him.﻿﻿ … But still she kept silence, and sat scanning him intently from head to foot, herself as motionless as a statue; her hands folded together before her, over the manuscript which lay upon her knee. If there was a blush on her cheek at her own daring, his eyes swam too much to notice it.

When would the intolerable suspense end? She was, perhaps, as unwilling to speak as he. But someone must strike the first blow: and, as often happens, the weaker party, impelled by sheer fear, struck it, and broke the silence in a tone half indignant, half apologetic—

“You sent for me hither!”

“I did. It seemed to me, as I watched you during my lecture, both before and after you were rude enough to interrupt me, that your offence was one of mere youthful ignorance. It seemed to me that your countenance bespoke a nobler nature than that which the gods are usually pleased to bestow upon monks. That I may now ascertain whether or not my surmises were correct, I ask you for what purpose are you come hither?”

===Chinese===
菲拉蒙站在那里，浑身发抖，气都透不过来，两眼盯着地板。他为这场合精心预备的那一套漂亮话都到哪里去了？他不敢抬头看那张脸，怕那脸会把它们从他脑子里赶走。然而他越是把眼睛从那张脸移开，便越意识到它，越意识到它正在注视他；而那些漂亮话也就因这意识而被赶出了他的脑子。……她什么时候才开口？也许她要他先开口。该她先开口，因为是她在召见他。……可她仍然沉默着，坐在那里目不转睛地从上到下打量他，自己则纹丝不动，如一座雕像；她的双手在身前交握，覆在膝上那卷手稿上。若说她脸上有为自己这一着胆大之举而泛起的红晕，他的眼睛也早已昏花得看不出来。

这难堪的悬念几时才是个头？也许她和他一样不愿开口。然而总得有人先打出第一拳：果然不出所料，弱的一方被纯粹的恐惧所驱使，率先动了手，以一种半是愤慨、半是抱歉的口气打破了沉默——

「是你召我到这里来的！」

「是我。我在讲学时观察你——无论在你粗暴地打断我之前还是之后——都觉得你的过错不过是年轻人的无知罢了。我觉得你的面容所昭示的，是一种比众神平日所乐于赐给修士的更高贵的本性。为要证实我的猜测是否正确，我现在问你：你到此地来，为的是什么？」

===Original===
Philammon hailed the question as a godsend.—Now for his message! And yet he faltered as he answered, with a desperate effort—“To rebuke you for your sins.”

“My sins! What sins?” she asked, as she looked up with a stately, slow surprise in those large gray eyes, before which his own glance sank abashed, he knew not why. What sins?—He knew not. Did she look like a Messalina? But was she not a heathen and a sorceress?—And yet he blushed, and stammered, and hung down his head, as, shrinking at the sound of his own words, he replied—

“The foul sorceries—and profligacy worse than sorceries, in which, they say—” He could get no farther: for he looked up again and saw an awful quiet smile upon that face. His words had raised no blush upon the marble cheek.

“They say! The bigots and slanderers; wild beasts of the desert, and fanatic intriguers, who, in the words of Him they call their master, compass heaven and earth to make one proselyte, and when they have found him, make him twofold more the child of hell than themselves. Go—I forgive you: you are young, and know not yet the mystery of the world. Science will teach you some day that the outward frame is the sacrament of the soul’s inward beauty. Such a soul I had fancied your face expressed; but I was mistaken. Foul hearts alone harbour such foul suspicions, and fancy others to be what they know they might become themselves. Go! Do I look like—? The very tapering of these fingers, if you could read their symbolism, would give your dream the lie.” And she flashed full on him, like sun-rays from a mirror, the full radiance of her glorious countenance.

===Chinese===
菲拉蒙把这问题当作天赐良机。——如今可以传他的信息了！然而他还是踌躇着，使尽全身力气答道——「为要指斥你的罪。」

「我的罪！什么罪？」她抬起头来，那双灰色的大眼睛里含着一种庄严而迟缓的惊异，他自己的目光不知为何便在这目光下羞怯地垂了下去。什么罪？——他不知道。她看起来像一个梅莎琳娜（Messalina）么？可她岂不是一个异教徒、一个女巫？——然而他还是红了脸，结结巴巴，垂下了头，一边畏缩于自己口中的话，一边答道——
