One's only hope of comfort lies in kicking feebly against the tyranny of one's own boring notions and sensations—every philosopher confesses that—and what god is logic, pray, that it is to be the sole exception?… What, old lady? I give you fair warning, you must choose this day, like any nun, between the ties of family and those of duty."

===Chinese===
可是那狗抬头望着他的脸——只有狗才会那样望着——朝废墟后面跑去，又跑回他跟前，又跑回去，直把他引了过去。

「这是怎么回事？这可真是一个厉害的新感觉！噢，物质表象的风暴与乌云啊，你们本来难道还不够多，非得把这一伙也算进你们的数目里去么？布朗！布朗！一年三百六十日，你就找不到别的一天，偏偏今日拿这些——一只——两只——三只——九只瞎眼小狗崽的尖叫声来伺候我的耳朵？」

布朗答道：一头冲进那洞里——她的新家小正在那里头打滚尖叫——叼出一只来，放在他脚边。

「不必了，我向你保证。事情是什么光景，我已经一清二楚。怎么！又一只？傻老家伙！——你也学那些贵妇人的样，以为用你自己那金贵模样的吵闹副本去连累这世界，是一件值得骄傲的事么？怎么，她要把整窝都搬出来！……我方才在想什么来着？啊——那论据是自相矛盾的，是么，因为我一面论证，一面却不得不用我所正要排斥的字眼。好。……而且——它为什么就不该自相矛盾？为什么不？这件事到底也只得认了。为什么一样东西就不能既真又假？一样东西是假的，又有什么坏处？它非真不可，又有何必要？真？真理是什么？一样东西因为不合逻辑就不好，又是何道理？到底为什么要有什么逻辑？我可曾见过哪只小虫子背上写着『逻辑』二字飞来飞去？我对它知道什么，无非是我自己心中的一种感觉——如果我有的话？凭什么这就证明我该服从它，而不是它服从我？跳蚤咬我，我便把那种感觉除去；逻辑烦我，我也把它除去。幻影必须学着知礼地退场。一个人唯一可指望的安慰，便在于对自己那些讨厌的念头与感觉的暴政作无力的踢蹬——每一位哲学家都承认这一点——请问，逻辑是什么神明，偏偏它可以独享例外？……怎么，老太太？我先警告你，你今日得像任何修女一样，在骨肉之情与本分之间选一样。」

===Original===
Bran seized him by the skirt, and pulled him down towards the puppies; took up one of the puppies and lifted it towards him; and then repeated the action with another.

"You unconscionable old brute! You don't actually dare to expect me to carry your puppies for you?" and he turned to go.

Bran sat down on her tail and began howling.

"Farewell, old dog! you have been a pleasant dream after all.… But if you will go the way of all phantasms.…" And he walked away.

Bran ran with him, leaping and barking; then recollected her family and ran back; tried to bring them, one by one, in her mouth, and then to bring them all at once; and failing sat down and howled.

"Come, Bran! Come, old girl!"

She raced halfway up to him; then halfway back again to the puppies; then towards him again: and then suddenly gave it up, and dropping her tail, walked slowly back to the blind suppliants, with a deep reproachful growl.

"——!" said Raphael with a mighty oath; "you are right after all! Here are nine things come into the world, phantasms or not, there it is; I can't deny it. They are something, and you are something, old dog; or at least like enough to something to do instead of it; and you are not I, and as good as I, and they too, for aught I know, and have as good a right to live as I; and by the seven planets and all the rest of it, I'll carry them!"

===Chinese===
布朗咬住他的衣襟，把他往小狗那边拽；叼起一只小狗，举到他跟前；然后又对另一只重复了一遍这个动作。

「你这不要脸的老畜生！你该不会当真指望我替你驮这些小狗崽吧？」他转身要走。

布朗一屁股坐到尾巴上，开始嚎叫。

「再会吧，老狗！你到底还是一场快活的梦。……只是你既执意要随一切幻影而去……」他大步走开了。

布朗跟着他跑，又蹦又叫；忽又想起她那一家子，跑回去；试着一只一只地把它们叼过来，又想一下子把它们全都叼来；都不成，便坐下来嚎叫。

「来吧，布朗！来呀，老妈！」

她朝他跑了一半；又朝小狗跑回一半；又朝他跑来：随即忽然放弃，耷拉着尾巴，慢慢地走回那些瞎眼的求告者身边，发出一声深沉的、含怨的低吼。

「——！」拉斐尔咒了一声重誓，「到底还是你对！这世上有九样东西出生了，是不是幻影且不论，反正就是这样；我推不开它。它们是有那么点东西，你也是那么点东西，老狗；或者至少像那么点东西，像得足以凑合顶用；而你并非我，且与我一样好，它们呢，就我所知，也与我一样好，与我一样有活的权利；凭着七大行星以及一切别的什么，我驮它们就是了！」
===Original===
And he went back, tied up the puppies in his blanket, and set forth, Bran barking, squeaking, wagging, leaping, running between his legs and upsetting him, in her agonies of joy.

"Forward! Whither you will, old lady! The world is wide. You shall be my guide, tutor, queen of philosophy, for the sake of this mere common sense of yours. Forward, you new Hypatia! I promise you I will attend no lectures but yours this day!"

He toiled on, every now and then stepping across a dead body, or clambering a wall out of the road, to avoid some plunging, shrieking horse, or obscene knot of prowling camp followers, who were already stripping and plundering the slain.… At last, in front of a large villa, now a black and smoking skeleton, he leaped a wall, and found himself landed on a heap of corpses.… They were piled up against the garden fence for many yards. The struggle had been fierce there some three hours before.

"Put me out of my misery! In mercy kill me!" moaned a voice beneath his feet.

Raphael looked down; the poor wretch was slashed and mutilated beyond all hope.

"Certainly, friend, if you wish it," and he drew his dagger. The poor fellow stretched out his throat, and awaited the stroke with a ghastly smile. Raphael caught his eye; his heart failed him, and he rose.

"What do you advise, Bran?" But the dog was far ahead, leaping and barking impatiently.

"I obey," said Raphael; and he followed her, while the wounded man called piteously and upbraidingly after him.

"He will not have long to wait. Those plunderers will not be as squeamish as I.… Strange, now! From Armenian reminiscences I should have fancied myself as free from such tender weakness as any of my Canaanite-slaying ancestors.… And yet by some mere spirit of contradiction, I couldn't kill that fellow, exactly because he asked me to do it.… There is more in that than will fit into the great inverted pyramid of 'I am I.…' Never mind, let me get the dog's lessons by heart first. What next, Bran? Ah! Could one believe the transformation? Why, this is the very trim villa which I passed yesterday morning, with the garden-chairs standing among the flowerbeds, just as the young ladies had left them, and the peacocks and silver pheasants running about, wondering why their pretty mistresses did not come to feed them. And here is a trampled mass of wreck and corruption for the girls to find, when they venture back from Rome, and complain how horrible war is for breaking down all their shrubs, and how cruel soldiers must be to kill and cook all their poor dear tame turtledoves! Why not? Why should they lament over other things—which they can just as little mend—and which perhaps need no more mending? Ah! there lies a gallant fellow underneath that fruit-tree!"

===Chinese===
于是他折回去，把小狗们裹在他的毯子里，动身上路；布朗又吠又吱、摇尾蹦跳、在他两腿之间窜来窜去把他绊倒，狂喜得几乎发狂。

「前进！随你去哪儿，老太太！天地很宽。就凭你这股子常识，你做我的向导、导师、哲学女王好了。前进吧，你这新希帕蒂娅！我答应你，今日我只听你一人讲学，旁人的课一概不上！」

他一路辛苦地走着，时而跨过一具死尸，时而翻过一道墙绕开大路，以避开那些惊跳嘶鸣的马匹，或是一伙一伙下流地四处游荡、已经在剥劫死者衣物的随营匪徒。……终于，在一座大别墅前——如今只剩一副乌黑冒烟的骨架——他跃过一道墙，落在一堆尸体上。……尸体沿着花园栅栏堆了有好几码远。约莫三个钟头前，这里有过一场恶战。

「给我个痛快吧！发发慈悲杀了我吧！」他脚下传来一声呻吟。

拉斐尔低头一看；那可怜人已被砍得血肉模糊，毫无指望。

「自然可以，朋友，只要你愿意，」他抽出了匕首。那可怜人伸长了脖子，带着一丝惨笑等候那一刀。拉斐尔触到他的目光；心一软，便站起身来。

「你以为如何，布朗？」可那狗早已远远跑在前头，急不可耐地又蹦又叫。

「我服从，」拉斐尔说；便跟了上去，任那伤者在身后凄厉而怨责地唤他。

「他用不着等多久。那些劫掠的人不会像我这样手软。……奇了！凭我在亚美尼亚（Armenia）的那些回忆，我本该以为自己像任何一位杀迦南人（Canaanite-slaying）的祖先一样，丝毫没有这种软心肠的弱点。……可偏偏凭着一种纯粹的逆反心理，我没能杀那个家伙，恰是因为他求我杀他。……这里头有东西，是塞不进『我是我』那座倒立金字塔里去的……罢了，且让我先把这狗的课背熟再说。下一步去哪儿，布朗？啊！这变化谁信得过？这可不是我昨天早上经过的那座整整齐齐的别墅么？花园椅子还摆在花床之间，正如小姐们离去时的模样，孔雀和银雉在四下乱跑，纳罕它们漂亮的女主人怎么不来喂食。如今却是一堆被践踏过的残骸与腐肉，等着姑娘们从罗马（Rome）壮着胆子回来时去发现，再去抱怨战争可真可怕，把她们的灌木都踩倒了，又抱怨那些士兵真残忍，竟把她们心爱的驯斑鸠统统杀掉煮吃了！有何不可？她们为什么就不去为别的事物——那些她们同样补救不了、也许同样无须补救的事物——哀悼呢？啊！那棵果树底下躺着一位好汉！」

===Original===
Raphael walked up to a ring of dead, in the midst of which lay, half-sitting against the trunk of the tree, a tall and noble officer in the first bloom of manhood. His casque and armour, gorgeously inlaid with gold, were hewn and battered by a hundred blows; his shield was cloven through and through; his sword broken in the stiffened hand which grasped it still. Cut off from his troop, he had made his last stand beneath the tree, knee-deep in the gay summer flowers, and there he lay, bestrewn, as if by some mockery—or pity—of mother nature, with faded roses, and golden fruit, shaken from off the boughs in that last deadly struggle. Raphael stood and watched him with a sad sneer.

"Well!—you have sold your fancied personality dear! How many dead men?… Nine.… Eleven! Conceited fellow! Who told you that your one life was worth the eleven which you have taken?"

Bran went up to the corpse—perhaps from its sitting posture fancying it still living—smelt the cold cheek, and recoiled with a mournful whine.

"Eh? That is the right way to look at the phenomena, is it? Well, after all, I am sorry for you… almost like you.… All your wounds in front, as a man's should be. Poor fop! Lais and Thais will never curl those dainty ringlets for you again! What is that bas-relief upon your shield? Venus receiving Psyche into the abode of the gods!… Ah! you have found out all about Psyche's wings by this time.… How do I know that? And yet, why am I, in spite of my common sense—if I have any—talking to you as you, and liking you, and pitying you, if you are nothing now, and probably never were anything? Bran! What right had you to pity him without giving your reasons in due form, as Hypatia would have done? Forgive me, sir, however—whether you exist or not, I cannot leave that collar round your neck for these camp-wolves to convert into strong liquor."

===Chinese===
拉斐尔走到一圈死人跟前；圈中央，半倚着树干坐着的，是一位高大威武的军官，正当盛年。他那华丽地嵌着金线的头盔与铠甲，被上百下刀砍斧砸剁得坑坑洼洼；盾牌被一劈两半；剑在一只早已僵硬却仍紧握着它的手中折断。他与自己的队伍失散，在这棵树下作了最后的抵抗，双膝没入灿烂的夏花之中；他便这样躺着，身上撒满了——仿佛出于大自然母亲某种嘲弄——或者怜悯——从那场最后殊死搏斗中抖落的枯萎玫瑰与金色果实。拉斐尔站着，带着一种凄凉的讥笑注视着他。

「好哇！——你把你那自以为有的人格卖了个好价钱！有几个死人？……九个。……十一个！自负的家伙！谁告诉你，你这一条命抵得过你夺走的十一条命？」

布朗走近尸体——也许是看那坐姿，以为他还活着——嗅了嗅那冰冷的面颊，哀呜一声退了回来。

「嗯？看现象原该这么看，是么？也罢，说到底我替你可惜……几乎有点喜欢你了。……你所有的伤都在前面，正是一个男子汉所该有的。可怜的花花公子！拉伊斯（Lais）和泰伊斯（Thais）再也不能替你卷那一头精致的鬈发了！你盾牌上那幅浮雕是什么？维纳斯（Venus）接纳普赛克（Psyche）入众神之所！……啊！普赛克那双翅膀是怎么一回事，你此时总该全弄明白了。……我怎么知道这个？可是，尽管你如今什么也不是——多半也从未是什么——我为什么罔顾我的常识——如果我有的话——把你当作你来同你说话、喜欢你、可怜你呢？布朗！你有什么权利，不像希帕蒂娅那样按规矩陈述理由，就去可怜他？不过，先生，恕我——不管你存不存在，我都不能把那串项圈留在你脖子上，让这些营中豺狼拿去换烈酒喝。」

===Original===
And as he spoke, he bent down, and detached, gently enough, a magnificent necklace.

"Not for myself, I assure you. Like Ate's golden apple, it shall go to the fairest. Here, Bran!" And he wreathed the jewels round the neck of the mastiff, who, evidently exalted in her own eyes by the burden, leaped and barked forward again, taking, apparently as a matter of course, the road back towards Ostia, by which they had come thither from the sea. And as he followed, careless where he went, he continued talking to himself aloud after the manner of restless self-discontented men.

"… And then man talks big about his dignity and his intellect, and his heavenly parentage, and his aspirations after the unseen, and the beautiful, and the infinite—and everything else unlike himself. How can he prove it? Why, these poor blackguards lying about are very fair specimens of humanity.—And how much have they been bothered since they were born with aspirations after anything infinite, except infinite sour wine? To eat, to drink; to destroy a certain number of their species; to reproduce a certain number of the same, two-thirds of whom will die in infancy, a dead waste of pain to their mothers and of expense to their putative sires… and then—what says Solomon? What befalls them befalls beasts. As one dies, so dies the other; so that they have all one breath, and a man has no preeminence over a beast; for all is vanity. All go to one place; all are of the dust, and turn to dust again. Who knows that the breath of man goes upward, and that the breath of the beast goes downward to the earth? Who, indeed, my most wise ancestor? Not I, certainly. Raphael Aben-Ezra, how art thou better than a beast? What preeminence hast thou, not merely over this dog, But over the fleas whom thou so wantonly cursest? Man must painfully win house, clothes, fire.… A pretty proof of his wisdom, when every flea has the wit to make my blanket, without any labour of his own, lodge him a great deal better than it lodges me! Man makes clothes, and the fleas live in them.… Which is the wiser of the two?…

===Chinese===
他说着，便弯下腰，相当轻手轻脚地解下一条华丽的项圈。

「不是为我自己，我向你保证。它要像阿忒（Ate）的金苹果一样，归于最美者。给你，布朗！」他把那些宝石绕在那大獒犬的脖子上；那狗显然因这份重负而在自家眼里荣光了不少，又蹦又吠地朝前开路，并且理所当然地走上了回奥斯提亚（Ostia）的那条路——他们当初便是从海边经这条路来到此处的。他漫不经心地跟着走，一面像那些不得安宁、自怨自艾的人那样，继续高声自言自语。

「……然后人便大吹大擂，谈他的尊严、他的理智、他的天家血统、他对那不可见、那美、那无限——以及一切与他自家不相像之物——的向往。他怎么证明呢？这些东一个西一个躺着的可怜无赖，可算是人类的很好标本。——他们自打出生以来，除了对无限的酸酒有所向往之外，被对任何无限之物的向往烦扰过多少呢？吃，喝；毁灭一定数目的同类；再繁育一定数目的同类，其中三分之二死于襁褓，白白地叫他们的母亲受苦、叫他们名义上的父亲破费……然后——所罗门（Solomon）怎么说？临到兽的，也临到人；这个怎样死，那个也怎样死；它们都有一样的气息，人并不比兽强；因为都是虚空。都归一处，都是出于尘土，也都归于尘土。谁知道人的气息是向上，兽的气息是下入地呢？谁又知道呢，我最最明智的祖先？我自然是不知道的。拉斐尔·阿本-以斯拉，你比一只兽强在哪里？你不单比这条狗，便比那些你如此恶毒咒骂的跳蚤，又强在哪里？人要辛辛苦苦才弄到房子、衣服、火。……这正是他的智慧的大证据——每一只跳蚤都有那份聪明，不费一点力气，便叫我的毯子供它住得比供我住的好得多！人造衣服，跳蚤住在里头。……这两者谁更聪明些？……

===Original===
"Ah, but—man is fallen.… Well—and the flea is not. So much better he than the man; for he is what he was intended to be, and so fulfils the very definition of virtue, which no one can say of us of the red-ochre vein. And even if the old myth be true, and the man only fell, because he was set to do higher work than the flea, what does that prove—but that he could not do it?

"But his arts and his sciences?… Apage! The very sound of those grown-children's rattles turns me sick.… One conceited ass in a generation increasing labour and sorrow, and dying after all even as the fool dies, and ten million brutes and slaves, just where their forefathers were, and where their children will be after them, to the end of the farce.… The thing that has been, it is that which shall be; and there is no new thing under the sun.…

"And as for your palaces, and cities, and temples… look at this Campagna, and judge. Flea-bites go down after a while—and so do they. What are they but the bumps which we human fleas make in the old earth's skin?… Make them? We only cause them, as fleas cause flea-bites.… What are all the works of man, but a sort of cutaneous disorder in this unhealthy earth-hide, and we a race of larger fleas, running about among its fur, which we call trees? Why should not the earth be an animal? How do I know it is not? Because it is too big? Bah! What is big, and what is little? Because it has not the shape of one?… Look into a fisherman's net, and see what forms are there! Because it does not speak?… Perhaps it has nothing to say, being too busy. Perhaps it can talk no more sense than we.… In both cases it shows its wisdom by holding its tongue. Because it moves in one necessary direction?… How do I know that it does? How can I tell that it is not flirting with all the seven spheres at once, at this moment? But if it does—so much the wiser of it, if that be the best direction for it. Oh, what a base satire on ourselves and our notions of the fair and fitting, to say that a thing cannot be alive and rational, just because it goes steadily on upon its own road, instead of skipping and scrambling fantastically up and down without method or order, like us and the fleas, from the cradle to the grave! Besides, if you grant, with the rest of the world, that fleas are less noble than we, because they are our parasites, then you are bound to grant that we are less noble than the earth, because we are its parasites.… Positively, it looks more probable than anything I have seen for many a day.… And, by the by, why should not earthquakes, and floods, and pestilences, be only just so many ways which the cunning old brute earth has of scratching herself when the human fleas and their palace and city bites get too troublesome?"

===Chinese===
「啊，可是——人堕落了。……好——跳蚤却没有。可见跳蚤比人强；因为它正是它被造时所定意要成为的样子，所以恰恰符合了德行的定义，这一点我们这些红土血脉的人是没人能说的。就算那古老的神话是真的，人之堕落只是因为他被派去做比跳蚤更高的事——那又证明了什么？——无非证明他做不来罢了。

「可他的那些艺术和科学呢？……去你的（Apage）！光听这些大孩子的拨浪鼓那声响，便叫我作呕。……一代出一个自大的蠢驴，加重劳苦与忧愁，到头来仍然和愚昧人一样地死；而一千万的禽兽和奴隶，仍然在他们祖宗所在的所在，他们的子孙也将要在他们之后的所在，直到这出滑稽戏演完。……已有的事，后必再有；日光之下，并无新事。……

「至于你的那些宫殿、城市、神庙……且看这片坎帕尼亚，自己判断吧。跳蚤叮的包过一阵子便消下去——它们也如此。它们不外是我们这些人形跳蚤，在老地球的皮肤上鼓起的一个个疙瘩。……鼓起的？我们只是引起了它们，正如跳蚤引起跳蚤叮的包。……人的一切作品，不外是这病态的兽皮上的一种皮肤病，而我们是一种更大的跳蚤，在它的毛——我们称之为树——之间到处乱跑罢了。为什么地球就不可以是一头动物？我怎么知道它不是？因为它太大？呸！什么叫大，什么叫小？因为它没有动物的样子？……去瞧瞧渔人的网里都有些什么形状的东西！因为它不说话？……也许它无话可说，因为它太忙。也许它说不出比我们更有道理的话来。……这两种情形下，它都因沉默而显出它的智慧。因为它只朝一个必须的方向走？……我怎么知道它是这样？我怎么知道它此刻不是正和那七重天界一齐调情呢？就算它是——若那是它最好的方向，那它便越发聪明了。噢，说一样东西不能是活的、不能是理性的，只因为它稳稳地走自己的路，而不像我们和跳蚤那样从摇篮到坟墓毫无章法地上蹿下跳、乱爬乱钻——这是对我们自己、对我们那套关于妥当与合宜之观念，何等卑劣的讥讽！况且，你若与世人一同承认跳蚤比我们低贱，因为它们是我们的寄生物；那么你也得承认我们比地球低贱，因为我们是它的寄生物。……说真的，这看起来比我好多天以来所见的一切都更可信。……而且，顺便问一句，为什么地震、洪水、瘟疫，不可以正是那狡猾的老兽——地球——在人形跳蚤以及它们的宫殿、城市之包叮得太烦人时，给自己搔痒的种种法子呢？」

===Original===
At a turn of the road he was aroused from this profitable meditation by a shriek, the shrillness of which told him that it was a woman's. He looked up, and saw close to him, among the smouldering ruins of a farmhouse, two ruffians driving before them a young girl, with her hands tied behind her, while the poor creature was looking back piteously after something among the ruins, and struggling in vain, bound as she was, to escape from her captors and return.

"Conduct unjustifiable in any fleas—eh, Bran? How do I know that, though? Why should it not be a piece of excellent fortune for her, if she had but the equanimity to see it? Why—what will happen to her? She will be taken to Rome, and sold as a slave.… And in spite of a few discomforts in the transfer, and the prejudice which some persons have against standing an hour on the *catasta* to be handled from head to foot in the minimum of clothing, she will most probably end in being far better housed, fed, bedizened, and pampered to her heart's desire, than ninety-nine out of a hundred of her sister fleas… till she begins to grow old… which she must do in any case.… And if she have not contrived to wheedle her master out of her liberty, and to make tip a pretty little purse of savings, by that time—why, it is her own fault. Eh, Bran?"

But Bran by no means agreed with his view of the case; for after watching the two ruffians, with her head stuck on one side, for a minute or two, she suddenly and silently, after the manner of mastiffs, sprang upon them, and dragged one to the ground.

"Oh! that is the 'fit and beautiful,' in this case, as they say in Alexandria, is it? Well—I obey. You are at least a more practical teacher than ever Hypatia was. Heaven grant that there may be no more of them in the ruins!"

===Chinese===
在路的一个拐弯处，他这番大有收益的冥想被一声尖叫打断；那尖叫的尖锐告诉他，这是女人的声音。他抬头一看，就在近旁，一处农舍仍在冒烟的废墟之间，两个恶汉正赶着一个少女在前头走；她的双手被反绑着，那可怜人正频频回首，凄然望着废墟中的某样东西，被捆着挣扎着想脱离掳她的人、回到那里去，却只是徒然。

「无论对哪只跳蚤来说，这都是不可辩解的行径——是吧，布朗？可我怎么知道就是这样呢？为什么这就不可以是她的一桩大好运，只要她有那份泰然去看得明白？为什么——她将如何？她将被带到罗马（Rome），卖作奴隶。……尽管在转手之间有些不适，又尽管有些人对在那*catasta*上站着任人从头到脚、近乎赤身地捏摸一个钟头存有偏见，她最终的结局多半是住得更宽敞、吃得更好、打扮得更珠光宝气、被娇纵到心满意足，比她一百个姐妹跳蚤中的九十九个都要强……直到她开始老了……而她无论如何总要老的。……若到那时她没能哄得主人放她自由、攒下一小笔体己钱——那便是她自己的不是了。嗯，布朗？」

但布朗一点也不以为然；她歪着头瞧了那两个恶汉一两分钟，便按照獒犬的做派，无声无息地忽然一扑，把其中一个拖翻在地。

「哦！这便是亚历山大城（Alexandria）人所说的『适宜而美』（fit and beautiful），是么？好——我服从。你至少比希帕蒂娅向来是个更实际的老师。但愿废墟里再没有别的恶汉了！」

===Original===
And rushing on the second plunderer, he laid him dead with a blow of his dagger, and then turned to the first, whom Bran was holding down by the throat.

"Mercy, mercy!" shrieked the wretch. "Life! only life!"

"There was a fellow half a mile back begging me to kill him: with which of you two am I to agree?—for you can't both be right."

"Life! Only life!"

"A carnal appetite, which man must learn to conquer," said Raphael, as he raised the poniard.… In a moment it was over, and Bran and he rose—Where was the girl? She had rushed back to the ruins, whither Raphael followed her; while Bran ran to the puppies, which he had laid upon a stone, and commenced her maternal cares.

"What do you want, my poor girl?" asked he in Latin. "I will not hurt you."

"My father! My father!"

He untied her bruised and swollen wrists; and without stopping to thank him, she ran to a heap of fallen stones and beams, and began digging wildly with all her little strength, breathlessly calling "Father!"

"Such is the gratitude of flea to flea! What is there, now, in the mere fact of being accustomed to call another person father, and not master, or slave, which should produce such passion as that?… Brute habit!… What services can the said man render, or have rendered, which make him worth—Here is Bran!… What do you think of that, my female philosopher?"

===Chinese===
他随即朝第二个劫匪扑去，一刀便结果了他；然后转向第一个——布朗正按住他的喉咙。

「饶命，饶命！」那可怜虫尖叫，「活命！只要活命！」

「半里外有个家伙求我杀他：你们两位到底是谁对？——你们俩总不能都对吧。」

「活命！只要活命！」

「一种肉体的食欲，人必须学着克服它，」拉斐尔一面说，一面举起了匕首。……一瞬之间便了结了；布朗和他一起站起身——那姑娘呢？她已奔回废墟去了，拉斐尔便跟了过去；布朗则跑到他放在一块石头上的小狗崽那里，开始尽她做母亲的职分。

「你要什么，可怜的姑娘？」他用拉丁语问。「我不会伤你。」

「我的父亲！我的父亲！」

他解开她那又青又肿的手腕；她顾不上道谢，便跑到一堆坍塌的石头与梁木前，使出小小的全身气力拼命地刨，气喘吁吁地连声唤着「父亲！」

「跳蚤对跳蚤的感激，便是如此！仅仅因为惯于把另一个人叫作父亲、而不是主人或奴仆，这一事实中究竟有什么，竟能生出这般激情？……盲目的习惯！……那个人所能效的、或曾经效过什么劳，使他值得——布朗来了！……女哲学家，这事你怎么看？」

===Original===
Bran sat down and watched too. The poor girl's tender hands were bleeding from the stones, while her golden tresses rolled down over her eyes, and entangled in her impatient fingers; but still she worked frantically. Bran seemed suddenly to comprehend the case, rushed to the rescue, and began digging too, with all her might.

Raphael rose with a shrug, and joined in the work.


===Chinese===
布朗坐下，也看着。那可怜姑娘娇嫩的手被石头磨出血来；她金色的长发披散下来遮住眼睛，缠在她焦躁的指间；可她仍旧发疯似的刨着。布朗似乎忽然明白了这是怎么回事，冲上去帮忙，也使出全力刨了起来。

拉斐尔耸耸肩站起身，加入了这工作。

---

===Original===

"Hang these brute instincts! They make one very hot. What was that?"

A feeble moan rose from under the stones. A human limb was uncovered. The girl threw herself on the place, shrieking her father's name. Raphael put her gently back and exerting his whole strength, drew out of the ruins a stalwart elderly man, in the dress of an officer of high rank.

He still breathed. The girl lifted up his head and covered him with wild kisses. Raphael looked round for water; found a spring and a broken sherd, and bathed the wounded man's temples till he opened his eyes and showed signs of returning life.

The girl still sat by him, fondling her recovered treasure, and bathing the grizzled face in holy tears.

"It is no business of mine," said Raphael. "Come, Bran!"

The girl sprang up, threw herself at his feet, kissed his hands, called him her saviour, her deliverer, sent by God.

"Not in the least, my child. You must thank my teacher the dog, not me."

===Chinese===

「这些畜生本能真要命！干得人浑身发热。那是什么？」

一声微弱的呻吟从石下传来。一条人的肢体露了出来。姑娘扑到那地方，尖叫着她父亲的名字。拉斐尔轻轻把她推开，使出全力，从废墟里拖出一个健壮的汉子，年事已长，穿着高级军官的服饰。

他还在喘息。姑娘捧起他的头，发狂似地亲遍他的脸。拉斐尔四处找水；寻见一处泉眼和一块破陶片，便替那伤者擦拭太阳穴，直擦得他睁开眼睛，显出回生的征兆。

姑娘仍坐在他身旁，抚爱着她失而复得的珍宝，用圣洁的泪水洗着那张斑白鬓发的脸。

「这不干我的事，」拉斐尔说，「走吧，布朗！」

姑娘一跃而起，扑倒在他脚前，亲吻他的双手，唤他作救命恩人、解救者，是上帝差他来的。

「完全不，孩子。你该谢我的老师那条狗，不是我。」

===Original===
And she took him at his word, and threw her soft arms round Bran's neck; and Bran understood it, and wagged her tail, and licked the gentle face lovingly.

"Intolerably absurd, all this!" said Raphael. "I must be going, Bran."

"You will not leave us? You surely will not leave an old man to die here?"

"Why not? What better thing could happen to him?"

"Nothing," murmured the officer, who had not spoken before.

"Ah, God! he is my father!"

"Well?"

"He is my father!"

"Well?"

"You must save him! You shall, I say!" And she seized Raphael's arm in the imperiousness of her passion.

He shrugged his shoulders: but felt, he knew not why, marvellously inclined to obey her.

"I may as well do this as anything else, having nothing else to do. Whither now, sir?"

"Whither you will. Our troops are disgraced, our eagles taken. We are your prisoners by right of war. We follow you."

===Chinese===
她便当真听信了他的话，把柔软的双臂搂住布朗的脖子；布朗心领神会，摇着尾巴，亲昵地舔那张温柔的脸。

「这一切荒唐得叫人受不了！」拉斐尔说，「我该走了，布朗。」

「你不留下我们？你总不至于把一个老人丢在这里送死吧？」

「为什么不？还有比这更好的事落到他头上么？」

「没有了，」那位此前一直未开口的军官低声道。

「啊，上帝！他是我的父亲！」

「怎样？」

「他是我的父亲！」

「怎样？」

「你非救他不可！我一定要你救他！」她在一腔激情的专横中抓住了拉斐尔的胳膊。

他耸耸肩：却不知为何，竟觉得分外愿意依她。

「我闲着也是闲着，做这件事与做别的事也无分别。这便往哪儿去，先生？」

「随你的意。我军已蒙羞，我们的鹰帜已被夺去。按战时之权，我们是你的俘虏。我们随你走。」

===Original===
"Oh, my fortune! A new responsibility! Why cannot I stir, without live animals, from fleas upward, attaching themselves to me? Is it not enough to have nine blind puppies at my back, and an old brute at my heels, who will persist in saving my life, that I must be burdened over and above with a respectable elderly rebel and his daughter? Why am I not allowed by fate to care for nobody but myself? Sir, I give you both your freedom. The world is wide enough for us all. I really ask no ransom."

"You seem philosophically disposed, my friend."

"I? Heaven forbid! I have gone right through that slough, and come out sheer on the other side. For sweeping the last lingering taint of it out of me, I have to thank, not sulphur and exorcisms, but your soldiers and their morning's work. Philosophy is superfluous in a world where all are fools."

"Do you include yourself under that title?"

"Most certainly, my best sir. Don't fancy that I make any exceptions. If I can in any way prove my folly to you, I will do it."

"Then help me and my daughter to Ostia."

"A very fair instance. Well—my dog happens to be going that way; and after all, you seem to have a sufficient share of human imbecility to be a very fit companion for me. I hope, though, you do not set up for a wise man!"

===Chinese===
「哎，我的命！又是一桩新差使！我怎么一动弹，从跳蚤往上，一切活物便都要来黏上我？背上九只瞎眼小狗崽、脚跟一条死活要救我命的老畜生，还不够么，偏偏又得再加上一位体面的老叛党和他女儿？命运怎么就不许我只关心我自己呢？先生，我把你二位的自由都还给你们。天地很宽，容得下我们大家。我当真一文赎金也不要。」

「你似乎生就一副哲人脾性呢，朋友。」

「我？上天不容！那一片泥潭我已从头蹚过，干干净净地到了那一边。能把我身上最后一点那泥潭的余毒都扫净的，不是硫磺与驱邪术，倒要感谢你们的兵士和他们今早的杰作。一个人人皆蠢的世界里，哲学是多余的。」

「这称号你也把自己算在里头么？」

「最当然不过了，我的好先生。别以为我会做任何例外。我若能以任何方式向你证明我的愚拙，我一定去证明。」

「那么帮我父女二人到奥斯提亚（Ostia）去。」

「这倒是一个相当好的例子。好——我的狗恰好也要往那边去；说到底，你似乎也有够多的人之愚拙，足以做我十分合适的旅伴。但愿你别自命为智者才好！」

===Original===
"God knows—no! Am I not of Heraclian's army?"

"True; and the young lady here made herself so great a fool about you, that she actually infected the very dog."

"So we three fools will forth together."

"And the greatest one, as usual, must help the rest. But I have nine puppies in my family already. How am I to carry you and them?"

"I will take them," said the girl; and Bran, after looking on at the transfer with a somewhat dubious face, seemed to satisfy herself that all was right, and put her head contentedly under the girl's hand.

"Eh? You trust her, Bran?" said Raphael, in an undertone. "I must really emancipate myself from your instructions if you require a similar simplicity in me. Stay! there wanders a mule without a rider; we may as well press into the service."

He caught the mule, lifted the wounded man into the saddle, and the cavalcade set forth, turning out of the highroad into a by-lane, which the officer, who seemed to know the country thoroughly, assured would lead them to Ostia by an unfrequented route.

"If we arrive there before sundown, we are saved," said he.

===Chinese===
「上帝鉴察——断断不是！我岂不也是赫拉克利安（Heraclian）军中之人？」

「不错；这位姑娘方才为你急成了那般大傻瓜，竟连这条狗都受了她的传染。」

「那么我们这三个蠢货便一同上路吧。」

「而最大的那个蠢货，照例还得帮扶其余的。可我家里已经有九只小狗崽了。我怎能连你带它们一齐驮上？」

「我来抱它们，」姑娘说；布朗瞧着这交接，面带几分犹疑，随后似乎打定了主意，一切都妥当，便心满意足地把头伸到姑娘手底下。

「咦？你信得过她，布朗？」拉斐尔低声道。「你若也要我同样地单纯，我可真得从你的指教里解放出来了。且住！那边 wandering 有一头没人骑的骡子；不妨也征用它入役。」

他捉住那骡子，把伤者扶上鞍，一行人便出发了；他们离开大路，拐进一条小径——那军官似乎对这一带烂熟于胸，保证这条路能经由一条僻径把他们带到奥斯提亚。

「若我们在日落前赶到那里，便有救了，」他说。

===Original===
"And in the meantime," answered Raphael, "between the dog and this dagger, which, as I take care to inform all comers, is delicately poisoned, we may keep ourselves clear of marauders. And yet, what a meddling fool I am!" he went on to himself. "What possible interest can I have in this uncircumcised rebel! The least evil is, that if we are taken, which we most probably shall be, I shall be crucified for helping to escape. But even if we get safe off—here is a fresh tie between me and those very brother fleas, to be rid of whom I have chosen beggary and starvation. Who knows where it may end? Pooh! The man is like other men. He is certain, before the day is over, to prove ungrateful, or attempt the mountebank-heroic, or give me some other excuse for bidding good evening. And in the meantime there is something quaint in the fact of finding so sober a respectability, with a young daughter too, abroad on this fool's errand, which really makes me curious to discover with what variety of flea I am to class him."

But while Aben-Ezra was talking to himself about the father, he could not help, somehow, thinking about the daughter. Again and again he found himself looking at her. She was, undeniably, most beautiful. Her features were not as regularly perfect as Hypatia's, nor her stature so commanding; but her face shone with a clear and joyful determination, and with a tender and modest thoughtfulness, such as he had never beheld before united in one countenance; and as she stepped along, firmly and lightly, by her father's side, looping up her scattered tresses as she went, laughing at the struggles of her noisy burden, and looking up with rapture at her father's gradually brightening face, Raphael could not help stealing glance after glance, and was surprised to find them returned with a bright, honest, smiling gratitude, which met full-eyed, as free from prudery as it was from coquetry.…"A lady she is," said he to himself; "but evidently no city one. There is nature—or something else, there, pure and unadulterated, without any of man's additions or beautifications." And as he looked, he began to feel it a pleasure such as his weary heart had not known for many a year, simply to watch her.…

"Positively there is a foolish enjoyment after all in making other fleas smile.… Ass that I am! As if I had not drunk all that ditch-water cup to the dregs years ago!"

===Chinese===
「这其间，」拉斐尔回答，「凭这条狗和这把匕首——我向来不忘告诉一切来人，这匕首上精巧地淬了毒——我们足以叫劫匪不敢近身。可我究竟是个多管闲事的蠢货！」他暗自接着想道。「这个未受割礼的叛党，与我有什么相干！往轻处说，若我们被捉住——这是十之八九的事——我便要因助人逃走而被钉上十字架。就算我们侥幸脱身——这又是我和那些我本欲摆脱、为此才甘心行乞挨饿的同类跳蚤之间一条新的羁绊。谁知它会引出什么来？呸！这人既和别人一样，这一日没过完，他必定要么忘恩负义，要么演一出逞英雄的把戏，要么给我别的什么借口，叫我与他道晚安。不过话说回来，这般庄重体面的人物，还带着一个年轻女儿，竟会在这桩蠢差事上漂泊在外，倒也有几分古怪，倒叫我着实好奇，要把他归入哪一类的跳蚤才好。」

可阿本-以斯拉一面心里嘀咕着那位父亲，不知怎地，却忍不住去想那女儿。他一次又一次地发觉自己在看她。她确是美极了。她的容貌不如希帕蒂娅那样规整无瑕，身量也不那样雍容夺人；可她的脸上闪着一种明朗而喜悦的果决，又闪着一种温柔而端庄的深思——他从未见过这两者如此合并在一张脸上；她迈步走在父亲身侧，步履坚定而轻盈，一面随手挽起散乱的长发，一面笑看那吵闹累赘在她怀中挣扎，又满怀欣喜地仰望父亲渐渐明朗的脸色——拉斐尔禁不住一道道目光偷瞧过去，却吃惊地发现，那目光竟被一道明亮、坦诚、含笑的感激迎了回来，那感激直直地正眼相迎，既无矫情，亦无卖弄。……「她是一位淑女，」他暗想，「但显然不是城里的淑女。那里头有自然——或者是别的什么——纯粹而不掺杂，不带半点人的增添与修饰。」他看着看着，便觉得光是看着她，便是他那颗倦心多年来未识的一种快乐。……

「说到底，叫别的跳蚤微笑，到底也有一桩愚蠢的乐趣。……我这头蠢驴！好像我多年之前没有把那沟里的臭水喝个涓滴不剩似的！」

===Original===
They went on for some time in silence, till the officer, turning to him—

"And may I ask you, my quaint preserver, whom I would have thanked before but for this foolish faintness, which is now going off, what and who you are?"

"A flea, sir—a flea—nothing more."

"But a patrician flea, surely, to judge by your language and manners?"

"Not that exactly. True, I have been rich, as the saying is; I may be rich again, they tell me, when I am fool enough to choose."

"Oh if we were but rich!" sighed the girl.

"You would be very unhappy, my dear young lady. Believe a flea who has tried the experiment thoroughly."

"Ah! but we could ransom my brother! and now we can find no money till we get back to Africa."

"And none then," said the officer, in a low voice. "You forget, my poor child, that I mortgaged the whole estate to raise my legion. We must not shrink from looking at things as they are."

"Ah! and he is prisoner! he will be sold for a slave—perhaps—ah! perhaps crucified, for he is not a Roman! Oh, he will be crucified!" and she burst into an agony of weeping.… Suddenly she dashed away her tears and looked up clear and bright once more.

"No! forgive me, father! God will protect His own!"

===Chinese===
他们默默走了一阵，后来那军官转向他——

「我可不可以请问，我这位古怪的救命恩人——若不是为这愚蠢的虚晕，此刻已渐散了，我早便要谢你——你是什么人，姓甚名谁？」

「一只跳蚤，先生——一只跳蚤——再无别的。」

「可是一只贵族跳蚤吧，看你的谈吐举止？」

「倒也不尽然。不错，我曾是所谓富有的；他们告诉我，等我蠢到甘心拣选那一条路时，我还可以再富起来。」

「啊，但愿我们能富起来！」姑娘叹道。

「那你就很不快活了，我亲爱的小姐。这话你该信一只把那实验做透了的跳蚤。」

「啊！可我们便能赎回我的兄弟！而眼下我们一文不名，非得回到非洲（Africa）去不可。」

「回了非洲也没有了，」那军官低声道，「你忘了，我可怜的孩子，我为筹措我这一军，已把整座田产都抵出去了。我们不可不敢正视事情的真相。」

「啊！而且他被俘了！他会被卖作奴隶——也许——啊！也许被钉十字架，因为他不是罗马人！噢，他会被钉十字架的！」她忽然痛哭起来。……猛然间她抹去眼泪，又抬起头来，眸子清亮如初。

「不！原谅我，父亲！上帝必保护属他的人！」

===Original===
"My dear young lady," said Raphael, "if you really dislike such a prospect for your brother, and are in want of a few dirty coins wherewith to prevent it, perhaps I may be able to find you them in Ostia."

She looked at incredulously, as her eye glanced over his rags, and then, blushing, begged his pardon for her unspoken thoughts.

"Well, as you choose to suppose. But my dog has been so civil to you already, that perhaps she may have no objection to make you a present of that necklace of hers. I will go to the Rabbis, and we will make all right; so don't cry. I hate crying; and the puppies are quite chorus enough for the present tragedy."

"The Rabbis? Are you a Jew?" asked the officer.

"Yes, sir, a Jew. And you, I presume, a Christian: perhaps you may have scruples about receiving—your sect has generally none about taking—from one of our stubborn and unbelieving race. Don't be frightened, though, for your conscience; I assure you I am no more a Jew at heart than I am a Christian."

"God help you then!"

"Someone, or something, has helped me a great deal too much, for three-and-thirty years of pampering. But, pardon me, that was a strange speech for a Christian."

"You must be a good Jew, sir, before you can be a good Christian."

"Possibly. I intend to be neither—nor a good Pagan either. My dear sir, let us drop the subject. It is beyond me. If I can be as good a brute animal as my dog there—it being first demonstrated that it is good to be good—I shall be very well content."

===Chinese===
「亲爱的小姐，」拉斐尔说，「你若当真不愿令兄落到这般境地，又缺几枚脏铜钱去拦阻它，那么我也许能在奥斯提亚替你找着它们。」

她抬眼瞅着他那一身破衣烂衫，满脸不信；随即红了脸，为方才心中的想法请他恕罪。

「好，随你怎么想吧。不过我这狗待你已经这般客气，说不定她也愿意把她脖子上那串项圈送给你。我去找拉比们（the Rabbis），一切都会办妥的；所以别哭了。我讨厌哭；眼前这出悲剧，有小狗崽们做歌队已经够了。」

「拉比们？你是犹太人？」那军官问。

「是的，先生，犹太人（Jew）。至于你，我想是基督徒（Christian）：你或许对于收受——你们这一教派对于索取一般是毫无顾虑的——我们这顽梗不化之族的东西，未免有所顾忌。不过，为你的良心起见，不必担心；我向你保证，我心里既不是犹太人，也不是基督徒。」

「那愿上帝帮助你！」

「某一位，或某一样东西，已经帮得我太多太多了——足足娇养了我三十三年。不过，恕我直言，这话出自一位基督徒之口，倒颇古怪。」

「先生，要做一名好的基督徒，必先做一名好的犹太人。」

「或许吧。我两样都不打算做——也不打算做个好的异教徒。我亲爱的先生，这个话题便到此为止吧。这超乎我的范围。我若能像我那条狗那样做一头好的畜生——并且先证明做一头好的畜生是一件好事——我就心满意足了。」

===Original===
The officer looked down on with a stately, loving sorrow. Raphael caught his eye, and felt that he was in the presence of no common man.

"I must take care what I say here, I suspect, or I shall be entangled shortly in a regular Socratic dialogue.… And now, sir, may I return your question, and ask who and what are you? I really have no intention of giving you up to any Caesar, Antiochus, Tiglath-Pileser, or other flea-devouring flea.… They will fatten well enough without your blood. So I only ask as a student of the great nothing-in-general, which men call the universe."

"I was prefect of a legion this morning. What I am now, you know as well as I."

"Just what I do not. I am in deep wonder at seeing your hilarity, when, by all flea-analogies, you ought to be either be howling your fate like Achilles on the shores of Styx, or pretending to grin and bear it, as I was taught to do when I played at Stoicism. You are not of that sect certainly, for you confessed yourself a fool just now."

"And it would be long, would it not, before you made one of them do as much? Well, be it so. A fool I am; yet, if God helps us as far as Ostia, why should I not be cheerful?"

"Why should you?"

"What better thing can happen to a fool, than that God should teach that he is one, when he fancied himself the wisest of the wise? Listen to me, sir. Four mouths ago I was blessed with health, honour, lands, friends—all for which the heart of man could wish. And if, for an insane ambition, I have chosen to risk all those, against the solemn warnings of the truest friend, and the wisest saint who treads this earth of God's—should I not rejoice to have it proved to me, even by such a lesson as this, that the friend who never deceived me before was right in this case too; and that the God who has checked and turned me for forty years of wild toil and warfare, whenever I dared to do what was right in the sight of my own eyes, has not forgotten me yet, or given up the thankless task of my education?"

"And who, pray, is this peerless friend?"

"Augustine of Hippo."

===Chinese===
那军官望着他，目光雍容而含着慈爱的悲悯。拉斐尔触到他的目光，觉得自己面对的绝非寻常之人。

「我瞧我在这里说话得小心些，」他暗想，「否则不多时便要陷入一场正经的苏格拉底式问答了。……那么先生，我可否把你方才的问题奉还，问你是何人、所事何事？我实在无意把你交给任何凯撒（Caesar）、安提阿古（Antiochus）、提革拉毗列色（Tiglath-Pileser），或其他吞吃跳蚤的跳蚤。……没有你的血，他们也尽可养得肥肥的。所以我只是作为『那大而无当、人称之为宇宙者』的研究者，才动此一问。」

「今早我还是一军之帅。此刻我是什么，你知道得和我一般清楚。」

「偏偏我不知道。我深为诧异于你这份快活劲儿，因为按照一切跳蚤的类比，你此刻本该要么像阿喀琉斯（Achilles）在斯提克斯河（Styx）畔号哭自己的命运，要么像我从前玩斯多葛派（Stoicism）那一套时所学的那样，装出一副咬牙苦忍的笑脸。你当然不属于那一派，因为你方才已自承是个愚人。」

「而要叫他们当中任何一位做到你方才所作的，只怕还得很久呢，是不是？好，便如此吧。我是愚人；可是，倘若上帝帮助我们到了奥斯提亚，我为何不该快活呢？」

「你为何该呢？」

「一个愚人发现自己原是愚人——而他原以为自己是最有智慧者之一——有上帝来这样教训他，还有什么比这更好的事么？听我说，先生。四个月前，我还享有健康、荣名、田产、朋友——人心所能愿望的一切。倘若我为一念癫狂的野心，竟不顾最真心的朋友、踏在这上帝之地上的最睿智的圣徒的谆谆告诫，甘冒失掉这一切之险——那么，如今既有这番教训来向我证明：那位向来不曾欺我的朋友在这事上也是对的；那位四十年来每当敢行自己眼中看为正之事便拦阻我、扭转我的上帝，也仍未丢弃我，仍未放弃我这份不知感恩的教化之工——我岂不应当欢喜么？」

「请问这位无与伦比的朋友是谁？」

「希波的奥古斯丁（Augustine of Hippo）。」

===Original===
"Humph! It had been better for the world in general, if the great dialectician had exerted his powers of persuasion on Heraclian himself."

"He did so, but in vain."

"I don't doubt it. I know the sleek Count well enough to judge what effect a sermon would have upon that smooth vulpine determination of his.… 'An instrument in the hands of God, my dear brother.… We must obey His call, even to the death,' etc. etc." And Raphael laughed bitterly.

"You know the Count?"

"As well, sir, as I care to know any man."

"I am sorry for your eyesight, then, sir," said the Prefect severely, "if it has been able to discern no more than that in so august a character."

"My dear sir, I do not doubt his excellence—nay, his inspiration. How well he divined the perfectly fit moment for stabbing his old comrade Stilicho! But really, as two men of the world, we must be aware by this time that every man has his price.…"

"Oh, hush! hush!" whispered the girl. "You cannot guess how you pain him. He worships the Count. It was not ambition, as he pretends, but merely loyalty to him, which brought here against his will."

"My dear madam, forgive me. For your sake I am silent.…"

"For her sake! A pretty speech for me! What next?" said he to himself. "Ah, Bran, Bran, this is all your fault!"

"For my sake! Oh, why not for your own sake? How sad to hear one—one like you, only sneering and speaking evil!"

"Why then? If fools are fools, and one can safely call them so, why not do it?"

"Ah—if God was merciful enough to send down His own Son to die for them, should we not be merciful enough not to judge their failings harshly!"

"My dear young lady, spare a worn-out philosopher any new anthropologic theories. We really must push on a little faster, if we intend to reach Ostia tonight."

But, for some reason or other, Raphael sneered no more for a full half-hour.

===Chinese===
「哼！那位大辩证家若是把他那套说服的本事用在赫拉克利安本人身上，于天下苍生或更为有益。」

「他这样做了，却徒然。」

「我并不怀疑。那位油头滑面的伯爵我是知道得够清楚的，一篇说教在那副油滑狐一般的决断上能起什么效用，我自能判断。……『上帝手中之器也，我亲爱的弟兄。……我们必须顺服他的呼召，虽至于死，云云。』」拉斐尔苦笑起来。

「你认识伯爵？」

「认识得跟我愿认识任何一个人一样深，先生。」

「那我替你的眼力惋惜，先生，」那总督严厉地说，「若你所见的那副堂皇气派仅止于此。」

「我亲爱的先生，我并不怀疑他的卓绝——乃至他的灵感。他当年选准了最恰当的时机，给他那位老袍泽斯提里科（Stilicho）一刀，何其精当！不过，说实在话，咱们两个历世之人，到此总该如何道：人各有其价。」

「哦，嘘！嘘！」姑娘低声道，「你猜不到你叫他多难受。他是崇拜伯爵的。带他到这里来的，并非他所假装的野心，而只是对伯爵的忠诚——他是违心而来的。」

「亲爱的夫人，恕我。为你的缘故，我缄口。……」

「为她的缘故！这话可真中听！接下来还怎样呢？」他暗想。「唉，布朗啊布朗，这全是你的不是！」

「为我的缘故！噢，为何不为你自己的缘故呢？听一个人——像你这般的人——一味讥嘲、一味说人坏话，多叫人难过！」

「那又为什么不该呢？愚人既是愚人，又能安然称之为愚人，为什么不该这样做？」

「啊——若是上帝慈悲到差遣他的独生子来为他们死，我们岂不也该慈悲，不苛刻地论断他们的过犯么！」

「亲爱的小姐，饶了一个筋疲力尽的哲学家吧，别再给他讲什么新的人类学理论了。我们今晚要赶到奥斯提亚，真得加快些才行。」

可是，不知为了什么缘故，足足半个钟头，拉斐尔没有再讥嘲过一句。

===Original===
Long, however, ere they reached Ostia, the night had fallen; and their situation began to be more than questionably safe. Now and then a wolf, slinking across the road towards his ghastly feast, glided like a lank ghost out of the darkness, and into it again, answering Bran's growl by a gleam of his white teeth. Then the voices of some marauding party rang coarse and loud through the still night, and made them hesitate and stop a while. And at last, worst of all, the measured tramp of an imperial column began to roll like distant thunder along the plain below. They were advancing upon Ostia! What if they arrived there before the routed army could rally, and defend themselves long enough to re-embark!… What if—a thousand ugly possibilities began to crowd up.

"Suppose we found the gates of Ostia shut, and the Imperialists bivouacked outside?" said Raphael half to himself.

"God would protect His own," answered the girl; and Raphael had no heart to rob her of her hope, though he looked upon their chances of escape as growing smaller and smaller every moment. The poor girl was weary; the mule weary also; and as they crawled along, at a pace which made it certain that the fast passing column would be at Ostia an hour before them, to join the vanguard of the pursuers, and aid them in investing the town, she had to lean again and again on Raphael's arm. Her shoes, unfitted for so rough a journey, had been long since torn off, and her tender feet were marking every step with blood. Raphael knew it by her faltering gait; and remarked, too, that neither sigh nor murmur passed her lips. But as for helping her, he could not; and began to curse the fancy which had led to eschew even sandals as unworthy the self-dependence of a Cynic.

And so they crawled along, while Raphael and the Prefect, each guessing the terrible thoughts of the other, were thankful for the darkness which hid their despairing countenances from the young girl; she, on the other hand, chatting cheerfully, almost laughingly, to her silent father.

At last the poor girl stepped on some stone more sharp than usual—and, with a sudden writhe and shriek, sank to the ground. Raphael lifted her up, and she tried to proceed, but sank down again.… What was to be done?

===Chinese===
然而，他们还没到奥斯提亚，夜色便已落下；他们的处境开始变得颇不安全了。不时有一只狼，悄悄穿过大路朝它那可怖的宴席走去，像一道瘦长的鬼影从黑暗里滑出，又滑进去，用一闪白牙回应布朗的低吼。接着，某一伙劫匪粗哑响亮的嗓音划破静谧的夜，叫他们迟疑着停了一会儿。最后，最糟糕的——御营一军那有节奏的脚步声，开始像远雷一般沿着下方平原滚将过来。他们正向奥斯提亚推进！若他们在溃军还来不及重整、自卫足够时间再度登船之前便赶到了那里，怎么办！……若是——一千种不妙的可能开始纷纷涌上心头。

「万一我们赶到奥斯提亚，城门紧闭，帝国军在外头露宿呢？」拉斐尔半自言自语地说。

「上帝必保护属他的人，」姑娘答道；拉斐尔虽眼看他们脱身的希望每时每刻都在变小，却也不忍夺去她这份盼望。那可怜的姑娘已筋疲力尽；骡子也累了；他们这样磨蹭着走，按这速度，那支疾行而过的纵队必在他们之前一个钟头到达奥斯提亚，与追兵的前锋会合，协助他们包围这座城镇；她不得不一次又一次地靠在拉斐尔臂上。她的鞋不适于这样崎岖的赶路，早已磨烂脱落，娇嫩的双脚每走一步都留下血迹。拉斐尔从她踉跄的步态便知道；他也注意到，她唇间不曾漏出半声叹息、半句怨言。可要帮她，他却不能；他开始咒骂自己当初那念头——为了不配犬儒派（Cynic）自立的精神，竟连便鞋也不肯穿。

他们就这样磨蹭着前行；拉斐尔与那总督各自揣着对方那可怖的心思，都为那遮住自己绝望面容、不叫姑娘看见的夜色而暗暗庆幸；她呢，却一路叽叽喳喳、几乎带着笑，跟她那沉默的父亲说着话。

终于，那可怜的姑娘踩到一块比平常更尖的石子——猛地一扭，一声尖叫，跌倒在地。拉斐尔把她扶起来，她想再走，却又跌了下去。……可怎么办？

===Original===
"I expected this," said the Prefect, in a slow stately voice. "Hear me, sir! Jew, Christian, or philosopher, God seems to have bestowed on you a heart which I can trust. To your care I commit this girl—your property, like me, by right of war. Mount her upon this mule. Hasten with her—where you will—for God will be there also. And may He so deal with you as you deal with her henceforth. An old and disgraced soldier can do no more than die."

And he made an effort to dismount; but fainting from his wounds, sank upon the neck of the mule. Raphael and his daughter caught in their arms.

"Father! Father! Impossible! Cruel! Oh—do you think that I would have followed you hither from Africa, against your own entreaties, to desert you now?"

"My daughter, I command!"

The girl remained firm and sound.

"How long have you learned to disobey me? Lift the old disgraced man down, sir, and leave to die in the right place—on the battlefield where his general sent him."

The girl sank down on the road in an agony of weeping. "I must help myself, I see," said her father, dropping to the ground. "Authority vanishes before old age and humiliation. Victoria! has your father no sins to answer for already, that you will send before his God with your blood too upon his head?"

Still the girl sat weeping on the ground; while Raphael, utterly at his wits end, tried hard to persuade himself that it was no concern of his.

"I am at the service of either or of both, for life or death; only be so good as to settle it quickly.… Hell! here it is settled for us, with a vengeance!"

And as he spoke, the tramp and jingle of horsemen rang along the lane, approaching rapidly.

In an instant Victoria had sprung to her feet—weakness and pain had vanished.

"There is one chance—one chance for him! Lift over the bank, sir! Lift over, while I run forward and meet them. My death will delay them long enough for you to save him!"

"Death?" cried Raphael, seizing her by the arm. "If that were all—"

"God will protect His own," answered she calmly, laying her finger on her lips; and then breaking from his grasp in the strength of her heroism, vanished into the night.

===Chinese===
「我料到这一着了，」那总督缓缓地、庄重地说。「听我说，先生！不论你是犹太人、基督徒，还是哲学家，上帝似乎已赐予你一颗我所能信任的心。这姑娘我便托付给你——按战时之权，她和我一样是你的财物。把她扶上这匹骡子。带着她——随你去哪里——赶紧走——上帝也必在那里。愿他此后怎样待你，全看你怎样待她。一个蒙羞的老兵，所能做的，不过一死而已。」

他挣扎着要下骡；却因伤口昏厥，倒在了骡子颈上。拉斐尔和他女儿一齐把他接住。

「父亲！父亲！万万不可！太狠心了！噢——你以为我既不顾你苦劝、从非洲跟你来到这里，今夜便会舍你而去么？」

「女儿，我命令你！」

姑娘仍站得稳稳的。

「你几时学会违抗我了？把这位蒙羞的老人扶下来，先生，让他死在该死的地方——死在他将军派他去的战场上。」

姑娘痛哭着瘫倒在大路上。「看来我得自己来，」她父亲说着，跌到地上。「在老迈与屈辱面前，威严便荡然无存。维多利亚（Victoria）！你父亲要担当的罪还不够多么，你还要让自己的血也算在他头上、叫他去见他的上帝么？」

姑娘仍坐在地上哭泣；拉斐尔一筹莫展，拼命想说服自己这不关他的事。

「生也好，死也好，你们一位或二位，我都听命；只是劳驾快些定夺。……见鬼！这可倒好，有人替我们定夺了！」

他正说着，骑兵的马蹄声与甲片的叮当声便顺着小径响来，来得飞快。

一霎间维多利亚已一跃而起——软弱与疼痛一扫而空。

「还有一个机会——一个救他的机会！把他抬过那道坡，先生！抬过去，我迎上前去会他们。我的死会耽搁他们，足够你们救他！」

「死？」拉斐尔一把抓住她的胳膊叫道，「倘若只是这一桩——」

「上帝必保护属他的人，」她平静地答道，一指按在唇上；随即以她那股英雄气概挣脱了他的手，消失在夜色中。

===Original===
Her father tried to follow her, but fell on his face, groaning. Raphael lifted him, strove to drag up the steep bank: but his knees knocked together; a faint sweat seemed to melt every limb.… There was a pause, which secured ages long.… Nearer and nearer came the trampling.… A sudden gleam of the moon revealed Victoria standing with outspread arms, right before the horses' heads. A heavenly glory seemed to bathe her from head to foot… or was it tears sparkling in his own eyes?… Then the grate and jar of the horse-hoofs on the road, as they pulled up suddenly.… He turned his face away and shut his eyes.…

"What are you?" thundered a voice.

"Victoria, the daughter of Majoricus the Prefect."

The voice was low, but yet so clear and calm, that every syllable rang through Aben-Ezra's tingling ears.…

A shout—a shriek—the confused murmur of many voices.… He looked up, in spite of himself—a horseman had sprung to the ground, and clasped Victoria in his arms. The human heart of flesh, asleep for many a year, leaped into mad life within his breast, and drawing his dagger, he rushed into the throng—

"Villains! Hellhounds! I will balk you! She shall die first!"

And the bright blade gleamed over Victoria's head.… He was struck down—blinded—half-stunned—but rose again with the energy of madness.… What was this? Soft arms around him.… Victoria's!

"Save him! spare him! He saved us! Sir! It is my brother! We are safe! Oh, spare the dog! It saved my father!"

"We have mistaken each other, indeed, sir!" said a gay young Tribune, in a voice trembling with joy. "Where is my father?"

"Fifty yards behind. Down, Bran! Quiet! O Solomon, mine ancestor, why did you not prevent me making such an egregious fool of myself? Why, I shall be forced, in self-justification, to carry through the farce!"

===Chinese===
她父亲想追上去，却面朝地栽倒，呻吟起来。拉斐尔扶起他，想把他拖上那道陡坡：可他自己却双膝打颤；一阵虚汗似乎把每一肢都融化了。……停了一阵——这几秒钟长得有如几个世纪。……马蹄声越来越近。……一道突如其来的月光，照见维多利亚张开双臂、正立在那些马头之前。一种天上的荣光似乎从头到脚沐浴着她……还是他自己眼中闪烁的泪光？……接着是马蹄在路面上猛然收住时的那一阵刺耳的摩擦与颠簸。……他把脸转开，闭上了眼睛……

「你是什么人？」一个声音如雷轰般问道。

「维多利亚，马约里库斯（Majoricus）总督之女。」

那声音虽低，却如此清朗沉静，每一个字都钻进阿本-以斯拉那嗡嗡作响的耳朵……

一声喊——一声尖叫——许多人声嘈杂交错。……他不由自主地抬头看——一名骑兵已跳到地上，把维多利亚搂在怀里。那颗沉睡了许多年的肉做的人心，在他胸中疯狂地跳活了；他抽出匕首，冲进人群——

「恶棍！地狱的恶犬！我偏不让你们如愿！我先叫她死！」

明晃晃的刀锋在维多利亚头上闪耀……他被打倒——眼前发黑——半昏过去——却又带着一股疯劲爬起来……这是什么？一双柔软的胳膊搂住了他……维多利亚的！

「救他！饶他！他救了我们！先生！这是我哥哥！我们没事了！噢，饶了那条狗吧！它救了我父亲！」

「我们果真是彼此误会了，先生！」一位年轻的护民官（Tribune）欢快地说，声音因喜悦而发颤。「我父亲在哪里？」

「五十步开外。布朗，趴下！安静！噢，我的祖先所罗门啊，你为何不拦着我，叫我出了这么大的洋相？哎呀，为给自己遮羞，我倒非把这出闹剧演到底不可了！」

===Original===
There is no use telling what followed during the next five minutes, at the end of which time Raphael found himself astride of a goodly warhorse, by the side of the young Tribune, who carried Victoria before him. Two soldiers in the meantime were supporting the Prefect on his mule, and convincing that stubborn bearer of burdens that it was not quite so unable to trot as it had fancied, by the combined arguments of a drench of wine and two sword-points, while they heaped their general with blessings, and kissed his hands and feet.

"Your father's soldiers seem to consider themselves in debt to him: not, surely, for taking them where they could best run away?"

"Ah, poor fellows!" said the Tribune; "we have had as real a panic among us as I ever read of in Arrian or Polybius. But he has been a father rather than a general to them. It is not often that, out of a routed army, twenty gallant men will volunteer to ride back into the enemy's ranks, on the chance of an old man's breathing still."

"Then you knew where to find us?" said Victoria.

"Some of them knew. And he himself showed us this very byroad yesterday, when we took up our ground, and told us it might be of service on occasion—and so it has been."

"But they told me that you were taken prisoner. Oh, the torture I have suffered for you!"

"Silly child! Did you fancy my father's son would be taken alive? I and the first troop got away over the garden walls, and cut our way out into the plain, three hours ago."

"Did I not tell you," said Victoria, leaning toward Raphael, "that God would protect His own?"

"You did," answered he; and fell into a long and silent meditation.
===Chinese===
接下来五分钟的事，不必细述；五分钟之末，拉斐尔发觉自己已跨在一匹神骏的战马上，与那年轻的护民官并辔而行——护民官把维多利亚抱在自己身前。这其间，两名士兵正扶着那总督骑在他的骡子上，用酒灌下去与剑尖抵上去这两条道理双管齐下，说服那头倔强的驮兽：它原不像它自以为的那样不善于小跑；他们一边给他们的将军堆上祝福，一边亲他的手和脚。

「你父亲的兵士似乎觉得欠了他的恩——总不会是因为他带他们到了一个最便于逃命的地方吧？」

「啊，可怜的人们！」护民官说，「我们当中这场惊慌大溃逃，是千真万确的，与我在阿里安（Arrian）或波利比乌斯（Polybius）书里读到过的一样真切。可他对他们与其说是一位将军，不如说是一位父亲。一支溃军之中，竟有二十位壮士自愿骑马重返敌阵，只为碰运气看一位老人是否还在喘息——这是寻常能见的事么。」

「那么你们是知道到哪儿来找我们了？」维多利亚说。

「他们当中有人知道。昨日我们安营时，正是他亲自把这条小径指给我们看，说万一或可派上用场——果然派上了用场。」

「可他们对我说你已被俘。啊，我为你受了多少苦！」

「傻孩子！你以为我父亲的儿子会被人活捉么？我和第一队人马早在三个钟头前便翻过花园的墙，杀出去冲到平原上了。」

「我不是跟你说过么，」维多利亚侧过身朝拉斐尔说，「上帝必保护属他的人？」

「你说过的，」他答道；随即陷入了长久的、默默的沉思。

## XIV / XIV

### The Rocks of the Sirens / 塞壬的礁石

===Original===
These four months had been busy and eventful enough to Hypatia and to Philammon; yet the events and the business were of so gradual and uniform a tenor, that it is as well to pass quickly over them, and show what had happened principally by its effects.

The robust and fiery desert-lad was now metamorphosed into the pale and thoughtful student, oppressed with the weight of careful thought and weary memory. But those remembrances were all recent ones. With his entrance into Hypatia’s lecture-room, and into the fairy realms of Greek thought, a new life had begun for him; and the Laura, and Pambo, and Arsenius, seemed dim phantoms from some antenatal existence, which faded day by day before the inrush of new and startling knowledge.

===Chinese===
这四个月，对希帕蒂娅（Hypatia）和菲拉蒙（Philammon）而言，都可谓忙碌而多事；然而这些事变与事务进展得那样和缓、那样一律，倒不如将它们略过，只由它们留下的痕迹来看究竟发生了什么。

那个壮健、火爆的沙漠少年，如今已化作一个苍白而多思的学生，被审慎的思虑与疲惫的记忆压得喘不过气来。然而这些回忆全是新近的。自他踏进希帕蒂娅的讲学堂、踏进希腊思想的仙境之日起，一种全新的生活便已为他展开；至于劳拉（the Laura）、庞波（Pambo）、阿尔塞尼乌斯（Arsenius），则成了某种前生存在的朦胧幻影，在汹涌而来的、令人惊骇的新知面前，一日淡似一日。

===Original===
But though the friends and scenes of his childhood had fallen back so swiftly into the far horizon, he was not lonely. His heart found a lovelier, if not a healthier home, than it had ever known before. For during those four peaceful and busy months of study there had sprung up between Hypatia and the beautiful boy one of those pure and yet passionate friendships﻿—call them rather, with St. Augustine, by the sacred name of love﻿—which, fair and holy as they are when they link youth to youth, or girl to girl, reach their full perfection only between man and woman. The unselfish adoration with which a maiden may bow down before some strong and holy priest, or with which an enthusiastic boy may cling to the wise and tender matron, who, amid the turmoil of the world, and the pride of beauty, and the cares of wifehood, bends down to with counsel and encouragement﻿—earth knows no fairer bonds than these, save wedded love itself. And that second relation, motherly rather than sisterly, had bound Philammon with a golden chain to the wondrous maid of Alexandria.

===Chinese===
然而，尽管他童年的朋友与旧景已如此迅速地退入遥远的天际，他并不孤单。他的心找到了一个比它所曾知道的任何归宿都更可爱——若不更健康——的家。因为在这平静而忙碌的四个月的学习里，希帕蒂娅与这美少年之间，已生发出一段又纯洁又热烈的友谊——倒不如借圣奥古斯丁（St. Augustine）之口，称之为「爱」这个神圣的名字——这类情谊，在少年与少年、女子与女子之间固然美好而圣洁，却只有在男女之间才能臻于圆满。一个少女可以在某位刚强圣洁的教士面前倾心崇拜；一个热烈的少年可以依恋那位明智而慈爱的妇人，她在人世的纷扰、美貌的骄傲、为人妻的诸般挂虑之中，仍俯身赐他以劝勉与鼓励——人间不知有比这更美的羁绊，除了夫妻之爱本身。正是这第二种情谊——更近乎母爱，而非姊姊之爱——用一条金链将菲拉蒙系在了亚历山大城这位奇女子的身上。

===Original===
From the commencement of his attendance in her lecture-room she had suited her discourses to what she fancied were his especial spiritual needs; and many a glance of the eye towards him, on any peculiarly important sentence, set the poor boy’s heart beating at that sign that the words were meant for him. But before a month was past, won by the intense attention with which he watched for every utterance of hers, she had persuaded her father to give a place in the library as one of his pupils, among the youths who were employed there daily in transcribing, as well as in studying, the authors then in fashion.

===Chinese===
自从他来到她的讲学堂听讲，她便将她所讲授的内容，针对她所臆想的他特有的灵性需求加以调配；每逢一句尤其要紧的话，她便向他投去一瞥，这暗示「这话是冲着他来的」，教可怜的少年的心怦怦直跳。然而不出一个月，他便以他等候她每一句话时所流露的那种全神贯注，赢得了她的欢心；她说服了自己的父亲，在图书室里给他安了一个座次，收为门生，混迹于那些每日在那里既抄写、又研读当时风行诸家的少年们之间。

===Original===
She saw him at first but seldom﻿—more seldom than she would have wished; but she dreaded the tongue of scandal, heathen as well as Christian, and contented herself with inquiring daily from her father about the progress of the boy. And when at times she entered for a moment the library, where he sat writing, or passed him on her way to the Museum, a look was interchanged, on her part of most gracious approval, and on his of adoring gratitude, which was enough for both. Her spell was working surely; and she was too confident in her own cause and her own powers to wish to hurry that transformation for which she so fondly hoped.

“He must begin at the beginning,” thought she to herself. “Mathematics and the Parmenides are enough for him as yet. Without a training in the liberal sciences he cannot gain a faith worthy of those gods to whom some day I shall present him; and I should find his Christian ignorance and fanaticism transferred, whole and rude, to the service of those gods whose shrine is unapproachable save to the spiritual man, who has passed through the successive vestibules of science and philosophy.”

===Chinese===
起初她见他的次数并不频繁——比她自己所愿见的还少；可她惧怕流言蜚语，异教徒的、基督徒的都不例外，于是只好每日向父亲打听这少年的进益。偶尔她踏入他伏案抄写的图书室片刻，或是在去博物院（the Museum）的路上从他身旁经过，两人便交换一个眼色：她那一边是极其恩慈的嘉许，他这一边是崇拜的感激——这一瞥于双方都已足够。她的法术正在稳稳地奏效；她对自己的事业、对自己的力量都太过自信，反倒不愿催促那她如此殷切期盼的改变早日到来。

「他必须从头学起，」她暗自思忖，「眼下数学和《巴门尼德斯》（Parmenides）对他已足够。不经 liberal sciences 自由学问的熏陶，他无从为那些有朝一日我要引他皈依的神明赢得一种相称的信仰；他的基督教式的无知与狂热，若原封不动地、粗鄙地搬到那些神明的座前效力，只怕我也要失望——那些神明的圣龛，唯有那已依次穿过科学与哲学一重重前厅的属灵之人，方能企及。」

===Original===
But soon, attracted herself, as much as wishing to attract him, she employed him in copying manuscripts for her own use. She sent back his themes and declamations, corrected with her own hand; and Philammon laid them by in his little garret at Eudaimon’s house as precious badges of honour, after exhibiting them to the reverential and envious gaze of the little porter. So he toiled on, early and late, counting himself well paid for a week’s intense exertion by a single smile or word of approbation, and went home to pour out his soul to his host on the one inexhaustible theme which they had in common﻿—Hypatia and her perfections. He would have raved often enough on the same subject to his fellow-pupils, but he shrank not only from their artificial city manners, but also from their morality, for suspecting which he saw but too good cause. He longed to go out into the streets, to proclaim to the whole world the treasure which he had found, and call on all to come and share it with him. For there was no jealousy in that pure love of his. Could he have seen her lavishing on thousands far greater favours than she had conferred on him, he would have rejoiced in the thought that there were so many more blest beings upon earth, and have loved them all and everyone as brothers, for having deserved her notice. Her very beauty, when his first flush of wonder was past, he ceased to mention﻿—ceased even to think of it. Of course she must be beautiful. It was her right; the natural complement of her other graces but it was to him only what the mother’s smile is to the infant, the sunlight to the skylark, the mountain-breeze to the hunter﻿—an inspiring element, on which he fed unconsciously. Only when he doubted for a moment some especially startling or fanciful assertion, did he become really aware of the great loveliness of her who made it; and then his heart silenced his judgment with the thought﻿—Could any but true words come out of those perfect lips?﻿—any but royal thoughts take shape within that queenly head?﻿ ﻿… Poor fool! Yet was it not natural enough?

===Chinese===
然而不久，她自己也被他所吸引——这一点丝毫不亚于她之欲吸引他——她便差他为自己抄写手稿。她把他交上来的作文与演说辞用朱笔批改后发还；菲拉蒙把它们当作珍贵的勋衔，珍藏在他欧代蒙（Eudaimon）家那间小阁楼里，珍藏之前还先拿到那小门房跟前，让他怀着敬畏与妒羡的心情瞻仰一番。他就这样早晚操劳不息，一整周紧张的劳作，只要换得她一个微笑、一句嘉许，他便觉得报酬已足；他又回到家里，向他的房东倾吐衷肠，絮絮叨叨地讲着他们二人唯一讲不完的共同话题——希帕蒂娅，以及她的种种美德。他本也大可以在他的同窗面前把同一题目吹嘘个够；可他不仅畏避他们那做作的城里人作派，也畏避他们的德行——他大有理由怀疑那德行究竟如何。他巴不得冲到街上去，向全世界宣告他所寻得的宝藏，呼唤众人都来与他一同分享。因为他那份纯洁的爱里没有半分嫉妒。倘若他亲眼看见她把远胜于她所赐予他的恩惠，慷慨地分给成千上万的人，他也会因想到地上竟有这么多蒙福的人而满心欢喜，并且爱他们每一个人如同兄弟，因为他们竟配得她的青眼。就连她的美貌——当初第一次惊叹的狂喜过去之后——他也不再提起，甚至也不再挂怀。她当然必须是美的。这本是她的权利，是她其余诸般恩赐的自然补足；然而对他而言，那美不过是母亲对婴孩的微笑、阳光对云雀、山风对猎人那样——一种鼓舞人心的元素，他在不知不觉中以此为养。唯有当他一时对她某句尤其骇人或离奇的断语生出疑惑时，他才真正意识到开口之人是何等的动人；这时他的心便以这样一个念头堵住了他的判断——除了真话，难道还能从那完美的双唇里吐出别的么？——除了王者之思，难道还能在那王者的头颅里成形的么？……可怜的痴人！然而这岂不也是再自然不过的么？

===Original===
Then, gradually, as she passed the boy, poring over his book, in some alcove of the Museum Gardens, she would invite him by a glance to join the knot of loungers and questioners who dangled about her and her father, and fancied themselves to be reproducing the days of the Athenian sages amid the groves of another Academus. Sometimes, even, she had beckoned him to her side as she sat in some retired arbour, attended only by her father; and there some passing observation, earnest and personal, however lofty and measured, made him aware, as it was intended to do, that she had a deeper interest in him, a livelier sympathy for him, than for the many; that he was in her eyes not merely a pupil to be instructed, but a soul whom she desired to educate. And those delicious gleams of sunlight grew more frequent and more protracted; for by each she satisfied herself more and more that she had not mistaken either his powers or his susceptibilities: and in each, whether in public or private, Philammon seemed to bear himself more worthily. For over and above the natural ease and dignity which accompanies physical beauty, and the modesty, self-restraint, and deep earnestness which he had acquired under the discipline of the Laura, his Greek character was developing itself in all its quickness, subtlety, and versatility, until he seemed to Hypatia some young Titan, by the side of the flippant, hasty, and insincere talkers who made up her chosen circle.

===Chinese===
其后，渐渐地，当她在博物院花园（Museum Gardens）的某处壁龛前走过，看见那少年埋头读书时，她便以一瞥眼色，邀他加入那一小簇在她和她父亲身旁转悠的闲人与发问者——这些人自以为是在另一座阿卡德穆（Academus）的林下重温雅典先哲的旧梦。有时她甚至会在某处幽僻的凉亭里向他招手，唤他到她身侧，那时在场的唯有她父亲一人；在那里，她随便说出的一两句虽则高远矜持、却恳切而切中他本人的话，便如她所愿地让他觉察到：她对他怀着比别人更深的关切、更切的同情；在她眼中，他不仅是一个待教的门生，更是一个她意欲陶冶的灵魂。而那一线一线甘美的阳光，也越发频繁、越发绵长；因为每经历一回，她便愈加确信自己没有看错他的资质，也没有看错他的可塑性；而在每一回里，无论公开场合还是私下，菲拉蒙似乎都表现得更为得体。因为除了那与体魄之美相伴而来的天然从容与庄重、以及他在劳拉的管教下养成的谦逊、自制与深沉的真诚之外，他那希腊人的天性也正以其全部的敏捷、微妙与多才多艺显露出来，直至在希帕蒂娅眼中，与那一群组成她精选圈子、轻浮、浮躁而又言不由衷的清谈客相比，他简直像一位年轻的提坦（Titan）。

===Original===
But man can no more live upon Platonic love than on the more prolific species of that common ailment; and for the first month Philammon would have gone hungry to his couch full many a night, to lie awake from baser causes than philosophic meditation, had it not been for his magnanimous host, who never lost heart for a moment, either about himself, or any other human being. As for Philammon’s going out with him to earn his bread, he would not hear of it. Did he suppose that he could meet any of those monkish rascals in the street, without being knocked down and carried off by main force? And besides there was a sort of impiety in allowing so hopeful a student to neglect the “Divine Ineffable” in order to supply the base necessities of the teeth. So he should pay no rent for his lodgings﻿—positively none; and as for eatables﻿—why, he must himself work a little harder in order to cater for both. Had not all his neighbours their litters of children to provide for, while he, thanks to the immortals, had been far too wise to burden the earth with animals who would add to the ugliness of their father the Tartarean hue of their mother? And after all, Philammon could pay him back when he became a great sophist, and made money, as of course he would some day or other; and in the meantime, something might turn up﻿—things were always turning up for those whom the gods favoured; and besides, he had fully ascertained that on the day on which he first met Philammon, the planets were favourable, the Mercury being in something or other, he forgot what, with Helios, which portended for Philammon, in his opinion, a similar career with that of the glorious and devout Emperor Julian.

===Chinese===
然而人不能靠柏拉图式的爱情果腹，正如不能靠那种更为多产的世俗病症果腹一样；头一个月里，若不是他那宽宏大量的房东——无论对别人还是对自己，从来不曾片刻灰心——菲拉蒙怕是有许多个夜晚要饿着肚子上床，并且彻夜难眠，但那却不是出于哲学冥想，而是出于更俗气的原因。至于让菲拉蒙跟他一道出去挣饭吃，他简直听都不愿听。难道菲拉蒙以为，他在街上随便撞见那些修士恶棍，能不被人家一拳打翻、强行掳走么？况且，让一个如此有指望的学生为供给牙齿那卑下的需求，而荒废了「神圣不可言说者」（the Divine Ineffable），未免也有几分不敬。所以他的房租——一文也不必付，坚决不付；至于吃的——好罢，他自己只好再多操些劳，好为两个人张罗。他的邻居们哪一个不是拖着一窝孩子要养活，而他呢，感谢诸位不朽之神，向来太过明智，绝不肯给大地再添累赘，添上一群既承袭乃父的丑陋、又染上乃母那塔耳塔洛斯（Tartarean）式幽暗肤色的生物？再说，待到菲拉蒙日后成了一位大智辩家、挣了大钱——这当然是早晚的事——总会还他的；而在那之前，总会有什么转机的——受神明眷顾之人，从来都不愁转机；况且他早已仔细查算过，他初次遇见菲拉蒙的那一日，星辰大吉，水星正处于某宫——他忘了是哪一宫——与赫利俄斯（Helios）同度；据他看来，这正预示着菲拉蒙将有一条与那位光荣而虔诚的尤利安皇帝（Emperor Julian）相仿佛的命运。

===Original===
Philammon winced somewhat at the hint; which seemed to have an ugly verisimilitude in it: but still, philosophy he must learn, and bread he must eat; so he submitted.

But one evening, a few days after he had been admitted as Theon’s pupil, he found, much to his astonishment, lying on the table in his garret, an undeniable glittering gold piece. He took it down to the porter the next morning, and begged him to discover the owner of the lost coin, and return it duly. But what was his surprise, when the little man, amid endless capers and gesticulations, informed him with an air of mystery, that it was anything but lost; that his arrears of rent had been paid for him; and that by the bounty of the upper powers, a fresh piece of coin would be forthcoming every month! In vain Philammon demanded to know who was his benefactor. Eudaimon resolutely kept the secret and imprecated a whole Tartarus of unnecessary curses on his wife if she allowed her female garrulity﻿—though the poor creature seemed never to open her lips from morning till night﻿—to betray so great a mystery.

===Chinese===
这暗示使菲拉蒙不免瑟缩了一下；它似乎含着一种可憎的近真意味：然而无论如何，哲学他是要学的，面包他也是要吃的；于是他便屈服了。

可是一天傍晚——此时他入提昂（Theon）门下已有数日——他十分诧异地发现，自己阁楼的桌上赫然躺着一块无可置疑地闪着金光的金币。第二天早晨他把它拿下去交给门房，求他查访失主，妥为归还。然而那小个子却在连串的蹦跳与比划之中，一脸神秘地告诉他：这金币压根儿不曾丢失；他所欠的房租已有人替他付清；而且承蒙上界诸神的恩泽，今后每月还会有一块崭新的金币送到！菲拉蒙再三追问这位恩主究竟是谁，却全属徒然。欧代蒙死守着这个秘密，还把整整一座塔耳塔洛斯的多余诅咒一股脑儿堆到他妻子头上——倘若她听任自己身为女子的多嘴多舌——尽管那可怜虫似乎从早到晚从未启过唇——泄露这般重大的机密的话。

===Original===
Who was the unknown friend? There was but one person who could have done it.﻿ ﻿… And yet he dared not﻿—the thought was too delightful﻿—think it was she. It must have been her father. The old man had asked him more than once about the state of his purse. True, he had always returned evasive answers; but the kind old man must have divined the truth. Ought he not﻿—must he not﻿—go and thank him? No; perhaps it was more courteous to say nothing. If he﻿—she﻿—for of course she had permitted, perhaps advised, the gift﻿—had intended him to thank them, would they have so carefully concealed their own generosity?﻿ ﻿… Be it so, then. But how would he not repay them for it! How delightful to be in her debt for anything﻿—for everything! Would that he could have the enjoyment of owing her existence itself!

So he took the coin, bought unto himself a cloak of the most philosophic fashion, and went his way, such as it was, rejoicing.

===Chinese===
这位素未谋面的恩人究竟是谁？能做这事的人只有一个。……然而他不敢——这念头太令人快慰了——想那人就是她。那必然是她的父亲。老人曾不止一次问起他钱囊的宽紧。不错，他总拿含糊其辞的话搪塞过去；可这位好心的老人必已窥破真情。他该不该——他能不能——去向他道谢？不；也许什么都不说才更合礼数。如果他——她——因为这份馈赠当然是她所允准的，甚或是她所建议的——有意让他去致谢，他们又何至于这般小心翼翼地隐匿自己的善举？……那就这样罢。然而他将怎样报答他们啊！欠她任何东西——欠她一切——竟是何等令人喜悦！但愿他能享有欠她一条性命的恩情！

于是他收下了那枚金币，给自己买了一件最合哲学家身份的斗篷，便满心欢喜地——尽管一仍旧贯——上路了。

===Original===
But his faith in Christianity? What had become of that?

What usually happens in such cases. It was not dead; but nevertheless it had fallen fast asleep for the time being. He did not disbelieve it; he would have been shocked to hear such a thing asserted of him: but he happened to be busy believing something else﻿—geometry, conic sections, cosmogonies, psychologies, and whatnot. And so it befell that he had not just then time to believe in Christianity. He recollected at times its existence; but even then he neither affirmed nor denied it. When he had solved the great questions﻿—those which Hypatia set forth as the roots of all knowledge﻿—how the world was made, and what was the origin of evil, and what his own personality was, and﻿—that being settled﻿—whether he had one, with a few other preliminary matters, then it would be time to return, with his enlarged light, to the study of Christianity; and if, of course, Christianity should be found to be at variance with that enlarged light, as Hypatia seemed to think.﻿ ﻿… Why, then﻿—What then?﻿ ﻿… He would not think about such disagreeable possibilities. Sufficient for the day was the evil thereof.

===Chinese===
然而他对基督教的信仰呢？那信仰又落到何种田地了？

这原是这类情形下常有的事。它并未死去；然而此刻却已沉沉地睡去了。他并不否定它；若有人把这话加在他身上，他定要大为震骇：只是他碰巧正忙着相信别的什么——几何学、圆锥曲线、宇宙生成论、种种灵魂论，以及诸如此类。于是乎，他一时竟没有工夫再去信基督教了。他偶或想起还有基督教这回事；可即便在那时，他既不肯定它，也不否定它。待他解决了那些大问题——那些被希帕蒂娅宣称为一切学问之根的问题——世界是怎样造成的、恶的根源何在、他自己的人格是什么，以及——把这先弄明白之后——他到底有没有一个人格，再加上其余几桩先决的事——到那时，他自可带着他已扩充了的光明，回过头来研究基督教；而倘若——当然啦——基督教竟被发现与那扩充了的光明相左，正如希帕蒂娅似乎所暗示的那样。……那么，到那时——到那时又怎样呢？……他不愿去想这般不快的可能。一天的难处一天当就够了。

===Original===
Possibilities? It was impossible.﻿ ﻿… Philosophy could not mislead. Had not Hypatia defined it, as man’s search after the unseen? And if he found the unseen by it, did it not come to just the same thing as if the unseen had revealed itself to him? And he must find it﻿—for logic and mathematics could not err. If every step was correct, the conclusion must be correct also; so he must end, after all, in the right path﻿—that is, of course, supposing Christianity to be the right path﻿—and return to fight the Church’s battles, with the sword which he had wrested from Goliath the Philistine.﻿ ﻿… But he had not won the sword yet.; and in the meanwhile, learning was weary work; and sufficient for the day was the good, as well as the evil, thereof.

So, enabled by his gold coin each month to devote himself entirely to study, he became very much what Peter would have coarsely termed a heathen. At first, indeed, he slipped into the Christian churches, from a habit of conscience. But habits soon grow sleepy; the fear of discovery and recapture made his attendance more and more of a labour. And keeping himself apart as much as possible from the congregation, as a lonely and secret worshipper, he soon found himself as separate from them in heart as in daily life. He felt that they, and even more than they, those flowery and bombastic pulpit rhetoricians, who were paid for their sermons by the clapping and cheering of the congregation, were not thinking of, longing after, the same things as himself. Besides, he never spoke to a Christian; for the negress at his lodgings seemed to avoid him﻿—whether from modesty or terror, he could not tell; and cut off thus from the outward “communion of saints,” he found himself fast parting away from the inward one. So he went no more to church, and looked the other way, he hardly knew why, whenever he passed the Caesareum; and Cyril, and all his mighty organisation, became to him another world, with which he had even less to do than with those planets over his head, whose mysterious movements, and symbolisms, and influences Hypatia’s lectures on astronomy were just opening before his bewildered imagination.

===Chinese===
可能？那是不可能的。……哲学岂能引人入歧途。希帕蒂娅岂不曾把哲学界定为人对那不可见者的追寻么？他若借哲学而寻得那不可见者，岂不是与那不可见者主动向他启示，殊途同归么？而他必能寻得——因为逻辑与数学不会出错。每一步若都正确，结论也必然正确；所以他终归必将走到正路上——当然，这是假定基督教才是正路——然后再回过头来，用他从非利士人歌利亚（Goliath the Philistine）手中夺来的剑，去为教会征战。……只是那把剑他眼下还没夺到手呢；而在此期间，做学问乃是苦差事；那么，一天的好处一天享也就够了。

于是，靠着每月那枚金币，得以全副心力扑在学问上，他变成了一个彼得（Peter）用粗俗的话怕要称作「异教徒」的人。起初，他确实还因良心的习惯，悄悄溜进基督教的教堂。然而习惯很快便会打盹；被人发觉、重新抓回去的恐惧，使他上教堂越来越像是一种苦役。他尽量躲开会众，作为一个孤独而隐秘的敬拜者待在一旁，不久便发觉自己与他们在心里，也如在日常生活中一样，已隔得远远的了。他感到他们——甚至更甚于他们的，是那些花团锦簇、夸夸其谈的讲坛演说家，他们靠会众的鼓掌欢呼领取讲道的报酬——所思所慕的，与他所思所慕的，全然不是一回事。况且他从不和一个基督徒交谈；因为他住处那个黑女人似乎有意躲着他——是出于羞怯，还是出于恐惧，他无从判断；既与外在的「圣徒相通」（communion of saints）断了来往，他发觉自己与那内在的相通也正迅速地疏离。于是他再也不上教堂了，每逢经过凯撒里乌姆（the Caesareum），他便把头扭向另一边——连他自己也说不清是为什么；至于区利罗（Cyril）以及他那强大的整套组织，在他眼中已成了另一个世界，他与之的瓜葛，甚至比头顶那些星辰还要少——而那些星辰神秘的运动、象征与影响，希帕蒂娅的天文学讲座正一一展现在他那目眩神迷的想象之前。

===Original===
Hypatia watched all this with growing self-satisfaction, and fed herself with the dream that through Philammon she might see her wildest hopes realised. After the manner of women, she crowned him, in her own imagination, with all powers and excellences which she would have wished him to possess, as well as with those which he actually manifested, till Philammon would have been as much astonished as self-glorified could he have seen the idealised caricature of himself which the sweet enthusiast had painted for her private enjoyment. They were blissful months those to poor Hypatia. Orestes, for some reason or other, had neglected to urge his suit, and the Iphigenia-sacrifice had retired mercifully into the background. Perhaps she should be able now to accomplish all without it. And yet﻿—it was so long to wait! Years might pass before Philammon’s education was matured, and with them golden opportunities which might never recur again.

===Chinese===
希帕蒂娅目睹这一切，日益沾沾自喜；她拿一个梦餍养自己：也许借菲拉蒙之手，她那些最狂妄的盼望竟可一一成真。凭着女子的脾性，她在自己的想象里，把一切她巴望他具备的才情美德，连同他实已显露的那些，统统加冕在他头上；以至于菲拉蒙若能瞧见这位甜蜜的狂热者私下为自己取乐而为他描绘的那幅理想化的漫画，怕是要既大吃一惊、又沾沾自喜了。对可怜的希帕蒂娅而言，那几个月是幸福的几个月。不知为了什么缘故，俄瑞斯忒斯（Orestes）竟不曾紧逼着求婚，而那伊菲革涅亚式的牺牲（Iphigenia-sacrifice），也慈惠地退到了幕后。也许她如今无需那牺牲，便能成就一切。然而——这要等多久啊！菲拉蒙的教育要待到成熟，恐怕还要过好几年；而与年俱逝的，将是那些再也不会重来的黄金良机。

===Original===
“Ah!” she sighed at times, “that Julian had lived a generation later! That I could have brought all my hard-earned treasures to the feet of the Poet of the Sun, and cried, ‘Take me!﻿—Hero, warrior, statesman, sage, priest of the God of Light! Take thy slave! Command her﻿—send her﻿—to martyrdom, if thou wilt!’ A pretty price would that have been wherewith to buy the honour of being the meanest of thy apostles, the fellow-labourer of Iamblichus, Maximus, Libanius, and the choir of sages who upheld the throne of the last true Caesar!”

===Chinese===
「啊！」她有时叹息道，「但愿尤利安晚生一代！但愿我能把所有这些我辛苦得来的珍宝，捧到那位太阳诗人脚下，高呼：『收下我罢！——英雄、武士、政治家、智者、光明之神的祭司啊！收下你的奴婢！差遣她——遣她——去殉道，随你的便罢！』以这样的代价，去买那做你最微贱一个使徒的荣名，去买那与杨布里库（Iamblichus）、马克西穆斯（Maximus）、利巴尼乌斯（Libanius），以及那一班扶持末代真正凯撒宝座的哲人群星并肩辛劳的荣名——这代价，又算得了什么呢！」

## XV / XV

### Nephelococcugia / 涅斐罗科库吉亚

===Original===
Hypatia had always avoided carefully discussing with Philammon any of those points on which she differed from his former faith. She was content to let the divine light of philosophy penetrate by its own power, and educe its own conclusions. But one day, at the very time at which this history reopens, she was tempted to speak more openly to her pupil than she yet had done. Her father had introduced him, a few days before, to a new work of hers on Mathematics; and the delighted and adoring look with which the boy welcomed her, as he met her in the Museum Gardens, pardonably tempted her curiosity to inquire what miracles her own wisdom might have already worked. She stopped in her walk, and motioned her father to begin a conversation with Philammon.

===Chinese===
希帕蒂娅向来小心地回避着，不去与菲拉蒙讨论任何她与他旧日信仰相左之处。她甘愿让哲学那属神的光借其自身的力量渗入，自行引出其结论。可有一天——正是在这部历史重新展开的那一刻——她忍不住要比往日更坦率地对她的学生开口。几天前，她父亲把她的新一卷数学著作引荐给了他；而那少年在博物院（Museum）花园里迎上她时，眼中那欣喜若狂、近乎崇拜的神色，也情有可原地勾起了她的好奇，想去探问自己的智慧究竟已行了什么神迹。她停下脚步，示意父亲去与菲拉蒙攀谈。

===Original===
“Well!” asked the old man, with an encouraging smile, “and how does our pupil like his new﻿—”

“You mean my conic sections, father? It is hardly fair to expect an unbiased answer in my presence.”

“Why so?” said Philammon. “Why should I not tell you, as well as all the world, the fresh and wonderful field of thought which they have opened to me in a few short hours?”

“What then?” asked Hypatia, smiling, as if she knew what the answer would be. “In what does my commentary differ from the original text of Apollonius, on which I have so faithfully based it?”

“Oh, as much as a living body differs from a dead one. Instead of mere dry disquisitions on the properties of lines and curves, I found a mine of poetry and theology. Every dull mathematical formula seemed transfigured, as if by a miracle, into the symbol of some deep and noble principle of the unseen world.”

===Chinese===
「那么！」老人含着鼓励的微笑问道，「咱们这位学生可喜欢他新——」

「您是指我的圆锥曲线论吧，父亲？当着我的面，要指望一个不带偏见的回答，未免不太公道。」

「为何不能？」菲拉蒙说，「我为何不能像对天下人一样，把那在短短几个时辰里向我豁然洞开的新奇而瑰丽的思想天地，告诉您呢？」

「那又如何？」希帕蒂娅含笑问，仿佛早已知晓答案，「我的评注，与我忠实地据以为本的那个阿波罗尼奥斯（Apollonius）的原典，究竟有何不同？」

「噢，其间差别，如同活人的身躯与死人的不同。我所遇见的，不再是关于线与曲线之性质的干巴巴的论说，而是一座诗与神学的宝矿。每一条枯燥的数学公式，都仿佛经了神迹一般变了模样，化作那未见之世界里某个深邃而崇高的原理的象征。」

===Original===
“And do you think that he of Perga did not see as much? or that we can pretend to surpass, in depth of insight, the sages of the elder world? Be sure that they, like the poets, meant only spiritual things, even when they seem to talk only of physical ones, and concealed heaven under an earthly garb, only to hide it from the eyes of the profane; while we, in these degenerate days, must interpret and display each detail to the dull ears of men.”

“Do you think, my young friend,” asked Theon, “that mathematics can be valuable to the philosopher otherwise than as vehicles of spiritual truth? Are we to study numbers merely that we may be able to keep accounts; or as Pythagoras did, in order to deduce from their laws the ideas by which the universe, man, Divinity itself, consists?”

“That seems to me certainly to be the nobler purpose.”

“Or conic sections, that we may know better how to construct machinery; or rather to devise from them symbols of the relations of Deity to its various emanations?”

“You use your dialectic like Socrates himself, my father,” said Hypatia.

===Chinese===
「你难道以为，佩尔加的那位就没有看到这些么？抑或我们竟能妄称，在洞见之深上，还要超过上古的哲人？你只管放心：他们和诗人一样，所说的无非属灵之事，哪怕表面看来只谈物质之物；他们把天上的事裹上一件尘世的外衣，不过是好从凡俗之人的眼中将它藏起罢了；而我们，在这衰颓之世，却不得不向人们迟钝的耳朵逐一讲解、铺陈每一处细节。」

「你可觉得，我的年轻朋友，」提昂问，「数学对哲人，除了作属灵真理的载体之外，还能别有价值么？我们研究数目，难道只为了好记账；抑或如毕达哥拉斯（Pythagoras）那样，是为了从数目的法则中，推出那使宇宙、人、乃至神性本身得以成立的诸般理念？」

「在我看来，那确是更为崇高的目的。」

「抑或研究圆锥曲线，只为好更精巧地制造机械；还是为了从其中构想出神性与其种种流溢之间关系的象征？」

「您运使辩证法，简直如苏格拉底（Socrates）本人一般，父亲，」希帕蒂娅说。

===Original===
“If I do, it is only for a temporary purpose. I should be sorry to accustom Philammon to suppose that the essence of philosophy was to be found in those minute investigations of words and analyses of notions, which seem to constitute Plato’s chief power in the eyes of those who, like the Christian sophist Augustine, worship his letter while they neglect his spirit; not seeing that those dialogues, which they fancy the shrine itself, are but vestibules﻿—”

“Say rather, veils, father.”

“Veils, indeed, which were intended to baffle the rude gaze of the carnal-minded; but still vestibules, through which the enlightened soul might be led up to the inner sanctuary, to the Hesperid gardens and golden fruit of the Timaeus and the oracles.﻿﻿ … And for myself, were but those two books left, I care not whether every other writing in the world perished tomorrow.”

“You must except Homer, father.”

“Yes, for the herd.﻿﻿ … But of what use would he be to them without some spiritual commentary?”

“He would tell them as little, perhaps, as the circle tells to the carpenter who draws one with his compasses.”

===Chinese===
「纵然我如此，也不过是一时的权宜。我可不乐意让菲拉蒙养成一种习惯，以为哲学的精髓尽在那对字句的细枝末节的考求、对概念的条分缕析之中——在那些如同基督徒诡辩家奥古斯丁（Augustine）一般的人眼里，那似乎正是柏拉图（Plato）力量之所在；他们崇拜他的字句，却忽略了他的精神；他们不曾看出，那些被他们当作圣龛本身的对话录，不过是门廊——」

「不如说，是幔子，父亲。」

「是幔子，没错，原是要叫属肉体之人的粗鄙目光无从窥探；可到底仍是门廊，蒙了光照的灵魂，可以被引着穿过它们，直入内殿，走到《蒂迈欧篇》（Timaeus）与诸神谕那赫斯珀里得斯花园（Hesperid gardens）、那金苹果所在之处。……而就我自己而言，只要那两本书尚在，明日世间其余一切著述尽数亡佚，我也全不在意。」

「荷马（Homer），父亲，您总得除外。」

「除外，那是为芸芸众生。……可若没有某种属灵的诠释，荷马于他们又有何用？」

「也许，他能告诉他们的，并不比一个圆所能告诉那个用圆规画出它的木匠多。」

===Original===
“And what is the meaning of the circle?” asked Philammon.

“It may have infinite meanings, like every other natural phenomenon; and deeper meanings in proportion to the exaltation of the soul which beholds it. But, consider, is it not, as the one perfect figure, the very symbol of the totality of the spiritual world; which, like it, is invisible, except at its circumference, where it is limited by the dead gross phenomena of sensuous matter! and even as the circle takes its origin from one centre, itself unseen﻿—a point, as Euclid defines it, whereof neither parts nor magnitude can be predicated﻿—does not the world of spirits revolve round one abysmal being, unseen and undefinable﻿—in itself, as I have so often preached, nothing, for it is conceivable only by the negation of all properties, even of those of reason, virtue, force; and yet, like the centre of the circle, the cause of all other existences?”

“I see,” said Philammon; for the moment, certainly, the said abysmal Deity struck him as a somewhat chill and barren notion﻿﻿ … but that might be caused only by the dullness of his own spiritual perceptions. At all events, if it was a logical conclusion, it must be right.

===Chinese===
「那这个圆，又是什么意思呢？」菲拉蒙问。

「它也许有无穷多的含义，正如一切别的自然现象一般；而观照它的灵魂愈是高超，它所显出的含义便愈深。可你且想，作为唯一完美的图形，它岂不正是那整个属灵世界的象征么？那世界正如它一般，是不可见的，唯有在其周界处才得看见——在那周界上，它为感官物质那死而粗浊的现象所限！而正如圆从一个圆心发生——那圆心本身是看不见的，是一个点，如欧几里得（Euclid）所定义的，无法断言其有部分、有大小——那属灵的世界，岂不也是绕着一个深渊般的存有旋转，它不可见、不可定——其自身，如我时常宣讲的那样，是无，因为它唯有借着否定一切属性、甚至否定理性、德性、力量这些属性，方可思议；然而又如那圆心一般，是一切其他存在的根源？」

「我明白了，」菲拉蒙说；至少此刻，这位深渊般的神在他看来，未免是一个略嫌清冷、略嫌荒芜的观念……可那也许不过是他自己属灵知觉迟钝所致。无论如何，倘若它是一个合乎逻辑的结论，那它便一定是对的。

===Original===
“Let that be enough for the present. Hereafter you may be﻿—I fancy that I know you well enough to prophesy that you will be﻿—able to recognise in the equilateral triangle inscribed within the circle, and touching it only with its angles, the three supra-sensual principles of existence, which are contained in Deity as it manifests itself in the physical universe, coinciding with its utmost limits, and yet, like it, dependent on that unseen central One which none dare name.”

“Ah!” said poor Philammon, blushing scarlet at the sense of his own dullness, “I am, indeed, not worthy to have such wisdom wasted upon my imperfect apprehension.﻿﻿ … But, if I may dare to ask﻿﻿ … does not Apollonius regard the circle, like all other curves, as not depending primarily on its own centre for its existence, but as generated by the section of any cone by a plane at right angles to its axis?”
