“But must we not draw, or at least conceive a circle, in order to produce that cone? And is not the axis of that cone determined by the centre of that circle?”

Philammon stood rebuked.

“Do not be ashamed; you have only, unwittingly, laid open another, and perhaps, as deep a symbol. Can you guess what it is?”

Philammon puzzled in vain.

“Does it not show you this? That, as every conceivable right section of the cone discloses the circle, so in all which is fair and symmetric you will discover Deity, if you but analyse it in a right and symmetric direction?”

“Beautiful!” said Philammon, while the old man added﻿—

“And does it not show us, too, how the one perfect and original philosophy may be discovered in all great writers, if we have but that scientific knowledge which will enable us to extract it?”

===Chinese===
「这些眼下便够了。日后你也许会——我想我对你知之已深，大可预言你将来定能——在那内接于圆、仅以其三角触着圆周的等边三角形中，认出存在的那三个超感官的原则：它们含于神性之中，正如神性在物质宇宙中显出自己时那样，与其最外的边界相吻合，却又如那圆一般，依赖着那无人敢称其名的、不可见的中央之一。」

「哎呀！」可怜的菲拉蒙说，因自觉迟钝而涨得满脸通红，「我实在不配，竟将这样的智慧虚耗在我这拙劣的悟性之上。……可是，若我敢问一句……阿波罗尼奥斯岂不是把圆，和一切别的曲线一样，看作其存在并非根本地依赖它自身的圆心，而是由一个平面以直角切过任一圆锥而产生的么？」

「可要得出那个圆锥，我们难道不必先画出一个、至少先构想出一个圆么？而那圆锥的轴，难道不是由那个圆的圆心所决定的么？」

菲拉蒙挨了训，默然而立。

「不必羞愧；你不过是不知不觉间，又揭示出另一个、或许同样深刻的象征。你能猜出是什么么？」

菲拉蒙苦苦思索，终是徒然。

「它岂不是向你显出这事么？正如圆锥每一个可以想见的直角截面都显出一个圆，同样，在一切美好而对称的事物中，只要你沿着一个正确而对称的方向去剖析，你便会在其中发现神性？」

「美极了！」菲拉蒙说，老人接着补了一句——

「而它岂不也向我们显出：那一套完美而本源的哲学，可以怎样在一切大作家的著作里被寻见，只要我们具备那种能将其抽取出来的科学知识？」

===Original===
“True, my father: but just now, I wish Philammon, by such thoughts as I have suggested, to rise to that higher and more spiritual insight into nature, which reveals her to us as instinct throughout﻿—all fair and noble forms of her at least﻿—with Deity itself; to make him feel that it is not enough to say, with the Christians, that God has made the world, if we make that very assertion an excuse for believing that His presence has been ever since withdrawn from it.”

“Christians, I think, would hardly say that,” said Philammon.

“Not in words. But, in fact, they regard Deity as the maker of a dead machine, which, once made, will move of itself thenceforth, and repudiate as heretics every philosophic thinker, whether Gnostic or Platonist, who, unsatisfied with so dead, barren, and sordid a conception of the glorious all, wishes to honour the Deity by acknowledging His universal presence, and to believe, honestly, the assertion of their own Scriptures, that He lives and moves, and has His being in the universe.”

Philammon gently suggested that the passage in question was worded somewhat differently in the Scripture.

“True. But if the one be true, its converse will be true also. If the universe lives and moves, and has its being in Him, must He not necessarily pervade all things?”

“Why?﻿—Forgive my dullness, and explain.”

“Because, if He did not pervade all things, those things which He did not pervade would be as it were interstices in His being, and in so far, without Him.”

“True, but still they would be within His circumference.”

“Well argued. But yet they would not live in Him, but in themselves. To live in Him they must be pervaded by His life. Do you think it possible﻿—do you think it even reverent to affirm that there can be anything within the infinite glory of Deity which has the power of excluding from the space which it occupies that very being from which it draws its worth, and which must have originally pervaded that thing, in order to bestow on it its organisation and its life? Does He retire after creating, from the spaces which He occupied during creation, reduced to the base necessity of making room for His own universe, and endure the suffering﻿—for the analogy of all material nature tells us that it is suffering﻿—of a foreign body, like a thorn within the flesh, subsisting within His own substance? Rather believe that His wisdom and splendour, like a subtle and piercing fire, insinuates itself eternally with resistless force through every organised atom, and that were it withdrawn but for an instant from the petal of the meanest flower, gross matter, and the dead chaos from which it was formed, would be all which would remain of its loveliness.﻿﻿ …

===Chinese===
「不错，父亲：只是眼下，我愿菲拉蒙借我所提示的这些思想，升到那更高、更属灵的对自然的洞见，那洞见向我们揭示：自然通体——至少她一切美好而崇高的形态——都贯穿着神性自身；我要让他感到：仅如基督徒那样说上帝造了世界，是不够的，倘若我们把这话当作借口，借以相信祂的同在自此便从世界中退去。」

「我想，基督徒不会那样说的，」菲拉蒙说。

「不会照字面说。可事实上，他们把神性看作一部死机器的制造者，那机器一经造好，此后便会自行运转；而无论灵知派（Gnostic）还是柏拉图派（Platonist），凡是不能满足于对那荣耀的万有如此死寂、荒芜、鄙陋的构想、而愿意借着承认神性无所不在来尊崇神性、并诚心相信他们自己《圣经》上那句「祂在宇宙之中生活、动作、存在」的哲思之人，他们一概斥为异端。」

菲拉蒙委婉地指出，那段经文在《圣经》里的措辞，与此略有不同。

「不错。可那一句若是真，其反面亦必为真。倘若宇宙在祂里面生活、动作、存在，祂岂不必然贯通万有？」

「为何？——原谅我的愚钝，请讲解。」

「因为，祂若不贯通万有，那些祂所未曾贯通之物，便仿佛是祂存在之中的空隙，在那一范围里，便是在祂之外了。」

「不错，可它们到底仍在祂的周界之内。」

「辩得妙。然而它们仍不是在祂里面活，而是在它们自己里面活。要在祂里面活，它们便须被祂的生命所贯通。你以为，在神性那无限的荣耀之中，竟可能有何物，具有从其所占的空间里排斥那使其之所以有价值、且必曾先行贯通该物方能赋予它组织与生命的那个存有的力量——你以为这是可能的么？这甚至是可敬的说法么？祂在创造之后，可是从那创造之时所占的空间里退了出来，沦落到要为己所造的宇宙腾出位置的可悲地步，并忍受那痛苦——因为一切物质自然的类比都告诉我们，那确是痛苦——如同肉中一根刺那般，有个异己之体在祂自己的实体之中存留？你宁可相信：祂的智慧与荣光，如同一团精微而透入的火，以不可抵挡之力永远贯入每一个有组织的原子；而它若从最卑微的一朵花的一片花瓣上撤去，哪怕只是一瞬，那么粗浊的物质、与那花成形之前那死寂的混沌，便是它所有可爱之处所剩下的全部了。……

===Original===
“Yes”﻿—she went on, after the method of her school, who preferred, like most decaying ones, harangues to dialectic, and synthesis to induction.﻿﻿ … “Look at yon lotus-flower, rising like Aphrodite from the wave in which it has slept throughout the night, and saluting, with bending swan-neck, that sun which it will follow lovingly around the sky. Is there no more there than brute matter, pipes and fibres, colour and shape, and the meaningless life-in-death which men call vegetation? Those old Egyptian priests knew better, who could see in the number and the form of those ivory petals and golden stamina, in that mysterious daily birth out of the wave, in that nightly baptism, from which it rises each morning reborn to a new life, the signs of some divine idea, some mysterious law, common to the flower itself, to the white-robed priestess who held it in the temple rites, and to the goddess to whom they both were consecrated.﻿﻿ … The flower of Isis!﻿﻿ … Ah!﻿—well. Nature has her sad symbols, as well as her fair ones. And in proportion as a misguided nation has forgotten the worship of her to whom they owed their greatness, for novel and barbaric superstitions, so has her sacred flower grown rarer and more rare, till now﻿—fit emblem of the worship over which it used to shed its perfume﻿—it is only to be found in gardens such as these﻿—a curiosity to the vulgar, and, to such as me, a lingering monument of wisdom and of glory past away.”

Philammon, it may be seen, was far advanced by this time; for he bore the allusions to Isis without the slightest shudder. Nay﻿—he dared even to offer consolation to the beautiful mourner.

“The philosopher,” he said, “will hardly lament the loss of a mere outward idolatry. For if, as you seem to think, there were a root of spiritual truth in the symbolism of nature, that cannot die. And thus the lotus-flower must still retain its meaning, as long as its species exists on earth.”

===Chinese===
「是的」——她接着说，用的是她那一派的方法，那一派如大多没落之派一样，偏爱雄辩胜过辩证，偏爱综合胜过归纳。……「你看那朵莲花，如阿佛洛狄忒（Aphrodite）从它宿了一夜的波涛中升起，以天鹅般弯垂的颈项，向那轮它将痴情追随环绕天穹的太阳致意。那里难道仅是粗蠢的物质、管道与纤维、颜色与形状、以及那被人称作草木的、无意义的半死之活么？那些古埃及的祭司懂得更多，他们能在那些象牙色花瓣与金色花蕊的数目与形态中，在那每日从波涛中神秘的诞生中，在那每夜的洗礼——它每日清晨从中复活、得一新命——之中，看见某个属神意念的征兆，某条神秘的法则，为花本身、为在庙中典礼里手执此花的白衣女祭司、以及为他们共同奉敬的女神所共有的法则。……伊西斯（Isis）之花！……啊！——罢了。自然界既有她美好的象征，也有她可悲的象征。而一国误入歧途的百姓，既已为他们本应归功其伟大的那位女神之敬拜所遗忘，转而去追逐新奇而野蛮的迷信，她那圣花也就越长越稀、越长越罕，直至今日——恰如它昔日曾为之散发芳馨的那场敬拜一般，恰成其恰当的象征——只见于这样的花园之中——于庸人不过一件奇珍，于如我这般人，则是一座流连不去的、记述着业已逝去的智慧与荣光的纪念碑。」

菲拉蒙，可想而知，至此已大有长进；因为他对那些提及伊西斯的话，竟毫不战栗地承受了下来。非但如此——他甚至敢向这位美丽的哀悼者进一言宽慰。

「哲人，」他说，「恐怕不会为一种纯粹外在的偶像崇拜之失而哀伤。因为倘若如你似乎所想，自然的象征之中含有属灵真理的根，那根是不会死的。如此，莲花便仍必保其含义，只要它的族类尚存于世上。」

===Original===
“Idolatry!” answered she, with a smile. “My pupil must not repeat to me that worn-out Christian calumny. Into whatsoever low superstitions the pious vulgar may have fallen, it is the Christians now, and not the heathens, who are idolaters. They who ascribe miraculous power to dead men’s bones, who make temples of charnel-houses, and bow before the images of the meanest of mankind, have surely no right to accuse of idolatry the Greek or the Egyptian, who embodies in a form of symbolic beauty ideas beyond the reach of words!

“Idolatry? Do I worship the Pharos when I gaze at it, as I do for hours, with loving awe, as the token to me of the all-conquering might of Hellas? Do I worship the roll on which Homer’s words are written, when I welcome with delight the celestial truths which it unfolds to me, and even prize and love the material book for the sake of the message which it brings? Do you fancy that any but the vulgar worship the image itself, or dream that it can help or hear them? Does the lover mistake his mistress’s picture for the living, speaking reality? We worship the idea of which the image is a symbol. Will you blame us because we use that symbol to represent the idea to our own affections and emotions instead of leaving it a barren notion, a vague imagination of our own intellect?”

===Chinese===
「偶像崇拜！」她含笑答道，「我的学生不可向我重复那套用烂了的基督徒的诽谤。无论虔诚的庸人曾陷入何等低劣的迷信，如今拜偶像的，是基督徒，而非异教徒。那些把神奇之力归于死人骨头、把藏尸所当作庙宇、在全人类最卑微之人的像前叩拜的人，当然便没有资格指控那以象征之美来体现言语所不能及之观念的希腊人或埃及人为拜偶像！

「拜偶像？我凝望法罗斯（the Pharos），一连几个时辰，怀着爱戴与敬畏，视它为我心中希腊（Hellas）那战无不胜之力的标记——我难道是在崇拜法罗斯么？我捧着那卷写着荷马之语的书卷，欣喜地迎接它向我展开的属天真理，甚至为它所传的信息而珍爱那有形的书——我难道是在崇拜那卷书么？你难道以为，除了庸人之外，还有谁崇拜那神像本身，或幻想它能垂听、能救助他们？情人难道会把他情人的画像，误作那活着、会说话的真身么？我们所崇拜的，是神像所象征的那个观念。难道你要责备我们，只因我们用那象征，把那观念呈现给自己的情与意，而不肯让它留作一个枯燥的观念、留作我们自己理智中一个模糊的想象？」

===Original===
“Then,” asked Philammon, with a faltering voice, yet unable to restrain his curiosity, “then you do reverence the heathen gods?”

Why Hypatia should have felt this question a sore one, puzzled Philammon; but she evidently did feel it as such, for she answered haughtily enough﻿—

“If Cyril had asked me that question, I should have disdained to answer. To you I will tell, that before I can answer your question you must learn what those whom you call heathen gods are. The vulgar, or rather those who find it their interest to calumniate the vulgar for the sake of confounding philosophers with them, may fancy them mere human beings, subject like man to the sufferings of pain and love, to the limitations of personality. We, on the other hand, have been taught by the primeval philosophers of Greece, by the priests of ancient Egypt, and the sages of Babylon, to recognise in them the universal powers of nature, those children of the all-quickening spirit, which are but various emanations of the one primeval unity﻿—say rather, various phases of that unity, as it has been variously conceived, according to the differences of climate and race, by the wise of different nations. And thus, in our eyes, he who reverences the many, worships by that very act, with the highest and fullest adoration, the one of whose perfection they are the partial antitypes; perfect each in themselves, but each the image of only one of its perfections.”

===Chinese===
「那么，」菲拉蒙声音发颤地问道，却又按捺不住好奇，「那么，您确是敬奉那些异教之神的了？」

希帕蒂娅为何会把这问题视作一处痛处，菲拉蒙百思不得其解；但她显然确有此感，因为她的回答颇带几分倨傲——

「若是区利罗（Cyril）问我这话，我必不屑作答。对你，我倒可以说：在我能回答你的问题之前，你必须先弄清楚，你所称的异教之神，究竟是什么。庸人——或者更确切地说，那些为了把哲人和庸人搅作一谈、而觉得诽谤庸人于己有利的人——也许会以为那些神不过是些凡人，和人一样受苦痛与情欲的折磨，受人格之局限的束缚。而我们这一派，则由希腊最早的哲人、古埃及的祭司、与巴比伦的智者所教导，在他们之中认出那普遍的自然之力，认出那位使万物复苏之灵的众子，他们不过是那一个太初之太一的种种流溢——不如说，是那太一在不同的气候与种族之下、被列国智者以不同方式所构想出来的种种相态。如此，在我们眼中，凡敬奉那「多」的，便正是借着这一敬奉之举，以最高、最圆满的崇拜，敬奉了那「一」——那「多」不过是其一端一端的局部原型；每一原型本身各尽其美，却各自只映出那「一」的一种完美。」

===Original===
“Why, then,” said Philammon, much relieved by this explanation, “do you so dislike Christianity? may it not be one of the many methods﻿—”

“Because,” she answered, interrupting him impatiently, “because it denies itself to be one of those many methods, and stakes its existence on the denial; because it arrogates to itself the exclusive revelation of the Divine, and cannot see, in its self-conceit, that its own doctrines disprove that assumption by their similarity to those of all creeds. There is not a dogma of the Galileans which may not be found, under some form or other, in some of those very religions from which it pretends to disdain borrowing.”

“Except,” said Theon, “its exaltation of all which is human and lowborn, illiterate, and levelling.”

“Except that﻿—But look! here comes someone whom I cannot﻿—do not choose to meet. Turn this way﻿—quick!”

And Hypatia, turning pale as death, drew her father with unphilosophic haste down a sidewalk.

===Chinese===
「那么，」菲拉蒙说，这一番解释令他大感宽慰，「您又为何这般厌弃基督教呢？它难道不可能是那诸多法门之一——」

「因为，」她不耐烦地打断他答道，「因为它自己否认它是那诸多法门之一，并且把它的存亡押在这一否认之上；因为它僭称自己独占了属神的启示，却又在自负之中看不见：它自己的种种教义，正因其与一切信条的教义都相似，反而证明了它那一套声称是站不住脚的。那些加利利人（Galileans）的教义，没有一条不能在某些形式之下、从某些它佯装不屑借鉴的宗教里寻见。」

「除了一条，」提昂说，「它把一切属人的、出身卑微的、不识字的、以及那拉平一切的，都抬举了起来。」

「除那一条——可你看！那边来了一位我无法——不愿与之相见的人。往这边走——快！」

希帕蒂娅面无人色，以一种很不哲学的匆忙，拽着父亲转入了一条小径。

===Original===
“Yes,” she went on to herself, as soon as she had recovered her equanimity. “Were this Galilean superstition content to take its place humbly among the other ‘*religiones licitas*’ of the empire, one might tolerate it well enough, as an anthropomorphic adumbration of divine things fitted for the base and toiling herd; perhaps peculiarly fitted, because peculiarly flattering to them. But now﻿—”

“There is Miriam again,” said Philammon, “right before us!”

“Miriam?” asked Hypatia severely. “You know her then? How is that?”

“She lodges at Eudaimon’s house, as I do,” answered Philammon frankly. “Not that I ever interchanged, or wish to interchange, a word with so base a creature.”

“Do not! I charge you!” said Hypatia, almost imploringly. But there was now no way of avoiding her, and perforce Hypatia and her tormentress met face to face.

===Chinese===
「是啊，」她一恢复镇定，便自顾自地接下去，「这加利利人的迷信，若是甘愿谦卑地置身于帝国其他那些『合法宗教』（*religiones licitas*）之列，人也未尝不能容忍它——把它看作一种拟人化的、对属神之物的影写，正合那卑贱劳苦之群氓的胃口；也许尤其合他们的胃口，因为它尤其迎合他们。可如今——」

「米利暗（Miriam）又来了，」菲拉蒙说，「就在我们前头！」

「米利暗？」希帕蒂娅厉声问，「你竟认识她？这是怎么回事？」

「她寄宿在欧代蒙（Eudaimon）家里，和我一样，」菲拉蒙坦率地答，「我并非曾与她交谈过一句话，也无意与这般卑劣之人交谈。」

「不可！我嘱咐你！」希帕蒂娅近乎恳求地说。可此刻已无从回避她，希帕蒂娅与折磨她的那个女人，终于不得不迎面相逢。

===Original===
“One word! one moment, beautiful lady,” began the old woman, with a slavish obeisance. “Nay, do not push by so cruelly. I have﻿—see what I have for you!” and she held out with a mysterious air, The Rainbow of Solomon.

“Ah! I knew you would stop a moment﻿—not for the ring’s sake, of course, nor even for the sake of one who once offered it to you.﻿.—Ah! and where is he now? Dead of love, perhaps! at least, here is his last token to the fairest one, the cruel one.﻿﻿ … Well, perhaps she is right.﻿﻿ … To be an empress﻿—an empress!﻿﻿ … Far finer than anything the poor Jew could have offered.﻿﻿ … But still.﻿﻿ … An empress need not be above hearing her subject’s petition.﻿﻿ …”

All this was uttered rapidly, and in a wheedling undertone, with a continual snaky writhing of her whole body, except her eye, which seemed, in the intense fixity of its glare, to act as a fulcrum for all her limbs; and from that eye, as long as it kept its mysterious hold, there was no escaping.

===Chinese===
「一句话！就一会儿，美丽的夫人，」老妇开口道，奴颜婢膝地打了个躬，「哎，别这样狠心地把我推开。我有——您瞧我给您带来了什么！」她神色诡秘地递出那枚「所罗门的彩虹」（The Rainbow of Solomon）。

「啊！我就知道您会停一停——当然不是为了这戒指的缘故，也未必是为了那个曾把它献给您的人。……啊！他如今在何处呢？也许为情而死了吧！至少，这是他给那位最美人儿、那位狠心人儿的最后一件信物。……唉，也许她是对的。……去做一位皇后——一位皇后！……可比那可怜的犹太人所能献出的一切都要强得多。……可话又说回来。……一位皇后，总不至于不肯听一听她臣民的请求吧。……」

这一番话说得又急又快，声调是哄骗似的低语，整个身子不住地如蛇一般扭动，唯独那只眼睛除外——那只眼在那凝定不移的逼视中，仿佛为全身四肢充当着一个支点；而只要那只眼还那样神秘地攫住人，便无人能从中脱身。

===Original===
“What do you mean? What have I to do with this ring?” asked Hypatia, half frightened.

“He who owned it once, offers it to you now. You recollect a little black agate﻿—a paltry thing﻿﻿ … If you have not thrown it away, as you most likely have, he wishes to redeem it with this opal﻿﻿ … a gem surely more fit for such a hand as that.”

“He gave me the agate, and I shall keep it.”

“But this opal﻿—worth, oh, worth ten thousand gold pieces﻿—in exchange for that paltry broken thing not worth one?”

“I am not a dealer, like you, and have not yet learnt to value things by their money price. It that agate had been worth money, I would never have accepted it.”

“Take the ring, take it, my darling,” whispered Theon impatiently; “it will pay all our debts.”

“Ah, that it will﻿—pay them all,” answered the old woman, who seemed to have mysteriously overheard him.

===Chinese===
「你什么意思？这戒指与我何干？」希帕蒂娅半带惊惶地问。

「曾拥有它的人，如今把它献给您了。您总还记得一颗小小的黑玛瑙——一件不值钱的东西……您若还没有把它丢了——十之八九是丢了吧——他愿以这枚欧泊来赎它……这样一颗宝石，自然更配这样一只手。」

「那玛瑙是他送我的，我自当留下。」

「可这枚欧泊——价值，噢，值一万金笔呢——换您那不值一文、破破烂烂的小玩意儿？」

「我不是买卖人，不像您，还没学会按价钱来估量东西。那颗玛瑙若值钱，我当初根本不会收下。」

「收下这戒指，收下吧，我的宝贝，」提昂不耐烦地低声说，「它能还清我们一切的债。」

「啊，正是——能还清一切，」老妇应道，她似乎神秘地听见了他的话。

===Original===
“What!﻿—my father! Would you, too, counsel me to be so mercenary? My good woman,” she went on, turning to Miriam, “I cannot expect you to understand the reason of my refusal. You and I have a different standard of worth. But for the sake of the talisman engraven on that agate, if for no other reason, I cannot give it up.”

“Ah! for the sake of the talisman! That is wise, now! That is noble! Like a philosopher! Oh, I will not say a word more. Let the beautiful prophetess keep the agate, and take the opal too; for see, there is a charm on it also! The name by which Solomon compelled the demons to do his bidding. Look! What might you not do now, if you knew how to use that! To have great glorious angels, with six wings each, bowing at your feet whensoever you called them, and saying, ‘Here am I, mistress; send me.’ Only look at it!”

Hypatia took the tempting bait, and examined it with more curiosity than she would have wished to confess; while the old woman went on﻿—

“But the wise lady knows how to use the black agate, of course? Aben-Ezra told her that, did he not?”

===Chinese===
「什么！——父亲！连您也劝我这般见钱眼开么？好女人，」她转向米利暗，接着说，「我也不能指望您明白我拒绝的缘由。您和我，衡量事物的尺度本就不同。可单为那颗玛瑙上所刻的符箓，即便别无他故，我也不能把它放弃。」

「啊！为了那符箓！这才叫明智！这才叫高尚！不愧是个哲人！噢，我一个字也不再说了。让美丽的女先知留下那颗玛瑙，也收下这枚欧泊吧；因为您瞧，它上面也有一道符咒！就是所罗门（Solomon）用以驱使众魔听命的那个名字。您看！您若是懂得怎样用它，还有什么做不成的呢！只要您一呼唤，便有荣耀的大天使，各个生着六只翅膀，俯伏在您脚前，说：『我在这里，主母；差遣我吧。』您只管看一看！」

希帕蒂娅吞下了这诱人的饵，以一种她自己也不愿承认的好奇打量起它来；老妇则在一旁接着说——

「可那位聪慧的夫人，自然懂得怎样用那颗黑玛瑙了？阿本-以斯拉（Aben-Ezra）告诉过她的，是么？」

===Original===
Hypatia blushed somewhat; she was ashamed to confess that Aben-Ezra had not revealed the secret to her, probably not believing that there was any, and that the talisman had been to her only a curious plaything, of which she liked to believe one day that it might possibly have some occult virtue, and the next day to laugh at the notion as unphilosophical and barbaric; so she answered, rather severely, that her secrets were her own property.

“Ah, then! she knows it all﻿—the fortunate lady! And the talisman has told her whether Heraclian has lost or won Rome by this time, and whether she is to be the mother of a new dynasty of Ptolemies, or to die a virgin, which the Four Angels avert! And surely she has had the great demon come to her already, when she rubbed the flat side, has she not?”

“Go, foolish woman! I am not like you, the dupe of childish superstitions.”

“Childish superstitions! Ha! ha! ha!” said the old woman, as she turned to go, with obeisances more lowly than ever. “And she has not seen the Angels yet!﻿﻿ … Ah well! perhaps some day, when she wants to know how to use the talisman, the beautiful lady will condescend to let the poor old Jewess show her the way.”

And Miriam disappeared down an alley, and plunged into the thickest shrubberies, while the three dreamers went on their way.

Little thought Hypatia that the moment the old woman had found herself alone, she had dashed herself down on the turf, rolling and biting at the leaves like an infuriated wild beast﻿﻿ … “I will have it yet! I will have it, if I tear out her heart with it!”

===Chinese===
希帕蒂娅微微红了脸；她羞于承认阿本-以斯拉并未把那秘密传授给她——他大抵根本不信有什么秘密——而那符箓于她不过一件新奇的玩物，她喜欢某一日相信它或许真有某种隐秘的神力，次日又把这一念头当作不哲学、不文明的而加以哂笑；于是她颇为严厉地答道，她的秘密是她自己的事。

「啊，原来如此！她什么都知道——这位有福的夫人！那符箓已经告诉她，赫拉克利安（Heraclian）此刻是失了罗马还是得了罗马；已经告诉她，她究竟是要做一系新托勒密诸王（Ptolemies）之母，还是要终身作一处女而死——但愿四位天使不许如此！而且，她只要摩挲那平整的一面，那大恶魔便已经来过她那里了，是吧？」

「去吧，愚蠢的女人！我可不像你，做那孩童般迷信的傀儡。」

「孩童般的迷信！哈！哈！哈！」老妇说着转身要走，躬身之卑更甚于前，「而她竟还没有见过众天使！……唉，也好！也许有朝一日，这位美丽的夫人想知道怎样用那符箓时，肯俯允让这可怜的犹太老妪为她指点一二。」

米利暗消失在一条小径尽头，一头钻进了最茂密的灌木丛中，而那三位梦中人则继续上路。

希帕蒂娅哪里想得到，那老妇一待四下无人，便一头扑倒在草地上，如一头被激怒的野兽一般打滚、啃咬着落叶……「我总要把它弄到手！我总要把它弄到手，哪怕连着她的心一齐掏出来！」

## XVI / XVI

### Venus and Pallas / 维纳斯与帕拉斯

===Original===
As Hypatia was passing across to her lecture-room that afternoon, she was stopped midway by a procession of some twenty Goths and damsels, headed by Pelagia herself, in all her glory of jewels, shawls, and snow-white mule; while by her side rode the Amal, his long legs, like those of Gang-Rolf the Norseman, all but touching the ground, as he crushed down with his weight a delicate little barb, the best substitute to be found in Alexandria for the huge black chargers of his native land.

On they came, followed by a wondering and admiring mob, straight to the door of the Museum, and stopping began to dismount, while their slaves took charge of the mules and horses.

There was no escape for Hypatia; pride forbade her to follow her own maidenly instinct, and to recoil among the crowd behind her; and in another moment the Amal had lifted Pelagia from her mule, and the rival beauties of Alexandria stood, for the first time in their lives, face to face.

"May Athene befriend you this day, Hypatia!" said Pelagia with her sweetest smile. "I have brought my guards to hear somewhat of your wisdom this afternoon. I am anxious to know whether you can teach them anything more worth listening to than the foolish little songs which Aphrodite taught me, when she raised me from the sea-foam, as she rose herself, and named me Pelagia."

===Chinese===
那天午后，希帕蒂娅正穿过院落往讲学堂去，半道上便被一队人马拦住了去路——约莫二十来个哥特男女，为首的正是佩拉吉娅本人，浑身上下珠光宝气，肩披丽纱，骑着一头雪白的骡子，好不风光；她身旁骑着的是阿玛尔，他那两条长腿，活像北欧人「群·罗尔夫」（Gang-Rolf）一样，几乎要蹭着地面，把他那一身沉甸甸的分量压在一匹娇小的柏柏尔马上——这已是亚历山大城里所能寻觅到的、最差强人意的坐骑，聊以替代他故土那些高大的黑色战马。

一行人径直而来，身后跟着一群又惊又羡的闲汉，一直簇拥到博物院门前，方才停步下马，由随行的奴仆牵过骡马去照管。

希帕蒂娅已无处可避；自尊心不容她顺从自己少女的本能退缩到身后人堆里去；转眼之间，阿玛尔已把佩拉吉娅从骡子上抱了下来，于是亚历山大城里这两位争艳的美人，便平生头一遭面对面地站在了一处。

「愿雅典娜今日护佑你，希帕蒂娅！」佩拉吉娅笑得最甜地说道。「我带着我的卫队来听听你今天下午的什么高论。我倒急着要知道，你能不能教他们一些比阿佛洛狄忒教我的那些傻乎乎的小曲儿更值得一听的东西——当初她把我从海沫里托起来，一如她自己从海中升起一般，并给我取名佩拉吉娅。」

===Original===
Hypatia drew herself up to her stateliest height, and returned no answer.

"I think my bodyguard will well bear comparison with yours. At least they are the princes and descendants of deities. So it is but fitting that they should enter before your provincials. Will you show them the way?"

No answer.

"Then I must do it myself. Come, Amal!" and she swept up the steps, followed by the Goths, who put the Alexandrians aside right and left, as if they had been children.

"Ah! treacherous wanton that you are!" cried a young man's voice out of the murmuring crowd. "After having plundered us of every coin out of which you could dupe us, here you are squandering our patrimonies on barbarians!"

"Give us back our presents, Pelagia," cried another, "and you are welcome to your herd of wild bulls!"

===Chinese===
希帕蒂娅挺直了她那最为端庄高傲的身段，一言不发。

「我想我这支卫队，与你那帮人比起来倒也毫不逊色。至少他们都是亲王之裔、神祇之后。所以理当让他们走在你那些乡下人前头进去。你来为他们引路么？」

仍是没有回答。

「那我只好自己来了。来呀，阿玛尔！」说着她便裙裾飘飘地登上了台阶，身后跟着那群哥特人，把亚历山大人左一把右一把地拨开，仿佛拨开一群小孩子似的。

「啊！你这背信弃义的荡妇！」人丛中一个少年的声音从窃窃私议里嚷了出来。「你把我们能被骗走的每一个铜板都搜刮干净了，如今又来拿我们的家产去倒贴蛮子！」

「把那些礼物还给我们，佩拉吉娅，」另一个喊道，「那一群野牛你尽可领了去！」

===Original===
"And I will!" cried she, stopping suddenly; and clutching at her chains and bracelets, she was on the point of dashing them among the astonished crowd—

"There! take your gifts! Pelagia and her girls scorn to be debtors to boys, while they are worshipped by men like these!"

But the Amal, who, luckily for the students, had not understood a word of this conversation, seized her arm, asking if she were mad.

"No, no!" panted she, inarticulate with passion. "Give me gold—every coin you have. These wretches are twitting me with what they gave me before—before—oh Amal, you understand me?" And she clung imploringly to his arm.

"Oh! Heroes! each of you throw his purse among these fellows! they say that we and our ladies are living on their spoils!" And he tossed his purse among the crowd.

===Chinese===
「我还就还！」她嚷着，猛地收住脚；一把抓着自己的链子和镯子，眼看就要朝那惊愕的人群摔过去——

「拿去！拿了你们的礼物去！佩拉吉娅和她的姑娘们，既有这样的汉子供奉着，才不屑欠这群毛孩子的人情！」

可阿玛尔——幸而这番话他一字也没听懂，否则学生们可要遭殃——一把抓住她的胳膊，问她是不是疯了。

「不，不！」她气喘吁吁地说，激动得话也说不利落。「给我金子——你身上每一个铜板。这帮恶人拿从前——从前——他们给我的东西来奚落我……噢，阿玛尔，你明白我的意思吧？」她紧紧攀住他的胳膊，满眼恳求。

「噢！众位英雄！你们每人都把钱袋扔到这帮家伙中间去！他们说我们和我们的夫人靠他们的赃物过活呢！」说罢他便把自己的钱袋掷向人群。

===Original===
In an instant every Goth had followed his example: more than one following it up by dashing a bracelet or necklace into the face of some hapless philosophaster.

"I have no lady, my young friends," said old Wulf, in good enough Greek, "and owe you nothing: so I shall keep my money, as you might have kept yours; and as you might, too, old Smid, if you had been as wise as I."

"Don't be stingy, prince, for the honour of the Goths," said Smid, laughing.

"If I take in gold I pay in iron," answered Wulf, drawing half out of its sheath the huge broad blade, at the ominous brown stains of which the studentry recoiled; and the whole party swept into the empty lecture-room, and seated themselves at their ease in the front ranks.

===Chinese===
转眼之间，每个哥特人都依样而为：不止一人顺手又把手镯、项链摔到某个倒霉的「假哲学家」脸上。

「我没有夫人，年轻的朋友们，」老沃尔夫用一口颇为不错的希腊语说道，「也不欠你们什么：所以我的钱我自己留着，正如你们本也可以留着你们的钱一样；你也是一样啊，老斯密德，你要是跟我一样精明，也该如此。」

「别小气呀，亲王，为了哥特人的体面嘛，」斯密德笑道。

「我要收金子，就用铁来偿还，」沃尔夫答道，一面把那柄宽阔的大刀从鞘里抽出半截——刀上那 ominous 的褐色斑痕令学子们纷纷倒退；于是这一行人便长驱直入空荡荡的讲堂，大模大样地在最前排落了座。

===Original===
Poor Hypatia! At first she determined not to lecture—then to send for Orestes—then to call on her students to defend the sanctity of the Museum; but pride, as well as prudence, advised her better; to retreat would be to confess herself conquered—to disgrace philosophy—to lose her hold on the minds of all waverers. No! she would go on and brave everything, insults, even violence; and with trembling limbs and a pale cheek, she mounted the tribune and began.

To her surprise and delight, however, her barbarian auditors were perfectly well behaved. Pelagia, in childish good-humour at her triumph, and perhaps, too, determined to show her contempt for her adversary by giving her every chance, enforced silence and attention, and checked the tittering of the girls, for a full half-hour. But at the end of that time the heavy breathing of the slumbering Amal, who had been twice awoke by her, resounded unchecked through the lecture-room, and deepened into a snore; for Pelagia herself was as fast asleep as he. But now another censor took upon himself the office of keeping order. Old Wulf, from the moment Hypatia had begun, had never taken his eyes off her face; and again and again the maiden's weak heart had been cheered, as she saw the smile of sturdy intelligence and honest satisfaction which twinkled over that scarred and bristly visage; while every now and then the graybeard wagged approval, until she found herself, long before the end of the oration, addressing herself straight to her new admirer.

At last it was over, and the students behind, who had sat meekly through it all, without the slightest wish to "upset" the intruders, who had so thoroughly upset them, rose hurriedly, glad enough to get safe out of so dangerous a neighbourhood. But to their astonishment, as well as to that of Hypatia, old Wulf rose also, and stumbling along to the foot of the tribune, pulled out his purse, and laid it at Hypatia's feet.

===Chinese===
可怜的希帕蒂娅！起初她决意不开讲——继而想差人去请俄瑞斯忒斯——又想呼吁她的学生起来捍卫博物院的尊严；然而自尊心与审慎一并劝她打消了这些念头：退避便是自认败北——便是辱没哲学——便是失去一切动摇之人心上的凭据。不！她要讲下去，担当一切，屈辱也好、拳脚也罢；于是她四肢战栗、双颊苍白地登上了讲坛，开了口。

然而令她又惊又喜的是，她那群蛮族听众竟规规矩矩，毫无失仪之处。佩拉吉娅正因得胜而满心孩子气的欢畅，或许也有意要借这放对手一马的机会来显示自己的轻蔑，竟维持了足足半个钟头的安静与专注，连姑娘们的窃笑也被她制止了。可半个钟头一过，那酣睡的阿玛尔——其间已被她弄醒过两回——粗重的呼吸声便在讲堂里毫无遮拦地回荡起来，渐次化作鼾声；因为佩拉吉娅自己也和他一样睡熟了。然而此时另一位监察却自告奋勇地担起了维持秩序的差事。老沃尔夫自希帕蒂娅开口之时起，便目不转睛地盯着她的脸；少女那颗怯弱的心，一次又一次地被他鼓舞——只见那张伤痕累累、胡茬丛生的脸上，闪烁着刚毅的明悟与由衷的满意之色；那白胡子老头时不时点头赞许，到后来——远在演讲结束之前——她已不知不觉地把话直接对准了这位新添的倾慕者。

终于讲完了。后排那些学生，一路温顺地坐着听完，丝毫没有意思去「颠覆」这群把他们搅得一塌糊涂的不速之客——须知这群不速之客早已把他们颠覆得够呛——这时慌忙起身，巴不得早些脱离这等凶险的邻里。然而令他们、也令希帕蒂娅同样惊诧的是，老沃尔夫竟也站了起来，踉踉跄跄地走到讲坛脚下，掏出钱袋，放在了希帕蒂娅的足边。

===Original===
"What is this?" asked she, half terrified at the approach of a figure more rugged and barbaric than she had ever beheld before.

"My fee for what I have heard today. You are a right noble maiden, and may Freya send you a husband worthy of you, and make you the mother of kings!"

And Wulf retired with his party.

Open homage to her rival, before her very face! Pelagia felt quite inclined to hate old Wulf.

But at least he was the only traitor. The rest of the Goths agreed unanimously that Hypatia was a very foolish person, who was wasting her youth and beauty in talking to donkey-riders; and Pelagia remounted her mule, and the Goths their horses, for a triumphal procession homeward.

===Chinese===
「这是做什么？」她问道，对这个比她生平所见都更为粗犷、更为蛮荒的身影的逼近，半含着惊惶。

「我今日所闻的束脩。你是个真正高贵的小姐，愿弗蕾雅赐你一个配得上你的丈夫，叫你做众王之母！」

沃尔夫说罢便带着他那一行人退了出去。

当着自己的面，公然向情敌致敬！佩拉吉娅真有些恨起老沃尔夫来了。

但至少他是唯一的一个叛徒。其余的哥特人异口同声地认定，希帕蒂娅是个十足的蠢人，白白把青春美貌糟蹋在给骑驴的人讲道上；于是佩拉吉娅重新跨上她的骡子，哥特人们纷纷上马，排成凯旋的队伍打道回府。

===Original===
And yet her heart was sad, even in her triumph. Right and wrong were ideas as unknown to her as they were to hundreds of thousands in her day. As far as her own consciousness was concerned, she was as destitute of a soul as the mule on which she rode. Gifted by nature with boundless frolic and good-humour, wit and cunning, her Greek taste for the physically beautiful and graceful developed by long training, until she had become, without a rival, the most perfect pantomime, dancer, and musician who catered for the luxurious tastes of the Alexandrian theatres, she had lived since her childhood only for enjoyment and vanity, and wished for nothing more. But her new affection, or rather worship, for the huge manhood of her Gothic lover had awoke in her a new object—to keep him—to live for him—to follow him to the ends of the earth, even if he tired of her, ill-used her, despised her. And slowly, day by day, Wulf's sneers had awakened in her a dread that perhaps the Amal might despise her.… Why, she could not guess: but what sort of women were those Alrunas of whom Wulf sang, of whom even the Amal and his men spoke with reverence, as something nobler, not only than her, but even than themselves? And what was it which Wulf had recognised in Hypatia which had bowed the stern and coarse old warrior before her in that public homage?… it was not difficult to say what.… But why should that make Hypatia or anyone else attractive? And the poor little child of nature gazed in deep bewilderment at a crowd of new questions, as a butterfly might at the pages of the book on which it has settled, and was sad and discontented—not with herself, for was she not Pelagia the perfect?—but with these strange fancies which came into other people's heads.—Why should not everyone be as happy as they could? And who knew better than she how to be happy, and to make others happy?…

===Chinese===
然而即便在凯旋之中，她的心却是忧愁的。是非对错于她，正如于她那时代千千万万的人一样，是从未有过的一种观念。就她自己的意识而言，她之没有灵魂，正和她胯下那头骡子一样。她天生便有无穷的嬉闹与好脾气、机灵与狡黠，加上长久的训练养成了她那希腊式的对形体之美与仪态之雅的赏鉴力，直到她已无与伦比，成了供奉亚历山大诸剧院奢靡口味的最完美的哑剧演员、舞者和乐师——她自幼便只为享乐与虚荣而活，再无所求。可她对那位哥特情人磅礴阳刚之气的新的眷恋——不如说是崇拜——却唤醒了她一个新的目标：要留住他——要为他而活——要追随他到天涯海角，哪怕他厌倦了她、虐待她、鄙夷她。而慢慢地，日复一日，沃尔夫的冷嘲热讽在她心里唤起了一种忧惧：也许阿玛尔是鄙夷她的。……为什么，她猜不透：但沃尔夫歌中所唱的那些阿尔鲁娜女巫究竟是怎样的女子呢？连阿玛尔和他手下的人提起她们都满怀敬意，仿佛那是比她、甚至比他们自己都更为高贵的东西？而沃尔夫在希帕蒂娅身上看出了什么，竟能使这位冷峻粗豪的老战士当众向她俯首致敬？……要说是什么，倒也不难说。……可那又为何能使希帕蒂娅或任何旁人具有魅力呢？这可怜的自然之子于是一头雾水地瞪着一堆新的疑问，正如一只蝴蝶停在一本书上，瞪着书页发呆一般；她忧愁、不满——不是对自己不满，因为她岂不是完美无瑕的佩拉吉娅么？——而是对旁人脑子里钻出来的这些古怪念头不满。——为什么人人不能各尽其欢呢？又有谁比她更懂得怎样让自己快乐、怎样叫别人快乐呢？……

===Original===
"Look at that old monk standing on the pavement, Amalric! Why does he stare so at me? Tell him to go away."

The person at whom she pointed, a delicate-featured old man, with a venerable white beard, seemed to hear her; for he turned with a sudden start, and then, to Pelagia's astonishment, put his hands before his face, and burst convulsively into tears.

"What does he mean by behaving in that way? Bring him here to me this moment! I will know!" cried she, petulantly catching at the new object, in order to escape from her own thoughts.

In a moment a Goth had led up the weeper, who came without demur to the side of Pelagia's mule.

"Why were you so rude as to burst out crying in my face?" asked she petulantly.

The old man looked up sadly and tenderly, and answered in a low voice, meant only for her ear—

"And how can I help weeping, when I see anything as beautiful as you are destined to the flames of hell forever?"

"The flames of hell?" said Pelagia, with a shudder. "What for?"

"Do you not know?" asked the old man, with a look of sad surprise. "Have you forgotten what you are?"

"I? I never hurt a fly!"

===Chinese===
「瞧那个站在路边的老修士，阿玛尔里克！他干嘛那样盯着我？叫他走开。」

她所指的那人，一位眉目清癯的老人，蓄着令人起敬的白须，似乎听见了她的话；只见他猛地一惊，转过身来，随即——令佩拉吉娅大为诧异——双手掩面，抽搐似的痛哭起来。

「他这是做什么？马上把他带到我跟前来！我倒要问个明白！」她焦躁地嚷道，急于抓住这个新的对象，好从自己的心事里逃脱。

转眼便有一个哥特人把那哭泣的老人领了过来，他毫无推拒地走到佩拉吉娅的骡子旁。

「你怎么这么无礼，当着我的面大哭起来？」她没好气地问。

老人悲切而温厚地抬起头来，压低了声音，只说给她一人听——

「我看见像你这般美丽的人，竟注定要永永远远在地狱的烈火中焚烧，又怎能忍住不哭呢？」

「地狱的烈火？」佩拉吉娅打了个寒颤。「为什么？」

「你不知道么？」老人问道，神情悲戚而惊异。「你忘了自己是什么人么？」

「我？我连一只苍蝇都不曾伤害过！」

===Original===
"Why do you look so terrified, my darling? What have you been saying to her, you old villain?" and the Amal raised his whip.

"Oh! do not strike him. Come, come tomorrow, and tell me what you mean."

"No, we will have no monks within our doors, frightening silly women. Off, sirrah! and thank the lady that you have escaped with a whole skin." And the Amal caught the bridle of Pelagia's mule, and pushed forward, leaving the old man gazing sadly after them.

But the beautiful sinner was evidently not the object which had brought the old monk of the desert into a neighbourhood so strange and ungenial to his habits; for, recovering himself in a few moments, he hurried on to the door of the Museum, and there planted himself, scanning earnestly the faces of the passers-out, and meeting, of course, with his due share of student ribaldry.

"Well, old cat, and what mouse are you on the watch for, at the hole's mouth here?"

"Just come inside, and see whether the mice will not singe your whiskers for you.…"

"Here is my mouse, gentlemen," answered the old monk, with a bow and a smile, as he laid his hand on Philammon's arm, and presented to his astonished eyes the delicate features and high retreating forehead of Arsenius.

===Chinese===
「你为什么吓得这样，我的心肝？你这老贼，你对她说什么了？」阿玛尔扬起了马鞭。

「噢！别打他。来，明天来我那儿，把你那话的意思告诉我。」

「不，我们家里不许修士进门，吓唬愚蠢的女人。去你的，老东西！还得谢谢这位夫人，留了你一条整皮。」阿玛尔一把抓住佩拉吉娅骡子的缰绳，催着往前走了，把那老人撇在身后，怅然地目送他们远去。

然而这位美丽的罪人，显然并非把这位沙漠老修士引到如此陌生、如此不合他习性的地方来的缘由；因为不多一会儿他便回过神来，急匆匆地赶到博物院门口，在那儿站定了，细细地端详着每一个出来的人的面孔——当然，也照例招来了学生们应得的那份轻薄嘲骂。

「喂，老猫，你在洞口这儿守着，要逮哪只老鼠哇？」

「只管进来瞧瞧，看老鼠会不会把你的胡子燎了去……」

「诸位，我的老鼠在这里，」老修士一面答道，一面含笑躬身为礼，一面却伸手按住了菲拉蒙的胳膊——同时呈现在少年惊愕的眼前的，是阿尔塞尼乌斯那清癯的面目和高高的后退的额头。

===Original===
"My father," cried the boy, in the first impulse of affectionate recognition; and then—he had expected some such meeting all along, but now that it was come at last, he turned pale as death. The students saw his emotion.

"Hands off, old Heautontimoroumenos! He belongs to our guild now! Monks have no more business with sons than with wives. Shall we hustle him for you, Philammon?"

"Take care how you show off, gentlemen: the Goths are not yet out of hearing!" answered Philammon, who was learning fast how to give a smart answer; and then, fearing the temper of the young dandies, and shrinking from the notion of any insult to one so reverend and so beloved as Arsenius, he drew the old man gently away, and walked up the street with him in silence, dreading what was coming.

"And are these your friends?"

"Heaven forbid! I have nothing in common with such animals but flesh and blood, and a seat in the lecture-room!"

"Of the heathen woman?"

===Chinese===
「父亲！」少年一声喊，那是认出亲人时头一冲动里情不自禁的呼唤；紧接着——他一路就料着会有这样一场相会，可如今它真到了跟前，他却面如死灰。学生们看出了他的激动。

「撒手吧，老『自刑者』（Heautontimoroumenos）！他如今是我们这一行的人了！修士之于儿子，原与之于妻子一样，毫不相干。菲拉蒙，要不要我们替你把他撵走？」

「诸位，卖弄可得小心哪：哥特人还没走远呢，听得见的！」菲拉蒙答道——他如今学得很快，已懂得怎样回敬一句俏皮话了；继而，他忌惮那些年轻花花公子的脾气，又不愿见像阿尔塞尼乌斯这般可敬、这般亲爱的人受辱，便轻轻地引着老人走开，默默地与他沿街而行，心里却害怕着即将到来的事。

「这些就是你的朋友么？」

「天理不容！我跟这群禽兽除了血肉之躯和讲学堂里的一席之地，再无半点共同之处！」

「那异教女子的讲学堂？」

===Original===
Philammon, after the fashion of young men in fear, rushed desperately into the subject himself, just because he dreaded Arsenius's entering on it quietly.

"Yes, of the heathen woman. Of course you have seen Cyril before you came hither?"

"I have, and—"

"And," went on Philammon, interrupting him, "you have been told every lie which prurience, stupidity, and revenge can invent. That I have trampled on the cross—sacrificed to all the deities in the pantheon—and probably"—(and he blushed scarlet)—"that that purest and holiest of beings—who, if she were not what people call a pagan, would be, and deserves to be, worshipped as the queen of saints—that she—and I—" and he stopped.

"Have I said that I believed what I may have heard?"

"No—and therefore, as they are all simple and sheer falsehoods, there is no more to be said on the subject. Not that I shall not be delighted to answer any questions of yours, my dearest father—"

"Have I asked any, my child?"

"No. So we may as well change the subject for the present,"—and he began overwhelming the old man with inquiries about himself, Pambo, and each and all of the inhabitants of the Laura to which Arsenius, to the boy's infinite relief, answered cordially and minutely, and even vouchsafed a smile at some jest of Philammon's on the contrast between the monks of Nitria and those of Scetis.

===Chinese===
菲拉蒙依照那些心中有惧的少年的脾气，自己孤注一掷地闯到这话题上去，正因为他怕阿尔塞尼乌斯不慌不忙地先提起它。

「是的，那异教女子的讲学堂。您来此之前，自然已经见过区利罗了？」

「我见过了，而且——」

「而且，」菲拉蒙打断他，接着说道，「您已听信了淫邪、愚蠢和报复之心所能编造的每一句谎话。说我践踏了十字架——向万神殿里所有的神祇献了祭——说不定还——」（他涨红了脸）「——说那位最纯洁、最神圣的人——她若不是世人所谓的异教徒，本该、也配得被当作圣徒之后而受人敬奉——说她——和我——」他住了口。

「我可曾说过，我信了我可能听来的那些话？」

「没有——那么，既然那些话全是些单纯的、彻头彻尾的谎话，这话题也就不必再提了。这并不是说，我 dearest 的父亲，您若有任何问题要问我，我不会乐意回答——」

「我可曾问过一句么，我的孩子？」

「没有。那么我们暂且换个话题吧。」——于是他连珠炮似的向老人问起他本人、庞波，以及劳拉里这一个、那一个所有居民的情形来；阿尔塞尼乌斯则——令少年大大松了一口气——恳切而详尽地一一作答，甚至对菲拉蒙拿尼特拉的修士与塞提斯的修士作对比的一句戏言，也赏了一个微笑。

===Original===
Arsenius was too wise not to see well enough what all this flippancy meant; and too wise, also, not to know that Philammon's version was probably quite as near the truth as Peter's and Cyril's; but for reasons of his own, merely replied by an affectionate look, and a compliment to Philammon's growth.

"And yet you seem thin and pale, my boy."

"Study," said Philammon, "study. One cannot burn the midnight oil without paying some penalty for it.… However, I am richly repaid already; I shall be more so hereafter."

"Let us hope so. But who are those Goths whom I passed in the streets just now?"

"Ah! my father," said Philammon, glad in his heart of any excuse to turn the conversation, and yet half uneasy and suspicious at Arsenius's evident determination to avoid the very object of his visit. "It must have been you, then, whom I saw stop and speak to Pelagia at the farther end of the street. What words could you possibly have had wherewith to honour such a creature?"

"God knows. Some secret sympathy touched my heart.… Alas! poor child! But how came you to know her?"

===Chinese===
阿尔塞尼乌斯何等明智，岂会看不出这一切轻浮究竟何意；他也同样明智，岂会不知道菲拉蒙所说的，大概与彼得和区利罗所说的一样接近真相；然而为了他自己的缘故，他只以一个慈爱的眼色和一句夸赞菲拉蒙长高了的话作答。

「可你似乎又瘦又苍白啊，我的孩子。」

「用功啊，」菲拉蒙说，「用功。一个人挑灯夜读，总得付出些代价的。……不过，我已得了丰厚的报酬；日后还会更多。」

「但愿如此吧。只是我刚才在街上走过的那些哥特人，是谁？」

「啊！父亲，」菲拉蒙说——他心里正巴不得有个借口把话头岔开，却又半是忐忑、半是狐疑，因为阿尔塞尼乌斯分明打定主意要避开他此行正题——「那么，我在街那头看见停下身来跟佩拉吉娅说话的，必是您了。您对那样一种人，究竟能有什么话可说呢？」

「上帝知道。某种隐秘的同情触动了我的心。……唉！可怜的孩子！可你是怎么认得她的？」

===Original===
"All Alexandria knows the shameless abomination," interrupted a voice at their elbow—none other than that of the little porter, who had been dodging and watching the pair the whole way, and could no longer restrain his longing to meddle. "And well it had been for many a rich young man had odd Miriam never brought her over, in an evil day, from Athens hither."

"Miriam?"

"Yes, monk; a name not unknown, I am told, in palaces as well as in slave-markets."

"An evil-eyed old Jewess?"

"A Jewess she is, as her name might have informed you; and as for her eyes, I consider them, or used to do so, of course—for her injured nation have been long expelled from Alexandria by your fanatic tribe—as altogether divine and demoniac, let the base imagination of monks call them what it likes."

"But how did you know this Pelagia, my son? She is no fit company for such as you."

Philammon told, honestly enough, the story of his Nile journey, and Pelagia's invitation to him.

"You did not surely accept it?"

"Heaven forbid that Hypatia's scholar should so degrade himself!"

===Chinese===
「全亚历山大城都知道这无耻的妖孽，」一个声音在他们肘边插了进来——不是别人，正是那小个子看门人，他一路上躲躲闪闪地盯梢着这一老一少，再也按捺不住要多管闲事的渴望。「多少富家少年，当初若不是那古怪的米利暗在一个不吉利的日子里把她从雅典带到这里来，该有多好。」

「米利暗？」

「是的，修士；据我所知，这个名字在王宫里和在奴隶市场上一样，都并不陌生。」

「一个目光毒辣的犹太老妪？」

「她是犹太人，这从她的名字便可知道；至于她的眼睛嘛，我认为——或者过去曾认为——当然是过去的事了，因为她那受辱的民族早被你们这群狂热之徒赶出了亚历山大城——那双眼可完全是神妙的、魔性的，随修士们卑污的想象爱怎么说便怎么说去吧。」

「可你是怎么认得这佩拉吉娅的，我的孩子？她这种人，不是你所宜与之来往的。」

菲拉蒙颇为老实地把他在尼罗河上的旅程，以及佩拉吉娅对他的邀请，原原本本说了一遍。

「你总不至于答应了吧？」

「天理不容，希帕蒂娅的门生竟会这般自贬身份！」

===Original===
Arsenius shook his head sadly.

"You would not have had me go?"

"No, boy. But how long hast thou learned to call thyself Hypatia's scholar, or to call it a degradation to visit the most sinful, if thou mightest thereby bring back a lost lamb to the Good Shepherd? Nevertheless, thou art too young for such employment—and she meant to tempt thee doubtless."

"I do not think it. She seemed struck by my talking Athenian Greek, and having come from Athens."

"And how long since she came from Athens?" said Arsenius, after a pause. "Who knows?"

"Just after it was sacked by the barbarians," said the little porter, who, beginning to suspect a mystery, was peaking and peering like an excited parrot. "The old dame brought her hither among a cargo of captive boys and girls."

"The time agrees.… Can this Miriam be found?"

"A sapient and courteous question for a monk to ask! Do you not know that Cyril has expelled all Jews four months ago?"

===Chinese===
阿尔塞尼乌斯悲哀地摇了摇头。

「您总不至于要我去吧？」

「不，孩子。可是，你从何时起学会了自称希帕蒂娅的门生？又从何时起，把去看望最罪孽深重的人——倘若你能借此把一只迷羊领回好牧人身边——看作是有失身份的事？话虽如此，你还太年轻，不堪此任——而她，想必是存心要诱惑你。」

「我倒不这样想。她似乎因为我能说一口阿提卡的雅典希腊语、又来自雅典，而对我刮目相看。」

「那么她是多久以前从雅典来的呢？」阿尔塞尼乌斯顿了一顿，说道。「谁知道呢？」

「就在雅典被蛮族攻陷之后不久，」小个子看门人说——他已渐渐疑心这其中大有文章，正像一只受了惊的鹦鹉似地伸头探脑。「那老太婆是连同一船被掳的男女孩童，把她一道带到这儿来的。」

「时日倒是对得上。……这米利暗还能找到么？」

「修士问出这样一句话来，可真是又精明又客气啊！您莫非不知道，区利罗四个月前已把所有的犹太人驱逐出去了？」

===Original===
"True, true.… Alas!" said the old man to himself, "how little the rulers of this world guess their own power! They move a finger carelessly, and forget that that finger may crush to death hundreds whose names they never heard—and every soul of them as precious in God's sight as Cyril's own."

"What is the matter, my father?" asked Philammon. "You seem deeply moved about this woman.…"

"And she is Miriam's slave?"

"Her freedwoman this four years past," said the porter. "The good lady—for reasons doubtless excellent in themselves, though not altogether patent to the philosophic mind—thought good to turn her loose on the Alexandrian republic, to seek what she might devour."

"God help her! And you are certain that Miriam is not in Alexandria?"

The little porter turned very red, and Philammon did so likewise; but he remembered his promise, and kept it.

"You both know something of her, I can see. You cannot deceive an old statesman, sir!"—turning to the little porter with a look of authority—"poor monk though he be now. If you think fitting to tell me what you know, I promise you that neither she nor you shall be losers by your confidence in me. If not, I shall find means to discover."

Both stood silent.

===Chinese===
「是了，是了。……唉！」老人自言自语道，「这世上的掌权者，何曾知道自己手中的权力！他们漫不经心地动一动指头，便忘了那指头可能碾死几百个他们从未听过名字的人——而他们每一个人的灵魂，在上帝眼中都与区利罗本人一般宝贵。」

「怎么了，父亲？」菲拉蒙问道。「您似乎为这女子动了很深的情。……」

「她是米利暗的奴婢？」

「这四年以来，是她的 freedwoman，已获释放的释奴，」看门人说。「那位好夫人——自有她一番绝妙的道理，虽然这些道理在哲学的头脑看来不甚明了——认为把她放到亚历山大这个共和国里去自谋生路，倒也不错。」

「上帝可怜她！那么你们确信米利暗已不在亚历山大城了？」

小个子看门人脸涨得通红，菲拉蒙也是如此；可他记着自己的诺言，守口如瓶。

「你们两个都知道她的下落，我看得出来。你骗不过一个老政客的，先生！」他转向那小个子看门人，带着一副凛然的神色——「虽然他如今不过是个穷修士。你若觉得方便把你所知的告诉我，我答应你：她也好、你也罢，都绝不会因信了我而吃亏。如若不然，我自有法子打听出来。」

两人都默然不语。

===Original===
"Philammon, my son! and art thou too in league against—no, not against me; against thyself, poor misguided boy?"

"Against myself?"

"Yes—I have said it. But unless you will trust me, I cannot trust you."

"I have promised."

"And I, sir statesman, or monk, or both, or neither, have sworn by the immortal gods!" said the porter, looking very big.

Arsenius paused.

"There are those who hold that an oath by an idol, being nothing, is of itself void. I do not agree with them. If thou thinkest it sin to break thine oath, to thee it is sin. And for thee, my poor child, thy promise is sacred, were it made to Iscariot himself. But hear me. Can either of you, by asking this woman, be so far absolved as to give me speech of her? Tell her—that is, if she be in Alexandria, which God grant—all that has passed between us here, and tell her, on the solemn oath of a Christian, that Arsenius, whose name she knows well, will neither injure nor betray her. Will you do this?"

"Arsenius?" said the little porter, with a look of mingled awe and pity.

The old man smiled. "Arsenius, who was once called the Father of the Emperors. Even she will trust that name."

"I will go this moment, sir; I will fly!" and off rushed the little porter.

===Chinese===
「菲拉蒙，我的孩子！怎么连你也入了伙，来对付——不，不是对付我；是对付你自己，你这可怜的、误入歧途的孩子？」

「对付我自己？」

「是的——我说出口了。可你们若不肯信我，我也不能信你们。」

「我已立过誓。」

「而我，政客先生，或者修士，或者兼而有之，或者两者皆非，已指着不朽的众神起了誓！」看门人说，神气十分了得。

阿尔塞尼乌斯顿了一顿。

「有人主张，指着偶像所起的誓，本是虚无，故而本身便是无效的。我不同意他们。你若以为违背誓言是罪，那么对你而言便是罪。而对你，我可怜的孩子，你的诺言便是神圣的，哪怕是对着加略人犹大（Iscariot）起的。可是听我说。你们两位，能否在向那女子问讯之时，以此求得一种开脱——把她带到我这里，让我与她说上一席话？告诉她——假如她真在亚历山大城的话，但愿上帝成全——把我们在此间所谈的一切，都告诉她；并以一个基督徒的庄严誓言告诉她：阿尔塞尼乌斯——她对这个名字想必烂熟——既不会加害于她，也不会出卖她。你们肯做这件事么？」

「阿尔塞尼乌斯？」小个子看门人说道，神情里半是敬畏、半是怜悯。

老人微微一笑。「阿尔塞尼乌斯，昔日人称『众皇之父』（the Father of the Emperors）。便是她，也会信这个名字的。」

「我这就去，先生；我飞跑去！」小个子看门人一溜烟地跑了。

===Original===
"The little fellow forgets," said Arsenius, with a smile, "to how much he has confessed already, and how easy it were now to trace him to the old hag's lair.… Philammon, my son.… I have many tears to weep over thee—but they must wait a while, I have thee safe now," and the old man clutched his arm. "Thou wilt not leave thy poor old father? Thou wilt not desert me for the heathen woman?"

"I will stay with you, I promise you, indeed! if—if you will not say unjust things of her."

"I will speak evil of no one, accuse no one, but myself. I will not say one harsh word to thee, my poor boy. But listen now! Thou knowest that thou camest from Athens. Knowest thou that it was I who brought thee hither?"

"You?"

"I, my son: but when I brought thee to the Laura, it seemed right that thou, as the son of a noble gentleman, shouldest hear nothing of it. But tell me: dost thou recollect father or mother, brother or sister; or anything of thy home in Athens?"

"No."

"Thanks be to God. But, Philammon, if thou hadst had a sister—hush! And if—I only say if—"

===Chinese===
「这小个子倒忘了，」阿尔塞尼乌斯微笑道，「他已经招供了多少，如今要顺藤摸瓜找到那老妖婆的巢穴，又是何等容易。……菲拉蒙，我的孩子。……我有许多眼泪要为你而流——可这眼泪得暂且搁一搁，如今我可把你抓牢了，」老人紧紧攥住他的胳膊。「你不会丢下你这可怜的老父亲吧？你不会为了那异教女子而弃我不顾吧？」

「我留在您身边，我向您保证，真的！只要——只要您不说她不公道的话。」

「我不说任何人的坏话，不控告任何人，除了我自己。我绝不对你说一句狠话，我可怜的孩子。可你听好！你知道你是从雅典来的。你可知道，当初带你到这里来的，是我？」

「您？」

「是我，我的孩子：可我带你到劳拉之时，觉得你既是一位高贵绅士的儿子，便不宜知晓这事。可你告诉我：你还记得父亲或母亲、兄弟或姐妹么？还记得你在雅典的家么？」

「不记得。」

「感谢上帝。可是，菲拉蒙，倘若你有过一个姐妹——嘘！倘若——我只是说倘若——」

===Original===
"A sister!" interrupted Philammon. "Pelagia?"

"God forbid, my son! But a sister thou hadst once—some three years older than thee she seemed."

"What! did you know her?"

"I saw her but once—on one sad day.—Poor children both! I will not sadden you by telling you where and how."

"And why did you not bring her hither with me? You surely had not the heart to part us?"

"Ah, my son, what right had an old monk with a fair young girl? And, indeed, even had I had the courage, it would have been impossible. There were others, richer than I, to whose covetousness her youth and beauty seemed a precious prize. When I saw her last, she was in company with an ancient Jewess. Heaven grant that this Miriam may prove to be the one!"

"And I have a sister!" gasped Philammon, his eyes bursting with tears. "We must find her! You will help me?—Now—this moment! There is nothing else to be thought of, spoken of, done, henceforth, till she is found!"

===Chinese===
「一个姐妹！」菲拉蒙打断道。「佩拉吉娅？」

「上帝不容，我的孩子！可你的确曾有过一个姐妹——看上去比你年长约摸三岁。」

「怎么！您见过她？」

「我只见过她一次——在一个悲伤的日子。——两个可怜的孩子！她在哪里、是怎样一种情形，我就不细说了，免得叫你伤心。」

「那您当时为什么不把她和我一道带来？您总不至于狠得下心把我们分开吧？」

「唉，我的孩子，一个老修士，怎能带着一个如花似玉的小姑娘？再说，纵然我有那个胆量，也是万万不能。还有旁人，比我有钱有势，她的青春与美貌在他们贪婪的眼里，是一件宝贵的猎物。我最后一次见她时，她正与一个年老的犹太妇人在一起。但愿上天保佑，这个米利暗就是那一位！」

「我竟有一个姐妹！」菲拉蒙喘着气说，眼里涌出了泪水。「我们一定要找到她！您会帮我的吧？——现在——立刻！从今往后，在找到她之前，旁的事都不必想、不必说、不必做了！」

===Original===
"Ah, my son, my son! Better, better, perhaps, to leave her in the hands of God! What if she were dead? To discover that, would be to discover needless sorrow. And what if—God grant that it be not so! she had only a name to live, and were dead, worse than dead, in sinful pleasure—"

"We would save her, or die trying to save her! Is it not enough for me that she is my sister?" Arsenius shook his head. He little knew the strange new light and warmth which his words had poured in upon the young heart beside him. "A sister!" What mysterious virtue was there in that simple word, which made Philammon's brain reel and his heart throb madly? A sister! not merely a friend, an equal, a helpmate, given by God Himself, for loving whom none, not even a monk, could blame him.—Not merely something delicate, weak, beautiful—for of course she must be beautiful—whom he might cherish, guide, support, deliver, die for, and find death delicious. Yes—all that, and more than that, lay in the sacred word. For those divided and partial notions had flitted across his mind too rapidly to stir such passion as moved him now; even the hint of her sin and danger had been heard heedlessly, if heard at all. It was the word itself which bore its own message, its own spell to the heart of the fatherless and motherless foundling, as he faced for the first time the deep, everlasting, divine reality of kindred.… A sister! of his own flesh and blood—born of the same father, the same mother—his, his, forever! How hollow and fleeting seemed all "spiritual sonships," "spiritual daughterhoods," inventions of the changing fancy, the wayward will of man! Arsenius—Pambo—ay, Hypatia herself—what were they to him now? Here was a real relationship.… A sister! What else was worth caring for upon earth?

===Chinese===
「唉，我的孩子，我的孩子！也许还是把她交在上帝手中更好！万一她已经死了呢？查出这个来，不过是无端添一段哀痛罢了。万一——但愿不至于如此！——她只有活着之名，实则已死，甚至比死更坏，死在罪中之乐里——」

「我们要救她，否则就为救她而死！她是我的姐妹，这于我还不够么？」阿尔塞尼乌斯摇了摇头。他哪里知道，自己方才那番话，已把一种何等奇异的新光与新热，倾注进了身边这颗年轻的心。「一个姐妹！」这一个简单的字眼里，究竟藏着怎样神秘的德性，竟使菲拉蒙头晕目眩、心跳如狂？一个姐妹！不仅仅是朋友，是平等的人，是上帝亲自赐下的伴侣，爱她，没有任何人——哪怕是修士——能加以责备。——也不仅仅是某种纤弱、娇弱、美丽——她当然必须是美丽的——值得他去珍护、引领、扶持、搭救、为之赴死，且在死中尝到甘甜。是的——这一切，乃至比这一切更多的，都蕴含在这一个神圣的字眼里。因为那些零碎的、局部的念头，此前虽也曾一闪而过地掠过他心头，却远不足以激起如今这样撼动他的激情；便是关于她的罪与危险的暗示，他也听得不甚在意，若真的听见了的话。正是这个字本身，自带它的信息、自带它的咒语，直抵这无父无母的弃儿的心头——他有生以来头一遭，面对着亲族这一深沉、永恒、神圣的真实。……一个姐妹！与他同血同肉——同一个父亲、同一个母亲所生——他的，他的，永永远远的！一切「属灵的儿子」、「属灵的女儿」——那些出于人之变幻的幻想、任性的意志所造出来的东西——显得何等空洞、何等飘忽！阿尔塞尼乌斯——庞波——便是希帕蒂娅本人——如今于他又有何干？这里才是一桩真正的关系。……一个姐妹！世上还有别的什么值得挂念的呢？

===Original===
"And she was at Athens when Pelagia was—" he cried at last—"perhaps knew her—let us go to Pelagia herself!"

"Heaven forbid!" said Arsenius. "We must wait at least till Miriam's answer comes."

"I can show you her house at least in the meanwhile; and you can go in yourself when you will. I do not ask to enter. Come! I feel certain that my finding her is in some way bound up with Pelagia. Had I not met her on the Nile, had you not met her in the street, I might never have heard that I had a sister. And if she went with Miriam, Pelagia must know her—she may be in that very house at this moment!"

Arsenius had his reasons for suspecting that Philammon was but too right. But he contented himself with yielding to the boy's excitement, and set off with him in the direction of the dancer's house.

They were within a few yards of the gate, when hurried footsteps behind them, and voices calling them by name, made them turn; and behold, evidently to the disgust of Arsenius as much as Philammon himself, Peter the Reader and a large party of monks!

===Chinese===
「而佩拉吉娅在雅典之时，她也在——」他终于嚷了出来，「——说不定认得她——我们这就到佩拉吉娅本人那里去！」

「天理不容！」阿尔塞尼乌斯说。「至少也得等米利暗的回音来了再说。」

「至少我可以先把她的宅子指给您看；您何时高兴，尽可自己进去。我并不求跟着进去。来吧！我有一种预感：我找到她这件事，和佩拉吉娅脱不了干系。我若不是在尼罗河上遇见了她，您若不是在街上遇见了她，我也许永远也不会听说自己有一个姐妹。而她若是跟着米利暗走的，佩拉吉娅必然认得她——说不定此刻就在那宅子里！」

阿尔塞尼乌斯自有他的理由，怀疑菲拉蒙所说只怕不幸言中。可他只是顺着少年的兴奋，与他一道朝那舞娘的宅子走去。

他们离大门不过几步之遥，忽然身后传来匆匆的脚步声，和呼唤他们名字的喊声，叫他们不得不回头；一看——不由分说，使阿尔塞尼乌斯和菲拉蒙本人一样恼怒的——竟是读经员彼得，还带着一大帮修士！

===Original===
Philammon's first impulse was to escape; Arsenius himself caught him by the arm, and seemed inclined to hurry on.

"No!" thought the youth, "am I not a free man, and a philosopher?" and facing round, he awaited the enemy.

"Ah, young apostate! So you have found him, reverend and ill-used sir. Praised be Heaven for this rapid success!"

"My good friend," asked Arsenius, in a trembling voice, "what brings you here?"

"Heaven forbid that I should have allowed your sanctity and age to go forth without some guard against the insults and violence of this wretched youth and his profligate companions. We have been following you afar off all the morning, with hearts full of filial solicitude."

===Chinese===
菲拉蒙头一个冲动便是逃；阿尔塞尼乌斯自己也一把抓住他的胳膊，似乎也想加快脚步走开。

「不！」少年心想，「我岂不是个自由人，岂不是个哲人？」于是他转过身来，迎着敌人等候。

「啊，年轻的叛教者！这么说您找到他了，可敬的、受尽委屈的先生。赞美上天，竟这样快便马到成功了！」

「好朋友，」阿尔塞尼乌斯颤声问道，「是什么风把你们吹到这儿来了？」

「上天不容啊，我岂能让您这般圣德高年的人独自出门，而没有几分护卫，以防这可恶少年和他那伙浪荡同伴的侮辱与暴行？我们整整一上午都在远远地跟着您，满怀为人子者的一片殷殷牵挂。」

===Original===
"Many thanks; but indeed your kindness has been superfluous. My son here, from whom I have met with nothing but affection, and whom, indeed, I believe far more innocent than report declared him, is about to return peaceably with me. Are you not, Philammon?"

"Alas! my father," said Philammon, with an effort, "how can I find courage to say it'?—but I cannot return with you."

"Cannot return?"

"I vowed that I would never again cross that threshold till—"

"And Cyril does. He bade me, indeed he bade me, assure you that he would receive you back as a son, and forgive and forget all the past."

"Forgive and forget? That is my part—not his. Will he right me against that tyrant and his crew? Will he proclaim me openly to be an innocent and persecuted man, unjustly beaten and driven forth for obeying his own commands? Till he does that, I shall not forget that I am a free man."

"A free man!" said Peter, with an unpleasant smile; "that remains to be proved, my gay youth; and will need more evidence than that smart philosophic cloak and those well-curled locks which you have adopted since I saw you last."

===Chinese===
「多谢多谢；可你们的盛情实在是多余的。我这孩子，我一路上从他那里领受的不过是孝爱之情，而且说实在的，我相信他远比传闻所说的要清白得多；他正打算随我安安稳稳地回去呢。是不是，菲拉蒙？」

「唉！父亲，」菲拉蒙费力地说道，「我怎忍心说出口呢？——可是我不能跟您回去。」

「不能回去？」

「我发过誓，在……之前，我绝不再跨过那道门槛。」

「而区利罗也要如此。他吩咐我——他实在吩咐过我——向你保证，他会像接待儿子一样接待你回去，宽恕并忘却过去的一切。」

「宽恕并忘却？那该是我的事——不是他的。他肯不肯在那暴君及其一伙面前为我主持公道？他肯不肯公开宣告我是个清白无辜、横遭逼迫的人，只因遵行了他的命令，便被不义地殴打、驱逐？在他如此行之前，我不会忘记我是个自由人。」

「自由人！」彼得皮笑肉不笑地说，「这还有待证明呢，你这风流少年；而且，所需的证据，怕是远不止你上次见我之后才换上的这件花哨哲人斗篷、和你那卷得油光水滑的鬈发呢。」

===Original===
"Remains to be proved?"

Arsenius made an imploring gesture to Peter to be silent.

"Nay, sir. As I foretold to you, this one way alone remains; the blame of it, if there be blame, must rest on the unhappy youth whose perversity renders it necessary."

"For God's sake, spare me!" cried the old man, dragging Peter aside, while Philammon stood astonished, divided between indignation and vague dread.

"Did I not tell you again and again that I never could bring myself to call a Christian man my slave? And him, above all, my spiritual son?"

"And, most reverend sir, whose zeal is only surpassed by your tenderness and mercy, did not the holy patriarch assure you that your scruples were groundless? Do you think that either he or I can have less horror than you have of slavery in itself? Heaven forbid! But when an immortal soul is at stake—when a lost lamb is to be brought back to the fold—surely you may employ the authority which the law gives you for the salvation of that precious charge committed to you? What could be more conclusive than his Holiness's argument this morning? 'Christians are bound to obey the laws of this world for conscience' sake, even though, in the abstract, they may disapprove of them, and deny their authority. Then, by parity of reasoning, it must be lawful for them to take the advantage which those same laws offer them, when by so doing the glory of God may be advanced.'"

===Chinese===
「有待证明？」

阿尔塞尼乌斯向彼得做了一个恳求的手势，请他噤声。

「不成啊，先生。正如我事先跟您说过的，如今只剩这一条路可走了；这事若有不是，那罪责也只能落在那个不幸的少年头上——正是他的执拗使这事成为必要。」

「看在上帝份上，饶了我吧！」老人嚷着，把彼得拉到一旁，而菲拉蒙则惊愕地站在那里，又是愤慨、又是一种模糊的恐惧，两头拉扯。

「我不是三番五次跟您说过了么，我怎能下得了手，把一个基督徒称作我的奴隶？何况是他，尤其是他——我属灵的儿子？」

「而最可敬的先生啊——您的热心只有您的温厚与慈悲才能相比——那位神圣的宗主教岂不是已向您保证，您的顾虑是毫无根据的么？您以为，论到奴役一事本身，他或我会有比您更少的憎恶么？上天不容！可是，当一个不朽的灵魂岌岌可危——当一只迷羊要被领回羊圈——您难道不可以运用法律赋予您的权威，来拯救那交托给您看守的宝贵灵魂么？还有比宗座大人今早那番论证更无可辩驳的么？——『基督徒为良心的缘故，有责任顺服这世上的律法，即便他们在抽象的意义上不赞成这些律法、否认它们的权威。那么，依此类推，当他们借此可使上帝的荣耀得着彰显之时，取这些律法所赋予他们的便宜，也必是合法的了。』」

===Original===
Arsenius still hung back, with eyes brimming with tears; but Philammon himself put an end to the parley.

"What is the meaning of all this? Are you, too, in a conspiracy against me? Speak, Arsenius!"

"This is the meaning of it, blinded sinner!" cried Peter. "That you are by law the slave of Arsenius, lawfully bought with his money in the city of Ravenna; and that he has the power, and, as I trust, for the sake of your salvation, the will also, to compel you to accompany him."

Philammon recoiled across the pavement, with eyes flashing defiance. A slave! The light of heaven grew black to him.… Oh, that Hypatia might never know his shame! Yet it was impossible. Too dreadful to be true.…

"You lie!" almost shrieked he. "I am the son of a noble citizen of Athens. Arsenius told me so, but this moment, with his own lips!"

===Chinese===
阿尔塞尼乌斯仍迟迟不肯，眼中含着满满的热泪；倒是菲拉蒙自己结束了这一场交涉。

「这都是什么意思？难道您也和他们串通一气来对付我？说话呀，阿尔塞尼乌斯！」

「这就是意思，你这被蒙蔽的罪人！」彼得嚷道。「按着律法，你是阿尔塞尼乌斯的奴隶，是他在拉文纳城里用钱合法买下的；所以他既有权力——我也相信，为了你灵魂得救的缘故，他也有这个心意——强迫你随他同去。」

菲拉蒙倒退着横穿过石板地，眼里闪出反抗的光。一个奴隶！天上的光在他眼前变得漆黑。……噢，但愿希帕蒂娅永远不知道他的耻辱！可这怎么可能。太可怕了，不可能是真的。……

「你撒谎！」他几乎是尖叫着。「我是雅典一位高贵市民的儿子。阿尔塞尼乌斯方才亲口对我说的，就在这一刻，用他自己的嘴！」

===Original===
"Ah, but he bought you—bought you in the public market; and he can prove it!"

"Hear me—hear me, my son!" cried the old man, springing toward him. Philammon, in his fury, mistook the gesture and thrust him fiercely back.

"Your son!—your slave! Do not insult the name of son by applying it to me. Yes, sir; your slave in body, but not in soul! Ay, seize me—drag home the fugitive—scourge him—brand him—chain him in the mill, if you can; but even for that the free heart has a remedy. If you will not let me live as a philosopher, you shall see me die like one!"

"Seize the fellow, my brethren!" cried Peter, while Arsenius, utterly unable to restrain either party, hid his face and wept.

"Wretches!" cried the boy; "you shall never take me alive, while I have teeth or nails left. Treat me as a brute beast, and I will defend myself as such!"

"Out of the way there, rascals! Place for the Prefect! What are you squabbling about here, you unmannerly monks?" shouted peremptory voices from behind. The crowd parted, and disclosed the apparitors of Orestes, who followed in his robes of office.

===Chinese===
「啊，可他买了你——在公开的市场上买了你；他能拿出证据来！」

「听我说——听我说，我的孩子！」老人喊道，向他扑了过去。菲拉蒙在狂怒之中错会了这个手势，狠狠地一把将他推开。

「你的儿子！——你的奴隶！别拿『儿子』这名字来辱没我。是的，先生；身体上是您的奴隶，灵魂上却不是！好呀，抓我呀——把这逃奴拖回家去——鞭打他——烙他——把他锁在磨坊里，你们能办到的话；可即便如此，一颗自由的心也还有最后的办法。你们若不许我像哲人那样活着，我便要叫你们看看我怎样像哲人那样去死！」

「抓住这家伙，众位弟兄！」彼得喊道，而阿尔塞尼乌斯，两边都按捺不住，只得掩面而泣。

「恶人！」少年喊道，「只要我还有一颗牙、一片指甲，你们就休想活捉我。你们把我当畜生看待，我便像畜生一样自卫！」

「滚开，流氓们！给总督让路！你们这些没规矩的修士，在这儿吵些什么？」身后传来几声厉声断喝。人群一分，露出了俄瑞斯忒斯的扈卫，总督身着官服，随在他们身后。

===Original===
A sudden hope flashed before Philammon, and in an instant he had burst through the mob, and was clinging to the Prefect's chariot.

"I am a freeborn Athenian, whom these monks wish to kidnap back into slavery! I claim your protection!"

"And you shall have it, right or wrong, my handsome fellow. By Heaven, you are much too good-looking to be made a monk of! What do you mean, you villains, by attempting to kidnap free men? Is it not enough for you to lock up every mad girl whom you can dupe, but you must—"

"His master is here present, your Excellency, who will swear to the purchase."

"Or to anything else for the glory of God. Out of the way! And take care, you tall scoundrel, that I do not get a handle against you. You have been one of my marked men for many a month. Off!"

"His master demands the rights of the law as a Roman citizen," said Peter, pushing forward Arsenius.

===Chinese===
一线希望忽然在菲拉蒙眼前闪过，转眼之间他便冲出人群，紧紧攀住了总督的车驾。

「我是个生而自由的雅典人，这些修士要绑架我回去做奴隶！我求大人庇护！」

「庇护给你便是，有理没理都给你，俊俏的小伙子。老天作证，你生得这般好模样，做修士未免太可惜了！你们这帮恶棍，竟敢绑架自由人，是什么意思？你们把能骗到的每一个疯丫头都关起来还不够，如今又要——」

「大人，他的主人便在此处，可以起誓证明这桩买卖。」

「或者为了上帝的荣耀，起誓证明别的什么都行。滚开！还有你，高个子恶棍，当心别叫我抓住了把柄。多少个月来你早就是我的眼中钉了。去！」

「他的主人以罗马公民的身份，要求法律所赋予的权利，」彼得说着，把阿尔塞尼乌斯推上前去。

===Original===
"If he be a Roman citizen, let him come and make his claim at the tribune tomorrow, in legal form. But I would have you remember, ancient sir, that I shall require you to prove your citizenship before we proceed to the question of purchase."

"The law does not demand that," quoth Peter.

"Knock that fellow down, apparitor!" Whereat Peter vanished, and an ominous growl rose from the mob of monks.

"What am I to do, most noble sir?" said Philammon.

"Whatever you like, till the third hour tomorrow—if you are fool enough to appear at the tribune. If you will take my advice, you will knock down these fellows right and left, and run for your life." And Orestes drove on.

Philammon saw that it was his only chance, and did so; and in another minute he found himself rushing headlong into the archway of Pelagia's house, with a dozen monks at his heels. As luck would have it, the outer gates, at which the Goths had just entered, were still open; but the inner ones which led into the court beyond were fast. He tried them, but in vain. There was an open door in the wall on his right: he rushed through it, into a long range of stables, and into the arms of Wulf and Smid, who were unsaddling and feeding, like true warriors, their own horses.

===Chinese===
「他若是罗马公民，叫他明日到法庭上，按合法形式来提出要求便是。不过，老先生，我得提醒你，在我们审理这桩买卖之前，我得先要你证明你自己的公民身份。」

「律法并不要求这个，」彼得道。

「扈卫，把那家伙打翻在地！」话音未落，彼得便没了影，修士群中起了一阵不祥的咆哮。

「我该怎么办，最尊贵的先生？」菲拉蒙说。

「随你的便，直到明日第三时辰为止——假如你蠢到要去法庭的话。你若肯听我的劝，便把这些家伙左一拳右一脚地打翻，然后逃命去。」俄瑞斯忒斯说罢便驱车前行。

菲拉蒙看出这是他唯一的机会，便依言而行；转眼之间，他便发觉自己正一头撞进佩拉吉娅宅子的门洞，身后紧跟着十来个修士。也是他运气好，哥特人方才进入的外门还敞着；可通向里面院落的内门却紧闭着。他试了试，推不开。右边墙上有一扇敞开的门：他一头冲了进去，跑进一长排马厩，正撞进沃尔夫和斯密德的怀里——这两个真正的武人，正如实惯做的那样，亲手在卸鞍喂马。

===Original===
"Souls of my fathers!" shouted Smid, "here's our young monk come back! What brings you here head over heels in this way, young curly-pate?"

"Save me from those wretches!" pointing to the monks, who were peeping into the doorway.

Wulf seemed to understand it all in a moment; for, snatching up a heavy whip, he rushed at the foe, and with a few tremendous strokes cleared the doorway, and shut-to the door.

Philammon was going to explain and thank, but Smid stopped his mouth.

"Never mind, young one, you are our guest now. Come in, and you shall be as welcome as ever. See what comes of running away from us at first."

"You do not seem to have benefited much by leaving me for the monks," said old Wulf. "Come in by the inner door. Smid! go and turn those monks out of the gateway."

===Chinese===
「列祖列宗的英灵啊！」斯密德喊道，「咱们的年轻修士又回来啦！你这样连滚带爬地跑来，是为着什么呀，小卷毛？」

「救救我，别叫那帮恶人抓去！」他指着正探头探脑往门里张望的修士们说。

沃尔夫似乎一转眼便全明白了；只见他抄起一条重鞭，冲向敌人，三两下狠命的抽打，便把门口打得干干净净，随即将门砰地关严。

菲拉蒙正要道谢解释，斯密德却堵住了他的嘴。

「别客气，小家伙，你如今是我们的客人了。进来吧，你一定会像从前一样受欢迎的。瞧瞧，当初从我们这儿溜走，落得什么下场。」

「你当初离开我去投修士，看来也没捞着什么好处呀，」老沃尔夫说。「从里头的门进来吧。斯密德！去把那些修士从大门口赶走。」

===Original===
But the mob, after battering the door for a few minutes, had yielded to the agonised entreaties of Peter, who assured them that if those incarnate fiends once broke out upon them, they would not leave a Christian alive in Alexandria. So it was agreed to leave a few to watch for Philammon's coming out; and the rest, balked of their prey, turned the tide of their wrath against the Prefect, and rejoined the mass of their party, who were still hanging round his chariot, ready for mischief.

In vain the hapless shepherd of the people attempted to drive on. The apparitors were frightened and hung back; and without their help it was impossible to force the horses through the mass of tossing arms and beards in front. The matter was evidently growing serious.

"The bitterest ruffians in all Nitria, your Excellency," whispered one of the guards, with a pale face; "and two hundred of them at the least. The very same set, I will be sworn, who nearly murdered Dioscuros."

===Chinese===
然而那群暴民在门上捶打了几分钟之后，到底听了彼得苦苦的哀求——他向他们保证，那些化身恶魔一旦冲出门来，亚历山大城里便休想有一个基督徒活命。于是众人商定，留下几个人监视菲拉蒙出来；其余的人扑了个空，失了猎物，便把一腔怒火转向总督，重新与大队人马汇合——那一伙人仍围着总督的车驾，伺机滋事。

这倒霉的牧民之官想驱车前行，却是徒然。扈卫们都吓破了胆，裹足不前；没有他们帮忙，要叫马匹冲过前面那一大片挥舞的手臂和胡须，根本不可能。事态显然正在恶化。

「大人，这些都是尼特拉最凶狠的恶棍，」一个扈卫面色苍白地低声说道，「至少有两百人。我敢起誓，就是这同一伙人，险些把狄奥斯科鲁斯害死。」

===Original===
"If you will not allow me to proceed, my holy brethren," said Orestes, trying to look collected, "perhaps it will not be contrary to the canons of the Church if I turn back. Leave the horses' heads alone. Why, in God's name, what do you want?"

"Do you fancy we have forgotten Hieracas?" cried a voice from the rear; and at that name, yell upon yell arose, till the mob, gaining courage from its own noise, burst out into open threats. "Revenge for the blessed martyr Hieracas!" "Revenge for the wrongs of the Church!" "Down with the friend of Heathens, Jews, and Barbarians!" "Down with the favourite of Hypatia!" "Tyrant!" "Butcher!" And the last epithet so smote the delicate fancy of the crowd, that a general cry arose of "Kill the butcher!" and one furious monk attempted to clamber into the chariot. An apparitor tore him down, and was dragged to the ground in his turn. The monks closed in. The guards, finding the enemy number ten to their one, threw down their weapons in a panic, and vanished; and in another minute the hopes of Hypatia and the gods would have been lost forever, and Alexandria robbed of the blessing of being ruled by the most finished gentleman south of the Mediterranean, had it not been for unexpected succour; of which it will be time enough, considering who and what is in danger, to speak in a future chapter.

===Chinese===
「你们若不许我前行，众位圣洁的弟兄，」俄瑞斯忒斯强作镇定地说道，「那么，我掉头回去，大约也不算有违教会的法规吧。别揪着马头不放。究竟，看在上帝份上，你们要怎样？」

「你以为我们忘了希拉克斯么？」后面有人喊了一声；一提起这名字，叫骂之声便此起彼伏地响了起来，直至暴民们从自己的喧嚣里壮起了胆，公然发出了威胁。「为蒙福的殉道者希拉克斯报仇！」「为教会所受的冤屈报仇！」「打倒异教徒、犹太人和蛮子的朋友！」「打倒希帕蒂娅的宠臣！」「暴君！」「屠夫！」这最后一个称呼如此切中了人群的妙想，以至于众人齐声高呼「杀了那屠夫！」一个狂怒的修士竟试图爬上车主。一个扈卫把他扯了下来，自己却也跟着被拖倒在地。修士们围拢上来。扈卫们见敌人十倍于己，惊慌失措地抛下兵器，四散逃命；若不是意外之援及时赶到，再过一分钟，希帕蒂娅和众神的指望便要永永远远地断送，亚历山大城也要失去那项福分——受地中海以南最风雅的君子所治理——然而鉴于此刻身陷险境的是何等人物、何等大事，这桩救援之事，留待下一章再表，也为时不迟。

## XVII / XVII

### A Stray Gleam / 一缕流光

===Original===
The last blue headland of Sardinia was fading fast on the northwest horizon, and a steady breeze bore before it innumerable ships, the wrecks of Heraclian’s armament, plunging and tossing impatiently in their desperate homeward race toward the coast of Africa. Far and wide, under a sky of cloudless blue, the white sails glittered on the glittering sea, as gaily now, above their loads of shame and disappointment, terror and pain, as when, but one short month before, they bore with them only wild hopes and gallant daring. Who can calculate the sum of misery in that hapless flight?﻿… And yet it was but one, and that one of the least known and most trivial, of the tragedies of that age of woe; one petty death-spasm among the unnumbered throes which were shaking to dissolution the Babylon of the West. Her time had come. Even as Saint John beheld her in his vision, by agony after agony, she was rotting to her well-earned doom. Tyrannising it luxuriously over all nations, she had sat upon the mystic beast﻿—building her power on the brute animal appetites of her dupes and slaves: but she had duped herself even more than them. She was finding out by bitter lessons that it was “to the beast,” and not to her, that her vassal kings of the earth had been giving their power and strength; and the ferocity and lust which she had pampered so cunningly in them, had become her curse and her destruction.﻿… Drunk with the blood of the saints; blinded by her own conceit and jealousy to the fact that she had been crushing and extirpating out of her empire for centuries past all which was noble, purifying, regenerative, divine, she sat impotent and doting, the prey of every fresh adventurer, the slave of her own slaves.﻿… “And the kings of the earth, who had sinned with her, hated the harlot, and made her desolate and naked, and devoured her flesh, and burned her with fire. For God had put into their hearts to fulfil His will, and to agree, and to give their kingdom to the beast, until the words of God should be fulfilled.﻿…” Everywhere sensuality, division, hatred, treachery, cruelty, uncertainty, terror; the vials of God’s wrath poured out. “Where was to be the end of it all?” asked every man of his neighbour, generation after generation; and received for answer only, “It is better to die than to live.”

===Chinese===
撒丁岛（Sardinia）最后一抹青蓝的海岬正在西北天际飞快地淡去，一阵稳定的信风驱赶着面前无数的船只——那是赫拉克利安（Heraclian）舰队的残骸——向着非洲海岸，绝望地争先恐后、劈波斩浪地夺路归乡。万里海面之上，碧空如洗，白帆在粼粼的海上闪着光，此刻仍是那样轻快——纵然船舱里装满了羞耻与失意、恐惧与痛苦——正如短短一个月之前，它们所载的还不过是狂放的希望与豪勇的胆气。谁能算得出那不幸的奔逃中积聚了多少苦难呢？……然而那不过是那个多灾多难的时代里、一出最鲜为人知、最微不足道的悲剧而已；不过是那无数将西方的巴比伦（Babylon）撼向崩解的阵痛中，一次小小的临终痉挛罢了。她的时辰到了。正如圣约翰（St. John）在异象中所见的那样，她正一苦再苦地、腐烂到她那罪有应得的下场。她曾穷奢极欲地辖制万国，曾骑在那头奥秘的兽之上——把自己的权势建立在她那些受骗者和奴隶的兽性嗜欲之上：可她骗自己，比骗他们骗得更厉害。她正从惨痛的教训中逐渐明白：世上那些藩王所献出的大能与 strength，原是献给「那兽」的，而不是献给她的；她那般精明地纵养在他们身上的凶残与淫欲，如今已成了她的咒诅与毁灭。……她喝醉了圣徒的血；被自己的自负与嫉妒蒙蔽了双眼，看不见几个世纪以来她一直在把自己帝国里一切崇高、洁净、重生、属神之物碾杀殆尽；她瘫坐如痴，成了每一个新冒出来的冒险家口中之食，成了自己奴隶的奴隶。……「地上的君王，向来与她一同犯罪，如今却恨那淫妇，使她冷落赤身，又要吃她的肉，用火将她烧尽。因为神把祂的旨意放在他们心里，叫他们同心合意，把自己的国归给那兽，直到神的话都应验了。」……到处是淫欲、分裂、仇恨、背叛、残忍、动荡、恐怖；神愤怒的七碗倾泻而下。「这一切何时才是个头呢？」一代又一代，人人都这样问邻人；所得的回答不过是：「活着不如死了。」

===Original===
And yet in one ship out of that sad fleet, there was peace; peace amid shame and terror; amid the groans of the wounded, and the sighs of the starving; amid all but blank despair. The great triremes and quinqueremes rushed onward past the lagging transports, careless, in the mad race for safety, that they were leaving the greater number of their comrades defenceless in the rear of the flight; but from one little fishing-craft alone no base entreaties, no bitter execrations greeted the passing flash and roll of their mighty oars. One after another, day by day, they came rushing up out of the northern offing, each like a huge hundred-footed dragon, panting and quivering, as if with terror, at every loud pulse of its oars, hurling the wild water right and left with the mighty share of its beak, while from the bows some gorgon or chimaera, elephant or boar, stared out with brazen eyes toward the coast of Africa, as if it, too, like the human beings which it carried, was dead to every care but that of dastard flight. Past they rushed, one after another; and off the poop some shouting voice chilled all hearts for a moment, with the fearful news that the Emperor’s Neapolitan fleet was in full chase.﻿… And the soldiers on board that little vessel looked silently and steadfastly into the silent steadfast face of the old Prefect, and Victoria saw him shudder, and turn his eyes away﻿—and stood up among the rough fighting men, like a goddess, and cried aloud that “the Lord would protect His own”; and they believed her, and were still; till many days and many ships were passed, and the little fishing-craft, outstripped even by the transports and merchantmen, as it strained and crawled along before its single square-sail, was left alone upon the sea.

===Chinese===
然而，在那可悲的舰队中的某一艘船上，竟有平安；在羞耻与恐惧之中的平安；在伤者的呻吟、饿者的叹息之中的平安；在近乎一片空白的绝望之中的平安。巨大的三列桨座舰与五列桨座舰从落在后头的运兵船旁飞掠而过，在夺路逃生的疯狂竞赛中，根本不顾它们正把大多数战友丢在溃逃的末尾，任其毫无遮蔽；唯独从那一艘小小的渔船上，没有发出一句卑劣的乞求，没有发出一声恶毒的咒骂，去迎接那些巨桨掠过、翻滚而去的闪光与轰鸣。日复一日，它们一艘接一艘地从北方的海天相接处冲出，每一艘都像一条百足巨龙，桨每响亮地搏动一下，它便喘息、颤抖，仿佛吓得发抖，用它喙般巨大的冲角把狂涛向左右劈开；船首上，什么戈耳工（gorgon）、喀迈拉（chimaera）、大象或野猪，瞪着一双铜睛直瞪向非洲海岸，仿佛它也与它所载的那些人一样，除了怯懦逃命这一桩事外，对万事都死了心。它们一艘接一艘地飞掠而过；每一艘的船尾楼上，总有某个高喊的声音令人心一寒，带来那可怕的消息——皇帝的那不勒斯（Neapolitan）舰队正在穷追不舍。……而那小船上众兵士，默默而坚定地望着那位老总督那张同样沉默而坚定的脸，维多利亚（Victoria）看见他打了个寒颤，把目光移开——便在那些粗豪的战士之间挺身而立，宛如一位女神，高声呼喊说：「主必保护属祂自己的人」；他们便信了她，安静下来；直到许多天、许多船都过去了，那艘小小的渔船——甚至被运兵船和商船都甩在后面，只剩一面方帆，勉力地在海面上挣扎、爬行——终于孤零零地被撇在了大海上。

===Original===
And where was Raphael Aben-Ezra?

He was sitting, with Bran’s head between his knees, at the door of a temporary awning in the vessel’s stern, which shielded the wounded men from sun and spray; and as he sat he could hear from within the tent the gentle voices of Victoria and her brother, as they tended the sick like ministering angels, or read to them words of divine hope and comfort-in which his homeless heart felt that he had no share.﻿…

“As I live, I would change places now with any one of those poor mangled ruffians to have that voice speaking such words to me﻿… and to believe them.﻿…” And he went on perusing the manuscript which he held in his hand.

---

“Well!” he sighed to himself after a while, “at least it is the most complimentary, not to say hopeful, view of our destinies with which I have met since I threw away my curse’s belief that the seed of David was fated to conquer the whole earth, and set up a second Roman Empire at Jerusalem, only worse than the present one, in that the devils of superstition and bigotry would be added to those of tyranny and rapine.”

===Chinese===
那么，拉斐尔·阿本-以斯拉（Raphael Aben-Ezra）在哪里呢？

他正坐在船尾一面临时搭起的布篷门口，把布朗（Bran）的头夹在两膝之间——那篷子是替伤兵遮阳挡浪的；他坐在那里，听得见篷内维多利亚与她兄弟温柔的声音，他们如服侍人的天使一般照料着病人，或给他们念些属神的盼望与安慰的话语——而他这颗无家可归的心，却觉得自己全无份于其中。……

「我指着我的性命起誓，我此刻情愿和那些可怜的、血肉模糊的恶棍里随便哪一个调换位置，只要能叫那声音对我说这样的话……而且相信它们。」于是他继续读起手中那卷手稿来。

---

「好啦！」过了一阵，他对自己叹道，「至少，这是自从我抛弃了我那受咒诅之信仰——那信仰说大卫的子孙注定要征服全地，要在耶路撒冷（Jerusalem）建立一个第二罗马帝国，只不过比眼下这个更糟，因为除了暴政与劫掠的群魔之外，还要再加上迷信与偏狭的群魔——以来，我所遇见的、对我们前途最恭维、甚至可说是最有指望的看法了。」

===Original===
A hand was laid on his shoulder, and a voice asked, “And what may this so hopeful view be?”

“Ah! my dear General!” said Raphael, looking up. “I have a poor bill of fare whereon to exercise my culinary powers this morning. Had it not been for that shark who was so luckily deluded last night, I should have been reduced to the necessity of stewing my friend the fat decurion’s big boots.”

“They would have been savoury enough, I will warrant, after they had passed under your magical hand.”

“It is a comfort, certainly, to find that after all one did learn something useful in Alexandria! So I will even go forward at once, and employ my artistic skill.”

“Tell me first what it was about which I heard you just now soliloquising, as so hopeful a view of some matter or other?”

“Honestly﻿—if you will neither betray me to your son and daughter, nor consider me as having in anywise committed myself﻿—it was Paul of Tarsus’s notion of the history and destinies of our stiff-necked nation. See what your daughter has persuaded me into reading!” And he held up a manuscript of the Epistle to the Hebrews.

===Chinese===
一只手搭在他肩上，一个声音问道：「这一番如此令人鼓舞的看法，究竟是什么？」

「啊！亲爱的将军！」拉斐尔抬起头来说，「今早我手头的菜单可怜得很，没多少东西可供我施展厨艺。若不是昨夜那条鲨鱼那么幸运地被骗了过来，我便只好去炖我那位胖十户长朋友的大皮靴了。」

「它们一经你那神手调理过，我敢保准滋味定然不差。」

「能发现自己在亚历山大城到底还是学了点有用的东西，这自然是件令人安慰的事！那么我便索性这就上前去，施展我的手艺了。」

「先告诉我，我方才听见你自言自语，说什么颇有盼望的看法，究竟讲的是什么？」

「老实说吧——只要你不去向你那儿子女儿告发我，也不算我在任何意义上许下了什么承诺——那不过是保罗（Paul of Tarsus）对我们这硬着颈项之民族的历史与前途的看法。你瞧，这都是你那女儿劝我读的！」说着，他举起一卷《希伯来书》（Epistle to the Hebrews）的手稿。

===Original===
“It is execrable Greek. But it is sound philosophy, I cannot deny. He knows Plato better than all the ladies and gentlemen in Alexandria put together, if my opinion on the point be worth having.”

“I am a plain soldier, and no judge on that point, sir. He may or may not know Plato; but I am right sure that he knows God.”

“Not too fast,” said Raphael with a smile. “You do not know, perhaps, that I have spent the last ten years of my life among men who professed the same knowledge?”

“Augustine, too, spent the best ten years of his life among such; and yet he is now combating the very errors which he once taught.”

“Having found, he fancies, something better!”

“Having found it, most truly. But you must talk to him yourself, and argue the matter over, with one who can argue. To me such questions are an unknown land.”

===Chinese===
「这希腊文糟糕得很。可这是健全的哲学，我不得不承认。倘若我这方面的意见还值得采纳的话，那他对柏拉图（Plato）的熟稔，比亚历山大城里所有的先生太太加在一起都要深。」

「我是个粗人武夫，对此事并无见地，先生。他知不知道柏拉图，我说不准；可我深信不疑的是，他认识神。」

「别太急，」拉斐尔微笑着说，「你或许不知道，我平生最后十年，恰恰是在一群自称有同样见识的人中间度过的呢？」

「奥古斯丁（Augustine）平生最好的十年，也是在这样一群人中间度过的；可他如今正在驳斥的，正是他当年所传的那些谬误。」

「他自以为，找到了更好的东西罢了！」

「是真真确确找到了。可这事你得亲自去同他谈，把这件事同一个能辩论的人辩个明白。这类问题于我，则是一片未知的土地。」

===Original===
“Well.﻿… Perhaps I may be tempted to do even that. At least a thoroughly converted philosopher﻿—for poor dear Synesius is half heathen still, I often fancy, and hankers after the wisdom of the Egyptian﻿—will be a curious sight; and to talk with so famous and so learned a man would always be a pleasure; but to argue with him, or any other human being, none whatsoever.”

“Why, then?”

“My dear sir, I am sick of syllogisms, and probabilities, and pros and contras. What do I care if, on weighing both sides, the nineteen pounds weight of questionable arguments against, are overbalanced by the twenty pounds weight of equally questionable arguments for? Do you not see that my belief of the victorious proposition will be proportioned to the one overbalancing pound only, while the whole other nineteen will go for nothing?”

“I really do not.”

“Happy are you, then. I do, from many a sad experience. No, my worthy sir. I want a faith past arguments; one which, whether I can prove it or not to the satisfaction of the lawyers, I believe to my own satisfaction, and act on it as undoubtingly and unreasoningly as I do upon my own newly-rediscovered personal identity. I don’t want to possess a faith. I want a faith which will possess me. And if I ever arrived at such a one, believe me, it would be by some such practical demonstration as this very tent has given me.”

===Chinese===
「好。……说不定我还真会被引诱去做这件事。至少，一位彻彻底底悔改归正的哲学家——因为我常觉得可怜的叙内西乌斯（Synesius）至今仍是个半异教徒，老是恋慕埃及人的智慧——倒是一桩奇景；能与如此闻名、如此博学之人交谈，终归是一桩乐事；至于与他、或任何别的活人辩论，则毫无乐趣可言。」

「那又是为何？」

「亲爱的先生，我对三段论、对盖然之理、对正反两面之辩，已厌倦透顶。倘若把两边都放在秤上称，那十九磅可疑的反方论据，被同样可疑的二十磅正方论据所压倒——这于我又有何干？难道你看不见，我所信从那获胜之命题的信心，只会与那一磅多出来的分量成正比，而其余那整整十九磅，将全归无效？」

「我实在看不出。」
