He had long in private admired the man, as a magnificent human character, a fairer one, in his eyes, than either Alexander or Julius Caesar. … What if Augustine had given him a hint which might justify his admiration? … But more. … What if Augustine were right in going even further than Philo and Hypatia? What if this same Jehovah, Wisdom, Logos, call Him what they might, were actually the God of the spirits, as well as of the bodies of all flesh? What if he was as near—Augustine said that He was—to the hearts of those wild Markmen, Gauls, Thracians, as to Augustine's own heart? What if He were—Augustine said He was—yearning after, enlightening, leading home to Himself, the souls of the poorest, the most brutal, the most sinful?—What if He loved man as man, and not merely one favoured race or one favoured class of minds? … And in the light of that hypothesis, that strange story of the Cross of Calvary seemed not so impossible after all. … But then, celibacy and asceticism, utterly nonhuman as they were, what had they to do with the theory of a human God?

And filled with many questionings, Raphael was not sorry to have the matter brought to an issue that very evening in Synesius's sitting-room. Majoricus, in his blunt, soldierlike way, set Raphael and Augustine at each other without circumlocution; and Raphael, after trying to smile and pooh-pooh away the subject, was tempted to make a jest on a seeming fallacious conceit of Augustine's—found it more difficult than he thought to trip up the serious and wary logician, lost his temper a little—a sign, perhaps, of returning health in a sceptic—and soon found himself fighting desperately, with Synesius backing him, apparently for the mere pleasure of seeing a battle, and Majoricus making him more and more cross by the implicit dogmatic faith with which he hewed at one Gordian knot after another, till Augustine had to save himself from his friends by tripping the good Prefect gently up, and leaving him miles behind the disputants, who argued on and on, till broad daylight shone in, and the sight of the desolation below recalled all parties to more material weapons, and a sterner warfare.

But little thought Raphael Aben-Ezra, as he sat there, calling up every resource of his wit and learning, in the hope, half malicious, half honestly cautious, of upsetting the sage of Hippo, and forgetting all heaven and earth in the delight of battle with his peers, that in a neighbouring chamber, her tender limbs outspread upon the floor, her face buried in her dishevelled locks; lay Victoria, wrestling all night long for him in prayer and bitter tears, as the murmur of busy voices reached her eager ears, longing in vain to catch the sense of words, on which hung now her hopes and bliss—how utterly and entirely, she lead never yet confessed to herself, though she dare confess it to that Son of Man to whom she prayed, as to One who felt with tenderness and insight beyond that of a brother, a father, even of a mother, for her maiden's blushes and her maiden's woes.

===Chinese===
待到拉斐尔在这番奇异的讲论终了时立起身来，他觉得自己比自幼坐在奶娘膝头、听所罗门与示巴女王（Queen of Sheba）的传奇那时候起，更像一个古希伯来人了。万一奥古斯丁到底是对的呢？万一旧约《圣经》里的耶和华（Jehovah），并不像拉比们所说的那样，仅仅是亚伯拉罕子孙的民族守护神；也不像斐洛所主张的那样，是只启迪少数特选圣贤——异教中亦有其人——的神圣智慧；而是全地、全地列国的主呢？——忽然间，他有生以来头一遭，一些诗篇与先知书里的话从他心头闪过，似乎正是这意思。《但以理书》（Daniel）那一整卷、尼布甲尼撒（Nebuchadnezzar）的那段事迹，若不是这意思，还能是什么意思呢？哲学上的宽容之风，早已医好了他拉比式的成见——把那位巴比伦征服者看作一个被指派到地狱（Tophet）去的化身魔鬼，一如他之前的西拿基立（Sennacherib）。他早就在私下里钦佩此人了，视他为一个伟大的人格，一个在他眼中比亚历山大（Alexander）或尤利乌斯·凯撒（Julius Caesar）更美的伟大人格。……万一奥古斯丁给了他一线暗示，可为他这份钦佩正名呢？……还不止此。……万一奥古斯丁比斐洛和希帕蒂娅走得更远，却仍是对的呢？万一这位耶和华、这位智慧、这位逻各斯（Logos）——随他们怎么称呼他——其实就是凡有血气者之灵的上帝，也是凡有血气者之身的上帝呢？万一他——奥古斯丁说他正是——与那些野蛮的马克人、高卢人、色雷斯人的心，一如与奥古斯丁自己的心，同样地相近呢？万一他——奥古斯丁说他正是——正眷恋着、光照着、领归自己，那些最贫贱者、最粗野者、最罪大恶极者的灵魂呢？——万一他爱的乃是人之所以为人，而非仅仅一个受宠的种族、或一类受宠的心智呢？……在这一假设的光照之下，各各他（Calvary）十字架那段奇异的故事，似乎到底也未尝不可能了。……可是，独身与苦行，那般非人之物，与一位属乎人之上帝的学说，又有什么相干？

拉斐尔满怀诸多疑问，倒也乐见这事就在当晚，于叙内西乌斯的起居室里当面对质起来。马约里库斯以他那直率的武人做派，毫不兜圈子地使拉斐尔和奥古斯丁对垒起来；拉斐尔先想一笑置之、把这话题岔过去，却受了诱惑，对奥古斯丁一个似乎站不住脚的巧思讥诮了一句——结果发觉要绊倒这位严肃而警觉的逻辑学家，远比他所想的困难；他略略动了火——在一个怀疑论者身上，这也许正是元气渐复之兆——很快便发现自己陷入苦战，叙内西乌斯在旁给他帮腔，似乎只为看一场好戏，而马约里库斯却以那种不加思辨的、教条式的笃信，一刀砍断一个又一个戈尔迪之结（Gordian knot），把他弄得越来越恼火；直到奥古斯丁不得不从朋友手里救出自己，把这位好总督轻轻一绊，将他甩在论战双方身后几英里之遥；双方则一路辩下去，直到天光大亮，俯瞰下面那一片荒凉，才把众人都召回更切实的兵器、更严峻的争战里去了。

可是拉斐尔·阿本-以斯拉坐在那里，搜尽自己一切机智与学问的储备——其心半是恶意、半是诚实的小心，盼望能扳倒希波的那位圣者，又在与旗鼓相当之对手交锋的酣畅里忘却了天地——他却万万不曾想到：在隔壁的一间屋子里，维多利亚正把她柔弱的四肢摊开在地板上，把脸埋进她散乱的长发里；她整夜为他摔跤祷告，泪落如雨；那一阵阵低语的嗡嗡声传到她侧耳的耳中，她徒然地想听清那些话的意思，而她的盼望与福乐如今正悬于其上——这盼望与福乐究竟完完全全、彻彻底底到何等地步，她从未敢向自己承认过，虽然她敢向她所祷告的那位人子承认；因为那一位对她的少女之羞、少女之苦，所怀的温存与洞见，胜过兄弟，胜过父亲，甚至胜过母亲。

## XXII / XXII

### Pandemonium / 群魔之窟

===Original===
But where was Philammon all that week?

For the first day or two of his imprisonment he had raved like some wild beast entrapped. His newfound purpose and energy, thus suddenly dammed back and checked, boiled up in frantic rage. He tore at the bars of his prison; he rolled himself, shrieking, on the floor. He called in vain on Hypatia, on Pelagia, on Arsenius﻿—on all but God. Pray he could not, and dare not; for to whom was he to pray? To the stars?﻿—to the Abysses and the Eternities?﻿ ﻿…

Alas! as Augustine said once, bitterly enough, of his own Manichaean teachers, Hypatia had taken away the living God, and given him instead the four Elements.﻿ ﻿… And in utter bewilderment and hopeless terror he implored the pity of every guard and gaoler who passed along the corridor, and conjured them, as brothers, fathers, men, to help him. Moved at once by his agony and by his exceeding beauty, the rough Thracians, who knew enough of their employer’s character to have little difficulty in believing his victim to be innocent, listened to him and questioned him. But when they offered the very help which he implored, and asked him to tell his story, the poor boy’s tongue clove to the roof of his mouth. How could he publish his sister’s shame? And yet she was about to publish it herself!﻿ ﻿… And instead of words, he met their condolences with fresh agonies, till they gave him up as mad; and, tired by his violence, compelled him, with blows and curses, to remain quiet; and so the week wore out, in dull and stupefied despair, which trembled on the very edge of idiocy. Night and day were alike to him. The food which was thrust in through his grate remained untasted; hour after hour, day after day, he sat upon the ground, his head buried in his hands, half-dozing from mere exhaustion of body and mind. Why should he care to stir, to eat, to live? He had but one purpose in heaven and earth: and that one purpose was impossible.

===Chinese===
可是这一周菲拉蒙究竟到哪里去了？

被囚禁的头一两天，他像一头落了陷阱的野兽一般狂吼乱挣。他那新近觉醒的目的与力量，骤然被堵截、被遏住，便化作癫狂的怒火沸腾而起。他撕扯囚笼的铁栏；他在地上翻滚号叫。他徒然地呼求希帕蒂娅、呼求佩拉吉娅、呼求阿尔塞尼乌斯——唯独不呼求上帝。他不能祷告，也不敢；因为他能向谁祷告呢？向群星？——向那些深渊与永古？……

可叹哪！正如奥古斯丁（Augustine）昔日极其苦涩地论及他自己那些摩尼教（Manichaean）师傅时所说的那样，希帕蒂娅夺去了那位又活又真的上帝，而把他原先拥有的四大元素给了他。……他在全然的迷惘与无望的恐惧中，向那条走廊上经过的每一个狱卒、每一个看守乞求怜悯，以兄弟之情、以父亲之心、以人之所以为人的名义，恳求他们帮帮他。那些粗鲁的色雷斯人（Thracians）被他这份苦楚、又被他那出众的美貌所动，又素知他们主子的为人，所以毫不费力便信了这少年受害者是无辜的，便肯听他说话、盘问他。然而待他们真要把他所央求的援助给他，请他道出原委时，这可怜少年的舌头却贴在上颚，吐不出半个字来。他怎能将妹妹的羞耻公之于众？可她偏偏又要亲自当众张扬出来！……于是他非但说不出话来，反以新一轮的痛楚回报他们的慰问；他们便当他疯癫了；待被他的撒泼闹得厌烦，便用拳打脚踢和咒骂逼他安静下来；这一周便这样磨损过去，在一种近乎痴呆的、麻木而绝望的麻木之中度过。对他而言，昼与夜并无分别。从铁栅格里塞进来的食物原封不动；他一小时接一小时、一天接一天地坐在地上，把头埋在两手之间，因身心俱疲而半昏半睡。他何苦还要动弹、还要进食、还要活呢？他在天地之间只剩下一个目的：而那目的是不可能的了。

===Original===
At last his cell-door grated on its hinges.

“Up, my mad youth!” cried a rough voice. “Up, and thank the favour of the gods, and the bounty of our noble﻿—ahem!﻿—Prefect. Today he gives freedom to all prisoners. And I suppose a pretty boy like you may go about your business, as well as uglier rascals!”

Philammon looked up in the gaoler’s face with a dim half-comprehension of his meaning.

“Do you hear?” cried the man with a curse. “You are free. Jump up, or I shut the door again, and your one chance is over.”

“Did she dance Venus Anadyomene?”

“She! Who?”

“My sister! Pelagia!”

“Heaven only knows what she has not danced in her time! But they say she dances today once more. Quick! out, or I shall not be ready in time for the sports. They begin an hour hence. Free admission into the theatre today for all﻿—rogues and honest men, Christians and heathens﻿—Curse the boy! he’s as mad as ever.”

===Chinese===
终于，他囚室的门在铰链上吱呀一响。

「起来，你这发疯的少年！」一个粗嗓门喊道。「起来，去谢众神的恩典，去谢我们那位贵人——咳咳！——总督的恩赏。今日他开恩，释放全体囚犯。我想，像你这般俊俏的小哥，大可与那些丑陋的恶棍一道，各自走各自的路了！」

菲拉蒙抬头望着狱卒的脸，那意思他似懂非懂。

「你听见没有？」那人骂了一句。「你自由了。赶紧起来，否则我又把门关上，你那一线生机便没了。」

「她跳了维纳斯·阿娜狄俄墨涅没有？」

「她！谁？」

「我妹妹！佩拉吉娅！」

「天才知道她这半辈子还有什么舞不曾跳过！不过听说她今日又要再跳一回。快！出去，否则我便赶不上看热闹了。一个时辰后开场。今日剧院向所有人大开门庭——骗子和老实人、基督徒和异教徒，一视同仁——该死的疯小子！还是疯成这般模样。」

===Original===
So indeed Philammon seemed; for, springing suddenly to his feet, he rushed out past the gaoler, upsetting him into the corridor, and fled wildly from the prison among the crowd of liberated ruffians, ran from the prison home, from home to the baths, from the baths to the theatre, and was soon pushing his way, regardless of etiquette, towards the lower tiers of benches, in order, he hardly knew why, to place himself as near as possible to the very sight which he dreaded and abhorred.

As fate would have it, the passage by which he had entered opened close to the Prefect’s chair of state, where sat Orestes, gorgeous in his robes of office, and by him﻿—to Philammon’s surprise and horror﻿—Hypatia herself.

More beautiful than ever, her forehead sparkling, like Juno’s own, with a lofty tiara of jewels, her white Ionic robe half hidden by a crimson shawl, there sat the vestal, the philosopher. What did she there? But the boy’s eager eyes, accustomed but too well to note every light and shade of feeling which crossed that face, saw in a moment how wan and haggard was its expression. She wore a look of constraint, of half-terrified self-resolve, as of a martyr: and yet not an undoubting martyr; for as Orestes turned his head at the stir of Philammon’s intrusion, and flashing with anger at the sight, motioned him fiercely back, Hypatia turned too, and as her eyes met her pupil’s she blushed crimson, and started, and seemed in act to motion him back also; and then, recollecting herself, whispered something to Orestes which quieted his wrath, and composed herself, or rather sank into her place again, as one who was determined to abide the worst.

A knot of gay young gentlemen, Philammon’s fellow-students, pulled him down among them, with welcome and laughter; and before he could collect his thoughts, the curtain in front of the stage had fallen, and the sport began.

===Chinese===
菲拉蒙看起来确是疯了；因为他猛然一跃而起，从狱卒身边冲了出去，把狱卒撞翻在走廊里，便随着那一群被释的恶棍狂奔出狱；他从狱中奔到住所，从住所奔到浴场，从浴场奔到剧院，很快便顾不得什么礼数，硬挤着朝下面几排座位闯去，要尽可能靠近那他既惧怕又憎恶的场面——他自己也几乎不知是为何。

命中注定如此，他进来的那条甬道，正开在总督宝座旁边；俄瑞斯忒斯端坐其上，一身官服华贵灿烂；而在他身旁——令菲拉蒙又惊又骇的——竟是希帕蒂娅本人。

她比往日更美，额上闪烁着一顶高高的宝石冠冕，一如朱诺（Juno）之所戴；她那袭白色的爱奥尼亚式长袍，被一条猩红的披肩遮去了一半。这位维斯塔贞女、这位哲学家，她坐在这里做什么？但这少年那双急切的眼睛——太习惯于捕捉那张脸上每一丝情绪的光影——一眼便看出那神情何其苍白憔悴。她带着一种强自镇定的神情，一种半带恐惧的自我决断，仿佛一位殉道者：却又不全然是笃定的殉道者；因为当俄瑞斯忒斯因菲拉蒙闯入的响动而回过头来，一见他便怒目相向、凶狠地挥手斥退他时，希帕蒂娅也回过头来；当她的目光与她这学生的目光相遇，她涨红了脸，吃了一惊，似乎也要挥手令他退去；继而又定下神来，向俄瑞斯忒斯低声说了句什么，平息了他的怒气；她自己也好生端坐了，或者不如说是重新颓然落座，恰如一个已下定决心承受最坏结局之人。

一群衣饰鲜丽的少年公子，菲拉蒙的同窗学友，嬉笑着把他拽到他们中间坐下；他还来不及定下神来，台前那道帷幕便已落下，那场热闹开场了。

===Original===
The scene represented a background of desert mountains, and on the stage itself, before a group of temporary huts, stood huddling together the black Libyan prisoners, some fifty men, women, and children, bedizened with gaudy feathers and girdles of tasselled leather, brandishing their spears and targets, and glaring out with white eyes on the strange scene before them, in childish awe and wonder.

Along the front of the stage a wattled battlement had been erected, while below, the hyposcenium had been painted to represent rocks, thus completing the rough imitation of a village among the Libyan hills.

Amid breathless silence, a herald advanced, and proclaimed that these were prisoners taken in arms against the Roman senate and people, and therefore worthy of immediate death: but that the Prefect, in his exceeding clemency toward them, and especial anxiety to afford the greatest possible amusement to the obedient and loyal citizens of Alexandria, had determined, instead of giving them at once to the beasts, to allow them to fight for their lives, promising to the survivors a free pardon if they acquitted themselves valiantly.

The poor wretches on the stage, when this proclamation was translated to them, set up a barbaric yell of joy, and brandished their spears and targets more fiercely than ever.

===Chinese===
布景画的是一片荒山旷野；台上，在一簇临时搭起的茅棚前，挤作一团的是那些黑皮肤的利比亚（Libyan）俘虏，约有五十来个男女老幼，身上挂满艳丽的羽毛和缀着流苏的皮带，挥舞着他们的长矛和圆盾，瞪着一双双白亮亮的眼珠望着眼前这奇异场面，带着孩童般的敬畏与惊骇。

沿着台口搭起了一道枝条编成的胸墙；下方的下层台口（hyposcenium）则被画成嶙峋岩石，这样便粗粗凑成一个利比亚山间村落的样子。

在令人屏息的寂静中，一名传令官走上前来，宣布这些都是持兵反抗罗马元老院与罗马人民的俘虏，理当立即处死：但总督对他们怀着极大的慈悲，又格外急于为亚历山大城这些驯服而忠诚的公民提供尽可能盛大的助兴，便决定不立即将他们喂野兽，而是允许他们为性命而战，并许诺凡能奋勇作战的幸存者，一律予以赦免。

台上那些可怜人听见这番宣示被译给他们听，便发出野蛮而狂喜的呐喊，更加拼命地挥舞起长矛和圆盾来。

===Original===
But their joy was short. The trumpets sounded the attack: a body of gladiators, equal in number to the savages, marched out from one of the two great side passages, made their obeisance to the applauding spectators, and planting their scaling-ladders against the front of the stage, mounted to the attack.

The Libyans fought like tigers; yet from the first, Hypatia, and Philammon also, could see that their promised chance of life was a mere mockery. Their light darts and naked limbs were no match for the heavy swords and complete armour of their brutal assailants, who endured carelessly a storm of blows and thrusts on heads and faces protected by visored helmets: yet so fierce was the valour of the Libyans, that even they recoiled twice, and twice the scaling-ladders were hurled down again, while more than one gladiator lay below, rolling in the death-agony.

And then burst forth the sleeping devil in the hearts of that great brutalised multitude. Yell upon yell of savage triumph, and still more savage disappointment, rang from every tier of that vast ring of seats, at each blow and parry, onslaught and repulse; and Philammon saw with horror and surprise that luxury, refinement, philosophic culture itself, were no safeguards against the infection of bloodthirstiness. Gay and delicate ladies, whom he had seen three days before simpering delight at Hypatia’s heavenward aspirations, and some, too, whom he seemed to recollect in Christian churches, sprang from their seats, waved their hands and handkerchiefs, and clapped and shouted to the gladiators. For, alas! there was no doubt as to which side the favour of the spectators inclined. With taunts, jeers, applause, entreaties, the hired ruffians were urged on to their work of blood. The poor wretches heard no voice raised in their favour: nothing but contempt, hatred, eager lust of blood, glared from those thousands of pitiless eyes; and, brokenhearted, despairing, they flagged and drew back one by one. A shout of triumph greeted the gladiators as they climbed over the battlement, and gained a footing on the stage. The wretched blacks broke up, and fled wildly from corner to corner, looking vainly for an outlet.﻿ ﻿…

===Chinese===
然而他们的欢喜是短暂的。号角吹响了进攻的信号：一队与那些野蛮人数量相等的角斗士（gladiators），从两条大侧道之一里开出，向鼓掌的观众躬身行礼，便将攻城梯搭上台口，攀援而上，发起攻势。

利比亚人拼死如虎；然而从一开始，希帕蒂娅——还有菲拉蒙——便看得出他们所许诺的求生之机，不过是一个嘲弄。他们轻飘飘的标枪和赤裸的肢体，怎敌得过那些残暴进攻者的重剑和全身甲胄；那些人头戴带面甲的头盔，任凭拳打脚踢如雨点落在头脸上也满不在乎：然而利比亚人之勇猛如此炽烈，以致那些进攻者竟也两度退却，两度攻城梯被掀翻下来，不止一个角斗士在台下翻滚着作垂死的挣扎。

于是那沉沉睡在那一大群被驯化了的大众心中的魔鬼，猛然迸发出来。一声接一声的野蛮狂吼——胜利时的与更失望时的——从那一圈圈庞大的座位上层层响起，应着每一记劈刺、每一记格挡、每一次冲杀、每一次反扑；菲拉蒙惊骇而诧异地看见，奢华、文雅、乃至哲学的修养本身，都挡不住这嗜血之疫的传染。那些娇贵艳丽的贵妇——三天之前他还在希帕蒂娅那超凡入圣的玄思面前见过她们故作娇痴的欢喜——还有一些他似乎在基督教教堂里见过的面孔——都从座位上一跃而起，挥着手、挥着手帕，向角斗士们鼓掌呐喊。因为，唉！看客们究竟偏袒哪一方，那是毫无疑问的。在奚落、嘲骂、喝彩、恳求之中，那一群拿钱卖命的恶棍被怂恿着去干他们那嗜血的勾当。那些可怜人听不见一声替他们说情的言语：那成千上万双无情的眼睛里，只流露出蔑视、仇恨和急切的嗜血之欲；他们心碎了，绝望了，一个个萎顿下来，节节后退。角斗士们攀过胸墙、登上舞台时，迎接他们的是一阵胜利的欢呼。那些可怜的黑人四散奔逃，从一个角落疯窜到另一个角落，徒然地寻一条出路。……

===Original===
And then began a butchery.﻿ ﻿… Some fifty men, women, and children were cooped together in that narrow space.﻿ ﻿… And yet Hypatia’s countenance did not falter. Why should it? What were their numbers, beside the thousands who had perished year by year for centuries, by that and far worse deaths, in the amphitheatres of that empire, for that faith which she was vowed to reestablish. It was part of the great system; and she must endure it.

Not that she did not feel; for she, too, was woman; and her heart, raised far above the brutal excitement of the multitude, lay calmly open to the most poignant stings of pity. Again and again she was in the act to entreat mercy for some shrieking woman or struggling child; but before her lips could shape the words, the blow had fallen, or the wretch was whirled away from her sight in the dense undistinguishable mass of slayers and slain. Yes, she had begun, and she must follow to the end.﻿ ﻿… And, after all, what were the lives of those few semi-brutes, returning thus a few years earlier to the clay from which they sprang, compared with the regeneration of a world?﻿ ﻿… And it would be over in a few minutes more, and that black writhing heap be still forever, and the curtain fall.﻿ ﻿… And then for Venus Anadyomene, and art, and joy, and peace, and the graceful wisdom and beauty of the old Greek art, calming and civilising all hearts, and softening them into pure devotion for the immortal myths, the immortal deities, who had inspired their forefathers in the glorious days of old.﻿ ﻿… But still the black heap writhed; and she looked away, up, down, and round, everywhere, to avoid the sickening sight; and her eye caught Philammon’s gazing at her with looks of horror and disgust.﻿ ﻿… A thrill of shame rushed through her heart, and blushing scarlet, she sank her head, and whispered to Orestes﻿—

“Have mercy!﻿—spare the rest!”

“Nay, fairest vestal! The mob has tasted blood, and they must have their fill of it, or they will turn on us for aught I know. Nothing so dangerous as to check a brute, whether he be horse, dog, or man, when once his spirit is up. Ha! there is a fugitive! How well the little rascal runs!”

===Chinese===
于是一场屠杀开始了。……五十来个男女老幼，被关在那一方狭小的台面上。……然而希帕蒂娅的面色并无动摇。她又何必动摇？在那帝国各处圆剧场里，为了她立志要重建的那种信仰，几百年来年复一年死去的人成千上万，所死之状远比这更惨——与那相比，这点人数又算得什么？这是那一整套大体制的一部分；她必须忍受。

这并非她无所感；因为她到底是女子；她的心远高于那群氓的嗜血狂热，平静地敞开着，承受着怜悯最尖锐的刺痛。她一次又一次地正要为某个尖叫的妇人或挣扎的孩童开口求情；可还没等她双唇吐出半个字，那一刀已然落下，或那可怜人已在那一堆刀手与被杀者混作一团的稠密尸骸里被卷离了她的视线。是的，她既已开了头，便只得跟到尽头。……再说，与一个世界的再造相比，这几个近乎禽兽之人的性命——他们不过是早几年归回他们所从出的尘土——又算得什么？……再过几分钟这一切便要过去，那一堆蠕动的黑色将永远静下来，那帷幕也将落下。……接下去便是维纳斯·阿娜狄俄墨涅（Venus Anadyomene）登场了，是艺术、欢乐、和平，是古朴希腊艺术的优雅智慧与美，它要抚慰、要开化一切人心，将它们软化为对那不朽神话、对那激励他们列祖于往昔光辉岁月中的不朽神祇的纯粹虔敬。……然而那一堆黑色仍在蠕动；她把目光移开，向上、向下、向四围，到处转，要避开那令人作呕的景象；可她的目光却撞上了菲拉蒙那双正凝视着她的眼睛，眼中满是惊骇与厌恶。……一阵羞惭掠过她的心，她涨红了脸，低下头去，对俄瑞斯忒斯低声道——

「开恩吧！——饶了剩下的人吧！」

「不成啊，最美丽的贞女！这群氓既已尝到了血，便非喝个饱不可，否则他们便会反过来对付我们，也未可知。再没有比约束一头畜生——管它是马、是狗、还是人——更危险的事了，一旦它的性子被激起来的话。哈！那里有个逃跑的！这小家伙跑得倒真利落！」

===Original===
As he spoke, a boy, the only survivor, leaped from the stage, and rushed across the orchestra toward them, followed by a rough cur-dog.

“You shall have this youth, if he reaches us.”

Hypatia watched breathless. The boy had just arrived at the altar in the centre of the orchestra, when he saw a gladiator close upon him. The ruffian’s arm was raised to strike, when, to the astonishment of the whole theatre, boy and dog turned valiantly to bay, and leaping on the gladiator, dragged him between them to the ground. The triumph was momentary. The uplifted hands, the shout of “Spare him!” came too late. The man, as he lay, buried his sword in the slender body of the child, and then rising, walked coolly back to the side passages, while the poor cur stood over the little corpse, licking its hands and face, and making the whole building ring with his doleful cries. The attendants entered, and striking their hooks into corpse after corpse, dragged them out of sight, marking their path by long red furrows in the sand; while the dog followed, until his inauspicious howlings died away down distant passages.

Philammon felt sick and giddy, and half rose to escape. But Pelagia!﻿ ﻿… No﻿—he must sit it out, and see the worst, if worse than this was possible. He looked round. The people were coolly sipping wine and eating cakes, while they chatted admirably about the beauty of the great curtain, which had fallen and hidden the stage, and represented, on a ground of deep-blue sea, Europa carried by the bull across the Bosphorus, while Nereids and Tritons played around.

===Chinese===
说话间，一个男孩——唯一的幸存者——从台上跳下，穿过乐池朝他们奔来，后面跟着一条杂种小恶犬。

「他若跑到我们这里，这少年便归你。」

希帕蒂娅屏息看着。那男孩刚刚跑到乐池中央的祭坛边，便见一个角斗士逼到了跟前。那恶棍举臂欲劈，谁知——全场为之大骇——那男孩和那条狗竟勇猛地返身迎战，扑到角斗士身上，合力把他拽倒在地。然而这胜利只在一瞬。那一双双举起的手、那一声「饶了他！」都来得太迟了。那人倒在地上，将剑刺入那孩子纤弱的身躯；继而翻身而起，从容地走回侧道去了；那条可怜的杂种狗却守在那小小的尸体旁，舔着它的手和脸，那一声声哀嚎叫整座剧院都回响起来。几个执役进场，用带钩的长竿钩住一具又一具尸体，拖出去看不见的地方，在沙地上留下一道道长长的红色沟痕；那条狗跟在后面，直到它那不祥的哀嚎在遥远的过道里渐渐消失。

菲拉蒙只觉阵阵作呕、头昏目眩，半站起身要逃。可佩拉吉娅呢！……不——他得坐到底，要看那更坏的一幕，若还有比这更坏的话。他四下里看。众人正从从容容地呷着酒、吃着饼，一边赞叹地议论那幅大帷幕如何美丽；那帷幕已经落下，遮住了舞台，画的乃是深蓝的海面上，欧罗巴（Europa）被公牛驮着渡过博斯普鲁斯（Bosphorus），四周有涅瑞伊得斯（Nereids）和特里同们（Tritons）嬉戏。

===Original===
A single flute within the curtain began to send forth luscious strains, deadened and distant, as if through far-off glens and woodlands; and from the side passages issued three Graces, led by Peitho, the goddess of persuasion, bearing a herald’s staff in her hand. She advanced to the altar in the centre of the orchestra, and informed the spectators that, during the absence of Ares in aid of a certain great military expedition, which was shortly to decide the diadem of Rome, and the liberty, prosperity, and supremacy of Egypt and Alexandria, Aphrodite had returned to her lawful allegiance, and submitted for the time being to the commands of her husband, Hephaestus; that he, as the deity of artificers, felt a peculiar interest in the welfare of the city of Alexandria, the workshop of the world, and had, as a sign of his especial favour, prevailed upon his fair spouse to exhibit, for this once, her beauties to the assembled populace, and, in the unspoken poetry of motion, to represent to them the emotions with which, as she arose newborn from the sea, she first surveyed that fair expanse of heaven and earth of which she now reigned undisputed queen.

A shout of rapturous applause greeted this announcement, and forthwith limped from the opposite slip the lame deity himself, hammer and pincers on shoulder, followed by a train of gigantic cyclopes, who bore on their shoulders various pieces of gilded metal work.

Hephaestus, who was intended to supply the comic element in the vast pantomimic pageant, shambled forward with studied uncouthness, amid roars of laughter; surveyed the altar with ludicrous contempt; raised his mighty hammer, shivered it to pieces with a single blow, and beckoned to his attendants to carry off the fragments, and replace it with something more fitting for his august spouse.

===Chinese===
帷幕之内，一支独笛开始送出旖旎的乐声，沉闷而遥远，仿佛穿过遥远的幽谷与林莽；从侧道里走出三位美惠女神（Graces），由说服女神佩托（Peitho）引领，她手中执着一根传令官的杖。她走到乐池中央的祭坛前，向众看客禀告：因阿瑞斯（Ares）外出助阵于某桩重大军事远征——此远征不久将决定罗马帝冠之归属、决定埃及与亚历山大城的自由、繁荣与至尊——阿佛洛狄忒（Aphrodite）已归回她合法的臣服之位，暂时顺从其夫赫淮斯托斯（Hephaestus）之命；赫淮斯托斯作为百工之神，对亚历山大城这座「天下作坊」的福祉别有一份关切，遂以其特殊恩典之明证，劝服了他美丽的妻子，只此一次，将其美貌展示给在场的百姓，并以那无言的动作之诗，向他们演绎当其初自海中新生而起、初次眺望这片她如今无可争议地为之主宰的天地时，心中所生的种种情思。

一阵狂喜的喝彩迎接了这番宣告；紧接着，从对面侧幕里一瘸一拐地走出那位跛足的神明自己，肩上扛着锤子和铁钳，后面跟着一队硕大无朋的独眼巨人（cyclopes），肩上扛着各色镀金的金属器件。

赫淮斯托斯在这浩大的哑剧排场中原是要担当滑稽角色的，便装出笨拙丑怪的步态蹒跚上前，在哄堂大笑中走到祭坛前，以滑稽的蔑视神色打量那祭坛；继而高高举起他那把巨锤，只一击便把它砸得粉碎，又挥手吩咐侍从们把碎片抬走，换上与他那位庄严妻子更为相称之物。

===Original===
With wonderful quickness the metal openwork was put in its place, and fitted together, forming a frame of coral branches intermingled with dolphins, Nereids, and Tritons. Four gigantic cyclopes then approached, staggering under the weight of a circular slab of green marble, polished to a perfect mirror, which they placed on the framework. The Graces wreathed its circumference with garlands of seaweed, shells, and corallines, and the mimic sea was complete.

Peitho and the Graces retired a few steps, and grouped themselves with the cyclopes, whose grimed and brawny limbs, and hideous one-eyed masks, threw out in striking contrast the delicate hue and grace of the beautiful maiden figures; while Hephaestus turned toward the curtain, and seemed to await impatiently the forthcoming of the goddess.

Every lip was breathless with expectation as the flutes swelled louder and nearer; horns and cymbals took up the harmony; and, to a triumphant burst of music, the curtain rose, and a simultaneous shout of delight burst from ten thousand voices.

The scene behind represented a magnificent temple, half hidden in an artificial wood of tropic trees and shrubs, which filled the stage. Fauns and dryads peeped laughing from among their stems, and gorgeous birds, tethered by unseen threads, fluttered and sang among their branches. In the centre an overarching avenue of palms led from the temple doors to the front of the stage, from which the mimic battlements had disappeared, and had been replaced, in those few moments, by a broad slope of smooth greensward, leading down into the orchestra, and fringed with myrtles, roses, apple-trees, poppies, and crimson hyacinths, stained with the lifeblood of Adonis.

===Chinese===
那一件件金属透雕飞快地被安放就位、拼合起来，构成一个由珊瑚枝桠夹杂着海豚、涅瑞伊得斯和特里同们组成的框架。然后四个硕大的独眼巨人走上前来，步履蹒跚地扛着一块圆形的绿大理石板，磨得光可鉴人，把它安在那框架之上。美惠女神们用海草、贝壳和珊瑚虫的花环把它的边缘盘绕起来，那模拟的海洋便大功告成。

佩托和美惠女神们退后几步，与独眼巨人们站作一群，他们那沾满油污、青筋暴突的四肢和狰狞的独眼面具，恰恰把那几位美丽少女的娇嫩肤色与婀娜身姿衬得格外鲜明；赫淮斯托斯则转身朝着帷幕，似乎不耐烦地等候女神的现身。

笛声渐高渐近，嘹亮起来，众人都屏息以待；号角与铜钹接上和声；在一片胜利的乐曲声中，那帷幕冉冉升起，一万个声音同时迸发出一阵欣喜若狂的欢呼。

后面的布景是一座宏伟的神庙，半掩在一片人工栽植的热带林木之间，那林木布满了整个舞台。羊人萨提尔和树精仙女们从树干后探出头来嬉笑；一群一群艳丽的鸟儿，被看不见的丝线拴着，在枝叶间扑腾鸣唱。中央一道拱顶般的棕榈夹道从神庙大门直通台口；台口上那道模拟的胸墙已不翼而飞，短短片刻之间已被一片宽阔平滑的绿草坪所取代，斜斜地铺入乐池，草坪两边缀满了香桃木、玫瑰、苹果树、罂粟，以及那被阿多尼斯（Adonis）的鲜血染红的猩红风信子。

===Original===
The folding doors of the temple opened slowly, the crash of instruments resounded from within; and, preceded by the musicians, came forth the triumph of Aphrodite, and passed down the slope, and down the outer ring of the orchestra.

A splendid car, drawn by white oxen, bore the rarest and gaudiest of foreign flowers and fruits, which young girls, dressed as Hours and Seasons, strewed in front of the procession and among the spectators.

A long line of beautiful youths and maidens, crowned with garlands, and robed in scarfs of purple gauze, followed by two and two. Each pair carried or led a pair of wild animals, captives of the conquering might of Beauty.

Foremost were borne, on the wrists of the actors, the birds especially sacred to the goddess﻿—doves and sparrows, wrynecks and swallows; and a pair of gigantic Indian tortoises, each ridden by a lovely nymph, showed that Orestes had not forgotten one wish, at least, of his intended bride.

Then followed strange birds from India, parakeets, peacocks, pheasants silver and golden; bustards and ostriches: the latter, bestridden each by a tiny cupid, were led on in golden leashes, followed by antelopes and oryxes, elks from beyond the Danube, four-horned rams from the Isles of the Hyperborean Ocean, and the strange hybrid of the Libyan hills, believed by all spectators to be half-bull half-horse. And then a murmur of delighted awe ran through the theatre, as bears and leopards, lions and tigers, fettered in heavy chains of gold, and made gentle for the occasion by narcotics, paced sedately down the slope, obedient to their beautiful guides; while behind them, the unwieldy bulk of two double-horned rhinoceroses, from the far south, was overtopped by the long slender necks and large soft eyes of a pair of giraffes, such as had not been seen in Alexandria for more than fifty years.

===Chinese===
神庙的对开大门缓缓开启，里头乐声震天价响；乐师们在前引路，其后便涌出阿佛洛狄忒的凯旋行列，顺着斜坡下来，绕着乐池外圈行进。

一辆华美的车辇，由白牛拉着，载着种种最稀奇最艳丽的异邦花草果实；一群少女装扮成时序女神（Hours）和季候女神（Seasons）的模样，把花果撒在行列前面、撒在观众中间。

一长列美丽的少年男女，头戴花冠，身披紫色薄纱披肩，两人一排，鱼贯相随。每一对或抬或牵着一对走兽，这些走兽都是「美」之征服伟力的俘虏。

打头抬着的，是系在演员手腕上的那些特为属于该女神的圣鸟——鸽子与麻雀，巫鸟与燕子；还有一对硕大的印度陆龟，每只龟上都坐着一位可爱的仙女，可见俄瑞斯忒斯并未忘记他那位未婚妻的至少一个心愿。

其后跟着的是种种来自印度的奇鸟——长尾鹦鹉、孔雀、银雉与金雉；鸨与鸵鸟：后者每一只背上骑着一个细小的丘比特（cupid），被金链子牵着走在前面；跟在后面的，是羚羊与剑羚，多瑙河（Danube）外的驼鹿，来自极北之洋（Hyperborean Ocean）诸岛的四角羊，还有利比亚山间那种古怪的半牛半马之物，看客们无不以为它果真是半牛半马。随后，一阵惊喜的敬畏低语流过整个剧院，只见那些熊与豹、狮与虎，被沉甸甸的金链锁住，又被药物麻醉得此时温驯，便恭顺地由它们那些美丽的引导者牵引着，庄重地从斜坡上走下来；在它们身后，两只来自远南的双角犀牛那笨重的身躯之上，又高耸着一对长颈鹿那细长优美的颈项和那一双温柔的大眼睛——这种动物已有五十多年未曾在亚历山大城出现过了。

===Original===
A cry arose of “Orestes! Orestes! Health to the illustrious Prefect! Thanks for his bounty!” And a hired voice or two among the crowd cried, “Hail to Orestes! Hail, Emperor of Africa!”.﻿ ﻿… But there was no response.

“The rose is still in the bud,” simpered Orestes to Hypatia. He rose, beckoned and bowed the crowd into silence; and then, after a short pantomimic exhibition of rapturous gratitude and humility, pointed triumphantly to the palm avenue, among the shadows of which appeared the wonder of the day﻿—the huge tusks and trunk of the white elephant himself.

There it was at last! Not a doubt of it! A real elephant, and yet as white as snow. Sight never seen before in Alexandria﻿—never to be seen again! “Oh, thrice blest men of Macedonia!” shouted some worthy on high, “the gods are bountiful to you this day!” And all mouths and eyes confirmed the opinion, as they opened wider and yet wider to drink in the inexhaustible joy and glory.

On he paced solemnly, while the whole theatre resounded to his heavy tread, and the fauns and dryads fled in terror. A choir of nymphs swung round him hand in hand, and sang, as they danced along, the conquering might of Beauty, the tamer of beasts and men and deities. Skirmishing parties of little winged cupids spread themselves over the orchestra, from left to right, and pelted the spectators with perfumed comfits, shot among them from their tiny bows arrows of fragrant sandalwood, or swung smoking censers, which loaded the air with intoxicating odours.

===Chinese===
众人齐声高呼：「俄瑞斯忒斯！俄瑞斯忒斯！祝尊贵的总督康健！多谢他的恩赏！」人群中又有一两个花钱雇来的嗓子喊道：「俄瑞斯忒斯万岁！万岁，阿非利加之皇！」……然而并无回响。

「玫瑰还在含苞呢，」俄瑞斯忒斯对希帕蒂娅假笑了一声。他站起身来，招手、躬身，请众人安静；继而，做出一段短短的、欣喜感恩与谦逊自抑的哑剧，便得意地朝那棕榈夹道一指——只见夹道的阴影里现出了今日压轴的奇观——那头白象自身巨大的象牙与长鼻。

它到底在那里了！这没错！一头真正的大象，却白得像雪。这在亚历山大城是前所未见的奇景——也再不会重见！「啊，三倍有福的马其顿人啊！」上面有个好人喊道，「众神今日对你们真是慷慨哪！」所有的嘴和眼都附和这话，它们张得越来越大，要饮尽那不竭的欢乐与荣光。

它迈着庄重的步子走来，整座剧院都回响着它沉重的足音，那些萨提尔与树精则惊惶逃窜。一队仙女手拉着手围着它翩翩旋转，边舞边歌，唱着「美」那征服万物的伟力，那驯服走兽、凡人与神祇的伟力。一队队长着翅膀的小丘比特三五成群地散开，从左到右掠过乐池，把芳香的糖渍蜜饯投向看客，从他们的小弓里把芳香的檀香木箭射向人群，或摇摆着冒烟的香炉，叫空气里满是醉人的香气。

===Original===
The procession came on down the slope, and the elephant approached the spectators; his tusks were wreathed with roses and myrtles; his ears were pierced with splendid earrings, a jewelled frontlet hung between his eyes; Eros himself, a lovely winged boy, sat on his neck, and guided him with the point of a golden arrow. But what precious thing was it which that shell-formed car upon his back contained? The goddess! Pelagia Aphrodite herself?

Yes; whiter than the snow-white elephant﻿—more rosy than the pink-tipped shell in which she lay, among crimson cushions and silver gauze, there shone the goddess, thrilling all hearts with those delicious smiles, and glances of the bashful playful eyes, and grateful wavings of her tiny hand, as the whole theatre rose with one accord, and ten thousand eyes were concentrated on the unequalled loveliness beneath them.

Twice the procession passed round the whole circumference of the orchestra, and then returning from the foot of the slope towards the central group around Hephaestus, deployed right and left in front of the stage. The lions and tigers were led away into the side passages; the youths and maidens combined themselves with the gentler animals into groups lessening gradually from the centre to the wings, and stood expectant, while the elephant came forward, and knelt behind the platform destined for the goddess.

The valves of the shell closed. The Graces unloosed the fastenings of the car. The elephant turned his trunk over his back, and, guided by the hands of the girls, grasped the shell, and lifting it high in air, deposited it on the steps at the back of the platform.

Hephaestus limped forward, and, with his most uncouth gestures, signified the delight which he had in bestowing such a sight upon his faithful artisans of Alexandria, and the unspeakable enjoyment which they were to expect from the mystic dance of the goddess; and then retired, leaving the Graces to advance in front of the platform, and with their arms twined round each other, begin Hypatia’s song of invocation.

===Chinese===
行列顺着斜坡下来，那大象挨近了观众；它的牙上盘绕着玫瑰和香桃木；它的耳朵上穿着华美的耳环，两眼之间悬着一面宝石额带；厄洛斯（Eros）本人——一个长着翅膀的可爱男孩——坐在它颈上，用一支金箭的箭头指引着它。可它背上那辆贝形车辇里所盛的，究竟是什么珍贵之物呢？是女神！是佩拉吉娅·阿佛洛狄忒本人么？

是的；比那雪白的大象更白——比她所卧其中的那只尖端粉红的贝壳更嫣红，她卧在猩红的软垫和银色的薄纱之间；这位女神璀璨夺目，她那醉人的微笑、那娇羞而俏皮的眼波、那纤手感激的轻挥，使全剧场的人都为之倾倒；整座剧院的人都不约而同地站了起来，一万双眼睛都集中在他们脚下那举世无双的美貌之上。

行列绕着乐池整整走了两圈，然后从斜坡脚下折回，朝着赫淮斯托斯周围那一簇中心人物行去，在台前排开左右两翼。狮和虎被牵入侧道；少年男女们与那些较温驯的动物搭配成一组一组的图案，从中央向两翼逐渐缩小，肃立以待；那大象则走上前来，跪在为女神所设的平台之后。

那贝壳的两瓣合拢了。美惠女神们解开车辇上的系绳。大象把长鼻反伸过背，由那些姑娘们的手引导着，抓住那贝壳，把它高高举到空中，又稳稳地放在平台后侧的台阶之上。

赫淮斯托斯一瘸一拐地上前来，用他那最笨拙丑怪的姿势，表示他多么乐于把这一番景象赏给他忠心的亚历山大城的工匠们，又表示他们将从女神那神秘的舞蹈中获得何等难以言喻的欢愉；说罢便退下去，让美惠女神们走到平台之前，彼此搂着腰，开始唱希帕蒂娅所作的祈神之歌。

===Original===
As the first strophe died away, the valves of the shell reopened, and discovered Aphrodite crouching on one knee within. She raised her head, and gazed around the vast circle of seats. A mild surprise was on her countenance, which quickened into delightful wonder, and bashfulness struggling with the sense of new enjoyment and new powers. She glanced downward at herself; and smiled, astonished at her own loveliness; then upward at the sky; and seemed ready, with an awful joy, to spring up into the boundless void. Her whole figure dilated; she seemed to drink in strength from every object which met her in the great universe around; and slowly, from among the shells and seaweeds, she rose to her full height, the mystic cestus glittering round her waist, in deep festoons of emeralds and pearls, and stepped forward upon the marble sea-floor, wringing the dripping perfume from her locks, as Aphrodite rose of old.

For the first minute the crowd was too breathless with pleasure to think of applause. But the goddess seemed to require due homage; and when she folded her arms across her bosom, and stood motionless for an instant, as if to demand the worship of the universe, every tongue was loosed, and a thunderclap of “Aphrodite!” rang out across the roofs of Alexandria, and startled Cyril in his chamber at the Serapeium, and weary muleteers on distant sand-hills, and dozing mariners far out at sea.

And then began a miracle of art, such as was only possible among a people of the free and exquisite physical training, and the delicate aesthetic perception of those old Greeks, even in their most fallen days. A dance, in which every motion was a word, and rest as eloquent as motion; in which every attitude was a fresh motive for a sculptor of the purest school, and the highest physical activity was manifested, not as in the coarser comic pantomimes, in fantastic bounds and unnatural distortions, but in perpetual delicate modulations of a stately and self-restraining grace. The artist was for the moment transformed into the goddess. The theatre, and Alexandria, and the gorgeous pageant beyond, had vanished from her imagination, and therefore from the imagination of the spectators, under the constraining inspiration of her art, and they and she alike saw nothing but the lonely sea around Cytherea, and the goddess hovering above its emerald mirror, saying forth on sea, and air, and shore, beauty, and joy, and love.﻿ ﻿…

===Chinese===
待到第一段颂歌余音将尽，那贝壳的两瓣重新开启，只见阿佛洛狄忒正以一膝跪在里边。她抬起头来，环顾那一圈庞大的座位。她面带一种温和的惊讶，这惊讶迅即化作甜美的惊奇，化作羞涩与新生的喜悦和新生的力量感彼此相争。她俯首看了一看自己；嫣然一笑，惊异于自己的美貌；继而仰望苍穹；仿佛怀着一种可畏的欢喜，便要纵身跃入那无垠的虚空。她整个身姿舒展开来；她仿佛从她周围那大千世界中每一个所见之物上汲取了力量；慢慢地，从那些贝壳与海草之间，她长身而起，立直了她整个高度，那条神秘的塞斯图斯（cestus）在她腰间熠熠生辉，以绿宝石与珍珠作成深深的垂坠；她踏上前去，立于那大理石的海底之上，拧着从发丝间滴落的香膏，一如阿佛洛狄忒古时初升之时。

头一分钟，众人因喜悦而屏息，竟来不及喝彩。但女神似在要求应得的敬拜；当她双臂交叉在胸前、一动不动地伫立片刻，仿佛要求全宇宙的崇拜时，所有舌头都松开了，一声惊雷似的「阿佛洛狄忒！」响彻亚历山大城千家万户的屋顶，惊动了远在塞拉匹斯神庙（Serapeium）密室中的区利罗（Cyril），惊动了远处沙丘上疲惫的赶骡人，也惊动了远在海上的打盹的水手。

于是一场艺术的奇迹开始了，这般奇迹唯有在一个拥有自由而精妙之身体训练、拥有细腻审美感觉的民族中才有可能——即便是这些古朴希腊人最堕落的时代里也仍然有可能。一支舞，其中每一个动作都是一个字眼，而停顿也如动作一般雄辩；其中每一个姿态都是最纯粹流派的雕塑家的新题材，而最高的身体活力之表现，并不像粗俗的滑稽哑剧里那样见于荒唐的跳跃和不自然的扭曲，而是见于一种庄严而自我克制的优雅之永不间断的精微起伏。这位艺人此刻已化为女神。剧院、亚历山大城、以及那一头那华美的排场，都已从她的想象中消失了——因而也就从看客们的想象中消失了——在她那艺术的不容置疑的灵感支配之下；她与众人一样，眼前所见唯有昔瑟里亚（Cytherea）四周那寂寥的大海，唯有那女神翱翔于其碧绿如镜的海面之上，向海、向空、向岸，倾吐着美、喜悦与爱。……

===Original===
Philammon’s eyes were bursting from his head with shame and horror: and yet he could not hate her; not even despise her. He would have done so, had there been the faintest trace of human feeling in her countenance to prove that some germ of moral sense lingered within: but even the faint blush and the downcast eye with which she had entered the theatre were gone; and the only expression on her face was that of intense enjoyment of her own activity and skill, and satisfied vanity, as of a petted child.﻿ ﻿… Was she accountable? A reasonable soul, capable of right or wrong at all? He hoped not.﻿ ﻿… He would trust not.﻿ ﻿… And still Pelagia danced on; and for a whole age of agony, he could see nothing in heaven or earth but the bewildering maze of those white feet, as they twinkled over their white image in the marble mirror.﻿ ﻿… At last it was over. Every limb suddenly collapsed, and she stood drooping in soft self-satisfied fatigue, awaiting the burst of applause which rang through Philammon’s ears, proclaiming to heaven and earth, as with a mighty trumpet-blast, his sister’s shame.

The elephant rose, and moved forward to the side of the slabs. His back was covered with crimson cushions, on which it seemed Aphrodite was to return without her shell. She folded her arms across her bosom, and stood smiling, as the elephant gently wreathed his trunk around her waist, and lifted her slowly from the slab, in act to place her on his back.﻿ ﻿…

The little feet, clinging half fearfully together, had just risen from the marble﻿—The elephant started, dropped his delicate burden heavily on the slab, looked down, raised his forefoot, and throwing his trunk into the air, gave a shrill scream of terror and disgust.﻿ ﻿…

The foot was red with blood﻿—the young boy’s blood﻿—which was soaking and bubbling up through the fresh sand where the elephant had trodden, in a round, dark, purple spot.﻿ ﻿…

===Chinese===
菲拉蒙的双眼因羞耻与惊骇而几乎要从眼眶里迸出来：然而他无法恨她；甚至连轻视她也不能。倘若她脸上还有一丝一毫人之情感的痕迹，足以证明她心中尚存一星半点的道德感，他倒会恨她、轻视她了：可是她进剧院时那一丝淡淡的红晕和低垂的眼，如今也都消失了；她脸上唯一的神情，是全然沉醉于自己的灵动与技艺之中那种酣畅，是那种被宠坏了的孩童似的心满意足的虚荣。……她还有可责之处么？还是一颗能分辨善恶的理智之灵么？他但愿没有。……他宁愿相信没有。……然而佩拉吉娅仍一路舞下去；整整一个痛苦的时代里，无论在天上、在地上，他都看不见别的，只看见那一双白色的纤足所舞出的令人目眩的迷阵，它们在大理石如镜的平面上在自己白色倒影之上一闪一闪地掠过。……终于结束了。她的四肢突然一松，软软地垂着，带着一种温柔而自满的慵懒伫立，等候那一阵爆发的喝彩；那喝彩声在菲拉蒙耳中轰然作响，仿佛以一声宏大的号角，向天地宣告了他妹妹的羞耻。

大象立起身来，走到石板边上。它背上铺着猩红的软垫，阿佛洛狄忒似乎要弃去贝壳、改由这软垫返回。她双臂交叉在胸前，含笑而立；大象轻轻地用长鼻绕住她的腰，慢慢地把她从石板上举起，正要把她放到自己背上……

那双小小的脚，半带恐惧地紧紧相挨，刚刚离开那大理石——大象猛地一惊，把它这娇嫩的负担重重地摔在石板上，低头一看，抬起前足，把长鼻抛向空中，发出一声又惊又嫌的尖锐嘶鸣。……

它的脚被血染红了——是那少年的血——正从它踏过的新铺沙土底下，在一处圆圆的、深紫色的斑渍里渗出、冒着泡。……

===Original===
Philammon could bear no more. Another moment and he had hurled down through the dense mass of spectators, clearing rank after rank of seats by the sheer strength of madness, leaped the balustrade into the orchestra below, and rushed across the space to the foot of the platform.

“Pelagia! Sister! My sister! Have mercy on me! on yourself! I will hide you! save you! and we will flee together out of this infernal place! this world of devils! I am your brother! Come!”

She looked at him one moment with wide, wild eyes﻿—The truth flashed on her﻿—

“Brother!”

And she sprang from the platform into his arms.﻿ ﻿… A vision of a lofty window in Athens, looking out over far olive-yards and gardens, and the bright roofs and basins of the Piraeus, and the broad blue sea, with the purple peaks of Aegina beyond all.﻿ ﻿… And a dark-eyed boy, with his arm around her neck, pointed laughing to the twinkling masts in the far harbour, and called her sister.﻿ ﻿… The dead soul woke within her; and with a wild cry she recoiled from him in an agony of shame, and covering her face with both her hands, sank down among the bloodstained sand.

A yell, as of all hell broke loose, rang along that vast circle﻿—

“Down with him!” “Away with him!” “Crucify the slave!” “Give the barbarian to the beasts!” “To the beasts with him, noble Prefect!” A crowd of attendants rushed upon him, and many of the spectators sprang from their seats, and were on the point of leaping down into the orchestra.

Philammon turned upon them like a lion at bay; and clear and loud his voice rose through the roar of the multitude.

“Ay! murder me as the Romans murdered Saint Telemachus! Slaves as besotted and accursed as your besotted and accursed tyrants! Lower than the beasts whom you employ as your butchers! Murder and lust go fitly hand in hand, and the throne of my sister’s shame is well built on the blood of innocents! Let my death end the devil’s sacrifice, and fill up the cup of your iniquity!”

“To the beasts!” “Make the elephant trample him to powder!”

And the huge brute, goaded on by the attendants, rushed on the youth, while Eros leaped from his neck, and fled weeping up the slope.

===Chinese===
菲拉蒙再也忍不住了。再过一刻他便已纵身冲下，穿过那密密匝匝的看客，凭着癫狂蛮力一级一级地跳过座位，越过栏杆跳进下方的乐池，又冲过那片空地，奔到平台脚下。

「佩拉吉娅！妹妹！我的妹妹！可怜可怜我吧！可怜可怜你自己吧！我会把你藏起来！救你出去！我们要一同逃出这个地狱！这个群魔横行的世界！我是你的哥哥！来！」

她睁着一双又大又狂乱的眼，对他望了片刻——那真相在她心头一闪——

「哥哥！」

她便从平台上一跃，跳进他的怀里。……眼前闪现一幕景象：雅典一扇高窗，窗外是远处的橄榄园和花圃，是比雷埃夫斯（Piraeus）那明亮的屋顶与船坞，是那一片湛蓝的大海，海的那一边便是埃吉纳（Aegina）那紫色的群峰。……一个黑眼睛的男孩，一手搂着她的脖子，笑着指向远处港内闪烁的桅杆，唤她作姐姐。……那颗已死的灵魂在她体内苏醒过来；她狂叫一声，在羞耻的剧痛中从他面前退缩，双手掩面，颓然倒在染血的沙土之间。

一声怒吼，如同万鬼出狱，沿着那一圈庞大的座位响彻而去——

「揍他！」「除掉他！」「把这奴才钉十字架！」「把这野蛮人喂野兽！」「把他喂野兽吧，尊贵的总督！」一群执役朝他扑来，许多看客也从座位上一跃而起，正要跳下乐池。

菲拉蒙如同一头被围困的狮子般返身相向；他清亮而高亢的声音穿过众人的怒吼直冲而上。

「好啊！像罗马人谋害提勒马库斯（Saint Telemachus）圣徒那样谋害我吧！你们这些奴隶，与你们那醉生梦死、可咒可诅的暴君一样醉生梦死、可咒可诅！比你们雇来充当屠夫的那些畜生还不如！谋杀与淫欲本是天造地设的一对，我妹妹这羞耻的宝座，正该以无辜者的血来筑成！就让我的死来终结这场魔鬼的祭典，来填满你们罪孽的杯吧！」

「喂野兽！」「叫那大象把他踩成齑粉！」

那头巨兽，被执役们用叉戟撵着，朝少年冲去；厄洛斯从它颈上一跃而下，哭啼啼地朝斜坡上逃去。

===Original===
He caught Philammon in his trunk and raised him high in air. For an instant the great bellowing ocean of heads spun round and round. He tried to breathe one prayer, and shut his eyes﻿—Pelagia’s voice rang sweet and clear, even in the shrillness of intense agony﻿—

“Spare him! He is my brother! Forgive him, men of Macedonia! For Pelagia’s sake﻿—Your Pelagia! One boon﻿—only this one!”

And she stretched her arms imploringly toward the spectators, and then clasping the huge knees of the elephant, called madly to it in terms of passionate entreaty and endearment.

The men wavered. The brute did not. Quietly he lowered his trunk, and set down Philammon on his feet. The monk was saved. Breathless and dizzy, he found himself hurried away by the attendants, dragged through dark passages, and hurled out into the street, with curses, warnings, and congratulations, which fell on an unheeding ear.

But Pelagia kept her face still hidden in her hands, and rising, walked slowly back, crushed by the weight of some tremendous awe, across the orchestra, and up the slope; and vanished among the palms and oleanders, regardless of the applause and entreaties, and jeers, and threats, and curses, of that great multitude of sinful slaves.

===Chinese===
它用长鼻卷住菲拉蒙，把他高高举到空中。一时之间，那鼎沸如海的万千人头旋转了又旋转。他勉力想祷告一句，便闭上了眼——佩拉吉娅的声音甜畅清亮，即便在极度的剧痛之中也如此尖锐地响起来——

「饶了他吧！他是我的哥哥！原谅他吧，马其顿人啊！看在佩拉吉娅的份上——你们的佩拉吉娅！这一件事——只求这一件！」

她朝众人哀求地伸出双臂，继而抱住大象那粗大的双膝，疯狂地向它呼唤，言辞里满是恳求与亲昵。

众人动摇了。那畜生却不动摇。它静静地垂下长鼻，把菲拉蒙放回脚边。这位修士得救了。他气喘吁吁、头昏眼花，便被执役们匆匆带走，拖过一道道黑暗的过道，被摔到了街上，伴随他的是咒骂、警告与道贺——可这一切他都听而不闻。

然而佩拉吉娅仍把脸埋在双手之间；她站起身来，被某种惊人的敬畏所压倒，缓缓地走了回去，穿过乐池，爬上斜坡；消失在那棕榈与夹竹桃之间，对那大群罪奴的喝彩、恳求、嘲骂、恐吓、咒诅，一概充耳不闻。

===Original===
For a moment all Orestes’s spells seemed broken by this unexpected catastrophe. A cloud, whether of disgust or of disappointment, hung upon every brow. More than one Christian rose hastily to depart, touched with real remorse and shame at the horrors of which they had been the willing witnesses. The common people behind, having glutted their curiosity with all that there was to see, began openly to murmur at the cruelty and heathenry of it. Hypatia, utterly unnerved, hid her face in both her hands. Orestes alone rose with the crisis. Now, or never, was the time for action; and stepping forward, with his most graceful obeisance, waved his hand for silence, and began his well-studied oration.

“Let me not, O men of Macedonia, suppose that you can be disturbed from that equanimity which befits politicians, by so light an accident as the caprice of a dancer. The spectacle which I have had the honour and delight of exhibiting to you﻿—(Roars and applause from the liberated prisoners and the young gentlemen)﻿—and on which it seemed to me you have deigned to look with not altogether unkindly eyes﻿—(Fresh applause, in which the Christian mob, relenting, began to join)﻿—is but a pleasant prelude to that more serious business for which I have drawn you here together. Other testimonials of my good intentions have not been wanting in the release of suffering innocence, and in the largess of food, the growth and natural property of Egypt, destined by your late tyrants to pamper the luxury of a distant court.﻿ ﻿… Why should I boast?﻿—yet even now this head is weary, these limbs fail me, worn out in ceaseless efforts for your welfare, and in the perpetual administration of the strictest justice. For a time has come in which the Macedonian race, whose boast is the gorgeous city of Alexander, must rise again to the political preeminence which they held of old, and becoming once more the masters of one-third of the universe, be treated by their rulers as freemen, citizens, heroes, who have a right to choose and to employ their rulers﻿—Rulers, did I say? Let us forget the word, and substitute in its place the more philosophic term of ministers. To be your minister﻿—the servant of you all﻿—To sacrifice myself, my leisure, health, life, if need be, to the one great object of securing the independence of Alexandria﻿—This is my work, my hope, my glory﻿—longed for through weary years: now for the first time possible by the fall of the late puppet Emperor of Rome. Men of Macedonia, remember that Honorius reigns no more! An African sits on the throne of the Caesars! Heraclian, by one decisive victory, has gained, by the favour of﻿—of Heaven, the imperial purple; and a new era opens for the world. Let the conqueror of Rome balance his account with that Byzantine court, so long the incubus of our Trans-Mediterranean wealth and civilisation; and let a free, independent, and united Africa rally round the palaces and docks of Alexandria, and find there its natural centre of polity and of prosperity.”

A roar of hired applause interrupted him and not a few, half for the sake of his compliments and fine words, half from a natural wish to be on the right side﻿—namely, the one which happened to be in the ascendant for the time being﻿—joined.﻿ ﻿… The city authorities were on the point of crying, “Imperator Orestes,” but thought better of it; and waited for someone else to cry first﻿—being respectable. Whereon the Prefect of the Guards, being a man of some presence of mind, and also not in anywise respectable, pricked up the Prefect of the docks with the point of his dagger, and bade him, with a fearful threat, take care how he played traitor. The worthy burgher roared incontinently﻿—whether with pain or patriotism; and the whole array of respectabilities﻿—having found a Curtius who would leap into the gulf, joined in unanimous chorus, and saluted Orestes as Emperor; while Hypatia, amid the shouts of her aristocratic scholars, rose and knelt before him, writhing inwardly with shame and despair, and entreated him to accept that tutelage of Greek commerce, supremacy, and philosophy which was forced on him by the unanimous voice of an adoring people.﻿ ﻿…

===Chinese===
一时之间，这场突如其来的灾祸似乎把俄瑞斯忒斯的一切法术都打破了。每一道额头上都笼罩着一团云——也不知是厌恶还是失望。不止一个基督徒匆匆起身要走，他们既甘心甘意地做了这些惨剧的看客，如今真有了悔恨与惭愧。后头的平民百姓既已看足了想看的一切，便也公开地嘟囔起来，抱怨这场面太残暴、太异教了。希帕蒂娅则心神俱碎，把脸埋在两只手里。唯有俄瑞斯忒斯临危而起。此时不搏，更待何时；他向前一步，以最优雅的仪态躬身一礼，挥手要众人安静，便开始他那早已背熟的演说。

「马其顿人啊，」他说，「莫要让我以为，凭一个舞女的任性这般区区小事，便能扰乱你们作为政治家所应有的那份镇定。我所荣幸、所快慰地向诸位展示的这场盛观——（被释囚犯与那些少年公子发出阵阵喝彩）——在我看来，诸位亦曾垂以不算苛刻之眼光——（又是一阵喝彩，连那一群心软下来的基督徒暴民也开始附和）——只不过是那桩更重大之事的一段愉快序曲，正是为了那事我才把诸位召集于此。我善意之明证，亦不在少数：受苦之无辜者之得释，粮食之广赍——这粮食本是埃及的产物、埃及的天然产业，却被你们已故的暴君们拿去奉养远方朝廷的奢靡。……我又何必自夸？——然而时至今日，这颗头颅已然疲倦，这些肢体也已不支，为诸位的福祉无休无止地操劳，为最严格之公义的永恒施行而耗尽。因为这样一个时刻已经到来：以这辉煌的亚历山大城为荣的马其顿民族，必须重新登上它古时所拥有的政治至尊之位，重新成为天下三分之一的主宰；被其统治者视为自由人、公民、英雄——有权利选举和任用他们的统治者。统治者？我竟说了这个词？让我们忘掉它，代之以更具哲学意味的词——仆役。做诸位的仆役——做你们全体的仆人——牺牲我自己、我的闲暇、我的健康、我的性命——若有必要——为的是确保亚历山大城的独立这一唯一大目标——这便是我的事业、我的盼望、我的荣耀——这盼望在疲惫的岁月中久久萦怀：如今因罗马那位傀儡皇帝之倒台，方才头一次成为可能。马其顿人啊，请记取：霍诺留（Honorius）不再为帝了！一位阿非利加人坐在凯撒（Caesar）的宝座之上！赫拉克利安（Heraclian）凭着一场决定性的胜利，已蒙——蒙天之恩宠——夺得皇紫；一个新的时代为世界开启。且让这位罗马的征服者，与那座拜占庭朝廷清算账目罢——那朝廷长久以来便是我们地中海彼岸之财富与文明的祸胎；且让一个自由、独立、统一的阿非利加，团结到亚历山大城的宫殿与船坞的周围，在那里寻得它天然的政治与繁荣的中心。」

一阵花钱雇来的喝彩声打断了他；也有不少人——半是为他那番恭维与漂亮话，半是出于一种自然而然、想站在正确一边的愿望——所谓正确一边，即眼下正好得势的那一边——也跟着附和起来。……城中那些显贵们正要高呼「大将军俄瑞斯忒斯」，又转念一想，便按住了；他们要等别人先喊——到底都是体面人。于是那位卫兵长，倒是个颇有急智、而且毫不顾体面之人，便用匕首尖去戳那位船坞总监，附耳以可怖之言恐吓他，叫他小心休要变节。那位可敬的市绅登时大叫一声——是痛还是爱国心切，便不得而知了；那全体体面人——既已找到一个肯纵身跳入深渊的库尔提乌斯（Curtius），便齐声合唱起来，一致向俄瑞斯忒斯拥戴致敬，奉之为皇；而希帕蒂娅，在她那些贵族弟子的欢呼声中，立起身来，跪在他面前——内心因羞耻与绝望而痉挛——恳请他接受希腊之商业、至尊与哲学的监护之位，而这一监护之位，乃是由一位爱戴他之百姓齐声所强加于他的。……

===Original===
“It is false!” shouted a voice from the highest tiers, appropriated to the women of the lower classes, which made all turn their heads in bewilderment.

“False! false! you are tricked! He is tricked! Heraclian was utterly routed at Ostia, and is fled to Carthage, with the emperor’s fleet in chase.”

“She lies! Drag the beast down!” cried Orestes, utterly thrown off his balance by the sudden check.

“She? He! I, a monk, brought the news! Cyril has known it﻿—every Jew in the Delta has known it, for a week past! So perish all the enemies of the Lord, caught in their own snare!”

And bursting desperately through the women who surrounded him, the monk vanished.

An awful silence fell on all who heard. For a minute every man looked in his neighbour’s face as if he longed to cut his throat, and get rid of one witness, at least, of his treason. And then arose a tumult, which Orestes in vain attempted to subdue. Whether the populace believed the monk’s words or not, they were panic-stricken at the mere possibility of their truth. Hoarse with denying, protesting, appealing, the would-be emperor had at last to summon his guards around him and Hypatia, and make his way out of the theatre as best he could; while the multitude melted away like snow before the rain, and poured out into the streets in eddying and roaring streams, to find every church placarded by Cyril with the particulars of Heraclian’s ruin.

===Chinese===
「那是假的！」一个声音从最高几排——专供下等妇人坐的地方——喊了出来，叫众人都不知所措地回过头去。

「假的！假的！你们上当了！他上当了！赫拉克利安在奥斯提亚（Ostia）一败涂地，已逃往迦太基（Carthage），皇帝的舰队正在后面追击。」

「她胡说！把这畜生拖下来！」俄瑞斯忒斯喊道，被这突如其来的当头一棒打得完全失去了镇定。

「她？他是他！我，一个修士，亲带来的消息！区利罗早已知晓——三角洲（the Delta）里每一个犹太人一周前就已知晓！愿耶和华的一切仇敌都如此灭亡，自投网罗！」

那修士拼命地从围着他的妇人们中间挤出去，便不见了。

一种可怖的寂静降临在所有听见之人心头。足足有一分钟，每个人都望着邻人的脸，仿佛巴不得割断那喉管，好除掉他叛逆勾当的至少一个见证人。继而一阵骚乱涌起，俄瑞斯忒斯徒然地想加以压制。那群氓信也罢、不信也罢，单是这话有可能为真，便足以使他们魂飞魄散。这位准皇帝竭力否认、抗议、申诉，喊得嗓音嘶哑，最后只好召集卫兵护住自己与希帕蒂娅，勉力挤出剧院；而那一群人则如雨前的残雪般消融，化作漩涡翻腾、咆哮的一股股人流涌到街上——只见每一座教堂的大门上，区利罗都已贴出赫拉克利安覆灭的详情。

## XXIII / XXIII

### Nemesis / 报应

===Original===
That evening was a hideous one in the palace of Orestes. His agonies of disappointment, rage, and terror were at once so shameful and so fearful, that none of his slaves dare approach him; and it was not till late that his confidential secretary, the Chaldean eunuch, driven by terror of the exasperated Catholics, ventured into the tiger's den, and represented to him the immediate necessity for action.

What could he do? He was committed—Cyril only knew how deeply. What might not the wily archbishop have discovered? What might not he pretend to have discovered? What accusations might he not send off on the spot to the Byzantine Court?

"Let the gates be guarded, and no one allowed to leave the city," suggested the Chaldee.

"Keep in monks? as well keep in rats! No; we must send off a counter-report, instantly."

===Chinese===
那天傍晚，俄瑞斯忒斯（Orestes）的总督府里是一片可怖的景象。他那失望、狂怒与惊恐交加的煎熬，既如此可耻，又如此骇人，以致他的奴仆没有一个敢走近他；直到夜深，他那心腹秘书——那个迦勒底人（the Chaldean eunuch）太监——被激怒的天主教徒吓得没了法子，才斗胆闯进这虎穴，向他陈述必须立即行事的紧要。

他能做什么呢？他已经陷进去了——只有区利罗（Cyril）知道陷得有多深。那位狡黠的宗主教可能已发现了多少秘密？他又可能假装发现了多少？他岂不能当场就向拜占庭朝廷递上一纸怎样的控告？

「把守城门，不许任何人离城，」迦勒底人献策道。

「关得住修士？那还不如去关老鼠！不；我们得立刻发一份反制的报告出去。」

===Original===
"What shall I say, your Excellency?" quoth the ready scribe, pulling out pen and inkhorn from his sash.

"What do I care? Any lie which comes to hand. What in the devil's name are you here for at all, but to invent a lie when I want one?"

"True, most noble," and the worthy sat meekly down to his paper … but did not proceed rapidly.

"I don't see anything that would suit the emergency, unless I stated, with your august leave, that Cyril, and not you, celebrated the gladiatorial exhibition; which might hardly appear credible?"

Orestes burst out laughing, in spite of himself. The sleek Chaldee smiled and purred in return. The victory was won; and Orestes, somewhat more master of himself, began to turn his vulpine cunning to the one absorbing question of the saving of his worthless neck.

"No, that would be too good. Write, that we had discovered a plot on Cyril's part to incorporate the whole of the African churches (mind and specify Carthage and Hippo) under his own jurisdiction, and to throw off allegiance to the Patriarch of Constantinople, in case of Heraclian's success."

The secretary purred delighted approval, and scribbled away now with right good heart.

"Heraclian's success, your Excellency."

===Chinese===
「阁下要我怎么说呢？」这干练的书吏一边问，一边从腰带里抽出笔和墨角。

「我管那个？随手拈来的谎话都成。你他妈待在这儿到底是干什么吃的，不就是为了我要谎话时给我编一个么？」

「阁下说得是，」这位好人便乖乖地在纸前坐下……可落笔并不算快。

「我看眼下这当口没什么顶用的，除非——得蒙阁下恩准——我说，办那角斗表演的乃是区利罗，而非阁下您；可这话只怕难以叫人信罢？」

俄瑞斯忒斯不由得放声大笑起来。那油头滑脑的迦勒底人便陪着微笑、打着哼儿作答。这一仗是打赢了；俄瑞斯忒斯多少恢复了几分自制，开始把那狐狸般的狡狯转到那一桩吞没一切的紧要问题上去——救他自己那条不值钱的脖子。

「不，那未免太妙了。写上：我们已发觉区利罗有一个阴谋，要在赫拉克利安（Heraclian）得手之时，把全阿非利加的教会（务必点明迦太基（Carthage）和希波（Hippo））都纳入自己的治下，并摆脱君士坦丁堡宗主教的统辖。」

那秘书高兴得直打哼儿地赞成，这下子提起精神来奋笔疾书了。

「赫拉克利安得手之时，阁下。」

===Original===
"We of course desired, by every means in our power, to gratify the people of Alexandria, and, as was our duty, to excite by every lawful method their loyalty toward the throne of the Caesars (never mind who sat on it) at so critical a moment."

"So critical a moment. …"

"But as faithful Catholics, and abhorring even in the extremest need, the sin of Uzzah, we dreaded to touch with the unsanctified hands of laymen the consecrated ark of the Church, even though for its preservation. …"

"Its preservation, your Excellency. …"

"We, therefore, as civil magistrates, felt bound to confine ourselves to those means which were already allowed by law and custom to our jurisdiction; and accordingly made use of those largesses, spectacles, and public execution of rebels, which have unhappily appeared to his holiness the patriarch (too ready, perhaps, to find a cause of complaint against faithful adherents of the Byzantine See) to partake of the nature of those gladiatorial exhibitions, which are equally abhorrent to the spirit of the Catholic Church, and to the charity of the sainted emperors by whose pious edicts they have been long since abolished."

===Chinese===
「我们自当竭尽所能，使亚历山大城的百姓心满意足；又按本分所当为，在此等危急之时，以一切合法之法，激发他们对凯撒宝座（管它上面坐的是谁）的忠忱。」

「此等危急之时。……」

「然我等既为忠信之天主教徒，即便在万分不得已之际，亦深恶乌撒（Uzzah）之罪，断不敢以平俗未圣别之手，擅触教会那已分别为圣之约柜，纵为保全其安亦所不欲。……」

「保全其安，阁下。……」

「故此，我等身为世俗之官长，唯有自限于律法与惯例所已归于我等权限之内的种种手段；相应地，便用上了那些赏赐、那些表演、以及处决叛逆示众之于民等措施——这些措施，不幸地，在宗主教圣座看来（他老人家或许太乐于在拜占庭宗座忠信之附庸身上找出攻讦之由了），似乎带上了几分角斗表演的性质；而角斗一事实为天主教会之精神、亦为那几位曾以虔敬诏令将其久远废除之受封圣的皇帝之仁心，所同样深恶痛绝。」

===Original===
"Your Excellency is indeed great … but—pardon your slave's remark—my simplicity is of opinion that it may be asked why you did not inform the Augusta Pulcheria of Cyril's conspiracy?"

"Say that we sent a messenger off three months ago, but that. … Make something happen to him, stupid, and save me the trouble."

"Shall I kill him by Arabs in the neighbourhood of Palmyra, your Excellency?"

"Let me see. … No. They may make inquiries there. Drown him at sea. Nobody can ask questions of the sharks."

"Foundered between Tyre and Crete, from which sad calamity only one man escaped on a raft, and being picked up, after three weeks' exposure to the fury of the elements, by a returning wheat-ship—By the by, most noble, what am I to say about those wheat-ships not having even sailed?"

===Chinese===
「阁下诚然英明……不过——恕奴才斗胆一言——奴才这点愚钝之见以为：人家或会问，阁下何以不曾将区利罗的阴谋奏知奥古斯塔普尔凯丽娅（the Augusta Pulcheria）？」

「就说我们三个月前已派出一名信使，可是那……替我给那信使安排点什么意外罢，蠢货，省得我费这个心。」

「要奴才让他死在帕尔米拉（Palmyra）附近、由阿拉伯人（Arabs）下手么，阁下？」

「我想想。……不成。人家会上那儿去查问。让他在海上淹死。鲨鱼可不会回答人家的问题。」

「船在推罗（Tyre）与克里特（Crete）之间沉没，那场可悲的灾难中仅一人靠一只木筏逃生，在风狂雨暴之中漂泊三周之后，为一艘返航的运麦船所救——顺便说一句，大人，那些运麦船根本尚未启航一事，我该怎么交代？」

===Original===
"Head of Augustus! I forgot them utterly. Say that—that the plague was making such ravages in the harbour quarter that we feared carrying the infection to the seat of the empire; and let them sail tomorrow."

The secretary's face lengthened.

"My fidelity is compelled to remark, even at the risk of your just indignation, that half of them have been unloaded again for your munificent largesses of the last two days."

Orestes swore a great oath.

"Oh, that the mob had but one throat, that I might give them an emetic! Well, we must buy more corn, that's all."

The secretary's face grew longer still.

"The Jews, most August—"

"What of them?" yelled the hapless Prefect. "Have they been forestalling?"

"My assiduity has discovered this afternoon that they have been buying up and exporting all the provisions which they could obtain."

"Scoundrels! Then they must have known of Heraclian's failure!"

===Chinese===
「奥古斯都（Augustus）的头颅啊！我把这事忘得一干二净了。就说——就说港埠一带瘟疫猖獗，我们唯恐把疫气带到帝国京畿去；让他们明日启航罢。」

那秘书的脸拉长了。

「奴才之忠诚，不得不冒犯阁下雷霆之怒，进一言：那些船里有一半已经重新卸了货，为的是阁下这两日来那慷慨豪奢的赏赐。」

俄瑞斯忒斯狠狠咒了一声。

「哼，这帮暴民要是只长着一条喉咙才好呢，我好给他们灌一服催吐药！罢了，我们只好再买些麦子，就这么办。」

那秘书的脸更长了。

「犹太人（The Jews），至圣的阁下——」

「他们怎么啦？」倒霉的总督吼道。「他们又囤积居奇了？」

「奴才的勤勉，今日午后已查得，他们一直在搜购一切能弄到手的粮食，并运出海外。」

「恶棍！那他们必是早知赫拉克利安兵败了！」

===Original===
"Your sagacity has, I fear, divined the truth. They have been betting largely against his success for the last week, both in Canopus and Pelusium."

"For the last week! Then Miriam betrayed me knowingly!" And Orestes broke forth again into a paroxysm of fury.

"Here—call the tribune of the guard! A hundred gold pieces to the man who brings me the witch alive!"

"She will never be taken alive."

"Dead, then—in any way! Go, you Chaldee hound! what are you hesitating about?"

"Most noble lord," said the secretary, prostrating himself upon the floor, and kissing his master's feet in an agony of fear. …

"Remember, that if you touch one Jew you touch all! Remember the bonds! remember the—the—your own most august reputation, in short."

===Chinese===
「阁下的圣明，只怕已洞察了实情。这一周来，他们在卡诺帕斯（Canopus）和佩卢西乌姆（Pelusium）两地，一直大笔押注他必败。」

「这一周来！那么米利暗（Miriam）是明知内情而出卖我了！」俄瑞斯忒斯便又是一阵狂怒的发作。

「来人——去叫护民官（tribune of the guard）！谁能把那女巫活捉来，赏他一百枚金币！」

「她绝不会被活捉。」

「那就要死的——不论用什么法子！去，你这迦勒底狗！你还犹豫什么？」

「至贵的主人，」那秘书一面说，一面五体投地趴在地上，在极度的恐惧中亲吻主人的脚……

「请记着，您动一个犹太人，便是动了所有的犹太人！记着那些债券！记着那——那——一句话，记着您自己至贵的名声。」

===Original===
"Get up, brute, and don't grovel there, but tell me what you mean, like a human being. If old Miriam is once dead, her bonds die with her, don't they?"

"Alas, my lord, you do not know the customs of that accursed folk. They have a damnable practice of treating every member of their nation as a brother, and helping each freely and faithfully without reward; whereby they are enabled to plunder all the rest of the world, and thrive themselves, from the least to the greatest. Don't fancy that your bonds are in Miriam's hands. They have been transferred months ago. Your real creditors may be in Carthage, or Rome, or Byzantium, and they will attack you from thence; while all that you would find if you seized the old witch's property, would be papers, useless to you, belonging to Jews all over the empire, who would rise as one man in defence of their money. I assure you, it is a net without a bound. If you touch one you touch all. … And besides, my diligence, expecting some such command, has already taken the liberty of making inquiries as to Miriam's place of abode; but it appears, I am sorry to say, utterly unknown to any of your Excellency's servants."

"You lie!" said Orestes. … "I would much sooner believe that you have been warning the hag to keep out of the way."

Orestes had spoken, for that once in his life, the exact truth.

===Chinese===
「起来，畜生，别在那儿趴着了，像个人样地告诉我你到底是什么意思。老米利暗一旦死了，她的债券也就随之作废了，不是么？」

「唉，我的主上，您不晓得那可诅咒之族的规矩。他们有一个可恶的习俗：把自己族中每一个人都当作兄弟看待，彼此白白地、忠实地相助，不图报偿；他们便是仗着这一点，去劫掠世上所有其余的人，而自己从最小的到最大的，一齐兴旺发达。您切莫以为您的债券还在米利暗手里。几月之前它们早已经转手了。您真正的债主也许在迦太基，也许在罗马（Rome），也许在拜占庭（Byzantium），他们将从那里向您发难；而您即便抄了那老巫婆的家产，所能找到的，也只是一堆对您毫无用处的文书，它们分属散在帝国各地的犹太人，那些人将如一人而起，来捍卫他们的钱财。奴才敢向您保证，这是一张无边无际的网。动一个，便是动了全部。……再者，奴才虑及阁下或会下此一令，已斗胆先行打听米利暗的住处；可惜——奴才不得不说——似乎您阁下的任何仆役都全然不知其所在。」

「你撒谎！」俄瑞斯忒斯道。……「我倒宁可相信，是你去向那老妖婆通风报信、叫她躲起来的。」

这是俄瑞斯忒斯生平仅有的一次，恰好说中了实情。

===Original===
The secretary, who had his own private dealings with Miriam, felt every particular atom of his skin shudder at those words; and had he had hair on his head, it would certainly have betrayed him by standing visibly on end. But as he was, luckily for him, close shaven, his turban remained in its proper place, as he meekly replied—"Alas! a faithful servant can feel no keener woe than the causeless suspicion of that sun before whose rays he daily prostrates his—"

"Confound your periphrases! Do you know where she is?"

"No!" cried the wretched secretary, driven to the lie direct at last; and confirmed the negation with such a string of oaths, that Orestes stopped his volubility with a kick, borrowed of him, under threat of torture, a thousand gold pieces as largess to the soldiery, and ended by concentrating the stationaries round his own palace, for the double purpose of protecting himself in case of a riot, and of increasing the chances of the said riot, by leaving the distant quarters of the city without police.

"If Cyril would but make a fool of himself, now that he is in the full-blown pride of victory—the rascal!—about that Ammonius, or about Hypatia, or anything else, and give me a real handle against him! After all, truth works better than lying now and then. Oh, that I could poison him! But one can't bribe those ecclesiastics; and as for the dagger, one could not hire a man to be torn in pieces by monks. No; I must just sit still, and see what Fortune's dice may turn up. Well, your pedants like Aristides or Epaminondas—thank Heaven, the race of them has died out long ago!—might call this no very creditable piece of provincial legislation; but after all, it is about as good as any now going, or likely to be going till the world's end; and one can't be expected to strike out a new path. I shall stick to the wisdom of my predecessors, and—oh, that Cyril may make a fool of himself tonight!"

===Chinese===
那秘书原本与米利暗有他私下的来往，听了这话，只觉自己浑身上下每一颗极小的微粒都在打战；他若头上还有头发，那头发必定根根倒竖，明明白白地出卖了他。幸而他的头剃得精光，那头巾便仍端端正正地待在原处，他唯唯诺诺地答道——「唉！一个忠仆所能感到的最深的痛楚，莫过于被那轮红日无端地见疑——他本是日日俯伏在那太阳的光辉之下，将他那——」

「去你那套绕弯子！你到底知不知道她在哪儿？」

「不知道！」那可怜的秘书终于被逼得赤裸裸地撒了谎；又用一连串的咒赌发誓来坐实这句否认，弄得俄瑞斯忒斯一脚踹过去止住他的滔滔不绝，又借着严刑恫吓，向他「借」了一千枚金币充作赏兵之费，末了把守备兵团（the stationaries）尽数调集到自己总督府四周，一举两得：一来可在暴乱起时护住自己，二来因城内远处街区没了警察，倒也增加了那暴乱发生的可能。

「区利罗要是能在这个大获全胜、得意忘形的当口——这无赖！——在阿摩尼乌斯（Ammonius）那事上，或在希帕蒂娅（Hypatia）那事上，或在别的什么事上，犯一回蠢、给我一个实实在在的把柄，就好了！毕竟，真话有时比谎话还顶用。唉，我要是能毒死他就好了！可那些教职人员是收买不动的；至于匕首么，没人肯为了一点钱去被修士们撕成碎片。罢了；我只好安坐不动，看看命运（Fortune）的骰子能掷出什么来。哼，你们那些书呆子——像阿里斯提得斯（Aristides）或者埃帕米农达斯（Epaminondas）那种人——谢天谢地，这一族早就绝了种了！——许会说这算不上什么光彩的行省立法；可说到底，这也跟眼下正行着的、或直等到世界末日都未必会有更好的立法差不多；总不能指望一个人另辟一条新路罢。我还是要抱定我前人的那套智慧，并且——唉，但愿区利罗今夜就犯一回蠢罢！」

===Original===
And Cyril did make a fool of himself that night, for the first and last time in his life; and suffers for it, as wise men are wont to do when they err, to this very day and hour: but how much Orestes gained by his foe's false move cannot be decided till the end of this story; perhaps not even then.

===Chinese===
而区利罗那一夜当真犯了一回蠢，这是他平生头一遭，也是末一遭；而且正像一个智者偶有失着时那样，为此受累，一直受累到此时此刻：然而俄瑞斯忒斯从仇敌这一着失算里究竟得了多少好处，却要等到本故事的末尾方能见出分晓；只怕到那时也未必见得。

## XXIV / XXIV

### Lost Lambs / 迷失的羔羊

===Original===
And Philammon?

For a long while he stood in the street outside the theatre, too much maddened to determine on any course of action; and, ere he had recovered his self-possession, the crowd began to pour from every outlet, and filling the street, swept him away in its stream.

Then, as he heard his sister’s name, in every tone of pity, contempt, and horror, mingle with their angry exclamations, he awoke from his dream, and, bursting through the mob, made straight for Pelagia’s house.

It was fast closed; and his repeated knocks at the gate brought only, after long waiting, a surly negro face to a little wicket.

===Chinese===
菲拉蒙呢？

好一会儿，他呆立在剧院外的街心上，心神狂乱得定不下任何主意；还没等他恢复镇定，人群已开始从各个出口涌出，灌满整条街道，把他裹挟在人潮之中卷走了。

随后，他听见姐姐的名字以怜悯、鄙夷、惊骇的种种声调，夹杂在人们愤愤的喧嚷里，他这才如梦初醒，猛地冲出人群，直奔佩拉吉娅的宅子而去。

大门紧闭；他一遍又一遍地敲门，等了许久，才有一个面色阴沉的黑人来到小窗前。

===Original===
He asked eagerly and instinctively for Pelagia; of course she had not yet returned. For Wulf he was not within. And then he took his station close to the gateway, while his heart beat loud with hope and dread.

At last the Goths appeared, forcing their way through the mob in a close column. There were no litters with them. Where, then, were Pelagia and her girls? Where, too, was the hated figure of the Amal? and Wulf, and Smid? The men came on, led by Goderic and Agilmund, with folded arms, knitted brows, downcast eyes: a stern disgust, not unmingled with shame, on every countenance, told Philammon afresh of his sister’s infamy.

Goderic passed him close, and Philammon summoned up courage to ask for Wulf.﻿… Pelagia he had not courage to name.

===Chinese===
他急切地、近乎本能地要找佩拉吉娅；她当然还没回来。至于沃尔夫，他不在里面。于是他紧挨着门道站定，心怀希望，又怀着恐惧，心怦怦直跳。

哥特人终于出现了，他们排成密集的纵队，从人群里硬挤出来。他们身边没有一顶轿子。那么，佩拉吉娅和她的舞女们哪里去了？那可憎的阿玛尔的身影又在哪里？还有沃尔夫，还有斯密德？那些汉子由戈德里克与阿吉蒙德领着头，走上前来，双臂交叉、眉头紧锁、目光低垂：每一张脸上那种冷峻的厌恶——又掺杂着羞惭——再一次向菲拉蒙宣告了他姐姐的丑行。

戈德里克从他身边擦肩而过，菲拉蒙鼓起勇气问起沃尔夫。……至于佩拉吉娅，他没敢出口。

===Original===
“Out, Greek hound! we have seen enough of your accursed race today! What? are you trying to follow us in?” And the young man’s sword flashed from its sheath so swiftly, that Philammon had but just time enough to spring back into the street, and wait there, in an agony of disappointment and anxiety, as the gates slid together again, and the house was as silent as before.

For a miserable hour he waited, while the mob thickened instead of flowing away, and the scattered groups of chatterers began to form themselves into masses, and parade the streets with shouts of “Down with the heathen!” “Down with the idolaters!” “Vengeance on all blaspheming harlots!”

At last the steady tramp of legionaries, and in the midst of the glittering lines of armed men﻿—oh, joy!﻿—a string of litters!

===Chinese===
「滚开，希腊狗！你那该死的族类，我们今日可见够了！怎么？还想跟着我们进去？」那年青人的剑出鞘得如此之快，寒光一闪，菲拉蒙只来得及跳回街上；两扇门又滑拢了，那宅子重又静寂如初，他只好留在外面，在失望与焦虑的煎熬中等候。

他凄惨地等了一个钟头，人群非但不散，反而越聚越密；原先三三两两嚼舌根的人开始结成一团一团，在街上游行呐喊：「打倒异教徒！」「打倒拜偶像的！」「惩办一切亵渎上帝的淫妇！」

终于，传来了军团兵丁整齐的脚步声，在那闪闪发光的武装队列之中——噢，谢天谢地！——一长串轿子！

===Original===
He sprang forward, and called Pelagia’s name again and again. Once he fancied he heard an answer: but the soldiers thrust him back.

“She is safe here, young fool, and has seen and been seen quite enough today already. Back!”

“Let me speak to her!”

“That is her business. Ours is now to see her home safe.”

“Let me go in with you, I beseech!”

“If you want to go in, knock for yourself when we are gone. If you have any business in the house, they will open to you, I suppose. Out, you interfering puppy!”

===Chinese===
他扑上前去，一声又一声地唤着佩拉吉娅的名字。有一回他恍惚听见一声回答：可兵丁们把他推了回去。

「她在这里很安全，年轻傻瓜，她今日抛头露面得也够够的了。退后！」

「让我跟她说句话！」

「那是她的事。我们的事是把她平安送回家。」

「求你们让我一同进去吧！」

「你要进去，等我们走了自己去敲门。你要是在这宅子里有事，我想他们自会给你开门的。滚开，你这多管闲事的小狗！」

===Original===
And a blow of the spear-butt in his chest sent him rolling back into the middle of the street, while the soldiers, having delivered up their charge, returned with the same stolid indifference. In vain Philammon, returning, knocked at the gate. Curses and threats from the negro were all the answer which he received; and at last, wearied into desperation, he wandered away, up one street and down another, struggling in vain to form some plan of action for himself, until the sun was set.

Wearily he went homewards at last. Once the thought of Miriam crossed his mind. It was a disgusting alternative to ask help of her, the very author of his sister’s shame: but yet she at least could obtain for him a sight of Pelagia; she had promised as much. But then﻿—the condition which she had appended to her help! To see his sister, and yet to leave her as she was!﻿—Horrible contradiction! But could he not employ Miriam for his own ends?﻿—outwit her?﻿—deceive her?﻿—for it came to that. The temptation was intense: but it lasted only a moment. Could he defile so pure a cause by falsehood? And hurrying past the Jewess’s door, hardly daring to look at it, lest the temptation should return, he darted upstairs to his own little chamber, hastily flung open the door, and stopped short in astonishment.

A woman, covered from head to foot in a large dark veil, stood in the centre of the chamber.

===Chinese===
一记矛杆捣在他胸口，把他打得踉跄着退回街心；兵丁们交割了所护送的人，便带着同样木然的冷漠转身离去。菲拉蒙折回来再敲门，也是徒然。那黑人回他的，只有咒骂与威吓；末了，他被折磨到走投无路，便信步游荡开去，沿一条街、又一条街地走，拼命想给自己定出个主意，却总是徒劳，直到日头西沉。

他终于疲惫地往回走。有一刻，米利暗的念头掠过他的心头。去求这个亲手造成他姐姐耻辱的人帮忙，这种办法实在令人作呕：可她至少能为他弄到一见佩拉吉娅的机会；她曾答应过这一点。然而——她给她的帮助所附的那条件！能见到姐姐，却仍要把她留在如今这副模样！——可怕的矛盾！可他能不能利用米利暗来达到自己的目的？——智取她？——欺骗她？——事情说到底就是如此。这诱惑极是强烈：可也只持续了一瞬。他能让这么纯洁的事业被谎言玷污么？于是他匆匆从那犹太女人的门前掠过，几乎不敢朝它看一眼，生怕诱惑卷土重来，飞奔上楼，回到自己的小房间，猛地推开门——却愕然止步。

一个女人，从头到脚裹在一幅宽大的深色面纱里，正站在房间正中。

===Original===
“Who are you? This is no place for you!” cried he, after a minute’s pause. She replied only by a shudder and a sob.﻿… He caught sight, beneath the folds of the veil, of a too well-known saffron shawl, and springing upon her like the lion on the lamb, clasped to his bosom his sister.

The veil fell from her beautiful forehead. She gazed into his eyes one moment with a look of terrified inquiry, and saw nothing there but love.﻿… And clinging heart to heart, brother and sister mingled holy kisses, and strained nearer and nearer still, as if to satisfy their last lingering doubts of each other’s kin.

Many a minute passed in silent joy.﻿… Philammon dare not speak; he dare not ask her what brought her thither﻿—dare not wake her to recollect the frightful present by questions of the past, of his long forgotten parents, their home, her history.﻿… And, after all, was it not enough for him that he held her at last?﻿—her, there by her own will﻿—the lost lamb returned to him?﻿—and their tears mingled as their cheeks were pressed together.

===Chinese===
「你是谁？这里不是你该来的地方！」停了一刻，他喊道。她只是浑身一颤，抽泣了一声作答。……他在面纱的褶裥下瞥见了一方太熟悉不过的橘黄色披肩，便如狮子扑向羔羊一般扑上前去，把姐姐紧紧搂进怀里。

面纱从她美丽的额头上滑落。她凝视他的眼睛，目光里是惊恐的探问，只看了一瞬，便看见其中唯有爱。……兄妹二人紧紧相拥，心贴着心，交换着圣洁的亲吻，越抱越紧，仿佛要以此打消彼此心头最后一丝犹疑，确证彼此的血亲。

许多分钟在无言的喜悦中过去。……菲拉蒙不敢开口；他不敢问她是什么使她来到这里——不敢用关于往昔的发问——关于他那早已被遗忘的父母、他们的家、她的身世——把她唤醒、令她回想起方才那可怖的一幕而毁掉眼前这一刻。……再说，他终于抱住了她，这岂不就够了么？——是她在她自己意愿的驱使下来到这里——那只迷失的羔羊回到了他身边？——他们的脸颊紧紧相贴，泪水也交融在一起。

===Original===
At last she spoke.

“I ought to have known you﻿—I believe I did know you from the first day! When they mentioned your likeness to me, my heart leapt up within me; and a voice whispered﻿… but I would not hear it! I was ashamed﻿—ashamed to acknowledge my brother, for whom I had sought and longed for years﻿… ashamed to think that I had a brother.﻿… Ah, God! and ought I not to be ashamed?”

And she broke from him again, and threw herself on the floor.

“Trample upon me; curse me!﻿—anything but part me from him!”

Philammon had not the heart to answer her; but he made an involuntary gesture of sorrowful dissent.

“No! Call me what I am!﻿—what he called me just now!﻿—but do not take me away! Strike me, as he struck me!﻿—anything but parting!”

“Struck you? The curse of God be on him!”

===Chinese===
终于，她开口了。

「我本该认出你的——我想，从第一天起我就认出你了！当他们说起你与我长得相像，我的心在胸中猛地一跳；有一个声音在耳畔低语……可我不肯听！我羞愧——羞愧认自己的哥哥，我寻他、盼他，寻了这么多年……一想到自己还有个哥哥，便觉得羞愧。……啊，上帝！我怎能不羞愧呢？」

她又从他怀里挣脱出来，扑倒在地上。

「践踏我吧；咒骂我吧！——什么都行，只要别把我从他身边夺走！」

菲拉蒙没有心思答话；他不由自主地做了一个悲痛否定的手势。

「不！我是什么就叫我什么吧！——就照他方才叫我的那样叫我！——只是别把我带走！打我吧，就像他打我那样！——什么都行，只要不分离！」

「他打了你？愿上帝的咒诅临到他头上！」

===Original===
“Ah, do not curse him!﻿—not him! It was not a blow, indeed!﻿—only a push﻿—a touch﻿—and it was my fault﻿—all mine. I angered him﻿—I upbraided him;﻿—I was mad.﻿… Oh, why did he deceive me? Why did he let me dance?﻿—command me to dance?”

“Command you?”

“He said that we must not break our words. He would not hear me, when I told him that we could deny having promised. I said that promises made over the wine need never be kept. Who ever heard of keeping them? And Orestes was drunk, too. But he said that I might teach a Goth to be whatever I liked, except a liar.﻿… Was not that a strange speech?﻿… And Wulf bade him be strong, and blest him for it.”

“He was right,” sobbed Philammon.

===Chinese===
「啊，别咒他！——别咒他！那不算打，真的！——不过是推一下——碰一下——那都是我的错——全是我不好。我惹恼了他——我数落他；——我发了疯。……唉，他为什么要骗我？为什么让我去跳那舞？——还命令我去跳？」

「命令你？」

「他说我们不能说话不算话。我对他说，我们大可抵赖说根本没应承过，他却不听。我说席间酒醉时许下的诺言本来就不必当真。谁听说过这种应承还得算数的？何况俄瑞斯忒斯当时也醉了。可他说，他倒可以教一个哥特人做我乐意的任何一种人，唯独不能做说谎的人。……这话不是很怪么？……而沃尔夫也怂恿他硬起心肠，还为他祝福。」

「他做得对，」菲拉蒙抽泣着说。

===Original===
“Then I thought he would love me for obeying him, though I loathed it!﻿—Oh, God, how I loathed it!﻿… But how could I fancy that he did not like my doing it? Who ever heard of anyone doing of their own will what they did not like?”

Philammon sobbed again, as the poor civilised savage artlessly opened to him all her moral darkness. What could he say?﻿… he knew what to say. The disease was so utterly patent, that any of Cyril’s schoolchildren could have supplied the remedy. But how to speak it?﻿—how to tell her, before all things, as he longed to do, that there was no hope of her marrying the Amal, and, therefore, no peace for her till she left him.

“Then you did hate the﻿—the﻿—” said he, at last, catching at some gleam of light.

===Chinese===
「我那时想，他既叫我顺从他，便会因此爱我，虽然我心里厌烦透了！——噢，上帝，我是多么厌烦啊！……可我怎么会以为他不喜欢我那样做呢？谁听说过有人甘心情愿去做自己不喜欢的事呢？」

菲拉蒙又抽泣起来，这个可怜的、半开化的文明人，天真地向他把内心的道德黑暗和盘托出。他能说什么呢？……他其实知道该说什么。这病征已是如此昭然，区利罗主日学里任何一个孩童都能开出救药。可这话怎么说出口？——怎样首先告诉她——他多么想这么做——她要嫁给阿玛尔已毫无指望，因此，她非离开他便无安宁可言。

「那么，你确实是厌恶那——那——」终于，他抓住一线光亮，说道。

===Original===
“Hate it? Do I not belong, body and soul, to him?﻿—him only?﻿… And yet.﻿… Oh, I must tell you all! When I and the girls began to practise, all the old feelings came back﻿—the love of being admired, and applauded, and cheered; and dancing is so delicious!﻿—so delicious to feel that you are doing anything beautiful perfectly, and better than everyone else!﻿… And he saw that I liked it, and despised me for it.﻿… And, deceitful!﻿—he little guessed how much of the pains which I took were taken to please him, to do my best before him, to win admiration, only that I might take it home and throw it all at his beloved feet, and make the world say once more, ‘She has all Alexandria to worship her, and yet she cares for that one Goth more than for﻿—’ But he deceived me, true man that he is! He wished to enjoy my smiles to the last moment, and then to cast me off, when I had once given him an excuse.﻿… Too cowardly to upbraid me, he let me ruin myself, to save him the trouble of ruining me. Oh, men, men! all alike! They love us for their own sakes, and we love them for love’s sake. We live by love, we die for love, and yet we never find it, but only selfishness dressed up in love’s mask.﻿… And then we take up with that, poor, fond, self-blinded creatures that we are!﻿—and in spite of the poisoned hearts around us, persuade ourselves that our latest asp’s egg, at least, will hatch into a dove, and that though all men are faithless, our own tyrant can never change, for he is more than man!”

“But he has deceived you! You have found out your mistake. Leave him, then, as he deserves!”

Pelagia looked up, with something of a tender smile. “Poor darling! Little do you know of love!”

===Chinese===
「厌恶？我岂不是身心都属他——只属他一个人么？……然而。……噢，我得把什么都告诉你！当我和那些姑娘开始排练时，往日的一切心情都回来了——那种被人艳羡、被人喝彩、被人欢呼的滋味；而跳舞又是那么美妙！——那种感到自己把一件美好的事做得尽善尽美、做得比谁都好的滋味，多么美妙！……他看出了我喜欢，便因此瞧不起我。……而我呢，他这糊涂人！他哪里猜得到，我下的那些功夫里有多少是为讨他欢心，为在他跟前尽我所能，为赢得艳羡，好让我把这一切带回家、尽数抛在他那双亲爱的脚下，让世人再说一遍：『全亚历山大城的人都来拜倒在她脚下，她却只把那一个哥特人看得比——更重』——可他却骗了我，这个一本正经的人！他要享受我的笑靥到最后一刻，再等我一旦给了他借口便把我一脚踢开。……他没有胆量当面斥责我，便由我自毁，省得他亲自动手来毁我。唉，男人，男人！全都一个样！他们为着自私而爱我们，我们却为爱本身而爱他们。我们靠爱而活，为爱而死，可到头来却总寻不着爱，寻着的不过是戴着爱之面具的私心。……于是我们这些可怜的、痴心的、自欺欺人的生灵便认了命！——纵然四围尽是中了毒的心，我们还是劝自己说：我们最新孵化的那一枚蝮蛇之卵，总该能孵出一只鸽子来；纵然天下的男人都薄情，我们自己那个暴君却永远不会变，因为他不是凡人！」

「可他骗了你！你已看清了自己的错。那就离开他，让他罪有应得！」

佩拉吉娅抬起头来，脸上浮起一丝温柔的笑意：「可怜的宝贝！你对爱情真是全然不懂！」

===Original===
Philammon, utterly bewildered by this newest and strangest phase of human passion, could only gasp out﻿—

“But do you not love me, too, my sister?”

“Do I not love you? But not as I love him! Oh, hush, hush!﻿—you cannot understand yet!” And Pelagia hid her face in her hands, while convulsive shudderings ran through every limb.…

“I must do it! I must! I will dare everything, stoop to everything for love’s sake! Go to her!﻿—to the wise woman!﻿—to Hypatia! She loves you! I know that she loves you! She will hear you, though she will not me!”

“Hypatia? Do you know that she was sitting there unmoved at﻿—in the theatre?”

===Chinese===
菲拉蒙被人世间这最新奇、最费解的激情弄得完全摸不着头脑，只能喘着气说——

「可你难道不也爱我么，我的姐姐？」

「我难道不爱你？可不像我爱他那样地爱！噢，别说，别说！——你还无法明白！」佩拉吉娅双手掩面，一阵阵痉挛性的颤抖传遍她每一寸肢体……

「我一定要做！我一定要！为了爱，我什么险都敢冒，什么都肯低头！去找她！——去找那位有智慧的女人！——去找希帕蒂娅！她爱你！我知道她爱你！她肯听你的，虽然她不肯听我的！」

「希帕蒂娅？你可知道，她方才若无其事地坐在那里——在剧院里？」

===Original===
“She was forced! Orestes compelled her! Miriam told me so. And I saw it in her face. As I passed beneath her, I looked up; and she was as pale as ivory, trembling in every limb. There was a dark hollow round her eyes﻿—she had been weeping, I saw. And I sneered in my mad self-conceit, and said, ‘She looks as if she was going to be crucified, not married!’﻿… But now, now!﻿—Oh, go to her! Tell her that I will give her all I have﻿—jewels, money, dresses, house! Tell her that I﻿—I﻿—entreat her pardon, that I will crawl to her feet myself and ask it, if she requires!﻿—Only let her teach me﻿—teach me to be wise and good, and honoured, and respected, as she is! Ask her to tell a poor brokenhearted woman her secret. She can make old Wulf, and him, and Orestes even, and the magistrates, respect her.﻿… Ask her to teach me how to be like her, and to make him respect me again, and I will give her all﻿—all!”

===Chinese===
「她是被逼的！是俄瑞斯忒斯强迫她的！米利暗是这么对我说的。我也从她脸上看得出来。我从她身下经过时，抬头一望；她脸白得像象牙，四肢都在颤抖。她眼眶周围一圈发青的凹痕——她方才哭过，我看得出。而我那时却在我那疯狂的虚荣里冷笑，说：『她那副模样，倒像是要被钉十字架，不是要出嫁呢！』……可如今，如今！——噢，去找她吧！告诉她，我愿把我所有的都给她——珠宝、银钱、衣裳、宅子！告诉她，我——我恳求她的宽恕，只要她要，我愿亲自爬到她脚前去求！——只求她教我——教我做她那样有智慧、善良、受人敬重、受人尊崇的人！求她把她的秘诀告诉一个心碎的可怜女人。她能叫老沃尔夫、叫他、甚至叫俄瑞斯忒斯和那些官长都敬重她。……求她教我怎样才能像她那样，怎样才能让他重新敬重我，我便把我所有的一切——一切都给她！」

===Original===
Philammon hesitated. Something within warned him, as the Daemon used to warn Socrates, that his errand would be bootless. He thought of the theatre, and of that firm, compressed lip; and forgot the hollow eye of misery which accompanied it, in his wrath against his lately-worshipped idol.
