"So said Aristophanes of Socrates. But hear me once more, beloved Hypatia. You refuse to give up the beautiful, the sublime, the heavenly? What if Raphael Aben-Ezra, at least, had never found them till now? Recollect what I said just now—what if our old Beautiful, and Sublime, and Heavenly, had been the sheerest materialism, notions spun by our own brains out of the impressions of pleasant things, and high things, and low things, and awful things, which we had seen with our bodily eyes? What if I had discovered that the spiritual is not the intellectual, but the moral; and that the spiritual world is not, as we used to make it, a world of our own intellectual abstractions, or of our own physical emotions, religious or other, but a world of righteous or unrighteous persons?"

===Chinese===
然而他是个犹太人，且是男人：希帕蒂娅是希腊人，又是女人——就此而言，她那一派里的男人们也都是如此。在她看来，那普通人伦与日常职责所闪烁的敬畏而神圣的意味，远不及在归信的犹太人眼中所闪烁的那样——这犹太人有生以来头一回觉醒，去认识自己圣经的真义，成了真正的以色列人。何况拉斐尔的那些辩证，虽能叫她无言以对，却不能叫她心服。她的信条，一如她同道哲学家们的信条，是属于想象与宗教情感的，而非属于理智与道德意识的。她多年来在其中纵情遨游的那个辉煌的云雾世界——种种宇宙生成论、流溢说、亲和力、象征论、等级体系、深渊、永恒，以及其余种种——尽管她并不能在其中安息，甚至也并不真信它们——尽管它们在她最迫切的需要之时已化作轻烟消散——然而——它们毕竟太美了，不能就此永远弃之不顾；于是，她一面与她理智中日渐增长的信念相抗衡，一面终于答道——

「那么你是要我像你似乎已经做的那样，放弃那崇高的、美的、属天之物，换上一串枯燥而贫瘠的辩证之链——而在其中，天晓得——毕竟，拉斐尔，我争不过你——我是个女人——一个软弱的女人！」

她便用双手掩住了脸。

「天晓得什么？」拉斐尔柔声问。

「你也许把那较坏的道理，说成了较好的道理。」

「阿里斯托芬（Aristophanes）当年也是这样论苏格拉底（Socrates）的。可是再听我说一次，敬爱的希帕蒂娅。你不肯放弃美、放弃崇高、放弃属天之物？倘若拉斐尔·阿本-以斯拉——至少——直到如今才头一回寻见它们呢？回想我方才所说的话——倘若我们旧日那『美』、那『崇高』、那『属天之物』，原来彻头彻尾是最粗俗的唯物主义，不过是我们自己的头脑从种种悦目之物、崇高之物、卑下之物、可畏之物——即我们以肉眼所见的那些事物——的印象中所抽绎出来的观念呢？倘若我发现，属灵之事并非理智之事，而是道德之事；而属灵世界也并不像我们从前所设想的那样，是一个由我们自己的理智抽象所构成的世界，或者由我们自己的肉体情感（无论宗教与否）所构成的世界，而是一个由公义或不义之人所构成的世界呢？」

===Original===
"What if I had discovered that one law of the spiritual world, in which all others were contained, was righteousness; and that disharmony with that law, which we called unspirituality, was not being vulgar, or clumsy, or ill-taught, or unimaginative, or dull, but simply being unrighteous? What if I had discovered that righteousness, and it alone, was the beautiful righteousness, the sublime, the heavenly, the Godlike—ay, God Himself? And what if it had dawned on me, as by a great sunrise, what that righteousness was like? What if I had seen a human being, a woman, too, a young weak girl, showing forth the glory and the beauty of God? Showing me that the beautiful was to mingle unshrinking, for duty's sake, with all that is most foul and loathsome; that the sublime was to stoop to the most menial offices, the most outwardly-degrading self-denials; that to be heavenly was to know that the commonest relations, the most vulgar duties, of earth, were God's commands, and only to be performed aright by the help of the same spirit by which He rules the Universe; that righteousness was to love, to help, to suffer for—if need be, to die for—those who, in themselves, seem fitted to arouse no feelings except indignation and disgust?"

"What if, for the first time, I trust not for the last time, in my life, I saw this vision; and at the sight of it my eyes were opened, and I knew it for the likeness and the glory of God? What if I, a Platonist, like John of Galilee, and Paul of Tarsus, yet, like them, a Hebrew of the Hebrews, had confessed to myself—If the creature can love thus, how much more its archetype? If weak woman can endure thus, how much more a Son of God? If for the good of others, man has strength to sacrifice himself in part, God will have strength to sacrifice Himself utterly. If He has not done it, He will do it: or He will be less beautiful, less sublime, less heavenly, less righteous than my poor conception of Him, ay, than this weak playful girl! Why should I not believe those who tell me that He has done it already? What if their evidence be, after all, only probability? I do not want mathematical demonstration to prove to me that when a child was in danger his father saved him—neither do I here. My reason, my heart, every faculty of me, except this stupid sensuous experience, which I find deceiving me every moment, which cannot even prove to me my own existence, accepts that story of Calvary as the most natural, most probable, most necessary of earthly events, assuming only that God is a righteous Person, and not some dream of an all-pervading necessary spirit-nonsense which, in its very terms, confesses its own materialism."

===Chinese===
「倘若我发现，属灵世界有一条总摄其余一切法则的法则，那就是公义；而我们之所谓『不属灵』，其实是对这条法则的不谐——这种不谐并非粗俗、并非笨拙、并非未受教化、并非缺乏想象力、并非迟钝，而是简简单单地就是不公义呢？倘若我发现，公义——而且唯独公义——才是那美的公义、那崇高、那属天、那如神——哎呀，就是上帝自己呢？倘若有一天，如同一轮大日初升，我骤然明白了那种公义是什么模样呢？倘若我看见一个人——而且是一个女子，一个年轻柔弱的少女——把上帝的荣耀与美彰显出来呢？她向我表明：所谓『美』，乃是为了本分的缘故，毫不畏缩地与众最污秽、最可憎之物相交往；所谓『崇高』，乃是俯身去做最卑微的差事、去做那些外表上最贬损人的舍己；所谓『属天』，乃是晓得地上最寻常的关系、最粗鄙的职责，都是上帝的命令，唯有靠着祂治理宇宙的那同一种灵才能行得合宜；所谓『公义』，乃是去爱、去扶助、为那些——就其自身而言——似乎只会激起愤慨与厌恶的人受苦，必要时为他们而死呢？」

「倘若——我有生以来头一回，但愿不是最后一回——我看见了这异象；并且在看见它的一刹那，我的眼睛开了，我便认出它是上帝的形象与荣耀呢？倘若我——一个柏拉图派，像加利利的约翰（John of Galilee）、像大数的保罗（Paul of Tarsus）一样，却又像他们一样，是希伯来人中的希伯来人——向我亲口承认：受造之物既能如此爱，它的原型岂不更能如此爱？柔弱的女子既能如此忍耐，上帝的儿子岂不更能如此忍耐？倘若人为了他人的益处，尚且有力量部分地牺牲自己，上帝必有力气彻底地牺牲自己。祂若未曾这样做，祂也必将这样做：否则祂便不如我那贫乏的构想那样美、那样崇高、那样属天、那样公义——哎呀，不如这个柔弱的戏耍的少女！那么，我为何不能信那告诉我『祂早已如此做了』之人呢？他们的证据，到头来即便只是或然之理，又当如何？我并不需要数学上的铁证来向我证明：当一个孩子有危险时，他的父亲救了他——在此处我亦不需要。我的理智、我的心、我的每一分官能——除了那愚蠢的感官经验，那每一刻都在欺骗我、甚至连我自己的存在都不能向我证明的经验——都接纳各各他（Calvary）那故事为地上最自然、最可能、最必然的事，只要一个前提：上帝是一位公义的位格，而不是某种无处不在、必然的『属灵胡言』之梦——这种梦，就其自身的说法而言，恰恰承认了它自己的唯物主义。」

===Original===
Hypatia answered with a forced smile.

"Raphael Aben-Ezra has deserted the method of the severe dialectician for that of the eloquent lover."

"Not altogether," said he, smiling in return. "For suppose that I had said to myself, 'We Platonists agree that the sight of God is the highest good.'"

Hypatia once more shuddered at last night's recollections.

"And if He be righteous, and righteousness be—as I know it to be—identical with love, then He will desire that highest good for men far more than they can desire it for themselves.… Then He will desire to show Himself and His own righteousness to them.… Will you make answer, dearest Hypatia, or shall I?… or does your silence give consent? At least let me go on to say this, that if God do desire to show His righteousness to men, His only perfect method, according to Plato, will be that of calumny, persecution, the scourge, and the cross, that so He, like Glaucon's righteous man, may remain forever free from any suspicion of selfish interest, or weakness of endurance.… Am I deserting the dialectic method now, Hypatia?… You are still silent? You will not hear me, I see.… At some future day, the philosopher may condescend to lend a kinder ear to the words of her greatest debtor.… Or, rather, she may condescend to hear, in her own heart, the voice of that Archetypal Man, who has been loving her, guiding her, heaping her with every perfection of body and of mind, inspiring her with all pure and noble longings, and only asks of her to listen to her own reason, her own philosophy, when they proclaim Him as the giver of them, and to impart them freely and humbly, as He has imparted them to her, to the poor, and the brutish, and the sinful, whom He loves as well as He loves her.… Farewell!"

===Chinese===
希帕蒂娅勉强地笑了笑。

「拉斐尔·阿本-以斯拉已舍弃了严谨辩证家的方法，改用雄辩情人那一套了。」

「也并非全然如此，」他微笑着回答。「因为假设我对自己说过这样的话：『我们柏拉图派一致认为，得见上帝乃是至善。』」

希帕蒂娅又因昨夜的回忆而战栗起来。

「而祂若是公义的，而公义——如我所知——与爱本是一回事，那么祂必会以这至善赐予人，远超过人自己所能渴慕的。……那么祂必会渴望向人彰显祂自己，并祂自己的公义。……你肯作答么，最亲爱的希帕蒂娅，还是由我代答？……或者，你的沉默便是应允？至少让我往下再说一句：倘若上帝果真渴望向人彰显祂的公义，那么按柏拉图所言，祂唯一完全的办法，便是那诽谤、逼迫、鞭笞与十字架之法，好叫祂像格劳孔那位公义之人一样，永远免受任何营私之嫌或忍耐薄弱之疑。……我此刻可是在背弃辩证之法么，希帕蒂娅？……你仍沉默？我看你是不肯听我了。……或有一日，这位哲学家肯屈尊，以更和善的耳朵听一听她最大欠债人的话罢。……或者，不如说，她肯屈尊，在她自己的心里，听见那位原型之人的声音——祂一直爱着她，引导她，把她身心一切完全堆在她身上，以一切纯洁高尚的渴慕感化她，只求她听凭自己的理智、自己的哲学——当它们宣称祂是这一切的赐予者之时——并且像祂赐给她那样，白白地、谦卑地把这一切传给那些贫穷的、粗野的、有罪的人，那些祂爱与爱她相同的人。……再会！」

===Original===
"Stay!" said she, springing up: "whither are you going?"

"To do a little good before I die, having done much evil. To farm, plant, and build, and rescue a little corner of Ormuzd's earth, as the Persians would say, out of the dominion of Ahriman. To fight Ausurian robbers, feed Thracian mercenaries, save a few widows from starvation, and a few orphans from slavery.… Perhaps to leave behind me a son of David's line, who will be a better Jew, because a better Christian, than his father.… We shall have trouble in the flesh, Augustine tells us.… But, as I answered him, I really have had so little thereof yet, that my fair share may probably be rather a useful education than otherwise. Farewell!"

"Stay!" said she. "Come again!—again! And her.… Bring her.… I must see her! She must be noble, indeed, to be worthy of you."

"She is many a hundred miles away."

"Ah! Perhaps she might have taught something to me—me, the philosopher! You need not have feared me.… I have no heart to make converts now.… Oh, Raphael Aben-Ezra, why break the bruised reed? My plans are scattered to the winds, my pupils worthless, my fair name tarnished, my conscience heavy with the thought of my own cruelty.… If you do not know all, you will know it but too soon.… My last hope, Synesius, implores for himself the hope which I need from him.… And, over and above it all.… You!… *Et tu, Brute!* Why not fold my mantle round me, like Julius of old, and die!"

Raphael stood looking sadly at her, as her whole face sank into utter prostration.

===Chinese===
「且慢！」她一跃而起：「你要去哪里？」

「趁我未死之前做一点善事，我已作了不少恶。去耕种、栽植、建造，用波斯人的话说，从阿赫里曼（Ahriman）的辖制之下，夺回奥尔穆兹德（Ormuzd）大地的一隅。去与奥苏里亚人（Ausurian）的强盗作战，养活色雷斯人（Thracian）的雇佣兵，从饥饿中救出几个寡妇，从奴役中救出几个孤儿。……也许还要留下一个大卫后裔的儿子，他将比他父亲做更好的犹太人——因为他做更好的基督徒。……奥古斯丁告诉我们，我们在肉体上是要受苦的。……可是，如我回答他的那样，我至今所受的苦实在少之又少，所以我那一份很可能是相当有用的教育，而非别的。再会！」

「且慢！」她说。「再来罢！——再来罢！还有她。……把她带来。……我必须见她！她一定是高贵的，才配得上你。」

「她在数百里之外。」

「啊！她也许本可以教我一些东西——教我，这位哲学家！你本不必怕我。……我如今已无心去劝人改宗了。……噢，拉斐尔·阿本-以斯拉，何必压伤那已折伤的芦苇呢？我的计划已随风飘散，我的学生不值一提，我的美名已经蒙尘，我的良心因想到自己的残忍而沉重不堪。……你若不全知，也很快便会知道得太清楚。……我最后的希望——叙内西乌斯——竟为他自己乞求那本是我要从他得着的希望。……更何况，这一切之外。……还有你！……*你也有份，布鲁图（Brute）！*我何不像从前的尤利乌斯（Julius）那样，把斗篷往脸上一蒙，死去算了！」

拉斐尔悲伤地站在那里看着她，只见她整张脸沉入了彻底的颓丧。

---

===Original===


"Yes—come.… The Galilaean.… If He conquers strong men, can the weak maid resist Him? Come soon.… This afternoon.… My heart is breaking fast."

"At the eighth hour this afternoon?"

"Yes.… At noon I lecture…take my farewell, rather, forever of the schools.… Gods! What have I to say?… And tell me about Him of Nazareth. Farewell!"

"Farewell, beloved lady! At the ninth hour, you shall hear of Him of Nazareth."

Why did his own words sound to him strangely pregnant, all but ominous? He almost fancied that not he, but some third person had spoken them. He kissed Hypatia's hand, it was as cold as ice; and his heart, too, in spite of all his bliss, felt cold and heavy, as he left the room.

As he went down the steps into the street, a young man sprang from behind one of the pillars, and seized his arm.

"Aha! my young Coryphaeus of pious plunderers! What do you want with me?"

Philammon, for it was he, looked at him an instant, and recognised him.

"Save her! for the love of God, save her!"

"Whom?"

"Hypatia!"

===Chinese===


「是——来罢。……那位加利利人。……祂若能征服强壮之人，这软弱的女子能抵抗祂么？快些来罢。……今日下午。……我的心正飞快地碎裂。」

「今日下午第八时？」

「是。……正午我要开讲……不如说，要向学坛作永远的告别。……众神啊！我还有什么可说的？……还有，告诉我一些关于那位拿撒勒人之事。再会！」

「再会，敬爱的女士！第九时，你必将听见关于那位拿撒勒人之事。」

为何他自己的话在他听来竟意味深长得离奇，几乎带着不祥？他几乎恍惚觉得，说出这话的不是他自己，而是某个第三者。他吻了吻希帕蒂娅的手，那只手冷若冰；而他的心——尽管他满怀幸福——却也觉得又冷又沉，他就这样走出了房间。

他走下台阶，进入街中时，一个少年从一根柱子后面窜出来，一把抓住他的手臂。

「啊哈！我这位率领一群敬虔劫匪的少年领班！你找我做什么？」

菲拉蒙——正是他——怔怔地看了他一眼，认出了他。

「救她！看在上帝的份上，救救她！」

「救谁？」

「希帕蒂娅！」

===Original===
"How long has her salvation been important to you, my good friend?"

"For God's sake," said Philammon, "go back and warn her! She will hear you—you are rich—you used to be her friend—I know you—I have heard of you.… Oh, if you ever cared for her—if you ever felt for her a thousandth part of what I feel—go in and warn her not to stir from home!"

"I must hear more of this," said Raphael, who saw that the boy was in earnest. "Come in with me, and speak to her father."

"No! not in that house! Never in that house again! Do not ask me why: but go yourself. She will not hear me. Did you—did you prevent her from listening?"

"What do you mean?"

"I have been here—ages! I sent a note in by her maid, and she returned no answer."

Raphael recollected then, for the first time, a note which he had seen brought to her during the conversation.

"I saw her receive a note. She tossed it away. Tell me your story. If there is reason in it, I will bear your message myself. Of what is she to be warned?"

"Of a plot—I know that there is a plot—against her among the monks and Parabolani. As I lay in bed this morning in Arsenius's room—they thought I was asleep—"

"Arsenius? Has that venerable fanatic, then, gone the way of all monastic flesh, and turned persecutor?"

===Chinese===
「她的得救，从何时起对你这般要紧了，我的好朋友？」

「看在上帝份上，」菲拉蒙说，「回去警告她！她会听你的——你有钱——你曾是她的朋友——我认得你——我听说过你。……噢，你若曾经在乎过她——你若曾对她有过我所感的千分之一——便进去警告她，叫她千万别踏出家门半步！」

「此事我得多听听，」拉斐尔说，他看出这少年是当真的。「跟我进去，对她父亲说罢。」

「不！不能进那宅子！永远不再进那宅子了！别问我为什么：可你自己去罢。她不会听我的。可是你——可是你从中作梗，不让她听么？」

「你这话是什么意思？」

「我在这里——已经好久了！我托她侍女送了张字条进去，她却半个字也没回。」

拉斐尔这才想起，方才谈话间曾见人送来一张字条。

「我看见她收到一张字条。她把它扔开了。把你的原委告诉我。倘若其中确有道理，我亲自替你传话。她要被警告的是什么？」

「是一个阴谋——我知道有一个阴谋——是修士和抚慰弟兄会（Parabolani）里那些人针对她的。今早我躺在床上，在阿尔塞尼乌斯（Arsenius）房里——他们以为我睡着了——」

「阿尔塞尼乌斯？难道那位可敬的狂热者也走了凡修士难免的路，转而作起逼迫人来了么？」

===Original===
"God forbid! I heard him beseeching Peter the Reader to refrain from something, I cannot tell what; but I caught her name.… I heard Peter say, 'She that hindereth will hinder till she be taken out of the way.' And when he went out into the passage I heard him say to another, 'That thou doest, do quickly!…'"

"These are slender grounds, my friend."

"Ah, you do not know of what those men are capable!"

"Do I not? Where did you and I meet last?"

Philammon blushed and burst forth again. "That was enough for me. I know the hatred which they bear her, the crimes which they attribute to her. Her house would have been attacked last night had it not been for Cyril.… And I knew Peter's tone. He spoke too gently and softly not to mean something devilish. I watched all the morning for an opportunity of escape, and here I am!—Will you take my message, or see her—"

"What?"

"God only knows, and the devil whom they worship instead of God."

Raphael hurried back into the house—"Could he see Hypatia?" She had shut herself up in her private room, strictly commanding that no visitor should be admitted.… "Where was Theon, then?" He had gone out by the canal gate half an hour before, with a bundle of mathematical papers under his arm, no one knew whither.… "Imbecile old idiot!" and he hastily wrote on his tablet—"Do not despise the young monk's warning. I believe him to speak the truth. As you love yourself and your father, Hypatia, stir not out today."

===Chinese===
「上帝不容！我听见他恳求读经员彼得（Peter the Reader）罢手某件事，我不知是什么；但我听得见她的名字。……我听见彼得说：『那阻挡的，必一直阻挡，直到她被除去。』等他出去走到过道里，我又听见他对另一个人说：『你所要做的，快做罢！……』」

「这些凭据太过单薄了，我的朋友。」

「啊，你不知道那些人能干出什么事来！」

「我岂不知？你我上次是在哪里相见的？」

菲拉蒙脸一红，又冲口而出：「那已够我明白的了。我知道他们对她怀的仇恨，知道他们加在她头上的种种罪名。昨夜若不是区利罗（Cyril），她的宅子早被攻破了。……而且我认得彼得说话的腔调。他说得太轻柔、太和缓了，不可能不怀着某种阴险的用意。我整整一上午都在伺机脱身，到底来了这儿！——你肯替我传话，还是去见她——」

「否则怎样？」

「只有上帝知道，还有他们所敬拜、用以代替上帝的那个魔鬼知道。」

拉斐尔匆匆奔回宅里——「他能见希帕蒂娅么？」她已把自己关在私室里，严命任何客人不得放进。……「那么提昂在哪里？」半小时前他已从运河门出去了，腋下夹着一卷数学论文，无人知其去向。……「老糊涂的蠢货！」他便在记事板上匆匆写下——「切勿轻视那少年修士的警告。我相信他说的属实。希帕蒂娅，你既爱你自己，又爱你的父亲，今日切莫踏出家门半步。」

===Original===
He bribed a maid to take the message upstairs; and passed his time in the hall in warning the servants. But they would not believe him. It was true the shops were shut in some quarters, and the Museum gardens empty; people were a little frightened after yesterday. But Cyril, they had heard for certain, had threatened excommunication only last night to any Christian who broke the peace; and there had not been a monk to be seen in the streets the whole morning. And as for any harm happening to their mistress—impossible! "The very wild beasts would not tear her," said the huge negro porter, "if she was thrown into the amphitheatre."

—Whereat a maid boxed his ears for talking of such a thing; and then, by way of mending it, declared that she knew for certain that her mistress could turn aside the lightning, and call legions of spirits to fight for her with a nod.… What was to be done with such idolaters? And yet who could help liking them the better for it?

At last the answer came down, in the old graceful, studied, self-conscious handwriting.

"It is a strange way of persuading me to your new faith, to bid me beware, on the very first day of your preaching, of the wickedness of those who believe it. I thank you: but your affection for me makes you timorous. I dread nothing. They will not dare. Did they dare now, they would have dared long ago. As for that youth—to obey or to believe his word, even to seem aware of his existence, were shame to me henceforth. Because he is insolent enough to warn me therefore I will go. Fear not for me. You would not wish me, for the first time in my life, to fear for myself. I must follow my destiny. I must speak the words which I have to speak. Above all, I must let no Christian say, that the philosopher dared less than the fanatic. If my Gods are Gods, then will they protect me: and if not, let your God prove His rule as seems to Him good."

===Chinese===
他贿赂一名侍女把这话送上去；自己则在前厅里警告仆人们。可他们都不肯信。诚然，有几处店铺关了门，博物院（Museum）的花园里空无一人；昨日之事之后，人心有些惶惶。可是他们确切听说，区利罗昨夜才威胁要开除任何破坏和平的基督徒的教籍；而且整整一上午，街上连一个修士的影子也看不见。至于他们女主人会遭什么祸——不可能！「便是把她扔进竞技场，」那身材魁伟的黑人看门人说，「就是野兽也不会撕碎她。」

——闻此，一名侍女一巴掌扇在他耳朵上，怪他说出这种话来；随即又补了一句，补救似地宣称：她确确实实地知道，她家女主人能叫闪电拐弯，能一颔首便召来万千精灵为她助战。……对这等把她当偶像来拜的仆人，还能怎样呢？可谁又忍心因此少喜欢他们几分呢？

终于，回话下来了，是那熟悉的、秀雅而讲究、矜持而自觉的旧日笔迹。

「你劝我皈依你的新信仰，方法倒也古怪：在你传道头一日，便叫我提防信这信仰之人的恶行。我谢你了：可你对我的关切叫你胆小了。我无所畏惧。他们不敢。他们今日若敢，早已敢了。至于那个少年——从此以后，听从他、相信他的话，甚至装出知道他存在的样子，于我都是耻辱。正因为他竟敢放肆地来警告我，所以我偏要出门。不必为我担心。你总不愿我生平头一遭为自己担惊受怕罢。我必须追随我的命运。我必须说出我必说的话。最重要的是，我绝不能让任何基督徒说：哲学家竟不如那狂徒勇敢。倘若我的众神是神，它们自会护佑我：倘若不然，便让你的上帝按祂看为好的方式来证明祂的治权罢。」

===Original===
Raphael tore the letter to fragments.… The guards, at least, were not gone mad like the rest of the world. It wanted half an hour of the time of her lecture. In the interval he might summon force enough to crush all Alexandria. And turning suddenly, he darted out of the room and out of the house.

"*Quem Deus vult perdere—!*" cried he to Philammon, with a gesture of grief. "Stay here and stop her!—make a last appeal! Drag the horses' heads down, if you can! I will be back in ten minutes." And he ran off for the nearest gate of the Museum gardens.

On the other side of the gardens lay the courtyard of the palace. There were gates in plenty communicating between them. If he could but see Orestes, even alarm the guard in time!…

And he hurried through the walks and alcoves, now deserted by the fearful citizens, to the nearest gate. It was fast, and barricaded firmly on the outside.

===Chinese===
拉斐尔把那信撕成碎片。……至少卫队还不至于像世上其余的人一样发了疯。离她开讲的时辰还有半个钟头。在这段时间里，他或能调集足够的力量，足以把整个亚历山大城碾碎。他猛地一转身，冲出房间，冲出宅子。

「*上帝要毁灭谁——！*」他对菲拉蒙悲伤地叫道，作了一个痛苦的手势。「你留在这里拦住她！——作最后一次恳求！你能把马头按下来便按下来！我十分钟后就回来。」说罢，他便朝博物院花园最近的一道门奔去。

花园的那一边便是宫殿的庭院。两处之间有许多门相通。他若能见到俄瑞斯忒斯（Orestes），即便及时惊动卫队也好！……

他匆匆穿过那些如今被惊惶的市民所遗弃的步道与凉亭，奔向最近的一道门。那门紧闭着，从外面牢牢地加了横闩。

===Original===
Terrified, he ran on to the next; it was barred also. He saw the reason in a moment, and maddened as he saw it. The guards, careless about the Museum, or reasonably fearing no danger from the Alexandrian populace to the glory and wonder of their city, or perhaps wishing wisely enough to concentrate their forces in the narrowest space, had contented themselves with cutting off all communication with the gardens, and so converting the lofty partition-wall into the outer enceinte of their marble citadel. At all events, the doors leading from the Museum itself might be open. He knew them every one, every hall, passage, statue, picture, almost every book in that vast treasure-house of ancient civilisation. He found an entrance; hurried through well-known corridors to a postern through which he and Orestes had lounged a hundred times, their lips full of bad words, their hearts of worse thoughts, gathered in those records of the fair wickedness of old.… It was fast. He beat upon it but no one answered. He rushed on and tried another. No one answered there. Another—still silence and despair!… He rushed upstairs, hoping that from the windows above he might be able to call to the guard. The prudent soldiers had locked and barricaded the entrances to the upper floors of the whole right wing, lest the palace court should be commanded from thence. Whither now? Back—and whither then? Back, round endless galleries, vaulted halls, staircases, doorways, some fast, some open, up and down, trying this way and that, losing himself at whiles in that enormous silent labyrinth. And his breath failed him, his throat was parched, his face burned as with the simoom wind, his legs were trembling under him. His presence of mind, usually so perfect, failed him utterly. He was baffled, netted; there was a spell upon him. Was it a dream? Was it all one of those hideous nightmares of endless pillars beyond pillars, stairs above stairs, rooms within rooms, changing, shifting, lengthening out forever and forever before the dreamer, narrowing, closing in on him, choking him?

Was it a dream? Was he doomed to wander forever and forever in some palace of the dead, to expiate the sin which he had learnt and done therein? His brain, for the first time in his life, began to reel. He could recollect nothing but that something dreadful was to happen—and that he had to prevent it, and could not.… Where was he now? In a little by-chamber.… He had talked with her there a hundred times, looking out over the Pharos and the blue Mediterranean.… What was that roar below? A sea of weltering yelling heads, thousands on thousands, down to the very beach; and from their innumerable throats one mighty war-cry—"God, and the mother of God!" Cyril's hounds were loose.… He reeled from the window, and darted frantically away again… whither, he knew not, and never knew until his dying day.

And Philammon?… Sufficient for the chapter, as for the day, is the evil thereof.

===Chinese===
他惊恐之下，又奔向下一道门；也闩着。他一刹那便明白了其中缘故，一看之下几乎发狂。卫队对博物院并不在意，或者合理地料想亚历山大城的百姓不会对他们城中的荣耀与奇观下手，又或者也许明智地要把兵力集中在最狭窄的地段上，便只顾把花园的一切通道切断，于是把那道高高的隔墙变成了他们那座大理石堡垒的外围城墙。无论如何，博物院本身通向外面的门也许是开着的。他认识它们每一处——每一座厅堂、每一条过道、每一尊雕像、每一幅画，乃至那座古代文明的巨大宝库里几乎每一本书。他寻得一个入口，匆匆穿过熟悉的走廊，奔到一道后门——从前他和俄瑞斯忒斯曾在此处懒洋洋地进进出出上百回，嘴里说着污言秽语，心里怀着更恶的念头，正是在那些古老而艳丽的罪恶记载之中所培养出来的。……门紧闭着。他捶打着，却无人应答。他冲出去试另一道。那里也无人应答。再一道——依旧是一片沉默与绝望！……他冲上楼梯，指望从楼上的窗口也许能向卫兵呼喊。那些谨慎的士兵早已把整座右翼楼上各层的入口都上了锁、加了横闩，以免宫殿庭院从那里被瞰制。此刻往何处去？回头——回头又往哪里？回头，绕过无穷无尽的画廊、穹顶大厅、楼梯、门洞，有的紧闭、有的敞开，上上下下，这条路那条路地试，时而在这座庞大的、死寂的迷宫里迷失了方向。他的气力已尽，喉咙干焦，脸上灼热如炙着西蒙风，两腿在他身下颤抖。他那向来无懈可击的镇定，此刻全然失灵。他一筹莫展，落入了罗网；仿佛有一道咒语降在他身上。这是一场梦么？这莫非就是那种可怖的噩梦——一根柱子接一根柱子、一道楼梯压一道楼梯、一间屋子套一间屋子，无穷无尽地在做梦的人面前变幻、移位、无限延伸，又不断收窄、朝他合拢、叫他窒息？

这是梦么？难道他注定要在这死者之宫中永远、永远地漂泊下去，以赎他在其中所学到、所行过的罪？他一生之中头一回，脑子开始发晕。他什么也记不起来，只记得有一桩可怕的事将要发生——而他必须阻止它，却不能够。……此刻他在哪里？在一间小小的偏室里。……他曾在此处和她谈过上百次话，窗外便是法罗斯（Pharos）和碧蓝的地中海（Mediterranean）。……底下那一阵吼声是什么？一片翻腾呐喊的人头之海，成千上万，一直漫到海边；从他们无数喉咙里发出一声宏大的战吼——「上帝，和上帝之母！」区利罗的猎犬已经被放出来了。……他从窗口一个踉跄，又疯狂地冲了出去……冲向何处，他自己也不知道，至死也不曾知道。

至于菲拉蒙？……本章之恶，一如一日之恶，已自够受的了。

## XXVIII / XXVIII

### Woman's Love / 女人的爱

===Original===
Pelagia had passed that night alone in sleepless sorrow, which was not diminished by her finding herself the next morning palpably a prisoner in her own house. Her girls told her that they had orders—they would not say from whom—to prevent her leaving her own apartments. And though some of them made the announcement with sighs and tears of condolence, yet more than one, she could see, was well inclined to make her feel that her power was over, and that there were others besides herself who might aspire to the honour of reigning favourite.

What matter to her? Whispers, sneers, and saucy answers fell on her ear unheeded. She had one idol, and she had lost it; one power, and it had failed her. In the heaven above, and in the earth beneath, was neither peace, nor help, nor hope; nothing but black, blank, stupid terror and despair. The little weak infant soul, which had just awakened in her, had been crushed and stunned in its very birth-hour; and instinctively she crept away to the roof of the tower where her apartments were, to sit and weep alone.

There she sat, hour after hour, beneath the shade of the large windsail, which served in all Alexandrian houses the double purpose of a shelter from the sun and a ventilator for the rooms below; and her eye roved carelessly over that endless sea of roofs and towers, and masts, and glittering canals, and gliding boats; but she saw none of them—nothing but one beloved face, lost, lost forever.

===Chinese===
佩拉吉娅（Pelagia）独自熬过了那个不眠的忧愁之夜；及至次日清晨，她分明发觉自己竟成了自家宅中的囚徒，愁苦更未稍减。她的侍女们告诉她，她们奉了命令——却不肯说是奉谁之命——不许她离开自己的寝居。其中几个宣布此事时尚且叹息垂泪，以示同情；可她看得出来，不止一人倒颇乐意叫她明白：她的权势已经到头了，除了她之外，旁人也大可觊觎那得宠掌权的殊荣。

这于她又有何干？切切私语、冷嘲热讽、放肆的顶撞，落在她耳中她全不理会。她曾有一个偶像，如今已经失去了；曾有一种力量，如今已经弃她而去。天上地下，再无安宁，再无援助，再无希望；唯有漆黑、空洞、愚钝的恐怖与绝望。那刚刚在她体内苏醒的、幼弱如婴儿的灵魂，在诞生的那一刻便已被碾碎、被震昏；她本能地悄悄攀到自己所居寝阁的那座塔楼顶上，独坐着哭泣。

她便那样一小时一小时地坐在那里，在一面大风帆的阴影底下——这风帆在亚历山大城各家宅中都是必备之物，既可遮阳，又可为楼下各室通风换气；她的目光漫不经心地掠过那一望无尽的屋顶与塔楼之海，掠过桅杆、闪光的运河和悠悠滑行的小舟；可她什么也看不见——眼前只有一个心爱的面容，失却了，永远地失却了。

===Original===
At last a low whistle roused her from her dream. She looked up. Across the narrow lane, from one of the embrasures of the opposite house-parapet bright eyes were peering at her. She moved angrily to escape them.

The whistle was repeated, and a head rose cautiously above the parapet. … It was Miriam's. Casting a careful look around, Pelagia went forward. What could the old woman want with her?

Miriam made interrogative signs, which Pelagia understood as asking her whether she was alone; and the moment that an answer in the negative was returned, Miriam rose, tossed over to her feet a letter weighted with a pebble, and then vanished again.

"I have watched here all day! They refused me admittance below. Beware of Wulf, of everyone. Do not stir from your chamber. There is a plot to carry you off tonight, and give you up to your brother the monk; you are betrayed; be brave!"

===Chinese===
终于，一声低低的口哨把她从梦中惊醒。她抬起头。隔着那条窄巷，从对面宅子女儿墙的一个雉堞后面，有明亮的眼睛正向她窥视。她恼怒地挪动身子，想躲开那目光。

口哨声又响了一次，一颗脑袋小心翼翼地从墙头探了出来。……是米利暗（Miriam）。佩拉吉娅四下里仔细望了望，便走上前去。这老妖婆找她做什么？

米利暗做出询问的手势，佩拉吉娅明白那是问她是否独自一人；她才一示意说自己并非独处，米利暗便探出身来，朝她脚边抛过一封系着小石子的信，随即又隐没了。

「我在这里守了一整天！楼下那些人不许我进去。当心沃尔夫·奥维达之子（Wulf），当心每一个人。千万别踏出你的寝居半步。今夜有人设下计谋，要把你劫走，交给你的修士哥哥；你已被人出卖了；要勇敢！」

===Original===
Pelagia read it with blanching cheek and staring eyes; and took, at least, the last part of Miriam's advice. For walking down the stair, she passed proudly through her own rooms, and commanding back the girls who would have stayed her, with a voice and gesture at which they quailed, went straight down, the letter in her hand, to the apartment where the Amal usually spent his midday hours.

As she approached the door, she heard loud voices within. … His!—yes; but Wulf's also. Her heart failed her, and she stopped a moment to listen. … She heard Hypatia's name; and mad with curiosity, crouched down at the lock, and hearkened to every word.

===Chinese===
佩拉吉娅脸色煞白、睁大了双眼读完了信；至少，她听从了米利暗临末那一句忠告。她步下楼梯，骄傲地穿过自己的内室，用一声口吻、一个手势喝退了要留住她的侍女——那口吻与手势叫她们不寒而栗——便手执那封信，径直下到阿玛尔（the Amal）惯常消磨午间时辰的那间屋子去。

将近门口时，她听见屋里有人高声说话。……是他的声音！——是的；可也有沃尔夫的。她的心一沉，便驻足倾听了片刻。……她听见了希帕蒂娅（Hypatia）的名字；于是好奇得发了狂，蹲身在锁孔旁，一字不漏地细听。

===Original===
"She will not accept me, Wulf."

"If she will not, she shall go farther and fare worse. Besides, I tell you, she is hard run. It is her last chance, and she will jump at it. The Christians are mad with her; if a storm blows up, her life is not worth—that!"

"It is a pity that we have not brought her hither already."

"It is; but we could not. We must not break with Orestes till the palace is in our hands."

"And will it ever be in our hands, friend?"

"Certain. We were round at every picquet last night, and the very notion of an Amal's heading them made them so eager, that we had to bribe them to be quiet rather than to rise."

===Chinese===
「她不肯接受我，沃尔夫。」

「她不肯，日后的下场只有更糟。再者我告诉你，她已被逼得走投无路。这是她最后的机会，她必定会一口应承。那些基督徒对她恨之入骨；一旦风浪起来，她的性命便不值——这一弹！」

「真可惜我们尚未把她接来这里。」

「是可惜；可我们办不到。在宫殿落入我们手中之前，不能与俄瑞斯忒斯（Orestes）翻脸。」

「可它当真会落入我们手中么，朋友？」

「必然。昨夜我们巡遍了每一处卫哨，单是有一位阿玛尔出头率领他们这个念头，便使他们踊跃之至——我们倒不得不出钱贿买他们安静下来，免得他们抢先哗变。」

===Original===
"Odin! I wish I were among them now!"

"Wait till the city rises. If the day pass over without a riot, I know nothing. The treasure is all on board, is it not?"

"Yes, and the galleys ready. I have been working like a horse at them all the morning, as you would let me do nothing else. And Goderic will not be back from the palace, you say, till nightfall!"

"If we are attacked first, we are to throw up a fire signal to him, and he is to come off hither with what Goths he can muster. If the palace is attacked first, he is to give us the signal, and we are to pack up and row round thither. And in the meanwhile he is to make that hound of a Greek prefect as drunk as he can."

"The Greek will see him under the table. He has drugs, I know, as all these Roman rascals have, to sober him when he likes; and then he sets to work and drinks again. Send off old Smid, and let him beat the armourer if he can."

"A very good thought!" said Wulf, and came out instantly for the purpose of putting it in practice.

===Chinese===
「奥丁（Odin）啊！我恨不得此刻就在他们中间！」

「且等全城起事。今日若无一場暴乱过去，我便什么都不懂了。财宝都已装上船了，是不是？」

「是的，桨船也都齐备了。我整整一上午像马一样在那上面卖力，因为你也不许我干别的。而你说戈德里克·厄门里克之子（Goderic）要到天黑才能从宫里回来！」

「倘若我们先遭攻击，便向他举起火号，他便尽其所能召集哥特人（Goths）赶来此地。倘若宫殿先遭攻击，他便向我们发号，我们便收拾行装，绕水路划过去。与此同时，他要尽力把那个希腊狗总督灌得烂醉如泥。」

「那希腊人倒能眼睁睁看着他醉倒在桌底下。他有解酒之药，我知道，这些罗马的无赖个个都有；他高兴时服下解酒，便又重新喝将起来。把老斯密德·特罗尔之子（Smid）打发去，让他去把那兵器匠揍一顿，要是他办得到的话。」

「好主意！」沃尔夫说着，当即出来要去照办。

===Original===
Pelagia had just time to retreat into an adjoining doorway: but she had heard enough; and as Wulf passed, she sprang to him and caught him by the arm.

"Oh, come in hither! Speak to me one moment; for mercy's sake speak to me!" and she drew him, half against his will, into the chamber, and throwing herself at his feet, broke out into a childlike wail.

Wulf stood silent, utterly discomfited by this unexpected submission, where he had expected petulant and artful resistance. He almost felt guilty and ashamed, as he looked down into that beautiful imploring face, convulsed with simple sorrow, as of a child for a broken toy. … At last she spoke.

"Oh, what have I done—what have I done? Why must you take him from me? What have I done but love him, honour him, worship him? I know you love him; and I love you for it.—I do indeed! But you—what is your love to mine? Oh, I would die for him—be torn in pieces for him—now, this moment! …"

Wulf was silent.

===Chinese===
佩拉吉娅堪堪来得及退进旁边一扇门里：可她已经听得够了；沃尔夫经过时，她一跃而起，一把抓住他的胳膊。

「噢，到这里头来！跟我说一句话罢；看在老天爷份上，跟我说句话罢！」她半拽半拉、违着他心意地把他拖进屋里，扑倒在他脚边，失声痛哭起来，像一个孩子。

沃尔夫默默站着，被这出乎意料的顺从弄得手足无措——他原以为会碰上撒泼取巧的反抗。他俯视着那张美丽的、苦苦哀求的脸，那脸因单纯的悲恸而抽搐，如同一个孩子为摔坏了的玩具而哭嚎。……他几乎觉得自己心虚、觉得羞惭。终于她开了口。

「噢，我做了什么——我做了什么呀？你们为什么非要把他从我身边夺走？我除了爱他、敬他、拜他，还做过什么？我知道你爱他；我也因此爱你。——我当真爱你的！可是你——你的爱怎能与我的相比？噢，我情愿为他去死——为他被撕成碎片——就在此刻，这一刹那！……」

沃尔夫沉默不语。

===Original===
Wulf was forced to be stern, or he would have melted at once.

"And what was your love worth to him? What has it done for him? It has made him a sot, an idler, a laughingstock to these Greek dogs, when he might have been their conqueror, their king. Foolish woman, who cannot see that your love has been his bane, his ruin! He, who ought by now to have been sitting upon the throne of the Ptolemies, the lord of all south of the Mediterranean—as he shall be still!"

===Chinese===
沃尔夫不得不硬起心肠，否则他当场便要心软了。

「那么，你的爱于他又有何益？它为他带来过什么？它不过叫他成了酒鬼、懒汉、成了那些希腊狗辈的笑柄，而他本可以做他们的征服者、他们的君王。你这痴愚的女子，竟看不出你的爱便是他的祸根、是他的毁灭！他此刻本该坐在托勒密诸王（the Ptolemies）的宝座上，做地中海（the Mediterranean）以南万物的主宰——他也仍将如此！」

===Original===
Pelagia looked tip at him wide-eyed, as if her mind was taking in slowly some vast new thought, under the weight of which it reeled already. Then she rose slowly.

"And he might be Emperor of Africa."

"And he shall be; but not—"

"Not with me!" she almost shrieked. "No! not with wretched, ignorant, polluted me! I see—oh God, I see it all! And this is why you want him to marry her—her—"

She could not utter the dreaded name.

Wulf could not trust himself to speak; but he bowed his head in acquiescence.

===Chinese===
佩拉吉娅睁大双眼仰望他，仿佛她的心正缓缓领受某个浩大的新念头，那念头之沉重已叫她心智摇摇欲坠。随后她缓缓站起身来。

「他本可以做非洲的皇帝。」

「他必将做到；只是不是——」

「不是与我！」她近乎尖叫。「不错！不能与我这可鄙、无知、污秽的人！我明白了——上帝啊，我全明白了！这便是你要他去娶她——娶她——」

她说不出那个叫她心惊的名字。

沃尔夫不敢信口开河；只得点了点头，表示应承。

---

===Original===
"Yes—I will go—up into the desert—with Philammon—and you shall never hear of me again. And I will be a nun, and pray for him, that he may be a great king, and conquer all the world. You will tell him why I went away, will you not? Yes, I will go—now, at once—"

She turned away hurriedly, as if to act upon her promise, and then she sprang again to Wulf with a sudden shudder.

"I cannot, Wulf!—I cannot leave him! I shall go mad if I do! Do not be angry;—I will promise anything—take any oath you like, if you will only let me stay here. Only as a slave—as anything—if I may but look at him sometimes. No—not even that—but to be under the same roof with him, only—Oh, let me be but a slave in the kitchen! I will make over all I have to him—to you—to anyone! And you shall tell him that I am gone—dead, if you will.—Only let me stay! And I will wear rags, and grind in the mill. … Even that will be delicious, to know that he is eating the bread which I have made! And if I ever dare speak to him—even to come near hint—let the steward hang me up by the wrists, and whip me, like the slave which I deserve to be! … And then shall I soon grow old and ugly with grief, and—there will be no more danger then, dear Wulf, will there, from this accursed face of mine? Only promise me that, and—There he is calling you! Don't let him come in and see me!—I cannot bear it! Go to him, quick, and tell him all.—No, don't tell him yet. …"

===Chinese===
「是——我走——到沙漠里去——跟菲拉蒙（Philammon）去——你们再也听不见我的音讯。我要去做修女，为他祷告，使他成为一代雄主，征服天下。你会告诉他我为何走，是不是？是，我走——此刻就走——」

她匆匆转身，像是要践行自己的诺言，可随即猛地一颤，又扑回到沃尔夫跟前。

「我不能，沃尔夫！——我不能离开他！我若离开他便会发疯！别生我的气；——我什么都可以答应——随你要我发什么誓，只要你让我留在这里。便是做个奴隶——做什么都行——只要偶尔能看他一眼。不——连这也不必——只要能与他同住一个屋檐下，便——噢，让我到厨房里去做个奴隶罢！我愿把我所有的一切都转让给他——给你——给任何人！你只管告诉他我走了——说我死了，由你。——只求让我留下！我肯穿破衣裳，肯到磨坊里去推磨。……便是那也甘美无比——想到他吃的是我亲手做的面包！倘若我胆敢跟他说话——甚至走近他身边——就让管家把我吊起手腕，鞭打我，像鞭打我这活该为奴的人！……到那时我自然会因忧愁而很快变得又老又丑，到——那时我这副招祸的脸便再没什么危险了，是不是，亲爱的沃尔夫？只要答应我这一件，就——他在叫你了！别让他进来瞧见我！——我受不了！快到他那里去，把一切都告诉他。——不，先别告诉他。……」

===Original===
And she sank down again on the floor, as Wulf went out murmuring to himself—

"Poor child! poor child! well for thee this clay if thou wert dead, and at the bottom of Hela!"

And Pelagia heard what he said.

===Chinese===
她又瘫倒在地板上，沃尔夫一面走出去，一面自言自语地咕哝着——

「苦命的孩子！苦命的孩子！你这泥身若死了，沉到海拉（Hela）的冥渊之底，倒好了！」

佩拉吉娅听清了他这话。

===Original===
Gradually, amid sobs and tears, and stormy confusion of impossible hopes and projects, those words took root in her mind, and spread, till they filled her whole heart and brain.

"Well for me if I were dead?"

And she rose slowly.

"Well for me if I were dead? And why not? Then it would indeed be all settled. There would be no more danger from poor little Pelagia then. …"

She went slowly, firmly, proudly, into the well-known chamber. … She threw herself upon the bed, and covered the pillow with kisses. Her eye fell on the Amal's sword, which hung across the bed's-head, after the custom of Gothic warriors. She seized it, and took it down, shuddering.

===Chinese===
渐渐地，在抽泣与眼泪之中，在种种不可能的希望与图谋翻江倒海般的混乱之中，那几个字在她心里生了根，蔓延开来，直到填满她整个心胸与脑海。

「我若是死了，倒好了？」

她缓缓站起身来。

「我若是死了，倒好了？为什么不呢？那样一来，一切当真就都了结啦。可怜的小佩拉吉娅便再也无足为患了。……」

她缓缓地、坚定地、骄傲地走进那间熟悉的寝阁。……她扑倒在床上，把枕头吻了个遍。她的目光落在阿玛尔的剑上——按哥特武士的习俗，那剑悬在床头的横梁上。她一阵战栗，伸手把它摘了下来。

===Original===
"Yes! … Let it be with this, if it must be. And it must be. I cannot bear it! Anything but shame! To have fancied all my life—vain fool that I was!—that everyone loved and admired me, and to find that they were despising me, hating me, all along! Those students at the lecture-room door told me I was despised. The old monk told me so—Fool that I was! I forgot it next day!—For he—he loved me still!—All—how could I believe them, till his own lips had said it? … Intolerable! … And yet women as bad as I am have been honoured—when they were dead. What was that song which I used to sing about Epicharis, who hung herself in the litter, and Leaina, who bit out her tongue, lest the torture should drive them to betray their lovers? There used to be a statue of Leaina, they say, at Athens—a lioness without a tongue. … And whenever I sang the song, the theatre used to rise, and shout, and call them noble and blessed. … I never could tell why then; but I know now!—I know now! Perhaps they may call me noble, after all. At least, they may say 'She was a—a—but she dare die for the man she loved!'.… Ay, but God despises me too, and elates me. He will send me to eternal fire. Philammon said so—though he was my brother. The old monk said so—though he wept as he said it. … The flames of hell forever! Oh, not forever! Great, dreadful God! Not forever! Indeed, I did not know! No one taught me about right and wrong, and I never knew that I had been baptized—Indeed, I never knew! And it was so pleasant—so pleasant to be happy, and praised, and loved, and to see happy faces round me. How could I help it? The birds there who are singing in the darling, beloved court—they do what they like, and Thou art not angry with them for being happy! And Thou wilt not be more cruel to me than to them, great God—for what did I know more than they? Thou hast made the beautiful sunshine, and the pleasant, pleasant world, and the flowers, and the birds—Thou wilt not send me to burn forever and ever? Will not a hundred years be punishment enough—or a thousand? Oh God! is not this punishment enough already—to have to leave him, just as just as I am beginning to long to be good, and to be worthy of him? … Oh, have mercy—mercy—mercy—and let me go after I have been punished enough! Why may I not turn into a bird, or even a worm, and come back again out of that horrible place, to see the sun shine, and the flowers grow once more? Oh, am I not punishing myself already? Will not this help to atone? … Yes—I will die!—and perhaps so God may pity me!"

===Chinese===
「好罢！……便用这把剑罢，倘若必须如此。而这是必须的。我受不了啦！什么都能受，唯独耻辱不能！我一生都自以为——我这虚荣的痴人！——人人都爱我、赞赏我，到头来才发现他们一直在轻蔑我、憎恨我！讲学堂门口那些学子曾说我为人所轻。那老修士也曾这样对我说——我这痴人！第二天我便把它忘了！——因为他——他仍然爱我！——是啊——在他们亲口说出之前，我怎能信他们？……不堪忍受！……然而和我一样坏的女人，也曾受过人敬重——当她们死了之后。我从前常唱的那支歌，唱的不是埃皮卡里斯（Epicharis）在肩舆里自缢、莱阿伊娜（Leaina）咬掉了自己的舌头，唯恐酷刑逼她们出卖所爱之人么？据说雅典（Athens）曾有一尊莱阿伊娜的像——一头没有舌头的母狮。……每逢我唱那支歌，满剧院的人都要起立、欢呼，称她们高贵、称她们有福。……那时我总不明白是为了什么；可如今我明白了！——如今我明白了！或许，他们到底也会称我高贵。至少，他们也许会说：『她是个——是个——可是她敢为所爱之人去死！』。……哎呀，可是上帝也鄙弃我、厌弃我。祂要把我送进永火里去。菲拉蒙这样说过——虽则他是我的哥哥。那老修士也这样说过——虽则他说时流了泪。……地狱的烈火，永远、永远！噢，不要永远！伟大而可畏的上帝啊！不要永远！实在的，我原本不知道！没有人教过我何为善恶，我也从不知道自己曾受过洗——实在的，我从来不知道！而那日子多么快活——多么快活啊，做快乐的人、受称赞、受宠爱，看见周围都是快活的面庞。我怎能由得自己呢？那边那个叫我心疼、叫我钟爱的小院里唱歌的鸟儿——它们爱做什么便做什么，它们因快乐，祢并不向它们发怒！伟大的上帝啊，祢对我总不至于比对它们更残酷罢——因为我所知的，哪里比它们多呢？祢造了那美丽的阳光，造了这快活、快活的世界，造了那些花草、那些飞鸟——祢总不至于叫我永永远远地燃烧罢？难道一百年还不够抵罪——或者一千年？噢，上帝啊！眼下这刑罚难道还不够——正当我刚起意要行善、要配得上他，却不得不离开他？……噢，开恩罢——开恩罢——开恩罢——等我受够了刑，便放我走罢！为什么我不能变作一只鸟，甚至一条虫，从那可怖之处再回到世上来，再看一看阳光、再看一看花开？噢，我不是已经在惩罚自己了么？这难道不能稍稍抵罪？……是——我愿意死！——或许上帝见我如此，便会怜悯我！」

===Original===
And with trembling hands she drew the sword from its sheath and covered the blade with kisses.

"Yes—on this sword—with which he won his battles. That is right—his to the last! How keen and cold it looks! Will it be very painful? … No—I will not try the point, or my heart might fail me. I will fall on it at once: let it hurt me as it may, it will be too late to draw back then. And after all it is his sword—It will not have the heart to torture me much. And yet he struck me himself this morning!"

===Chinese===
她用颤抖的双手将剑抽出鞘来，在剑刃上密密地吻了个遍。

「不错——在这把剑上——他曾用这把剑赢取过他的战绩。这就对了——到底还是他的！这剑刃看上去多么锋利、多么冰冷！会痛得很么？……不——我不去试那剑尖，否则我的心会软下来。我要一下子扑上去：随它怎么痛，到那时再要退缩也迟了。况且这到底是他的剑——它也狠不下心来折磨我多久。可是他今早竟亲手打了我！」

===Original===
And at that thought, a long wild cry of misery broke from her lips, and rang through the house. Hurriedly she fastened the sword upright to the foot of the bed, and tore open her tunic. … "Here—under this widowed bosom, where his head will never lie again! There are footsteps in the passage! Quick, Pelagia! Now—"

And she threw up her arms wildly, in act to fall. …

"It is his step! And he will find me, and never know that it is for him I die!"

===Chinese===
一念及此，一声悠长狂乱的哀号从她唇间迸出，响彻了整座宅子。她匆匆把剑竖直固定在床脚，扯开了自己的内衣。……「这儿——在这再不会有他头颅安枕的寡居胸怀里！过道里有脚步声！快，佩拉吉娅！此刻——」

她狂乱地把双臂一扬，作势要扑下去。……

「是他的脚步！他要找到我了，却永不知道我竟是为他而死！」

===Original===
The Amal tried the door. It was fast. With a single blow he burst it open, and demanded—

"What was that shriek? What is the meaning of this? Pelagia!"

Pelagia, like a child caught playing with a forbidden toy, hid her face in her hands and cowered down.

"What is it?" cried he, lifting her.

But she burst from his arms.

"No, no!—never more! I am not worthy of you! Let me die, wretch that I am! I can only drag you down. You must be a king. You must marry her—the wise woman!"

"Hypatia! She is dead!"

"Dead?" shrieked Pelagia.

===Chinese===
阿玛尔试了试门。门闩着。他一拳砸开，喝问——

「方才那声尖叫是怎么回事？这是干什么？佩拉吉娅！」

佩拉吉娅像一个被抓到玩弄禁物的小孩，双手掩面，缩成一团。

「怎么了？」他叫着，把她抱起来。

可她从他怀里挣脱出来。

「不，不！——再也不能了！我配不上你！让我死罢，我这可鄙的人！我只能把你拖累。你必须做国王。你必须娶她——那位有学问的女子！」

「希帕蒂娅！她已经死了！」

「死了？」佩拉吉娅尖叫。

===Original===
"Murdered, an hour ago, by those Christian devils."

Pelagia put her hands over her eyes, and burst into tears. Were they of pity or of joy? … She did not ask herself; and we will not ask her.

"Where is my sword? Soul of Odin! Why is it fastened here?"

"I was going to—Do not be angry! … They told me that I had better die, and—"

The Amal stood thunderstruck for a moment.

"Oh, do not strike me again! Send me to the mill. Kill me now with your own hand! Anything but another blow!"

===Chinese===
「一个钟头前被那些基督徒魔鬼谋害了。」

佩拉吉娅双手掩目，泪如雨下。那泪是为怜悯，还是为喜悦？……她自己没有追问；我们也不去问她。

「我的剑呢？奥丁之灵！它为何固定在这里？」

「我正要——你别生气！……他们对我说我最好去死，于是——」

阿玛尔如遭雷击，怔立了一刹那。

「噢，别再打我了！把我送到磨坊去。现在就亲手杀了我罢！只要别再打我一拳！」

===Original===
"A blow?—Noble woman!" cried the Amal, clasping her in his arms.

The storm was past; and Pelagia had been nestling to that beloved heart, cooing like a happy dove, for many a minute before the Amal aroused himself and her. …

"Now!—quick! We have not a moment to lose. Up to the tower, where you will be safe; and then to show these curs what comes of snarling round the wild wolves' den!"

===Chinese===
「打你？——高贵的女子！」阿玛尔叫着，把她紧紧搂进怀里。

暴风雨过去了；佩拉吉娅依偎在那颗她所钟爱的心头，像一只欢快的鸽子咕咕低语，过了好一会儿，阿玛尔才惊醒过来，也叫醒了她。……

「来！——快！我们一刻也耽误不得了。上塔楼去，那里你才安全；然后让这群癞皮狗见识见识，在野狼窟旁狺狺狂吠，是什么下场！」

## XXIX / XXIX

### Nemesis / 报应

===Original===
And was the Amal’s news true, then?

Philammon saw Raphael rush across the street into the Museum gardens. His last words had been a command to stay where he was; and the boy obeyed him. The black porter who let Raphael out told him somewhat insolently, that his mistress would see no one, and receive no messages: but he had made up his mind: complained of the sun, quietly ensconced himself behind a buttress, and sat coiled up on the pavement, ready for a desperate spring. The slave stared at him: but he was accustomed to the vagaries of philosophers; and thanking the gods that he was not born in that station of life, retired to his porter’s cell, and forgot the whole matter.

There Philammon awaited a full half-hour. It seemed to him hours, days, years. And yet Raphael did not return: and yet no guards appeared. Was the strange Jew a traitor? Impossible!—his face had shown a desperate earnestness of terror as intense as Philammon’s own.… Yet why did he not return?

===Chinese===
这么说，阿玛尔（the Amal）带来的消息竟是真的？

菲拉蒙（Philammon）眼看着拉斐尔·阿本-以斯拉（Raphael Aben-Ezra）冲过街心，奔进博物院（Museum）的园林。他临走时留下的话，是命菲拉蒙原地等候；少年听从了他。放拉斐尔出门的黑皮肤看门人带着几分倨傲告诉他：自家女主人谁也不见，任何口信也不收。可菲拉蒙心意已决：他抱怨日头毒辣，悄悄躲到一道扶壁背后，蜷身坐在石板地上，蓄势待发，只待最后一拼。那奴隶瞠目看着他：可他早已见惯了哲学家们种种古怪的行径；便谢过众神，庆幸自己不曾投生到这一种身份里，退回他那看门的小屋，把整件事忘到脑后。

菲拉蒙就在那里足足候了一个半钟头。在他心目中，那仿佛是几个时辰、几日、几年。可拉斐尔仍不回来：也没有卫兵出现。那个奇怪的犹太人莫非是个奸细？绝不可能！——他脸上那一副拼命般的、极其恳切的恐惧之色，与菲拉蒙自己心头之惧同样深切。……可他为何还不回来？

===Original===
Perhaps he had found out that the streets were clear; their mutual fears groundless.… What meant that black knot of men some two hundred yards off, hanging about the mouth of the side street, just opposite the door which led to her lecture-room? He moved to watch them: they had vanished. He lay down again and waited.… There they were again. It was a suspicious post. That street ran along the back of the Caesareum, a favourite haunt of monks, communicating by innumerable entries and back buildings with the great Church itself.… And yet, why should there not be a knot of monks there? What more common in every street of Alexandria? He tried to laugh away his own fears. And yet they ripened, by the very intensity of thinking on them, into certainty. He knew that something terrible was at hand. More than once he looked out from his hiding-place—the knot of men were still there;… it seemed to have increased, to draw nearer. If they found him, what would they not suspect? What did he care? He would die for her, if it came to that—not that it could come to that: but still he must speak to her—he must warn her. Passenger after passenger, carriage after carriage passed along the street: student after student entered the lecture-room; but he never saw them, not though they passed him close. The sun rose higher and higher, and turned his whole blaze upon the corner where Philammon crouched, till the pavement scorched like hot iron, and his eyes were dazzled by the blinding glare: but he never heeded it. His whole heart, and sense, and sight, were riveted upon that well-known door, expecting it to open.…

===Chinese===
莫非他已查明街上清静无事；二人彼此的忧虑都属无的放矢。……可离此约二百步开外、在那条正对着通向她讲学堂的小门的横街口上，那一簇黑压压的人影聚在那里作甚？他挪了挪身去看：他们已不见了。他再躺下等候……他们又出现了。这是个形迹可疑的去处。那条街沿着凯撒里乌姆（the Caesareum）的背后蜿蜒，是修士们爱出没之所，借无数夹道与后楼与大教堂本身相通。……可话说回来，那里怎么就不能有一簇修士呢？在亚历山大城（Alexandria）的每一条街上，这不都是最寻常不过的景象么？他试图把自己的忧虑一笑置之。然而这忧虑因他愈想愈深，反倒渐次凝结为确凿。他知道，一桩可怕的事即将临到。他不只一次从藏身处向外张望——那一簇人仍在那里；……似乎人数还增多了，离得也近了。倘若他们发现了他，还有什么不会被他们猜疑的？他管它呢？必要时他愿为她而死——其实事情也不至于到那一步：但他仍须对她说话——他必须警告她。一个又一个行人、一辆又一辆马车沿街而过：一个又一个学生走进讲学堂：可他全不曾看见他们，哪怕他们擦身而过。日头愈升愈高，把全部火焰似的骄阳都倾泻到菲拉蒙蜷伏的那个墙角，直晒得石板烫如热铁，他的双眼也被那炫目的强光耀得发花：可他全不理会。他整颗心、全副感官、整双眼睛，都钉在那扇熟识的门上，只盼它打开。……

===Original===
At last a curricle, glittering with silver, rattled round the corner and stopped opposite him. She must becoming now. The crowd had vanished. Perhaps it was, after all, a fancy of his own. No; there they were, peeping round the corner, close to the lecture-room—the hellhounds! A slave brought out an embroidered cushion—and then Hypatia herself came forth, looking more glorious than ever; her lips set in a sad firm smile; her eyes uplifted, inquiring, eager, and yet gentle, dimmed by some great inward awe, as if her soul was far away aloft, and face to face with God.

In a moment he sprang up to her, caught her robe convulsively, threw himself on his knees before her—

“Stop! Stay! You are going to destruction!”

Calmly she looked down upon him.

“Accomplice of witches! Would you make of Theon’s daughter a traitor like yourself?”

He sprang up, stepped back, and stood stupefied with shame and despair.…

She believed him guilty, then!… It was the will of God!

The plumes of the horses were waving far down the street before he recovered himself, and rushed after her, shouting he knew not what.

===Chinese===
终于，一辆银光闪闪的双轮轻车辚辚地转过街角，停在他对面。此刻她必是要出来了。那群人已然不见。或许那终究只是他自己凭空的疑心。不；他们在那里呢，正贴着讲学堂、在街角探头探脑——那些地狱里的恶犬！一个奴隶捧出一只绣花坐垫——接着希帕蒂娅（Hypatia）本人走了出来，比往日更为明艳照人；她的唇边含着一丝凄然坚定的微笑；她的双眸仰视着，带着探问、急切而又温柔的神情，被一股发自内心深处的巨大敬畏所蒙胧，仿佛她的灵魂已远在高天之上，与上帝面对面相对。

刹那间他纵身扑到她跟前，痉挛地抓住她的衣袍，扑倒在她膝前——

「停！等一等！您这是去送死啊！」

她平静地俯视着他。

「巫婆的同党！你要叫提昂（Theon）的女儿也像你一样做个叛徒么？」

他猛地站起来，倒退一步，羞惭与绝望使他呆立如木鸡。……

这么说，她竟信他是真有罪的！……这是上帝的旨意！

待他回过神来，马车早已驰出老远，马饰上的羽毛在街尽头飘拂，他这才拔步追了上去，嘴里狂喊着一些连自己也不知所云的话。

===Original===
It was too late! A dark wave of men rushed from the ambuscade, surged up round the car… swept forward… she had disappeared! and as Philammon followed breathless, the horses galloped past him madly homeward with the empty carriage.

Whither were they dragging her? To the Caesareum, the Church of God Himself? Impossible! Why thither of all places of the earth? Why did the mob, increasing momentarily by hundreds, pour down upon the beach, and return brandishing flints, shells, fragments of pottery?

She was upon the church steps before he caught them up, invisible among the crowd; but he could track her by the fragments of her dress.

Where were her gay pupils now? Alas! they had barricaded themselves shamefully in the Museum, at the first rush which swept her from the door of the lecture-room. Cowards! he would save her!

===Chinese===
太迟了！一股黑色的人潮从埋伏处涌出，在车四围旋转激荡……滚滚向前……她已不见了！菲拉蒙气喘吁吁地追在后面，只见那两匹马拖着一辆空车，发疯似地朝回家的方向从他身边疾驰而过。

他们要把她拖到哪里去？拖到凯撒里乌姆去，拖到上帝自己的教堂里去？断无此理！天底下何处不可去，偏偏要去那里？那群暴民缘何一刻不停地成百增加，又缘何冲到海边，挥舞着捡来的燧石、贝壳、碎陶片折返回来？

待他追上时，她已在教堂的台阶上，被人群吞没得无影无踪；但他还能凭她衣衫的残片追踪她的去向。

她那些鲜衣怒马的学生们如今都到哪里去了？唉！头一股人潮把她从讲学堂门口卷走之时，他们便无耻地把自己反锁进了博物院。一群懦夫！他要去救她！

===Original===
And he struggled in vain to pierce the dense mass of Parabolani and monks, who, mingled with the fishwives and dockworkers, leaped and yelled around their victim. But what he could not do another and a weaker did—even the little porter. Furiously—no one knew how or whence—he burst up as if from the ground in the thickest of the crowd, with knife, teeth, and nails, like a venomous wildcat, tearing his way towards his idol. Alas! he was torn down himself, rolled over the steps, and lay there half dead in an agony of weeping, as Philammon sprang up past him into the church.

Yes. On into the church itself! Into the cool dim shadow, with its fretted pillars, and lowering domes, and candles, and incense, and blazing altar, and great pictures looking from the walls athwart the gorgeous gloom. And right in front, above the altar, the colossal Christ watching unmoved from off the wall, His right hand raised to give a blessing—or a curse?

===Chinese===
他拼命想挤进那抚慰弟兄会（parabolani）的修士与修士所结成的人墙——他们与鱼妇和码头工人混作一处，围着他们的猎物又跳又喊：可徒劳无功。然而他所做不到的，另一个比他更弱小的人却做到了——正是那小个子看门人。他不知从何处、不知怎样，竟如从地底钻出一般，狂暴地跃起在人丛最稠密处，操着刀子、牙齿和指甲，像一只狠毒的野猫，朝他心目中的偶像一路撕扑过去。唉！他自己反倒被掀翻在地，从台阶上滚了下去，半死不活地躺在那里痛苦地哭泣；而菲拉蒙已趁势从他身边跃起，冲进了教堂。

是的。一直冲进教堂里头去！冲进那清凉昏暗的阴影里，那里有雕花的支柱、低垂的穹顶、摇曳的烛光、袅袅的香烟、烈焰熊熊的祭坛，还有从墙上透过那富丽的昏暗俯视下来的巨幅圣像。而在正前方、祭坛上方，那尊巨大的基督像从墙上冷然俯视，一动不动，祂的右手举起，正要降福——还是降祸？

===Original===
On, up the nave, fresh shreds of her dress strewing the holy pavement—up the chancel steps themselves—up to the altar—right underneath the great still Christ: and there even those hellhounds paused.

She shook herself free from her tormentors, and springing back, rose for one moment to her full height, naked, snow-white against the dusky mass around—shame and indignation in those wide clear eyes, but not a stain of fear. With one hand she clasped her golden locks around her; the other long white arm was stretched upward toward the great still Christ appealing—and who dare say in vain?—from man to God. Her lips were opened to speak: but the words that should have come from them reached God’s ear alone; for in an instant Peter struck her down, the dark mass closed over her again… and then wail on wail, long, wild, ear-piercing, rang along the vaulted roofs, and thrilled like the trumpet of avenging angels through Philammon’s ears.

===Chinese===
继续向前，沿着中殿直上，她衣裙新落的碎片一路撒在神圣的石板上——直上唱诗班的台阶——直上祭坛——一直到了那伟大静默的基督正下方：就在那里，连那些地狱恶犬也不禁驻足。

她挣脱了折磨她的人，向后一跃，有一刹那挺直了她整个身躯，赤裸着、雪白地映衬在四周黑压压的人丛之前——那双澄澈的大眼中是羞愤，却没有一丝惧色。她一只手把满头金发拢在胸前；另一只修长白皙的手臂向上伸向那伟大静默的基督，发出恳求——谁敢说这恳求是徒然的？——从人面前，向上帝而发。她的双唇张开，正要说话：可那本应从她唇间吐出的话语，唯有上帝的耳朵听见了；因为就在一瞬之间，彼得（Peter）一击把她打翻在地，那黑色的人潮又把她合拢淹没……随后一声接一声的长号，狂野而尖锐，刺透耳膜，沿着穹顶回荡，如复仇天使的号角一般，震彻菲拉蒙的双耳。

===Original===
Crushed against a pillar, unable to move in the dense mass, he pressed his hands over his ears. He could not shut out those shrieks! When would they end? What in the name of the God of mercy were they doing? Tearing her piecemeal? Yes, and worse than that. And still the shrieks rang on, and still the great Christ looked down on Philammon with that calm, intolerable eye, and would not turn away. And over His head was written in the rainbow, “I am the same, yesterday, today, and forever!” The same as He was in Judea of old, Philammon? Then what are these, and in whose temple? And he covered his face with his hands, and longed to die.

It was over. The shrieks had died away into moans; the moans to silence. How long had he been there? An hour, or an eternity? Thank God it was over! For her sake—but for theirs? But they thought not of that as a new cry rose through the dome.

“To the Cinaron! Burn the bones to ashes! Scatter them into the sea!” And the mob poured past him again.…

===Chinese===
他被挤在一根柱子上，在那稠密的人丛中动弹不得，只能用双手紧捂双耳。可他捂不住那一声声惨叫！它们何时才会了结？发慈悲的上帝啊，他们究竟在干什么？把她撕成碎片么？是的，而且比那更甚。然而惨叫仍在继续，那尊伟大的基督也仍以那双沉静、令人难以忍受的眼睛俯视着菲拉蒙，不肯转脸而去。在祂的头顶，那道虹彩里写着：「我昨日、今日、直到永远，都是一样的！」菲拉蒙啊，与祂昔日在那犹太地（Judea）时一样么？那么，这些人又是谁，他们又在谁的圣殿里？他双手掩面，恨不得死去。

结束了。惨叫已衰弱为呻吟；呻吟归于寂静。他在那里已经多久？一个时辰，还是一个永恒？谢天谢地，这事总算过去了！为她着想是解脱了——可他们呢？可他们无暇及此，因为穹顶之下又升起了一阵新的呼喊。

「到西纳隆（Cinaron）去！把骨头烧成灰！撒到海里去！」那群暴民又从他身边涌过。……

===Original===
He turned to flee: but, once outside the church, he sank exhausted, and lay upon the steps, watching with stupid horror the glaring of the fire, and the mob who leaped and yelled like demons round their Moloch sacrifice.

A hand grasped his arm; he looked up; it was the porter.

“And this, young butcher, is the Catholic and apostolic Church?”

“No! Eudaimon, it is the church of the devils of hell!” And gathering himself up, he sat upon the steps and buried his head within his hands. He would have given life itself for the power of weeping: but his eyes and brain were hot and dry as the desert.

Eudaimon looked at him a while. The shock had sobered the poor fop for once.

“I did what I could to die with her!” said he.

“I did what I could to save her!” answered Philammon.

“I know it. Forgive the words which I just spoke. Did we not both love her?”

And the little wretch sat down by Philammon’s side, and as the blood dripped from his wounds upon the pavement, broke out into a bitter agony of human tears.

===Chinese===
他转身要逃：可一出了教堂，他便筋疲力尽地瘫倒，躺在台阶上，以痴呆的恐怖望着那火光的灼照，望着那群如魔鬼般围绕他们摩洛（Moloch）的祭品又跳又喊的暴民。

一只手抓住了他的胳膊；他抬头一看；是那看门人。

「年轻的屠夫啊，这便是大公教会、使徒所传的教会么？」

「不！欧代蒙（Eudaimon），这是地狱群魔的教会！」他强撑着坐起来，坐在台阶上，把头埋进双手之间。他宁可以命相换，只求能痛哭一场：可他的眼和脑都滚烫干枯，一如那沙漠。

欧代蒙望着他看了一会儿。这场惊变竟使这可怜的花花公子头一次清醒过来。

「我尽我所能，要与她同死！」他说。

「我尽我所能，要救她性命！」菲拉蒙答道。

「我知道。原谅我刚才所说的话。我们两人，岂不是都爱她么？」

那可怜的小人物便挨着菲拉蒙坐下，他伤口淌下的血一滴一滴落在石板上，他放声痛哭起来，吐出一片痛彻人心的眼泪。

===Original===
There are times when the very intensity of our misery is a boon, and kindly stuns us till we are unable to torture ourselves by thought. And so it was with Philammon then. He sat there, he knew not how long.

“She is with the gods,” said Eudaimon at last.

“She is with the God of gods,” answered Philammon: and they both were silent again.

Suddenly a commanding voice aroused them.

They looked up, and saw before them Raphael Aben-Ezra.

He was pale as death, but calm as death. One look into his face told them that he knew all.

“Young monk,” he said, between his closed teeth, “you seem to have loved her?”

Philammon looked up, but could not speak.

“Then arise, and flee for your life into the farthest corner of the desert, ere the doom of Sodom and Gomorrha fall upon this accursed city. Have you father, mother, brother, sister—ay, cat, dog, or bird for which you care, within its walls?”

===Chinese===
有时，痛苦的极其深重反倒是一种恩赐，它仁慈地将我们击晕过去，使我们再不能用思虑来折磨自己。菲拉蒙此刻正是如此。他坐在那里，自己也坐了多久也不知道。

「她与众神同在了。」欧代蒙终于说道。

「她与万神之上帝同在了。」菲拉蒙答道：两人又都沉默下来。

忽然，一个威严的声音把他们惊起。

他们抬头一看，见面前站着的是拉斐尔·阿本-以斯拉。

他苍白如死，也沉静如死。朝他脸上一望，便知他已尽知其事。

「年轻的修士，」他从咬紧的牙缝里说，「你似乎是爱她的？」

菲拉蒙抬起头，却说不出话来。

「那就起来，逃命去罢，逃到沙漠最偏远的角落里去，趁着所多玛（Sodom）和蛾摩拉（Gomorrha）的刑罚尚未临到这座可咒诅的城。你可有父亲、母亲、兄弟、姊妹——甚至猫、狗，或一只你心疼的鸟儿——在这城墙之内么？」

===Original===
Philammon started; for he recollected Pelagia.… That evening, so Cyril had promised, twenty trusty monks were to have gone with him to seize her.

“You have? Then take them with you, and escape, and remember Lot’s wife. Eudaimon, come with me. You must lead me to your house, to the lodging of Miriam the Jewess. Do not deny! I know that she is there. For the sake of her who is gone I will hold you harmless, ay, reward you richly, if you prove faithful. Rise!”

Eudaimon, who knew Raphael’s face well, rose and led the way trembling; and Philammon was left alone.

They never met again. But Philammon knew that he had been in the presence of a stronger man than himself, and of one who hated even more bitterly than he himself that deed at which the very sun, it seemed, ought to have veiled his face. And his words, “Arise, and flee for thy life,” uttered as they were with the stern self-command and writhing lip of compressed agony, rang through his ears like the trump of doom. Yes, he would flee. He had gone forth to see the world, and he had seen it. Arsenius was in the right after all. Home to the desert! But first he would go himself, alone, to Pelagia, and implore her once more to flee with him. Beast, fool, that he had been to try to win her by force—by the help of such as these! God’s kingdom was not a kingdom of fanatics yelling for a doctrine, but of willing, loving, obedient hearts. If he could not win her heart, her will, he would go alone, and die praying for her.

===Chinese===
菲拉蒙猛然一惊：因为他想起了佩拉吉娅（Pelagia）。……就在那天傍晚，按照区利罗（Cyril）所应允的，本有二十名可靠修士要随他一同去劫取她。

「你有？那就带着他们一同逃，要记住罗得的妻子。欧代蒙，跟我来。你必须领我到你家去，到那犹太女人米利暗（Miriam）下榻之处。休要推托！我知道她在那里。念在那已逝之人的份上，你若忠心，我保你无虞，还要重重酬谢你。起来！」

欧代蒙深知拉斐尔的面孔，颤巍巍地起身在前引路；菲拉蒙被独自留下。

他们此后再未相见。但菲拉蒙知道，自己刚才置身于一个比他更刚强的人面前，置身于一个比他自己更深切痛恨那桩罪行的人面前——那桩罪行，连太阳似乎也本该掩面不愿看。他那句「起来，逃命去罢」，是用铁一般的自制力说出的，是在压抑的剧痛中咬着嘴唇说出的，如末日审判的号角般在他耳中震响。是的，他要逃。他出来要看世界，世界他也看过了。阿尔塞尼乌斯（Arsenius）到底是对的。回沙漠去！但他要先独自去见佩拉吉娅，再求她一次与他同逃。禽兽啊，蠢货啊，他竟想用强力——靠着这样一伙人——去赢取她！上帝的国，不是一群为教条嘶喊的狂热之徒的国，乃是甘心、相爱、顺服之心的国。他若赢不得她的心、她的意，他宁可独自前去，在那里为她祈祷至死。

===Original===
He sprang from the steps of the Caesareum, and turned up the street of the Museum. Alas! it was one roaring sea of heads! They were sacking Theon’s house—the house of so many memories! Perhaps the poor old man too had perished! Still—his sister! He must save her and flee. And he turned up a side street and tried to make his way onward.

Alas again! the whole of the dock-quarter was up and out. Every street poured its tide of furious fanatics into the main river; and ere he could reach Pelagia’s house the sun was set, and close behind him, echoed by ten thousand voices, was the cry of “Down with all heathens! Root out all Arian Goths! Down with idolatrous wantons! Down with Pelagia Aphrodite!”

===Chinese===
他从凯撒里乌姆的台阶上一跃而起，转入了博物院那条街。唉！那已是一片人头攒动、怒吼如海的汪洋！他们正在劫掠提昂的宅子——那装满了多少记忆的宅子！那可怜的老人或许也已遭了毒手！可是——他的妹妹！他必须救她同逃。他便转进一条横街，想设法挤向前去。

再一声唉！整个码头区的人都倾巢而出。每一条街都把自己那一股狂怒的狂热之徒倾入那主流之中；未等他赶到佩拉吉娅的宅子，日头已经落山，紧贴在他身后，由一万个声音齐声呼应的，是那呼喊：「打倒一切异教徒！铲除一切阿里乌派（Arian）的哥特人（Goth）！打倒拜偶像的淫妇！打倒佩拉吉娅·阿佛洛狄忒（Pelagia Aphrodite）！」

===Original===
He hurried down the alley, to the tower door, where Wulf had promised to meet him. It was half open, and in the dusk he could see a figure standing in the doorway. He sprang up the steps, and found, not Wulf, but Miriam.

“Let me pass!”

“Wherefore?”

He made no answer, and tried to push past her.

“Fool, fool, fool!” whispered the hag, holding the door against him with all her strength. “Where are your fellow-kidnappers? Where are your band of monks?”

Philammon started back. How had she discovered his plan?

“Ay—where are they? Besotted boy! Have you not seen enough of monkery this afternoon, that you must try still to make that poor girl even such a one as yourselves? Ay, you may root out your own human natures if you will, and make yourselves devils in trying to become angels: but woman she is, and woman she shall live or die!”

“Let me pass!” cried Philammon furiously.

“Raise your voice—and I raise mine: and then your life is not worth a moment’s purchase. Fool, do you think I speak as a Jewess? I speak as a woman—as a nun! I was a nun once, madman—the iron entered into my soul!—God do so to me, and more also, if it ever enter into another soul while I can prevent it! You shall not have her! I will strangle her with my own hand first!” And turning from him, she darted up the winding stair.

===Chinese===
他急急穿过那条小巷，赶到那塔楼的门前，沃尔夫·奥维达之子（Wulf the son of Ovida）本约好在那里与他相会。门半开着，昏暗中他看见一个人影立在门口。他冲上台阶，却发觉那不是沃尔夫，而是米利暗。

「让我过去！」

「为了何事？」

他不答，想从她身边硬挤过去。

「蠢货，蠢货，蠢货！」那老妖婆低声骂道，拼尽全身气力抵住门不让他进去。「你的劫掠同伙哪里去了？你那一伙修士哪里去了？」

菲拉蒙倒退一步。她是怎么识破他的计谋的？

「是啊——他们人呢？糊涂的傻小子！今天下午修士那一套你还没看够么，竟还要把那可怜的姑娘也变成你们这种人？是了，你们尽可以把自己的人性连根拔起，尽可以为了要做天使反倒把自己做成魔鬼：可她是女人，她生也是女人，死也是女人！」

「让我过去！」菲拉蒙怒吼道。

「你提高嗓门——我也提高嗓门：那时候你的命一文也不值。蠢货，你以为我是以犹太人的身份说话么？我是以女人的身份——以修女的身份说话！我从前做过修女，疯子啊——那铁已刺进我的灵魂！——上帝怎样待我，再加倍待我，若我还能阻止，竟让那铁再刺进别人的灵魂！你休想得到她！我宁可亲手把她掐死！」说罢她转身一闪，便顺着那盘旋的楼梯蹿了上去。

===Original===
He followed: but the intense passion of the old hag hurled her onward with the strength and speed of a young Maenad. Once Philammon was near passing her. But he recollected that he did not know his way, and contented himself with keeping close behind, and making the fugitive his guide.

Stair after stair, he fled upward, till she turned suddenly into a chamber door. Philammon paused. A few feet above him the open sky showed at the stairhead. They were close then to the roof! One moment more, and the hag darted out of the room again, and turned to flee upward still. Philammon caught her by the arm, hurled her back into the empty chamber, shut the door upon her; and with a few bounds gained the roof, and met Pelagia face to face.

“Come!” gasped he breathlessly. “Now is the moment! Come, while they are all below!” and he seized her hand.

But Pelagia only recoiled.

“No, no,” whispered she in answer, “I cannot, cannot—he has forgiven me all, all! and I am his forever! And now, just as he is in danger, when he may be wounded—ah, heaven! would you have me do anything so base as to desert him?”

“Pelagia, Pelagia, darling sister!” cried Philammon, in an agonised voice, “think of the doom of sin! Think of the pains of hell!”

“I have thought of them this day: and I do not believe you! No—I do not! God is not so cruel as you say! And if He were:—to lose my love, that is hell! Let me burn hereafter, if I do but keep him now!”

===Chinese===
他追上去：可那老妖婆激切之情把她推拥向前，竟有年轻迈纳德斯（Maenad）一般的力气和脚力。菲拉蒙有一度几乎要从她身边越过。可他记起自己不识路径，便只紧紧跟在后面，让这逃亡者给他领路。

一阶又一阶，他向上追，直到她忽然闪进一扇房门。菲拉蒙顿住。在他头顶几步之上，楼梯口露出了一片露天的夜空。那么他们已经接近屋顶了！又过片刻，那妖婆又从房里蹿出，转身仍要往上逃。菲拉蒙一把抓住她的胳膊，把她摔回那间空房，把她关在门里；便纵身几跃上了屋顶，与佩拉吉娅迎面相遇。

「来！」他气喘如牛地喘着。「就是这一刻！来罢，趁他们都在下面！」他说着便抓住了她的手。

可佩拉吉娅只是向后退缩。

「不，不，」她低声答道，「我不能，我不能——他已经全原谅我了，全都原谅了！我是永远属于他的了！此刻他正身陷险境，他也许会受伤——啊，天哪！难道你要我做下这等下贱的事，在他危难之际抛弃他么？」

「佩拉吉娅，佩拉吉娅，亲爱的妹妹！」菲拉蒙以哀痛欲绝的声音喊道，「想想罪的刑罚！想想地狱的痛苦！」

「今天我想过这些了：而我不信你那一套！不——我不信！上帝并不像你说的那样残忍！纵然祂果真如此：——失去我所爱，那才是地狱！日后的火烧由它去罢，只要我此刻还能留住他！」

===Original===
Philammon stood stupefied and shuddering. All his own early doubts flashed across him like a thunderbolt, when in the temple-cave he had seen those painted ladies at their revels, and shuddered, and asked himself, were they burning forever and ever?

“Come!” gasped he once again; and throwing himself on his knees before her, covered her hands with kisses, wildly entreating: but in vain.

“What is this?” thundered a voice; not Miriam’s, but the Amal’s. He was unarmed but he rushed straight upon Philammon.

“Do not harm him!” shrieked Pelagia; “he is my brother—my brother of whom I told you!”

“What does he here?” cried the Amal, who instantly divined the truth.

Pelagia was silent.

“I wish to deliver my sister, a Christian, from the sinful embraces of an Arian heretic; and deliver her I will, or die!”

“An Arian?” laughed the Amal. “Say a heathen at once, and tell the truth, young fool! Will you go with him, Pelagia, and turn nun in the sand-heaps?”

Pelagia sprang towards her lover: Philammon caught her by the arm for one last despairing appeal: and in a moment, neither knew how, the Goth and the Greek were locked in deadly struggle, while Pelagia stood in silent horror, knowing that a call for help would bring instant death to her brother.

===Chinese===
菲拉蒙呆立着，浑身发抖。他早年一切疑虑如一道电光闪过心头——那是在神庙洞穴之中，他曾看见那些浓妆艳抹的妇人在那里纵酒作乐，他为之战栗，问自己：她们要这样永远永远地燃烧下去么？

「来！」他再一次喘着气说；他扑倒在她膝前，狂乱地恳求着，把一连串的吻落在她手上：全是徒然。

「这是干什么？」一个声音如雷般喝道；不是米利暗的，而是阿玛尔的。他手无寸铁，却径直朝菲拉蒙扑来。

「不要伤他！」佩拉吉娅尖叫道，「他是我哥哥——我曾跟你说起的那个哥哥！」

「他来这里干什么？」阿玛尔喝道，他当即猜中了真相。

佩拉吉娅默然不语。

「我要把我这位信基督的妹妹，从一个阿里乌派异端的罪污拥抱中救出来；我非救她不可，否则便死！」

「阿里乌派？」阿玛尔笑道，「你不如干脆说异教徒，把实话讲出来罢，年轻的傻瓜！佩拉吉娅，你愿意跟他走么，到那沙堆里去做修女？」

佩拉吉娅朝她的情人扑过去：菲拉蒙抓住她的胳膊，作最后一次绝望的央求：刹那之间，谁也说不清是怎么回事，那哥特人和那希腊人已扭作一团，拼起命来；佩拉吉娅默默惊恐地站着——她知道，只要她一喊救命，便要立刻断送她哥哥的性命。

===Original===
It was over in a few seconds. The Goth lifted Philammon like a baby in his arms, and bearing him to the parapet, attempted to hurl him into the canal below. But the active Greek had wound himself like a snake around him, and held him by the throat with the strength of despair. Twice they rolled and tottered on the parapet; and twice recoiled. A third fearful lunge—the earthen wall gave way; and down to the dark depths, locked in each other’s arms, fell Goth and Greek.

Pelagia rushed to the brink, and gazed downward into the gloom, dumb and dry-eyed with horror. Twice they turned over together in midair.… The foot of the tower, as was usual in Egypt, sloped outwards towards the water. They must strike upon that—and then!… It seemed an eternity ere they touched the masonry.… The Amal was undermost.… She saw his fair floating locks dash against the cruel stone. His grasp suddenly loosened, his limbs collapsed; two distinct plunges broke the dark sullen water; and then all was still but the awakened ripple, lapping angrily against the wall.

Pelagia gazed down one moment more, and then, with a shriek which rang along roof and river, she turned, and fled down the stairs and out into the night.

===Chinese===
这一切只在几秒钟内便见分晓。那哥特人像抱婴儿一般把菲拉蒙举在臂间，把他抱到垛口，要扔进下面的运河里。可那灵巧的希腊人已如蛇一般缠住了他，以绝望中的气力扼住了他的咽喉。两人在垛口上翻滚踉跄了两次；两次都退了回来。第三次可怕的一冲——那土墙便塌了；哥特人和希腊人紧紧相抱着，一同坠入那幽暗的深处。

佩拉吉娅冲到垛口边，向那幽暗之中凝神下望，吓得呆了，欲哭无泪。他们在半空中一同翻转了两下。……那塔楼的墙脚，按埃及的惯例，向外侧朝水面倾斜出去。他们必然会撞在那上面——然后！……他们似乎过了整整一个永恒才触到那墙身。……阿玛尔在下面。……她看见他飘拂的金发撞在那无情石头上。他的攀握忽然松了，四肢一软；只听得两声清晰的扑通声，划破那阴沉沉的黑水；再之后，一切归于寂静，唯有被惊起的涟漪，愤怒地拍打着墙根。

佩拉吉娅又向下望了片刻，随即发出一声锐呼，沿着屋顶与河水远远传开，她转身奔下楼梯，逃进了夜色之中。

===Original===
Five minutes afterwards, Philammon, dripping, bruised, and bleeding, was crawling up the water-steps at the lower end of the lane. A woman rushed from the postern door, and stood on the quay edge, gazing with clasped hands into the canal. The moon fell full on her face. It was Pelagia. She saw him, knew him, and recoiled.

“Sister!—my sister! Forgive me!”

“Murderer!” she shrieked, and dashing aside his outspread hands, fled wildly up the passage.

The way was blocked with bales of merchandise: but the dancer bounded over them like a deer; while Philammon, half stunned by his fall, and blinded by his dripping locks, stumbled, fell, and lay, unable to rise. She held on for a few yards towards the torch-lit mob, which was surging and roaring in the main street above, then turned suddenly into a side alley, and vanished; while Philammon lay groaning upon the pavement, without a purpose or a hope upon earth.

Five minutes more, and Wulf was gazing over the broken parapet, at the head of twenty terrified spectators, male and female, whom Pelagia’s shriek had summoned.

He alone suspected that Philammon had been there; and shuddering at the thought of what might have happened, he kept his secret.

But all knew that Pelagia had been on the tower; all had seen the Amal go up thither. Where were they now? And why was the little postern gate found open, and shut only just in time to prevent the entrance of the mob?

===Chinese===
五分钟之后，菲拉蒙浑身湿透、青肿、淌着血，正沿着小巷尽头的水边石阶爬上来。一个妇人从那扇小角门里冲出，站在河岸的边上，双手紧握，向运河里凝望。明月正照在她脸上。那是佩拉吉娅。她看见了他，认出了他，便向后退。

「妹妹！——我的妹妹！原谅我！」

「杀人凶手！」她尖叫一声，把他伸出的双手一掌打开，发狂般顺着过道奔了上去。

路上堆着一捆捆货物拦住去路：可那舞女如鹿一般从上面一一跃过；菲拉蒙却因那一摔半发了昏，又被湿淋淋的头发遮住了眼睛，踉跄跌倒，再也爬不起来。她又朝那上面大街上汹涌吼叫、火把通明的暴民奔了几步，便忽地转进一条横巷，消失不见；菲拉蒙则躺在石板上呻吟，在这世上既无目的，也无指望。

又过了五分钟，沃尔夫已站在那坍塌的垛口边下望，身后是佩拉吉娅那一声尖叫所召来的二十名惊惶失措的男女看客。

唯独他怀疑菲拉蒙方才到过此处；他一想到可能发生之事便战栗，于是把这一桩秘密藏在心里。

但人人都知道佩拉吉娅方才在塔上；人人都亲眼看见阿玛尔上去过。他们如今在哪里？那扇小角门又为何被发现敞开着，而且只差一点便要合上，恰好挡住涌来的暴民？

===Original===
Wulf stood, revolving in a brain but too well practised in such cases, all possible contingencies of death and horror. At last—

“A rope and a light, Smid!” he almost whispered.

They were brought, and Wulf, resisting all the entreaties of the younger men to allow them to go on the perilous search, lowered himself through the breach.

He was about two-thirds down, when he shook the rope, and called in a stifled voice, to those above—

“Haul up. I have seen enough.”

Breathless with curiosity and fear, they hauled him up. He stood among them for a few moments, silent, as if stunned by the weight of some enormous woe.

“Is he dead?”

“Odin has taken his son home, wolves of the Goths!” And he held out his right hand to the awestruck ring, and burst into an agony of weeping.… A clotted tress of long fair hair lay in his palm.

===Chinese===
沃尔夫站着，那颗在诸如此类的场合里早已训练有素的脑子，把一切可能的人命与惨祸的变故一一盘算过去。终于——

「一条绳子，一盏灯，斯密德·特罗尔之子（Smid the son of Troll）！」他几乎是低声耳语。

东西取来了，沃尔夫不顾年轻人们一再恳求要去代他冒这趟险，自个儿从那破口缒了下去。

他下到约三分之二处，便抖了抖绳子，以压低的声音朝上面的人唤道——

「拉我上去。我看得够了。」

众人好奇又惊惧，屏息把他拉了上来。他在他们中间站了片刻，一言不发，仿佛被某种莫大的悲患压得怔住了。

「他死了么？」

「奥丁（Odin）已把他的儿子接回家了，哥特的群狼！」他向那惊惶失色的围圈伸出右手，放声痛哭起来。……他掌心里躺着一绺结着血块的修长金发。

===Original===
It was snatched; handed from man to man.… One after another recognised the beloved golden locks. And then, to the utter astonishment of the girls who stood round, the great simple hearts, too brave to be ashamed of tears, broke out and wailed like children.… Their Amal! Their heavenly man! Odin’s own son, their joy and pride, and glory! Their “Kingdom of heaven,” as his name declared him, who was all that each wished to be, and more, and yet belonged to them, bone of their bone, flesh of their flesh! Ah, it is bitter to all true human hearts to be robbed of their ideal, even though that ideal be that of a mere wild bull, and soulless gladiator.…

At last Smid spoke—

“Heroes, this is Odin’s doom; and the All-father is just. Had we listened to Prince Wulf four months ago, this had never been. We have been cowards and sluggards, and Odin is angry with his children. Let us swear to be Prince Wulf’s men and follow him tomorrow where he will!”

Wulf grasped his outstretched hand lovingly—“No, Smid, son of Troll! These words are not yours to speak. Agilmund son of Cniva, Goderic son of Ermenric, you are Balts, and to you the succession appertains. Draw lots here, which of you shall be our chieftain.”

“No! no! Wulf!” cried both the youths at once. “You are the hero! you are the Sagaman! We are not worthy; we have been cowards and sluggards, like the rest. Wolves of the Goths, follow the Wolf, even though he lead you to the land of the giants!”

A roar of applause followed.

“Lift him on the shield,” cried Goderic, tearing off his buckler. “Lift him on the shield! Hail, Wulf king! Wulf, king of Egypt!”

===Chinese===
那一绺头发被人夺了过去；从一只手传到另一只手。……一个接一个地认出了那可爱的金发。于是，那些伫立四周的姑娘们大惊失色地看见，这几颗质朴而伟大的心——它们勇敢得不知以眼泪为耻——骤然崩溃，如孩童一般嚎啕痛哭。……他们的阿玛尔啊！他们那如天神般的人物！奥丁自己的儿子，他们的喜乐、他们的骄傲、他们的荣耀！他的名字宣示他是他们的「天国」，而他是他们每一个人所愿成为的样子，甚至有过之而无不及，却又属于他们，与他们骨肉相连、血肉同源！啊，对一切真正的人心而言，被夺去他们心目中的理想，都是苦痛的——纵然那理想不过是一头野牛、一个没有灵魂的角斗士（gladiator）的理想。……

终于斯密德开口——

「众英雄，这是奥丁的判定；而众神之父是公义的。四个月前我们若听了沃尔夫亲王的话，此事便绝不会发生。我们做了懦夫和懒汉，奥丁向祂的儿女发怒了。让我们立誓，做沃尔夫亲王的人，明日他到哪里，我们便跟到哪里！」

沃尔夫亲切地握住他伸出的手——「不，斯密德·特罗尔之子！这话不该由你来说。阿吉蒙德·克尼瓦之子（Agilmund the son of Cniva），戈德里克·厄门里克之子（Goderic the son of Ermenric），你们是巴尔王族（Balts），继承之权属于你们。就在这里抽签罢，看你们哪一位做我们的首领。」

「不！不！沃尔夫！」两个少年齐声喊道，「你才是英雄！你才是萨迦（saga）的传唱者！我们不配；我们和众人一样，是懦夫和懒汉。哥特的群狼啊，跟着这头狼罢，哪怕他领你们到巨人的国土里去！」

一阵喝彩声随之而起。

「把他举到盾上，」戈德里克一面把自己小圆盾扯下一面喊，「把他举到盾上！沃尔夫王万岁！沃尔夫，埃及之王！」

===Original===
And the rest of the Goths, attracted by the noise, rushed up the tower-stairs in time to join in the mighty shout of “Wulf, king of Egypt!”—as careless of the vast multitude which yelled and surged without, as boys are of the snow against the windowpane.

“No!” said Wulf solemnly, as he stood on the uplifted shield. “If I be indeed your king, and ye my men, wolves of the Goths, tomorrow we will go forth of this place, hated of Odin, rank with the innocent blood of the Alruna maid. Back to Adolf; back to our own people! Will you go?”

“Back to Adolf!” shouted the men.

“You will not leave us to be murdered?” cried one of the girls. “The mob are breaking the gates already!”

“Silence, silly one! Men—we have one thing to do. The Amal must not go to the Valhalla without fair attendance.”

“Not the poor girls?” said Agilmund, who took for granted that Wulf would wish to celebrate the Amal’s funeral in true Gothic fashion by a slaughter of slaves.

“No.… One of them I saw behave this very afternoon worthy of a Vala. And they, too—they may make heroes’ wives after all, yet.… Women are better than I fancied, even the worst of them. No. Go down, heroes, and throw the gates open; and call in the Greek hounds to the funeral supper of a son of Odin.”

===Chinese===
其余的哥特人被这喧声惊动，纷纷冲上塔楼的楼梯，刚好来得及加入那一声响彻云霄的齐呼：「沃尔夫，埃及之王！」——他们对墙外那汹涌叫嚣的茫茫人海毫不在意，一如孩童不顾扑打窗棂的飞雪。

「不！」沃尔夫站在被举起的盾上庄严地说，「我若真是你们的王，你们真是我的部下，哥特的群狼，明日我们便要离开此地——这为奥丁所憎恶、沾满那位阿尔鲁娜少女（Alruna maid）无辜鲜血的地方。回到阿道夫（Adolf）那里去；回到我们自己的族人那里去！你们可愿去？」

「回阿道夫那里去！」众人喊道。

「你们不会丢下我们任人屠杀罢？」其中一个姑娘喊道，「暴民已经在砸门了！」

「安静，傻丫头！众兄弟——我们还有一桩事要办。阿玛尔总不能没有相当的随从，就这般前往瓦尔哈拉（Valhalla）。」

「不是要杀那些可怜的姑娘罢？」阿吉蒙德说，他理所当然地以为沃尔夫要按真正的哥特古礼，以屠杀奴隶来为阿玛尔举丧。

「不。……今日下午我亲眼看见她们之中有一位，行事颇有瓦拉（Vala）之风。而她们——她们说不定到底还能做英雄的妻子呢。……女人比我设想的要好，连她们之中最坏的也是。不必如此。下去罢，众英雄，把大门敞开；把那些希腊的猎狗请进来，赴一位奥丁之子的丧宴。」

===Original===
“Throw the gates open?”

“Yes. Goderic, take a dozen men, and be ready in the east hall. Agilmund, go with a dozen to the west side of the court—there in the kitchen; and wait till you hear my war-cry. Smid and the rest of you, come with me through the stables close to the gate—as silent as Hela.”

And they went down—to meet, full on the stairs below, old Miriam.

Breathless and exhausted by her exertion, she had fallen heavily before Philammon’s strong arm; and lying half stunned for a while, recovered just in time to meet her doom.

She knew that it was come, and faced it like herself.

“Take the witch!” said Wulf slowly—“Take the corrupter of heroes—the cause of all our sorrows!”

Miriam looked at him with a quiet smile.

“The witch is accustomed long ago to hear fools lay on her the consequences of their own lust and laziness.”

===Chinese===
「把大门敞开？」

「是的。戈德里克，带十二个人，到东厅里待命。阿吉蒙德，带十二个人到院子西头——就是厨房那里；等听见我的战吼再动手。斯密德和你其余的人，跟我从紧挨大门的马房进去——静得像海拉（Hela）一般。」

他们下了楼——却在楼梯下面，正面撞上了老米利暗。

她方才气喘吁吁、气力用尽，在菲拉蒙那双强健的胳膊前重重跌倒；半死不活地躺了一会儿，刚刚苏醒过来，便正赶上她的劫数。

她知道时辰已到，便以她素来的本色迎了上去。

「拿下那女巫！」沃尔夫缓缓地说——「拿下这败坏英雄的妖妇——我们一切灾祸的祸首！」

米利暗带着恬静的微笑看着他。

「这女巫早就听惯了：蠢货们把他们自己贪欲和懒惰所招来的恶果，一股脑儿推到她头上。」

===Original===
“Hew her down, Smid, son of Troll, that she may pass the Amal’s soul and gladden it on her way to Niflheim.”

Smid did it: but so terrible were the eyes which glared upon him from those sunken sockets, that his sight was dazzled. The axe turned aside, and struck her shoulder. She reeled, but did not fall.

“It is enough,” she said quietly.

“The accursed Grendel’s daughter numbed my arm!” said Smid. “Let her go! No man shall say that I struck a woman twice.”

“Nidhogg waits for her, soon or late,” answered Wulf.

And Miriam, coolly folding her shawl around her, turned and walked steadily down the stair; while all men breathed more freely, as if delivered from some accursed and supernatural spell.

“And now,” said Wulf, “to your posts, and vengeance!”

===Chinese===
「劈倒她，斯密德·特罗尔之子，好让她去尼弗尔海姆（Niflheim）的路上陪伴阿玛尔的灵魂，使它快活。」

斯密德依言而作：可那深陷的眼窝里瞪着他的两道目光可怖之极，竟晃得他眼花。那斧头一偏，砍在了她的肩上。她踉跄了一下，却没有倒。

「够了。」她平静地说。

「这可咒诅的格伦德尔（Grendel）的女儿，把我的胳膊都吓麻了！」斯密德说，「放她去罢！谁也不能说我砍一个女人两斧。」

「尼德霍格（Nidhogg）迟早会等着她的。」沃尔夫答道。

米利暗从容地把披肩拢了拢，转身稳步走下楼梯；众人尽皆如释重负地透了一口气，仿佛从某种可咒诅的、超自然的魔魇之下解脱出来。

「如今，」沃尔夫说，「各就各位，报仇！」

===Original===
The mob had weltered and howled ineffectually around the house for some half-hour. But the lofty walls, opening on the street only by a few narrow windows in the higher stories, rendered it an impregnable fortress. Suddenly, the iron gates were drawn back, disclosing to the front rank the court, glaring empty and silent and ghastly in the moonlight. For an instant they recoiled, with a vague horror, and dread of treachery: but the mass behind pressed them onward, and in swept the murderers of Hypatia, till the court was full of choking wretches, surging against the walls and pillars in aimless fury. And then, from under the archway on each side, rushed a body of tall armed men, driving back all incomers more; the gates slid together again upon their grooves and the wild beasts of Alexandria were trapped at last.

And then began a murder grim and great. From three different doors issued a line of Goths, whose helmets and mail-shirts made them invulnerable to the clumsy weapons of the mob, and began hewing their way right through the living mass, helpless from their close-packed array. True, they were but as one to ten; but what are ten curs before one lion?… And the moon rose higher and higher, staring down ghastly and unmoved upon that doomed court of the furies, and still the bills and swords hewed on and on, and the Goths drew the corpses, as they found room, towards a dark pile in the midst, where old Wulf sat upon a heap of slain, singing the praises of the Amal and the glories of Valhalla, while the shrieks of his lute rose shrill above the shrieks of the flying and the wounded, and its wild waltz-time danced and rollicked on swifter and swifter as the old singer maddened, in awful mockery of the terror and agony around.

===Chinese===
那群暴民围着这座宅子徒劳地咆哮鼓噪了约莫半个钟头。可那高耸的院墙——临街的一面只在高层开着几扇窄窗——使这宅子成了一座攻不破的堡垒。忽然，那两扇铁门朝里拉开，向最前排的人显出了那座庭院：在月光下空荡荡、死寂、白惨惨地泛着光。他们一时倒退了几步，怀着一种朦胧的恐怖，唯恐有诈：可后面的人潮仍把他们向前挤压，于是那些杀害希帕蒂娅的凶手便一涌而入，直到院子里挤满了一群窒息的可怜虫，徒然地、狂怒地朝墙和柱子挤压。这时，从两侧拱廊之下，各冲出一队高大甲胄之士，把后续挤入者顶了回去；铁门顺着滑轨再度合拢——亚历山大城的那群野兽，到底落入了陷阱。

于是开始了一场森严浩大的屠杀。从三道不同的门里，鱼贯走出一列列哥特人，他们的头盔和锁子甲使暴民手中笨拙的器械伤不得他们分毫，他们便在这挤作一团、无从施展的人肉之中一路砍杀过去。他们人数诚然不过一以当十；可十只癞皮狗在一头雄狮面前又算得了什么？……月轮愈升愈高，惨白而冷漠地俯视着那座厄运临头的复仇者之庭，阔剑与长刀仍在一路一路砍将下去；哥特人一有空隙便把尸首拖向中央那堆黑黝黝的尸山——老沃尔夫就坐在那一堆被杀之人上头，高唱着阿玛尔的功绩和瓦尔哈拉的荣光；他的琴声其声高亢，盖过了奔逃者和受伤者的惨叫，那狂野的圆舞曲节拍愈跳愈急，那老歌手自己也渐唱渐狂，以一种可怖的戏谑，嘲笑着四围的恐怖与苦痛。

===Original===
And so, by men and purposes which recked not of her, as is the wont of Providence, was the blood of Hypatia avenged in part that night. In part only. For Peter the Reader, and his especial associates, were safe in sanctuary at the Caesareum, clinging to the altar. Terrified at the storm which they had raised, and fearing the consequences of an attack upon the palace, they had left the mob to run riot at its will; and escaped the swords of the Goths to be reserved for the more awful punishment of impunity.

===Chinese===
希帕蒂娅之血，就在那一夜，由一些根本不曾把她放在心上的人和计谋，部分地得了报偿——这正是天意（Providence）的惯例。只是部分地而已。因为读经员彼得（Peter the Reader）和他那一伙死党，此刻正安然躲在凯撒里乌姆的避难所里，紧抱着祭坛不放。他们被自己一手掀起的狂风骤雨所惊吓，又怕攻打皇宫会招致何种后果，便索性听任暴民自行肆虐；他们逃过了哥特人的刀剑，却被留下来承受那更为可畏的刑罚——得以逍遥法外。

## XXX / XXX

### Every Man to His Own Place / 各归其所

===Original===
